fix: surface user-module load errors as ModuleLoadError + filter via Sentry user-error set (#1094)

## Summary

`flyte deploy <dir>` and `flyte deploy <file>` both invoke
`flyte._utils.module_loader.load_python_modules`. When a user `.py` file
fails at import time with `ModuleNotFoundError` (missing third-party
dep), `SyntaxError`, `NameError`, `KeyError`-via-bad-import,
`TypeError`,
etc., the bare exception bubbled past the Sentry `capture_errors`
decorator in `flyte/cli/_deploy.py` and landed in Sentry as an SDK
crash — even though the code that failed was in the user's workflow,
not in flyte.

## Changes

1. **`flyte._utils.module_loader.load_python_modules`** — catch
   `ImportError` / `SyntaxError` / `NameError` / `AttributeError` /
   `TypeError` / `ValueError` raised during `importlib.import_module`:
   - **Single-file path**: wrap in `flyte.errors.ModuleLoadError`
     (a `RuntimeUserError`), preserving the original traceback via
     `from e`, so the CLI surfaces an actionable message and the
     exception type itself signals "user error".
   - **Directory path**: record the failure in `failed_paths` so deploy
     either warns or aborts via `--ignore-load-errors`, matching how
     pre-existing `ModuleLoadError`s were already handled.

2. **`flyte._sentry._is_user_error`** — classify any `RuntimeUserError`
   subclass as a user error. Previously hard-coded to
   `(DeploymentError, ImageBuildError, InitializationError)`, missing
   the other ~20 `RuntimeUserError` subclasses (`ModuleLoadError`,
   `OOMError`, `TaskTimeoutError`, `RuntimeDataValidationError`,
   `CodeBundleError`, `RemoteTaskNotFoundError`, etc.). Filtering on
   the parent class is the right primitive — these errors are
   intentionally raised as user-facing messages, not crash reports.

## Closes

All match the same `module_loader` → `<frozen importlib._bootstrap>` →
user-module shape; this PR filters them out at the Sentry boundary:

- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3T
(`fold_to_ascii`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3R
(`langchain_community`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3Q
(`requests`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3P
(`google.oauth2`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3N
(`boto3`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3M
(`common`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3K
(`common`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3J
(`tqdm`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3H
(`cloudpathlib`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3E
(`flytelib.manifest`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3D
(KeyError 'GCP_ADR' from user `os.environ`)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3B
(TypeError `create_task_environment()` missing positional arg)
- fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3C
(NameError `gcp_adr` undefined)

## Test plan

- [x] New tests in `tests/flyte/utils/test_module_loader.py`:
  - Single-file `ModuleNotFoundError` is wrapped in `ModuleLoadError`
    with the original module name preserved.
  - Directory walk records `ModuleNotFoundError`s in `failed_paths`
    rather than crashing.
  - Same wrapping applies to `SyntaxError` / `NameError` /
`AttributeError` / `TypeError` / `ValueError` on the single-file path.
- [x] New tests in `tests/flyte/test_sentry.py`:
  - `ModuleLoadError` (a `RuntimeUserError`) is filtered.
  - Generic `RuntimeUserError` subclass (`OOMError`) is filtered.
  - Wrapped `ModuleLoadError` via `__cause__` is filtered.

Fix(anthropic): route tool input_schema through Flyte type engine (#702)

## Fix: Route Anthropic tool input_schema through Flyte type engine
The Anthropic plugin was generating input_schema for Claude tools using
a hand-written Python type mapper (`_python_type_to_json_schema`). This
mapper was unaware of Flyte's internal type system, causing correctness
failures - most critically, `Literal["C", "F"]` parameters produced
`{"type": "string"}` instead of `{"type": "string", "enum": ["C",
"F"]}`, because NativeInterface stores Literal as a dynamic Enum and the
old code didn't recognise it.

  This PR replaces the ad-hoc mapper with a proper type-engine.

  Changes:
- `src/flyte/_json_schema.py` (new) — converts a LiteralType protobuf to
a JSON schema dict
- `src/flyte/models.py` — adds `NativeInterface.json_schema` property,
which calls `TypeEngine.to_literal_type()` per input and converts via
`_json_schema.py`
- `src/flyte/_task.py` — adds `AsyncFunctionTaskTemplate.json_schema`
delegating to self.interface.json_schema
- `plugins/anthropic/.../agents/_function_tools.py` — removes TYPE_MAP,
_python_type_to_json_schema, _get_function_schema; replaces with
func.json_schema / NativeInterface.from_callable(func).json_schema
- `plugins/anthropic/tests/test_agents.py` — rewrites type schema tests
to use the new path; adds regression tests for Literal, datetime,
timedelta, Optional, nested collections, and true unions


  Design choices:

- json_schema lives on NativeInterface, not TypedInterface —
NativeInterface is the right home because it also holds parameter
defaults, which are needed to build the required list. TypedInterface is
a serialization-time artifact and
  not available during tool registration.
- Optional[X] is simplified to just X's schema — rather than emitting a
full oneOf + null variant. Claude tool use already communicates
optionality through the required array, so the null variant adds noise
without value.
- Deferred imports in json_schema — TypeEngine and flyteidl2 (protobuf)
are heavyweight. They are imported inside the property body rather than
at module load time to avoid slowing down every import of flyte.models.
- input_schema is computed once at function_tool() call time and stored
as a plain dict on the FunctionTool dataclass — it is never recomputed
during the agent loop.
  

Example:
- Literal["C","F"] → NativeInterface (Enum) → TypeEngine → LiteralType →
literal_type_to_json_schema → {"type":"string","enum":["C","F"]} →
FunctionTool.input_schema → Claude API
---

- Run the full test suite: cd plugins/anthropic && uv run pytest tests/
-v

fix: validate a bare `cache=` the way a `Cache(behavior=...)` is validated (#1597)

Direct sibling of #1594, three lines up in the same `__post_init__`.

## The bug

`TaskTemplate.__post_init__` normalized the bare `cache=` spelling with
a `match` that has **no `case _`**:

```python
if isinstance(self.cache, str):
    match self.cache:
        case "auto":     self.cache = Cache(behavior="auto")
        case "override": self.cache = Cache(behavior="override")
        case "disable":  self.cache = Cache(behavior="disable")
```

A `match` with no default is a silent no-op, so anything else stayed on
the task as the raw value the user typed.

| value | `Cache(behavior=...)` — the field spelling |
`@env.task(cache=...)` — the bare spelling |
|---|---|---|
| `"always"` (typo) | `ValueError: Invalid cache behavior: 'always'.
Must be one of ['auto', 'override', 'disable'] (aliases accepted: …)` |
**accepted**, stored as `'always'` |
| `"enable"` (documented alias) | normalized to `Cache("auto")` |
**accepted**, stored as `'enable'` |
| `5` | `ValueError` | **accepted**, stored as `5` |
| `True` | `ValueError` | **accepted**, stored as `True` |
| `"auto"` | `Cache("auto")` | `Cache("auto")` ✓ |

Same value, two spellings, opposite treatment — the shape #1582 and
#1594 both fixed.

## The alias table is the sharper half

`_CACHE_BEHAVIOR_ALIASES` maps nine spellings (`enable`, `enabled`,
`on`, `true`, `yes`, `off`, `false`, `no`, `none`) onto canonical
behaviors. Its own comment says why it exists:

> Common user-typed aliases mapped to their canonical CacheBehavior.
Keeps code like `cache="enable"` or `cache="off"` working instead of
crashing with a ValueError that ends up in Sentry as an SDK error.

**The task decorator is where that spelling gets typed, and it is the
one place the table never ran.** `@env.task(cache="enable")` left
`task.cache` as the `str` `'enable'`, and two consumers read that
attribute directly:

```
src/flyte/app/extras/_webhook_app.py:489    "behavior": task_details.cache.behavior,
src/flyte/ai/mcp/_tools.py:456              "behavior": td.cache.behavior,
```

Against a raw string that is `AttributeError: 'str' object has no
attribute 'behavior'` — the alias exists specifically to prevent a
crash, and skipping it produced a worse one.

## The fix

```python
self.cache = cache_from_request(self.cache)
```

`cache_from_request` is **the same coercion `task_serde.py:227` already
applies**, and it is the only path that runs `Cache.__post_init__` —
where the alias table and the "Invalid cache behavior" message both
live. The `match` was a subset re-implementation of it that drifted: it
never got the aliases, never got the error, and never got a default
case. Calling the helper deletes the duplicate rather than extending it,
and drops the now-unused `Cache` import.

Behaviour after:

```
cache='always'     -> ValueError: Invalid cache behavior: 'always'. Must be one of [...]
cache='enable'     -> 'auto'
cache='off'        -> 'disable'
cache='auto'       -> 'auto'
cache=5            -> ValueError: Invalid cache behavior: 5. ...
```

## Why this is a bug and not a matter of taste

Two independent witnesses, the pair this queue looks for:

1. **The consumer already asserts the invariant.** Two call sites do
`<task>.cache.behavior` with no guard, which is only correct if
`__post_init__` always leaves a `Cache`.
2. **The dataclass validates its other fields this way already.** In the
same `__post_init__`, `service_account` raises a clean `TypeError` and
`retries` raises a clean `ValueError` as of #1594. `cache` was the one
left silent.

## Not changed

`@env.task(cache="")` still falls back to the environment's default
rather than raising — the decorator's `cache or self.cache` treats the
empty string as "unset", which predates this and is a separate question
about falsy defaults across every kwarg.

## Tests

`tests/user_api/test_task_cache_request.py` — **23 tests**, following
#1594's file layout. Verified against pristine `main` with the
production change reverted:

```
18 failed, 5 passed
```

The 5 that pass both ways are the "accepts valid input" guards (the
three canonical behaviors, the default, and a `Cache` instance passed
straight through), so the suite pins the fix rather than the
implementation.

Full suite: **27 failed, 5934 passed** — the same 27 that fail on clean
`origin/main` in this sandbox (obstore/S3 with no sandbox running, the
three docker-builder tests with no daemon, keyring, roundtrip,
`test_ls_files_loaded_modules_*`, `test_real_build`). `make fmt`, `mypy`
(330 files), `ty` and `make check-docstrings` all clean.

## No Sentry issue

This is a code-audit PR. The silent half cannot produce one — a value
that serializes without raising never reports anything, which is exactly
why the corpus does not find this class.

fix(imagebuild): install local wheel by path so dev pre-release isn't dropped

PythonWheelHandler emitted two `uv pip install` commands per PythonWheels
layer: one to install the wheel (`--no-deps --no-index --reinstall`) and a
second to pull dependencies (`--find-links /dist <package_name>`). Once
`--no-index` was dropped in the second step, uv saw the package from two
sources -- the local `/dist` wheel (a `.dev` pre-release) and PyPI (a stable
release). By PEP 440, uv ignores pre-releases when a stable version satisfies
an unconstrained requirement, so the second step silently uninstalled the
local dev wheel and reinstalled the stable PyPI build. This made
`with_local_v2()` fail to pick up a locally-modified flyte once a competing
stable release existed on PyPI.

Install the wheel directly by file path instead:
`uv pip install <args> /dist/<package_name>-*.whl`. Pointing uv at the file
removes the resolution contest for the package itself (no pre-release
exclusion), while its dependencies still resolve from the index. This also
collapses the two commands into one. `package_name` is already the
underscore-normalized distribution name, and the build (`make dist` /
`dist-plugins`) cleans `dist/` first, so the dash-anchored glob matches
exactly one wheel for this package.

fix: async LocalDB connection never opened after sync-only init

A sync-only init (e.g. `flyte.init(local_persistence=True)` warming the
run-persistence DB at run start) set the shared `_initialized` flag
without opening the aiosqlite connection. `get_async()` then saw the
flag, skipped async init, and raised
`RuntimeError: LocalDB not properly initialized (async)` on every
cached child-task lookup. This is the Google Colab failure mode, where
aiosqlite is preinstalled (so the async path is taken) and the

feat(remote): fetch the code a run executed

The console shows a run's source under its "Code" tab, but the SDK had no way
to get at it: the pieces existed (extract_code_bundle, download_bundle) but
only as worker-side internals, with no method on remote.Run or remote.Action
and no CLI command.

Adds `Run.download_code` / `Action.download_code`, which pull the bundle down
and unpack it, `Run.code_bundle` / `ActionDetails.code_bundle` for the metadata
alone, and `flyte get code <run> [action]`, which lists the bundle's files or
unpacks it into `--dest`.

The bytes come from the same pre-signed link the console uses
(CreateDownloadLink with ARTIFACT_TYPE_CODE_BUNDLE), so no object-store
credentials are needed on the client. Backends that sign reports only, and
pickled bundles, which are deliberately refused there, fall back to reading the
bundle URI through flyte.storage.

extract_code_bundle also learns the two other places a bundle can be recorded —
the primary container of a K8sPod target, and task metadata's code_bundle_uri —
matching how the backend resolves it, so pod-template tasks are covered too.

feat(plugins): pydantic BaseModel batteries for typesafe-ai (#1609)

Follow-up to #1604. `ask()` already accepted a dataclass battery, a
single question type, or a mapping of them; it now also accepts a
**pydantic `BaseModel`**, so the answers land in a model you can
validate and pass around like any other.

## What actually needed changing

Transport already worked. A model holding `Choice[Intent]` round-trips
through the Pydantic transformer with the enum member and calibration
intact:

```
flyte transformer   Pydantic Transformer
flyte round-trip    ('Triage', <Intent.REFUND: 'refund'>, 'Choice')
compile_questions   BatteryError: ... is not a question    <- the only gap
```

So this is just the battery compiler learning to read pydantic fields:

- `Field(description=...)` → the question, which reads naturally
- `json_schema_extra={"question": ..., "criteria": ...}` → carries what
a description cannot, and overrides it
- `Annotated` metadata and enum docstrings behave exactly as on a
dataclass
- a required non-question field is rejected with the same message as the
dataclass path

Detection is duck-typed (`model_fields` + `model_validate`), so the
plugin still never imports pydantic.

## How this differs from Pydantic AI

[Pydantic AI's TypeSafe
integration](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/models/typesafe/) puts the
**question** in the field type — a `bool` is a yes/no question, a
`Literal` a pick-one, an `IntEnum` a rubric — and returns plain values
with the calibration alongside in `response.provider_details`.

This plugin puts the **answer** in the field type. A field is
`Choice[Intent]`, not `Intent`, so confidence and the full distribution
travel *with* the value: into the model, through validators, and across
Flyte task boundaries, with no side channel to thread through.
`examples/pydantic_battery.py` shows a `model_validator` acting on the
calibration directly — the case that gets awkward when it lives in a
separate response object.

Neither shape is better in the abstract; the README says when to reach
for each.

## Also here

One commit re-applies a type-checker fix to `examples/typesafe_ai/`.
`Score(criteria=...)` and `Choice(criteria=...)` are annotated with
invariant `list`/`dict`, so a `list[str]` literal is not assignable.
These only fail once `typesafe-sdk` is installed and the checkers can
see the real signatures — CI does not install it, which is why the
examples looked clean on #1602. Runtime was always fine.

## Testing

- 38 plugin tests, 7 of them new: compilation from pydantic fields, each
metadata source and its precedence, the required-field rejection,
`ask()` returning a populated model, a task-boundary round-trip, and
validators acting on the answers
- `make fmt`, `make mypy` (896 files), `make ty`, `check-docstrings`,
`codespell` clean
- The new example runs end to end against a live cluster: `route=review
intent=refund (p=1.00) severity=BLOCKING@2.6 refund_requested=0.99
conflicted=False`

fix: report a non-string memory/disk/shm against the field that was wrong (#1581)

## What

`Resources.memory`, `.disk` and `.shm` are declared as Kubernetes
quantity **strings** and are handed to protobuf string fields untouched,
so nothing ever checked them. A non-string survived `__post_init__` and
only failed much later, during serialization:

```
TypeError: bad argument type for built-in operation
```

raised inside `resources_serde` — SDK frames, naming neither the field
that was wrong nor the task it came from.

`cpu` never had the problem, because `_get_cpu_resource_entry` does
`str(cpu)` (it legitimately accepts an int or float core count). The
other three quantities have no such coercion, and that asymmetry is what
hid the gap:

```python
def _get_cpu_resource_entry(cpu: CPUBaseType) -> ...:
    return tasks_pb2.Resources.ResourceEntry(..., value=str(cpu))   # coerced

def _get_memory_resource_entry(memory: str) -> ...:
    return tasks_pb2.Resources.ResourceEntry(..., value=memory)     # not coerced
```

Reproduced on `main`, 4 for 4 — every one dies in serde, `cpu` is the
control:

| `Resources(...)` | before |
|---|---|
| `memory=1024` | `TypeError: bad argument type for built-in operation`
|
| `memory=(1024, 2048)` | `TypeError: bad argument type for built-in
operation` |
| `disk=10` | `TypeError: bad argument type for built-in operation` |
| `shm=1024` | `TypeError: bad argument type for built-in operation` |
| `cpu=2` *(control)* | serializes fine |

## Fix

Validate the three quantity fields in `__post_init__`, exactly the way
#1560 did for `gpu`, so the mistake is reported against the task
definition that caused it rather than surfacing as an opaque crash at
deploy time.

**Reject rather than coerce.** `memory=1024` is a plausible mistake, and
`str(1024)` is a *valid* Kubernetes quantity meaning 1024 **bytes** —
coercing would quietly deploy a task with a thousandth of the memory the
user asked for.

The guard deliberately does not narrow the accepted surface: `cpu` stays
untouched (it is not a quantity string), `shm="auto"`, the `(request,
limit)` pairs and every unset field all still work. It runs *after* the
existing pair-length check, so a 3-tuple keeps its own more specific
message.

## How this was found

Technique: audit the *fix sites* of a merged fix rather than the Sentry
corpus. #1560 added a guard for `gpu`, a field typed as a Union whose
unchecked arms only failed later in serialization. `memory`/`disk`/`shm`
are its siblings in the same dataclass with the same shape of gap.

## Notes

- **No Sentry issue and no GitHub issue to close.** This is a code-audit
finding, like #1537 / #1546 / #1549 / #1559 — there is no `fixes
FLYTE-SDK-XX` trailer because nothing in the corpus has fired for it. It
is capture-reachable, though: `cli/_deploy.py`'s `@capture_errors`
covers serialization, so this *would* be filed as an SDK crash if a user
hit it.
- Distinct from flyteorg/flyte#7991 (the `pod_spec_from_resources` key
map), which is closed and fixed by #1545.

## Test plan

- 5 new tests reproduce the crash for each affected field/shape;
verified they fail on `main` with `DID NOT RAISE` and pass with the fix.
- 9 new tests pin the accepted surface so the guard cannot narrow it,
plus one that the pair-length message still wins and one end-to-end
serialization check.
- `tests/user_api/test_resources.py` +
`tests/internal/runtime/test_resources_serde.py`: **135 passed**.
- Broader sweep (`-k "resource or serde or pod_spec or deploy"`): **442
passed**.
- `make fmt`, `ruff check`, `mypy`, `ty`, `check-docstrings` all clean.

fix: don't crash reading a non-JSON body from the IDP (FLYTE-SDK-60)

The OAuth token and device-code endpoints are specified to answer in JSON, but
what reaches the SDK is whatever a deployment puts in the way: a load balancer's
HTML 502 page, a proxy's plain-text "Internal Server Error", an SSO
interstitial. Four `response.json()` calls read those bodies unguarded, and two
of them sit on the *error* paths -- so the SDK crashed with a bare

SelectCluster/upload wrap unrecognized and lands in Sentry as an SDK bug, with
`Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)` as the only thing the user is told.

Making every command output json (In the future yaml too) (#56)

### PR Description

#### Overview

This pull request introduces significant improvements to the Flyte CLI
and SDK around output formatting and JSON serialization. The goal is to
make CLI output more flexible, scriptable, and user-friendly, especially
for automation and integration with other tools.

---

#### Key Changes

**1. Output Format Option for CLI**
- Replaces the boolean --simple flag with a new --output-format (or -of)
option.
- Supports multiple formats: table (default), table-simple, and json.
- All CLI commands that previously used get_table now use the new format
function, allowing consistent output formatting based on user
preference.

**2. Common Formatting Utilities**
- Introduces a new format function in _common.py that handles table,
simple table, and JSON output for iterable objects.
- get_panel is updated to respect output format for consistency.

**3. ToJSONMixin for Models**
- Adds a new ToJSONMixin class (in remote/_common.py) that provides
to_dict and to_json methods.
- All major API model classes (Project, Run, Task, Secret, Action,
ActionDetails, ActionInputs, ActionOutputs, RunDetails, TaskDetails) now
inherit from ToJSONMixin.
- This enables easy and consistent JSON serialization for CLI output and
programmatic use.

**4. Improved List Commands**
- All list commands (e.g., flyte get projects, flyte get runs, flyte get
tasks, etc.) now respect the --output-format option.
- Limits for listing are more consistently handled (e.g., flyte get
run/task now have a --limit option).

**5. Codebase Modernization**
- Refactors all usages of simple argument to output_format.
- Updates type annotations using Literal and typing_extensions.get_args
for CLI option validation.

---

#### Motivation

- Provides a more scriptable CLI experience for users and automation by
supporting JSON output.
- Makes the CLI more flexible for different use cases (human-friendly
tables, simple for scripting, JSON for parsing).
- Unifies output formatting and serialization logic across the codebase
for maintainability and consistency.

---

#### Backward Compatibility

- The --simple flag is removed and replaced by --output-format. The
default remains a rich table, so most users will not notice a change
unless they used --simple (who can now use --output-format
table-simple).
- All API models are backward compatible, now with additional methods
for JSON serialization.

---

#### How to Use

- Human-readable table (default):
  `flyte get projects`
- Simple table (for copy-pasting):
  `flyte get projects --output-format table-simple`
- JSON output (for scripting/automation):
  `flyte get projects --output-format json`

---

#### Example

```sh
flyte get tasks --output-format json --limit 10
```

---

#### Additional Notes

- All new output format logic is centralized, making future extensions
(e.g., YAML, CSV) easy to add.
- The ToJSONMixin is designed to work seamlessly with protobuf-based
models as well as plain dataclasses.

fix(controller): forward auth kwargs to the controller client

`create_remote_controller` accepted `command`, `proxy_command`, `http_proxy_url`
and `client_config` and then never passed them to `ControllerClient`, so they were
silently dropped on the way to `create_session_config`.

In-cluster that split the two halves apart: `init_in_cluster` builds the SDK client
and the controller from the same kwargs, so with `auth_type="ExternalCommand"` the
client authenticated correctly while the controller got the auth mode with no
command to run. That surfaced only when the controller made its first RPC, as
`AuthenticationError: Command cannot be empty for command authenticator` — and the
controller is what enqueues and watches child actions, so eager tasks failed at the
point of spawning work rather than at init.

Build the kwargs once and spread them into both the endpoint and api-key
constructors, with a note pointing at `_initialize._initialize_client` so the two
sets stay together. `rpc_retries` is deliberately still not forwarded: the
controller has never installed the retry interceptor and adding it here would
change retry behavior rather than fix a drop.

fix(controllers): bound informer watch establishment to recover from half-open reconnects

A flyte2 server restart left parent actions stuck "Running" for hours. The
runtime's watch informer reconnected onto a pooled keep-alive connection that
was half-open (peer gone, no RST), wrote the WatchForUpdates request, and then
blocked forever reading the chunked response: the transport's read_timeout is
unset and the intended watch_conn_timeout_sec guard was never wired in. A hung
read raises no exception, so the retry/backoff loop never fired and the parent
never re-synced its children's terminal states.

Wire watch_conn_timeout_sec in as a per-stream establishment deadline (applied
to each read up to the sentinel). A stalled reconnect now raises TimeoutError,
the existing backoff/retry re-issues the watch on a fresh connection, and the
server's snapshot re-syncs child state. The deadline is per-attempt (not
self._ready) because the incident hung on a reconnect after the informer was
already ready, and it is dropped once the sentinel arrives so healthy idle
streams are not recycled.

Env-var control of in-cluster auth mode (ExternalCommand without EAGER_API_KEY) (#1536)

## Problem

A customer does not want the control plane issuing eager API keys to
their task pods. They mint their own, more narrowly scoped tokens and
want the SDK to authenticate with `ExternalCommand`, which we already
support and prototyped with them.

`init_in_cluster` resolved credentials in this order:

1. an explicit `api_key=` argument
2. a mounted config file, if the pod has `UCTL_CONFIG` /
`FLYTECTL_CONFIG` set
3. the injected `_UNION_EAGER_API_KEY` / `EAGER_API_KEY`

So the only way to opt out of the injected key was to mount a config
file. There was no env-var-only route — even though every credentials
config entry already derives an env var (`admin.authType` →
`FLYTE_ADMIN_AUTHTYPE`).

Two things were also quietly broken along the way, and both had to be
fixed for the env-var route to work end to end.

## What this does

A task pod can now carry:

```
FLYTE_AUTH_TYPE=ExternalCommand
FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND="/usr/local/bin/mint-token --audience flyte"
```

and authenticate by running that command, with no API key issued to it
at all.

- `FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND` takes a shell-quoted command line, or a JSON
array when an argument contains spaces. Its stdout is the access token,
re-run on refresh.
- **Setting `FLYTE_AUTH_TYPE` disables the injected-key fallback
outright** rather than layering on top of it, so a cluster still
injecting a key mid-migration cannot have the two silently disagree.
- The endpoint still comes from the injected `_U_EP_OVERRIDE`, and now
also accepts `FLYTE_ADMIN_ENDPOINT` — dropping the API key drops the
endpoint it used to decode to.
- `FLYTE_AUTH_PROXY_COMMAND` is picked up independently of the auth
type.
- An explicit `api_key=` argument still wins, and logs that it is
ignoring the env vars instead of doing so quietly.
- `ExternalCommand` with no command raises at init, rather than
deferring to an `AuthenticationError` on the first RPC that names
neither env var.

The entries are read via `ConfigEntry.read()` with no config file, which
consults only the environment. That deliberately keeps the pod off
`resolve_config_path`, whose `git rev-parse` subprocess is wasted work
in a task pod.

## Two bugs fixed on the way

**`FLYTE_ADMIN_COMMAND` was unusable even on the existing config-file
path.** `ConfigEntry` applied no transform to env values, so a
`list`-typed entry came back as the raw string and
`asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(*self._cmd)` spread it *one argument per
character*. Same shape for the proxy command and scopes. YAML already
yields a list and is unaffected; the new transforms are idempotent on
that path.

**`create_remote_controller` accepted `command` and threw it away.** It
took `command`, `proxy_command`, `http_proxy_url` and `client_config`
and never forwarded them to `ControllerClient`. Since `init_in_cluster`
builds the SDK client and the controller from the same kwargs,
`auth_type="ExternalCommand"` would have authenticated the client
correctly while leaving the controller holding the auth mode with
nothing to run — surfacing only as `AuthenticationError: Command cannot
be empty for command authenticator` on the controller's first RPC. The
controller is what enqueues and watches child actions, so eager tasks
would have failed at the point of spawning work rather than at init.

`rpc_retries` is deliberately still not forwarded there: the controller
has never installed the retry interceptor, and adding it would change
retry behavior rather than fix a drop.

## On the env var names

These names are normally *derived*, not chosen: `get_env_name()` does
`FLYTE_{SWITCH_UPPERCASED}`, so `admin.authType` →
`FLYTE_ADMIN_AUTHTYPE`. That spelling leaks flyte-1 `flyteadmin` naming
into something a customer has to type into a pod spec, and
`read_from_env`'s docstring already called the scheme provisional.

Renaming outright would cost more than the wart. The scheme's one real
virtue is that env var and config key are derivable from each other both
ways; changing 2 of the 11 `admin.*` entries leaves no rule, just a
lookup table with exceptions. The derived names are also public surface
predating this feature — they are what the config-file path has always
used.

So the preferred name is now explicit rather than implicit.
`YamlConfigEntry` takes an `aliases` tuple checked ahead of the derived
name; `get_env_name()` reports the preferred one (docs, error messages)
and `env_names()` gives the precedence order.

| setting | preferred | still accepted |
|---|---|---|
| `admin.authType` | `FLYTE_AUTH_TYPE` | `FLYTE_ADMIN_AUTHTYPE` |
| `admin.command` | `FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND` | `FLYTE_ADMIN_COMMAND` |
| `admin.proxyCommand` | `FLYTE_AUTH_PROXY_COMMAND` |
`FLYTE_ADMIN_PROXYCOMMAND` |

Nothing that worked before stops working. When two names for one setting
disagree the higher-precedence one wins and the conflict is logged
rather than dropped silently — that ambiguity is how a migration goes
wrong quietly; identical values are not reported.

Scoped deliberately to the three auth entries this feature documents.
`FLYTE_ADMIN_ENDPOINT` keeps its derived name, since the endpoint is a
platform setting rather than an auth one. Renaming the rest of the
`admin.*` family is the scheme-wide change the code comment anticipates
and wants its own discussion.

## Known gap

The opt-in Rust controller (`_F_USE_RUST_CONTROLLER=1`) reads the
injected API key directly and does not honor these vars. Anyone on it
cannot drop the key yet. Called out in the `init_in_cluster` docstring.

## Testing

- 18 new tests in `tests/user_api/test_init_in_cluster_env_auth.py`
covering parsing (shlex, JSON array, quoted args), precedence (explicit
auth type beats the injected key; explicit `api_key` beats the env vars;
no env vars means unchanged legacy behavior), the endpoint fallback, the
loud-failure case, the controller forwarding, and the alias mechanism
(preferred name wins, derived name still honored, conflicts reported,
non-aliased entries unchanged).
- Verified end to end that the env vars produce an
`AsyncCommandAuthenticator` which runs the command and returns its
stdout as the token.
- Full suite failure set is byte-identical before and after this change.
`ruff` and `mypy` clean.

Note for reviewers running tests inside a Flyte task pod:
`_U_EP_OVERRIDE` and `_UNION_EAGER_API_KEY` are live in that environment
and leak into several tests, including a pre-existing one in
`test_init_in_cluster_fallback.py`. Unset them for a clean run.

## Summary

Fix `ContainerTask` deployment when it declares required inputs.

`ContainerTask` was constructing its `NativeInterface` with `None` as
the default for every input. During deployment,
`convert_upload_default_inputs` therefore treated required inputs as
optional defaults and attempted to serialize `None` using the declared
type. For inputs such as `str`, this failed with an error like:


- Represent `ContainerTask` inputs with `inspect.Parameter.empty`,
matching required inputs on function-backed tasks.
- Add a regression test that verifies:
  - declared inputs are reported as required;
  - their interface defaults use the required-parameter sentinel; and

feat(_task): allow secret overrides on reusable tasks

``task.override(secrets=...)`` previously raised when the task's env was
reusable. The intent was to keep one pool per env, but the actor pool
key (``extract_unique_id_and_image``) already includes the task's
``security_context`` — so a secret override deterministically maps to a
*different* actor pool, not a polluted one.

Concrete use case unblocked: per-user / per-identifier credentials
secrets on a reusable claude-session env. Each identifier gets its own
actor pod hosting that user's concurrent sessions; cross-identifier
isolation is preserved by the pool-key hash.

Resources and env_vars remain locked: they would change the pod spec
(CPU/memory limits, env values seen at exec time) without changing the
pool key, so the same actor pool could end up running tasks that disagree
on those values.

Claim new flyteplugins PyPI names at merge time, not release time (#1538)

## Why

PyPI limits each account to creating **4 new projects per 24 hours**
([pypi/support#10572](https://github.com/pypi/support/issues/10572)).
Uploads to existing projects are unlimited — the limit only bites on the
first-ever publish of a name. This broke the v2.7.0 release
([run](https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/actions/runs/33795996203)):
`flyteplugins-github` and `flyteplugins-llamacpp` were new names and got
`429 Too Many Requests` after earlier new names in the same run consumed
the budget.

Separately, a `flyteplugins-*` name that sits declared in the tree but
unpublished is squattable by anyone — `flyteplugins-redis`, `-echo`,
`-nsight`, and `-agento11y` were lost exactly that way and are now
quarantined on PyPI (PEP 541 requests pending).

## What

New `claim-plugin-names.yml` workflow:

- **`pull_request`** (touching `plugins/**/pyproject.toml`): fails early
if a single PR adds **more than 4** new `flyteplugins-*` distributions,
telling the author to split the PR and why (the PyPI new-project rate
limit).
- **`push` to `main`**: immediately publishes a `0.0.0a0` claim wheel
for every still-unregistered name, so the PyPI project is registered the
day the plugin merges instead of at the next release. If more than 4
names are somehow unregistered on a push (PR check bypassed), it fails
loudly before publishing anything.
- **daily `schedule` / `workflow_dispatch`**: drains any backlog at
4/day (e.g. names PyPI later frees from quarantine become 404 and get
claimed automatically).

`0.0.0a0` is a pre-release, so default `pip` resolution never picks the
claim wheel over a real release.

Also adds a cross-reference comment in `publish.yml`'s
`discover-plugin-packages` job: by release time every discovered name
should already exist, so releases only upload to existing projects and
never hit the creation limit.

## Validation

Dry-ran both scripts against the live repo/PyPI:
- name-diff logic: v2.6.10→HEAD correctly reports 6 new distributions;
HEAD→HEAD reports 0
- discovery over all 44 in-tree names: exactly 2 currently unclaimed
(`flyteplugins-github`, `flyteplugins-llamacpp`); the 4 quarantined
names correctly read as already-registered (HTTP 200) and are skipped
- both workflow files parse as valid YAML

First run of this workflow will claim `flyteplugins-github` and
`flyteplugins-llamacpp` (2 ≤ 4 budget).

## Notes for reviewers

- Consider making the `check-pr-plugin-count` job a required status
check on `main` so oversized plugin PRs can't merge.
- The claim job is gated to `github.repository == 'flyteorg/flyte-sdk'`
and uses the same `PYPI_USERNAME`/`PYPI_PASSWORD` secrets as
`publish.yml`.

fix: report a malformed auth env var against the variable that carried it

`FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND` / `FLYTE_AUTH_PROXY_COMMAND` are normalized with
`shlex.split`, which raises a bare `ValueError: No closing quotation` on an
unbalanced quote or a trailing escape. Nothing catches it, so a typo in the
command line aborts with a message that names neither the variable, the
setting, nor what a good value would look like:

    ValueError: No closing quotation

`read_from_env` now turns any transform failure into an `InitializationError`
naming the variable that carried the value and the setting it configures, and
`_as_argv` adds the two accepted forms to shlex's account of what is wrong:

fix(types): handle default_factory fields when reconstructing untagged outputs

Reconstructing a Pydantic/dataclass output from its schema (when the original
class isn't available) crashed for untagged outputs whose schema has
default_factory fields:

    TypeError: non-default argument '<field>' follows default argument

Pydantic omits the `default` key from the JSON schema for default_factory
fields, so they were handed to make_dataclass without a default. Whenever a
defaulted field happened to precede one in the hash-randomized schema order,
make_dataclass raised -- intermittently, ~80% of runs. Earlier SDKs instead
dropped these fields silently (lossy reconstruction).

Regression from #1171, which stopped dropping non-required fields but left
default_factory fields without a default on the dataclass path.

Give every non-required field a default during reconstruction, choosing a
faithful one by shape: list -> [], dict -> {}, nested model (no-arg
constructible) -> a constructed instance, everything else -> Optional[...] =
None. Fixes the crash and restores full-fidelity reconstruction on the untagged
path; the tagged Pydantic path was already correct.

replace with asyncssh so that no install at runtime (#1241)

## What

Replace the system `sshd` used by SSH-into-task debug with the
pure-Python **asyncssh** server, so there's **no runtime package
install** on the pod. The default task image runs as the non-root
`flyte` user with a root-owned venv, so `apt-get install openssh-server`
(or relying on a preinstalled `sshd`) isn't viable at runtime.
`asyncssh` is added as a flyte dependency (pure-Python, ~370 KB; its
only requirement `cryptography` already ships via pyOpenSSL), so it's
always present in the image.

The in-process `SshServer` (in `src/flyte/_debug/ssh.py`) generates its
host key and authorizes the user's key in-process, serves PTY login
shells and `ssh host <cmd>` execs, allows client-initiated TCP
forwarding (`ssh -L`/`-D`, needed by VS Code Remote-SSH), and exposes
SFTP. `import asyncssh` is kept local to the server methods so importing
the module (e.g. for the `WsBridge`) doesn't pull asyncssh.

## Changes

- `pyproject.toml`: add `asyncssh>=2.14` runtime dependency.
- `src/flyte/_debug/ssh.py`: in-process asyncssh server replacing the
`sshd` subprocess (host-key gen, key auth, PTY/pipe sessions, SFTP, TCP
forwarding); lazy `import asyncssh`.
- `src/flyte/_debug/vscode.py`: generated `.vscode/launch.json` now uses
the modern `"type": "debugpy"` instead of the deprecated `"type":
"python"`, which fails to resolve a debug adapter on current
`ms-python.debugpy` versions and would break F5 "Interactive Debugging"
over VS Code Remote-SSH.
- `tests/flyte/test_ssh_debug.py`: updated for the asyncssh server.
- `uv.lock` + all `plugins/*/uv.lock`: relock for the new asyncssh
dependency (it propagates into every plugin that depends on flyte).

## CI fixes (post-merge with `main`)

- **mypy**: annotated `SshServer._acceptor:
Optional["asyncssh.SSHAcceptor"]` (via a `TYPE_CHECKING` import) — now
that asyncssh is a hard dep, mypy resolves `asyncssh.listen()`'s return
type and flagged the assignment to the bare `_acceptor = None`.
- **check uv.lock**: regenerated every plugin lockfile so `uv lock
--check` is green across the repo.

## End-to-end validation (demo cluster: `demo.hosted.unionai.cloud`)

Built the local wheel (`make dist`, baked into a `from_debian_base`
image), ran a task, then `flyte debug <run>` to relaunch it with
ssh-debug and connected:

- ✅ SSH connect through the `:6060` WebSocket bridge → in-pod asyncssh
server (`asyncssh 2.24.0`, **baked into the image, no runtime install**)
- ✅ Command exec, PTY interactive shell (`/dev/pts/0`,
`TERM=xterm-256color`), and SFTP subsystem (VS Code Remote-SSH / scp)
- ✅ Workspace staged (code bundle downloaded) + debug helpers written
(`.vscode/launch.json`, `flyte-debug-task.sh` pdb helper)

**VS Code Remote-SSH debugging path** specifically verified:
- ✅ `x86_64` + glibc 2.36 → `server-linux-x64` compatible; egress to the
VS Code CDN returns HTTP 200 (server bootstraps)
- ✅ Local forward (`ssh -L`) and dynamic SOCKS forward (`ssh -D`) both
return HTTP 200 — `direct-tcpip` forwarding works (the extension host +
port forwarding Remote-SSH relies on)
- ✅ `launch.json` "Interactive Debugging" entrypoint
(`/opt/venv/bin/runtime.py`) present; debugpy is supplied by the VS Code
extension (not required in the task venv)

## Why

AWS `g7.4xlarge` nodes carry `k8s.amazonaws.com/accelerator:
nvidia-rtx-pro-4500`, but the v2 SDK has no way to request them through
the first-class API: `flyte.GPU("RTX PRO 4500", 1)` raises `Invalid GPU

workaround today is the escape hatch

device_class="GPU")`.

`RTX PRO 6000` (g7e) is already in `GPUType` but missing from
`ACCELERATOR_DEVICE_MAP`, so the SDK sends the raw `"RTX PRO 6000"`
string and relies on the control plane's alias map to normalize it.
Dual-GPU g7e instances also had no `"RTX PRO 6000:2"` accelerator
string.

"nvidia-rtx-pro-4500"` and `"RTX PRO 6000" -> "nvidia-rtx-pro-6000"` so
the SDK emits the node label value directly, consistent with the other
NVIDIA entries.

emitted `gpu_accelerator.device` and GPU quantity for the RTX PRO
strings.

Note: the control plane's `AcceleratorDevices` alias map
(`flyteplugins/.../flytek8s/config/config.go`) should get a matching
`"RTX PRO 4500"` entry so that older SDKs sending the human-readable
name also resolve.

fix(examples): repair the volume examples against flyteplugins-union 0.10.9 (#1584)

All four Volume examples failed on a real cluster. Three classes of rot,
plus two defects the verification runs surfaced.

## Hardcoded `/workspace`

The default mount path is now per-volume (`_default_mount_path()` keys
off the volume name), so an explicit `mount_path="/workspace"` in one
task and a bare `mount()` in the next landed in different directories:

```
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/workspace/hello.txt'
```

Every task now reads and writes under the `Path` that `mount()` returns.
In `bench.py` that means threading `root` into the workload functions;
in `volume_recover.py` the `mounted` bool is gone — `root:
Optional[Path]` does double duty as the mount-once flag.

## Version pin

`flyteplugins-union>=0.4.0` → `>=0.10.9`, in both the PEP 723 header and
`with_pip_packages`.

## `allow_fuse()` → `allow_volumes()`

The surrounding comments described the old in-process mount path
(smarter-devices/fuse, CAP_SYS_ADMIN); a brokered mount needs neither,
so the comments and the Prereqs docstrings now describe the CSI mount
broker instead.

## `bench.py`'s index-size probe was silently dead

It stat'd `/var/lib/flyte-volume/index.db`, which no longer exists, so
`index_bytes` was `0.0` for every cell. It now pins `meta_dir` on
`mount()` and stats that — the verification run reports real numbers
again (1.37 MB for `metadata_burst`, 156 KB for `fork_burst`).

## `volume_recover.py` was OOMKilled at `memory="1Gi"`

The first clean run took three attempts, not two: the intentional crash
after epoch 2, then an `OOMKilled` (exit 137) on the resume, and only
the third attempt finished. With `retries=2` that is one bad break from
failing outright. Raised the three demos to `cpu="1", memory="4Gi"` —
the mount client (JuiceFS plus its metadata store) and the memory-backed
staging emptyDir that `allow_volumes()` attaches both draw on the pod
limit. The re-run took exactly two attempts, the only failure being the
simulated crash.

`gcsfuse_example.py` is untouched: it is plain GKE gcsfuse CSI, not the
Volume plugin, and its `MOUNT_PATH` is already used consistently.

## Note for anyone reproducing

`with_local_v2()` bakes whatever wheel is already in `dist/` rather than
rebuilding from `src/`, so run `make dist` first. A stale wheel there is
what produced the original failure — `ImportError: cannot import name
'run_sync_in_thread'` — because the baked SDK predated #1472's rename
while the working tree did not.

Address review: directive injection, state suffixes, dropped directives

Three findings from the PR review, each verified against a live cluster.

Reject CR/LF in sbatch directive values. A newline ends the `#SBATCH`
comment and everything after it becomes script body, which Slurm runs as the
SSH user. Values reach the renderer from task config -- `sbatch_options` and
`working_dir` -- so they are not necessarily trusted. Shell arguments were
already quoted; directive values were not.

Normalize decorated job states. `sacct` reports `CANCELLED by 1234` and
suffixes a state with `+` when the field carries extra information. Only the
whitespace form was handled, so `CANCELLED+` fell through to the
unrecognized-state path, which reports RUNNING -- leaving a finished task
polling until it timed out.

Hoist a script task's own leading directives above the generated exports.
`sbatch` stops reading `#SBATCH` at the first executable line, so emitting
the exports before the user's script silently dropped every directive it
carried, contradicting the documented behaviour. Confirmed on a cluster: a
`--cpus-per-task` after an `echo` has no effect, and of two identical
options the last wins. The plugin's directives are therefore emitted after
the user's, so non-conflicting options survive and ours still win a
duplicate. A directive below an executable line was already inert and stays
in the body rather than being promoted, so wrapping cannot start applying an
option the cluster was ignoring.

Verified end to end: a wrapped script carrying `--cpus-per-task=3` now
allocates 3 CPUs where it previously got the default, while the plugin's
job name still overrides the script's.

without — and could not answer its own strongest counter-argument, the
first thing a sceptical reader says out loud: *the System 2 model could
have filled that schema itself, you just never asked it to.*

That objection was correct. The pair varied three things at once, so a
win for Jev was unattributable between them:

1. **who answers** the atomic questions,
2. whether the verdict is **composed in code** or reasoned out in a
prompt,
3. whether the pipeline may **abstain**.

Several scoring choices also leaned the same way — all of them in Jev's
favour.

## The fix: a third arm

`system2_structured` pins (2) and (3) down and varies only (1). System 2
answers exactly the battery Jev answers, against exactly the criteria
Jev is given, and runs through the same `derive()`, the same confidence
gate, the same tools and the same prose prompt.

| Arm | Fills the battery | Composes the verdict | May abstain |
|---|---|---|---|
| `with_system1` | System 1 (Jev), one parallel call |
`TaskSpec.derive()` | yes |
| `system2_structured` | System 2, autoregressively |
`TaskSpec.derive()` | yes |
| `without_system1` | System 2, autoregressively | the prompt | no |

Both composed arms call one shared `_compose_and_finish` rather than two
copies, so nothing downstream of the battery can drift apart and quietly
confound the comparison. Two independent readings fall out:

- **with Jev vs structured** — who is the better schema-filler,
everything else identical.
- **structured vs without** — what moving composition out of the prompt
and into Python is worth, model held fixed. This delta costs no System 1
vendor at all, and may be the more broadly useful number.

## Levelling the specification and the scoring

| Was | Now |
|---|---|
| Jev got `true`/`false` criteria, label descriptions and every severity
tier; System 2 got bare keys — it was graded against a rubric it had
never seen | Both System 2 arms get the identical specification via
`_battery_spec()` |
| System 2 sampled at the gateway default while Jev is deterministic |
`temperature=0`, so decision-stability measures the model, not the
sampler |
| A signal answered `"yes"` instead of `true` scored as a dropped field
| Lenient counting, with the strict count beside it as a reported
**format gap** |
| A battery truncated at `max_tokens` was indistinguishable from one the
model declined to answer | `max_tokens` 4096→8192 and
`finish_reason`/`stop_reason` captured as `truncated` |
| An arm that escalated everything scored 0% success while doing exactly
what it was designed to do | New **coverage** metric as the denominator
for selective accuracy |

Two asymmetries are kept **deliberately**, and both are flagged in the
report:

- The with-Jev arm spends a second Jev call verifying its own
generation, so the structured arm runs the same three checks through
System 2 and is billed for them — rather than looking cheaper for
skipping work.
- The two gates are not the same quantity. Jev's confidence is a
calibrated probability; the structured arm's is a number the model was
asked to state about itself. That makes their routing split a test of
**calibration** — a real difference between the approaches, not a flaw
in the setup — but it must be read as that and not as accuracy.

## Verification

`logic_check.py` gains a second offline proof alongside the existing
one: a *perfect* System 2 answer sheet derives the identical label, tool
and routing tier as a perfect Jev battery, across all 36 cases,
including deliberately mixed boolean spellings. Without it a lossy
adapter could handicap the challenger and the benchmark would confirm
its own hypothesis.

```
all composition rules reproduce ground truth
both composed arms derive identically from a perfect battery
```

Both run offline in under a second — no API key, no tokens. An
end-to-end smoke test with stubbed models also runs all three arms clean
and renders the full report; `ruff`, `mypy` and `ty` all pass.

## Note on the published results

The results table in the README is **marked stale rather than updated**.
Every change above moved the baseline it was measured against, and it
has no third-arm column — so it cannot distinguish "Jev answers the
battery better" from "composing in Python beats composing in a prompt".
A re-run at the same conditions as the last published run (`--num_cases
12 --repeats 5`) is in flight; the README section will be replaced with
its numbers in a follow-up.

The default matrix grows from 324 to 486 actions (3 tasks × 9
arm-provider cells × 6 cases × 3 repeats).

Conflicted with #1609, which fixed the same two pre-existing `_judge.py`
/ `durable_agent.py` type errors this branch had also fixed
incidentally. Resolved by taking `main`'s version of both files verbatim

fix: filter ConnectError(UNAVAILABLE/DEADLINE_EXCEEDED) from Sentry (#1137)

## Summary

SelectCluster failures land in Sentry as SDK crashes even though they
are transient infra problems — DNS lookup failed, TCP connect refused,
connection reset, deadline exceeded. The chain is:

```
ConnectError(UNAVAILABLE | DEADLINE_EXCEEDED)
  -> RuntimeError("SelectCluster failed for operation=...")        # _select_and_build
  -> RuntimeSystemError("Failed to get signed url for /tmp/...")   # _upload_single_file
```

The SDK cannot recover from these; they belong in the same user-error
bucket the CLI's `InvokeBaseMixin` (in `src/flyte/cli/_common.py`)
already routes to `ClickException`.

## Change

Extends `_USER_ACTIONABLE_CONNECT_CODES` in `src/flyte/_sentry.py` to
include:
- `UNAVAILABLE` — connection refused/reset, DNS lookup failure, backend
down.
- `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` — request timed out.

`INTERNAL` is intentionally **not** added — that code can indicate a
real backend/SDK bug worth a crash report. Docstring on
`_is_user_actionable_connect_error` is updated to spell out the
two-flavor (user-config + transient-infra) scope.

## Closes

- [FLYTE-SDK-29](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/FLYTE-SDK-29/) —
SelectCluster `Request timed out` (DEADLINE_EXCEEDED)
- [FLYTE-SDK-47](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/FLYTE-SDK-47/) —
SelectCluster `Connection refused` (UNAVAILABLE)
- [FLYTE-SDK-48](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/FLYTE-SDK-48/) —
SelectCluster transient failure (UNAVAILABLE)
- [FLYTE-SDK-3W](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/FLYTE-SDK-3W/) —
SelectCluster `Connection reset` (UNAVAILABLE)

\`fixes FLYTE-SDK-29\`
\`fixes FLYTE-SDK-47\`
\`fixes FLYTE-SDK-48\`
\`fixes FLYTE-SDK-3W\`

RuntimeSystemError — filtered.
- [x] New: `ConnectError(DEADLINE_EXCEEDED)` wrapped variant — filtered.

`test_capture_exception_still_reports_connect_error_internal` —

Add flyte.is_control_plane_available() and Run.first_failure() for agent edit-and-relaunch loops (#1522)

## Why

The agent-mediated forking example (unionai/unionai-examples#308) — an
agent task that launches a workflow, observes the failure, patches the
workflow's source on disk, reloads it, and `fork()`s the failed run with
the fixed code — had to reach into SDK internals:

1. `isinstance(get_controller(), RemoteController)` to decide whether
launching/forking real runs is possible, or whether to fall back to
running the workflow inline.
2. Hand-rolled `Action.listall(...FAILED...)` iteration to find which
step failed and its error message.
3. `flyte._code_bundle.bundle.build_code_bundle.cache_clear()` to make
the next fork ship the edited working tree — **no longer needed**: #1508
removed the code-bundle memoization entirely, so every launch re-bundles
from disk. This PR originally shipped a
`flyte.refresh_code_bundle_cache()` for that; it was dropped when
merging main, since the cache it managed no longer exists.

## What

**`flyte.is_control_plane_available()`** — True when the process can
submit work to a control plane (launch real runs whose actions can be
awaited and replayed/forked). Inside a task, the orchestration mode
decides (`remote`/`hybrid` → True, `local` → False, even when a client
is configured — `flyte run --local` configures one too); outside a task,
a configured client decides. This replaces the
isinstance-on-internal-controller probe with the `TaskContext.mode` the
runtime already maintains.

**`Run.first_failure()` and `ActionDetails.error_message`** — the
observation half of a repair loop: which step of a run failed, and why.
`first_failure()` returns the `ActionDetails` of the first failed action
in creation order, preferring a failed sub-action over the failed root
(whose error usually just repeats the sub-action's); `error_message` is
the failed action's message or `""`.

With these, the example's loop reduces to:

```python
run = await flyte.run.aio(wf.main, n_records=n_records)
await run.wait.aio(quiet=True)
if failure := await run.first_failure.aio():
    patch_workflow_source(failure.task_name, failure.error_message)
    importlib.reload(sys.modules["workflow"])
    run = await fork.aio(run.name, task_template=wf.main)
```

## Testing

- New unit tests: `is_control_plane_available()` across

Treat RST_STREAM-backed ConnectErrors as transient watch failures

The StreamError branch in _is_transient_watch_error was unreachable.
connectrpc catches the transport's pyqwest.StreamError and re-raises it as a
ConnectError (`raise rst_err from e`), and maybe_map_stream_reset sends the
NO_ERROR / INTERNAL_ERROR / PROTOCOL_ERROR reset codes onto Code.INTERNAL —
which _TRANSIENT_CONNECT_CODES deliberately excludes. So an intermediary
resetting an idle stream (an ALB at its default 60s idle timeout, say) still
surfaced as a fatal INTERNAL and the reconnect loop never ran:

    connectrpc.errors.ConnectError: Error reading content

Classify via __cause__ instead: a ConnectError is transient if its code is in
the transient set *or* a StreamError sits underneath it. A genuine server-side
INTERNAL is built from the response body and carries no such cause, so it stays
fatal.

Add flyte.replay() for re-executing runs with original or updated code

Replay lets users re-run a previous execution using the same inputs and
RunSpec, optionally swapping in a new TaskTemplate with updated code.
This is useful for:

- Debugging: reproduce a failed run locally with the exact same inputs
- Iterating: re-run with modified task code against production inputs
- Testing: verify a fix against the inputs that caused a failure

Usage examples:

    # Replay remotely with original task template
    flyte.replay("my-run-name")

    # Replay a specific action within a run
    flyte.replay("my-run-name", action_name="a1")

    # Replay with updated code
    flyte.replay("my-run-name", task_template=my_updated_task)

    # Replay locally (requires a task_template with executable code)
    flyte.with_replaycontext(mode="local").replay(
        "my-run-name", task_template=my_task
    )

    # Replay remotely with explicit mode
    flyte.with_replaycontext(mode="remote").replay("my-run-name")

Implementation notes:
- Follows the same _Runner/with_runcontext pattern: _Replayer holds config,
  with_replaycontext() returns a _Replayer, top-level replay() uses defaults
- Local replay always requires a task_template (validated early, before
  network calls) since there is no Python function to execute without one
- Extracts shared local execution logic into run_task_locally() in _run.py,
  eliminating duplication between _Runner._run_local and _Replayer._replay_local

fix: report a non-string memory/disk/shm against the field that was wrong (#1581)

## What

`Resources.memory`, `.disk` and `.shm` are declared as Kubernetes
quantity **strings** and are handed to protobuf string fields untouched,
so nothing ever checked them. A non-string survived `__post_init__` and
only failed much later, during serialization:

```
TypeError: bad argument type for built-in operation
```

raised inside `resources_serde` — SDK frames, naming neither the field
that was wrong nor the task it came from.

`cpu` never had the problem, because `_get_cpu_resource_entry` does
`str(cpu)` (it legitimately accepts an int or float core count). The
other three quantities have no such coercion, and that asymmetry is what
hid the gap:

```python
def _get_cpu_resource_entry(cpu: CPUBaseType) -> ...:
    return tasks_pb2.Resources.ResourceEntry(..., value=str(cpu))   # coerced

def _get_memory_resource_entry(memory: str) -> ...:
    return tasks_pb2.Resources.ResourceEntry(..., value=memory)     # not coerced
```

Reproduced on `main`, 4 for 4 — every one dies in serde, `cpu` is the
control:

| `Resources(...)` | before |
|---|---|
| `memory=1024` | `TypeError: bad argument type for built-in operation`
|
| `memory=(1024, 2048)` | `TypeError: bad argument type for built-in
operation` |
| `disk=10` | `TypeError: bad argument type for built-in operation` |
| `shm=1024` | `TypeError: bad argument type for built-in operation` |
| `cpu=2` *(control)* | serializes fine |

## Fix

Validate the three quantity fields in `__post_init__`, exactly the way
#1560 did for `gpu`, so the mistake is reported against the task
definition that caused it rather than surfacing as an opaque crash at
deploy time.

**Reject rather than coerce.** `memory=1024` is a plausible mistake, and
`str(1024)` is a *valid* Kubernetes quantity meaning 1024 **bytes** —
coercing would quietly deploy a task with a thousandth of the memory the
user asked for.

The guard deliberately does not narrow the accepted surface: `cpu` stays
untouched (it is not a quantity string), `shm="auto"`, the `(request,
limit)` pairs and every unset field all still work. It runs *after* the
existing pair-length check, so a 3-tuple keeps its own more specific
message.

## How this was found

Technique: audit the *fix sites* of a merged fix rather than the Sentry
corpus. #1560 added a guard for `gpu`, a field typed as a Union whose
unchecked arms only failed later in serialization. `memory`/`disk`/`shm`
are its siblings in the same dataclass with the same shape of gap.

## Notes

- **No Sentry issue and no GitHub issue to close.** This is a code-audit
finding, like #1537 / #1546 / #1549 / #1559 — there is no `fixes
FLYTE-SDK-XX` trailer because nothing in the corpus has fired for it. It
is capture-reachable, though: `cli/_deploy.py`'s `@capture_errors`
covers serialization, so this *would* be filed as an SDK crash if a user
hit it.
- Distinct from flyteorg/flyte#7991 (the `pod_spec_from_resources` key
map), which is closed and fixed by #1545.

## Test plan

- 5 new tests reproduce the crash for each affected field/shape;
verified they fail on `main` with `DID NOT RAISE` and pass with the fix.
- 9 new tests pin the accepted surface so the guard cannot narrow it,
plus one that the pair-length message still wins and one end-to-end
serialization check.
- `tests/user_api/test_resources.py` +
`tests/internal/runtime/test_resources_serde.py`: **135 passed**.
- Broader sweep (`-k "resource or serde or pod_spec or deploy"`): **442
passed**.
- `make fmt`, `ruff check`, `mypy`, `ty`, `check-docstrings` all clean.

fix: map disk to ephemeral-storage and skip shm in pod_spec_from_resources (#1545)

## Why

`pod_spec_from_resources` walks every field of `Resources` and looks
each one up in an unguarded dict:

```python
resources_map = {
    "cpu": "cpu",
    "memory": "memory",
    "gpu": k8s_gpu_resource_key,
    "ephemeral_storage": "ephemeral-storage",   # no such field on Resources
}
...
k8s_pod_resources[resources_map[resource.name]] = resource_value
```

`Resources` declares `cpu, memory, gpu, disk, shm`. The map is keyed on
`ephemeral_storage` — the flytekit v1 name for what v2 calls `disk` —
and has no entry for `shm`, so either field raises:

```python
pod_spec_from_resources(requests=Resources(cpu=1, disk="10Gi"))  # KeyError: 'disk'
pod_spec_from_resources(requests=Resources(cpu=1, shm="2Gi"))    # KeyError: 'shm'
```

`ephemeral_storage` was the only occurrence of that spelling left in
`src/`.

## Impact

The function is public — exported from `flyte.extend` and in its
`__all__` — and the Ray plugin calls it for every head/worker group that
sets resources (`plugins/ray/src/flyteplugins/ray/task.py:86`). Going
through the plugin's own `_build_node_pod_template`:

```
before:  ray worker, disk  -> KeyError: 'disk'
         ray worker, shm   -> KeyError: 'shm'
after:   ray worker, disk  -> {'cpu': 1, 'memory': '1Gi', 'ephemeral-storage': '10Gi'}
         ray worker, shm   -> {'cpu': 1, 'memory': '1Gi'}
```

So a Ray task requesting ephemeral disk — ordinary for a shuffle- or
spill-heavy job — failed before submitting anything. Both fields are
documented on `Resources`, and `shm` is documented as "useful for ML
data loading", squarely Ray's use case.

## What changed

The serde path already settles what both fields mean, so the mapping
isn't a judgement call:

- `disk` → `ResourceName.EPHEMERAL_STORAGE` via
`_get_disk_resource_entry` (`resources_serde.py:80`), i.e. the
`ephemeral-storage` container key.
- `shm` → `ExtendedResources.shared_memory` mounted at `/dev/shm` via
`get_proto_extended_resources` (`resources_serde.py:96`). That's a
volume, not a container resource key, so it must not appear under
`requests`/`limits`.

This keys `disk` to `ephemeral-storage`, drops the stale
`ephemeral_storage` entry, and skips fields with no entry in the map —
which leaves `shm` out of container resources where it belongs, and
makes a future `Resources` field a silent skip rather than a crash.

`cpu`, `memory`, and `gpu` behaviour is unchanged, including the
`nvidia.com/gpu` key and the requests/limits mirroring.

## Tests

Four tests added to `tests/user_api/test_resources.py` — the function
had no coverage at all:

- `test_pod_spec_from_resources_maps_disk_to_ephemeral_storage`
- `test_pod_spec_from_resources_skips_shm`
- `test_pod_spec_from_resources_all_fields` — cpu + memory + gpu + disk
+ shm together
- `test_pod_spec_from_resources_disk_in_requests_and_limits`

All four fail on `main` with the exact `KeyError`s and pass with this
change.

- `make fmt` — clean
- `make mypy` — `Success: no issues found in 870 source files`
- `make check-docstrings` — `523 files clean`
- `codespell` — clean
- `make unit_test` — no new failures
- Ray plugin suite — 15 passed

Let flyte.sandbox.orchestrator call local tasks

An orchestrator could only call remote references, because the worker
launches a child from its deployed spec. A local task has no deployed
spec, but the SDK already knows how to build one: it is what flyte.run
does for any task. So when an orchestrator is run, each local task it
calls is serialized (building its image and code bundle as usual) and
its spec is shipped in the orchestrator's template. The worker uses an
embedded spec when there is one and looks the task up otherwise.

Remote references still need nothing built. Durable operations are
rejected at decoration time, since only tasks can be launched.

Fall back to _F_PATH_REWRITE env var for actor tasks in rusty.run_task (#1384)

## TL;DR

`_bin/runtime.py` (regular tasks) reads `_F_PATH_REWRITE` from the pod
env to enable accelerated-inputs path rewriting. `rusty.py` (actor
tasks) never did — it only honored the `path_rewrite_cfg` kwarg, which
workers don't pass. This PR gives rusty the same env-var fallback
runtime.py already has.

## Before / after

**Regular task** (`_bin/runtime.py`, unchanged):
```
read _F_PATH_REWRITE env → verify local mount exists → rewrite input paths (else read remote)
```

**Actor task** (`rusty.run_task`):
```
before:  kwarg not passed → no rewrite → always reads remote storage, even with the local mirror mounted
after:   kwarg not passed → read _F_PATH_REWRITE env → same mount check → same rewrite
```

One consistent decision tree for both entrypoints: explicit kwarg wins,
else pod env, then the existing mount-existence check gates activation.

## Why it matters

Actors are the workload that benefits most from local dataset reads —
many short tasks on one warm worker, often re-reading the same shared
data. Without this, enabling accelerated inputs sped up regular tasks
but silently did nothing for actors.

## Safety

Every missing piece degrades to today's behavior (remote reads): env var
absent → no-op; mount not present → existing check falls back; old
workers → this is the only path that activates the feature for them;
workers that do forward the kwarg (worker-v2 change, separate) → kwarg
takes precedence.

fix(secret): normalize Secret mount to a POSIX path so image builds work on Windows

`Secret.__post_init__` compared `str(self.mount)` to "/etc/flyte/secrets". On
Windows, `str(pathlib.Path("/etc/flyte/secrets"))` is "\etc\flyte\secrets", so
any image with secret mounts failed to build: the remote builder itself builds
`Secret(..., mount=Path("/etc/flyte/secrets"))` in
`_get_build_secrets_from_image` and the check rejected it.

The mount is a path inside the Linux container, so normalize it to a
`PurePosixPath` once in `__post_init__`. That also keeps backslashes out of the
Dockerfile `--mount=type=secret,...,target=` and keeps `stable_hash` the same
across platforms. The remote builder now builds the default as a
`PurePosixPath` too.

fix: give `flyte deploy` a CLI config when the context has none (FLYTE-SDK-8N) (#1589)

## Problem

[FLYTE-SDK-8N](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/?query=FLYTE-SDK-8N) —
firing at release **2.8.0**, the current release:

```
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'output_format'
  flyte/cli/_deploy.py:242 in invoke
```

`DeployEnvRecursiveCommand.invoke` reads `ctx.obj` into a local
**before** calling `common.initialize_config(ctx=ctx, ...)`, and then
throws that call's return value away:

```python
obj: CLIConfig = ctx.obj          # None when nothing put a config on the context
common.initialize_config(         # <- builds one, returns it, return value discarded
    ctx=ctx, project=..., domain=..., ...
)
...
common.format("Loaded Environments", ..., obj.output_format)   # boom
```

`initialize_config` already handles this exact state — it has an `if obj
is None:` branch that builds a `CLIConfig` and hands it back. The repair
it performs simply never reached the caller.

`DeployEnvCommand.invoke` has the same root cause one step earlier. It
calls `ctx.obj.init(...)` directly, with no `initialize_config` call at
all, so the same context state gives:

```
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'init'
```

**A context arriving without a config is expected, not hypothetical.**
Two independent compensations for it already exist in the codebase —
`initialize_config`'s own `is None` branch, and
`_hello.py:_ensure_cli_config`, whose docstring states the case
outright:

> Give the context a CLIConfig when `run`/`serve` was invoked without
going through main.

`_deploy.py` was the caller of that shape benefiting from neither.

## Fix

- `DeployEnvRecursiveCommand.invoke` takes the config
`initialize_config` returns instead of the pre-call `ctx.obj`.
- `DeployEnvCommand.invoke` routes through `initialize_config`. The five
arguments it passed to `ctx.obj.init(...)` are exactly the five
`initialize_config` forwards to `CLIConfig.init`, so this is
behaviour-preserving when a config is present, and a repair when it is
not.
- `initialize_config` now also stores the config it builds on the
context rather than only returning it. The remaining callers invoke it
purely for its side effect (`list_commands`/`get_command` in `_deploy`,
`_serve` and `_run`); this leaves the context in a state where a later
`ctx.obj` read succeeds instead of silently building and discarding a
config.

## Verification

Both crash sites reproduce on `main` with the exact Sentry exception,
and pass after the change. 3 of the 4 new tests fail without the
production diff (the fourth is a guard that a context which *already*
carries a config keeps that exact object, and passes either way).

`tests/cli/` + `tests/flyte/cli/`: **537 passed**, no regressions. `make
fmt`, `make mypy`, `make ty` and `make check-docstrings` all clean.

docsy: hf_model docstring documents CLI flags as Python parameters (#1451)

## Summary

The `hf_model()` docstring describes an API the function does not have.

Found while documenting artifacts for the user guide
([unionai-docs#1454](https://github.com/unionai/unionai-docs/pull/1454))
— the docs example was written from this docstring and inherited the
error, so it shipped a snippet that raises.

## What is wrong

**The example passes a parameter that does not exist:**

```python
run = flyte.prefetch.hf_model(
    repo="meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-hf",
    shard_config=ShardConfig(engine="vllm", args=VLLMShardArgs(tensor_parallel_size=8)),
    accelerator="A100:8",     # <- not a parameter of hf_model
    hf_token_key="HF_TOKEN",
)
```

**And the `Args:` block documents six names that are not in the
signature**, while omitting two that are:

| | |
|---|---|
| Documented, nonexistent | `cpu` · `mem` · `disk` · `gpu` · `shm` ·
`wait` |
| Exists, undocumented | `raw_data_path` · `resources` |

Signature on `main` is `(repo, raw_data_path, artifact_name,
architecture, task, modality, serial_format, model_type,
short_description, shard_config, hf_token_key, resources, force)`.

## Why it drifted

Those six are **exactly** the flags on `flyte prefetch hf-model`
(`--cpu/--mem/--disk/--gpu/--shm/--wait`), which the CLI folds into a
single `Resources(...)` before calling this function. The docstring was
written against the CLI's surface and never updated when the Python API
consolidated them. `accelerator=` is a third spelling matching neither.

## Why it is not cosmetic

Copying the example gives a `TypeError`. Reading `Args:` to size a
sharding run points you at `gpu=`, which also does not exist — the
accelerator belongs in `Resources(gpu=...)`.

The example is the likelier path, because it is the only place showing
sharding, and **sharding is the one case that actually needs an
accelerator**. The default is `Resources(cpu="2", memory="8Gi",
disk="50Gi")` with no GPU, so a reader who follows the example as
written asks vLLM for `tensor_parallel_size=8` on a 70B model with two
CPUs and no accelerator.

## The fix

- Example passes `resources=flyte.Resources(cpu="8", memory="64Gi",
disk="500Gi", gpu="A100:8")`.
- `Args:` documents `resources` and `raw_data_path`, states that the
default carries **no accelerator** so sharding needs it set explicitly,
and points at the CLI's separate flags so the two surfaces are
reconcilable rather than silently contradictory.
- `raw_data_path` wording lifted from the CLI flag's own help text, so
the two agree.

## Also in here

`"the repo's README is attached as the model card"` is **conditional**.
The README fetch is wrapped in a `try/except` that logs `"No README.md
file found"`, and the card is only built `if card_md` — so a repo
without a README yields no card. Softened to say so.

## Second commit: the CLI's help advertises the same nonexistent flag

`src/flyte/cli/_prefetch.py:210` — the sharding example in `flyte
prefetch hf-model`'s help text passes `--accelerator A100:8`, but the
command defines **`--gpu`**. `--accelerator` appears nowhere in its own
option list.

**This one cannot be worked around downstream.** The help text is
rendered verbatim into the generated CLI reference page
(`api-reference/flyte-cli.md` on the docs site), so the published docs
carry the bad flag and the only fix is here.

After the change, every flag referenced in that module's help text is
one the command actually defines (checked programmatically: 17 defined
options, 0 referenced-but-undefined).

So this is **one drift in three places**: the `hf_model()` Python
docstring, the CLI help text, and the docs page written from them. The
docs page is fixed in
[unionai-docs#1454](https://github.com/unionai/unionai-docs/pull/1454);
the other two are here.

## Verification

- The docstring example now **parses as valid Python** and its call
matches the released signature.
- Signature and `Args:` now agree exactly: zero
documented-but-nonexistent, zero exists-but-undocumented.
- `ruff check` clean, `ruff format --check` clean.

Docs-only. No behavior change.

Add Slurm connector plugin

Run Flyte 2 tasks on an existing Slurm cluster, including Soperator-managed
clusters, without changing the cluster.

Two task types are served by one connector:

- `slurm`: a Python task submitted as an sbatch job that runs the task's own
  container image and Flyte entrypoint under Pyxis/Enroot, so typed I/O,
  caching, retries and error reporting work as they do for a Kubernetes pod.
  Removing `plugin_config` runs the identical task on Kubernetes.
- `slurm_script`: an existing sbatch script submitted unchanged; scalar
  inputs are exposed as FLYTE_INPUT_<NAME>. Phase, exit code and logs only.

Transport is SSH to a login node (asyncssh) behind a small SlurmTransport
protocol so a slurmrestd transport can be added later. One connection per
cluster is reused and status queries are batched (squeue, then sacct for
finished jobs). Slurm states map to Flyte phases with PENDING reported as
QUEUED rather than RUNNING, PREEMPTED as retryable, and CANCELLED as
ABORTED; failures carry Slurm's reason and the tail of stderr.

Connection details may be set per task or cluster-wide on the connector via
FLYTE_SLURM_HOST / FLYTE_SLURM_USERNAME / FLYTE_SLURM_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY.
The plugin is added to the default connector image build.

fix: report a non-string memory/disk/shm against the field that was wrong

`Resources.memory`, `.disk` and `.shm` are declared as Kubernetes quantity
strings and are handed to protobuf string fields untouched, so nothing ever
checked them. A non-string survived `__post_init__` and only failed much later,
during serialization, as:

    TypeError: bad argument type for built-in operation

raised inside `resources_serde` -- SDK frames, naming neither the field that was
wrong nor the task it came from. `cpu` never had the problem because
`_get_cpu_resource_entry` stringifies it (it legitimately takes an int or float
core count); the other three quantities have no such coercion.

Validate them in `__post_init__` instead, the same way #1560 did for `gpu`, so
the mistake is reported against the task definition that caused it.

Reject rather than coerce: `memory=1024` is a plausible mistake, and `str(1024)`
is a valid Kubernetes quantity meaning 1024 *bytes*, so coercing would quietly
deploy a task with a thousandth of the memory the user asked for.

The guard does not narrow the accepted surface -- `cpu` stays untouched, `shm="auto"`,
the `(request, limit)` pairs and every unset field all still work -- and it runs
after the existing pair-length check, so a 3-tuple keeps its own message.

`apply()` derives the deployment version by piping the user's envs and
image cache through `cloudpickle.dumps`. If anything in the user's
task or environment is unpicklable (e.g. a captured
`sys.stdin`/`stdout` tty handle, an open file, a thread, or a lock),
cloudpickle raises `PicklingError`/`TypeError` and the raw stack ends
up in Sentry.

This change wraps the version-hash computation and translates those
pickle failures into a `click.ClickException` that names the most
common cause and points the user at the `version=` escape hatch. The
new ClickException short-circuits the Sentry filter added in #1039 so
we stop logging user-side closure mistakes as SDK crashes.

## Closes

- [FLYTE-SDK-21](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/FLYTE-SDK-21) --
`PicklingError: Cannot pickle files that map to tty objects` from
`cloudpickle._file_reduce`

`fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-21`

## Test plan

- [x] New unit test in `tests/flyte/test_deploy.py` covers the
unpicklable-envs path.
