examples: add examples/rerun covering rerun, recover, forced replay, changed inputs

A pipeline that fans out four `prep` tasks into a `flaky_join` that fails
unless FLAKY_OK=1 is in the run environment. That yields a seed run with
four succeeded actions and one failed one -- the shape recovery exists for
-- so recovering it visibly reuses the preps and re-executes only the join.

Walks all four variants end to end, printing each action's phase after
every launch so RECOVERED (reused as-is) is distinguishable from a real
re-execution:

  1. rerun(run)                                  everything executes again
  2. rerun(run, recover=True)                    preps reused, join re-run
  3. rerun(run, recover=True, force_rerun_actions=[...])  force one anyway
  4. rerun(run, inputs={"n": 6})                 same code, new parameters

Also demonstrates the boundary: recover=True with changed inputs raises,
because replaying with new code or inputs is fork (flyteplugins-union).

The module docstring carries the equivalent `flyte` CLI command for each
variant, including `flyte get action <run>` to discover the deterministic
action-name hashes that --force-rerun-action takes.

Rebuild task as the plugin template class when overriding plugin_config

Plugin behavior lives on the template class, not on a field: `TaskEnvironment.task()`
resolves the class from `TaskPluginRegistry` at decoration time, and that class carries
the `task_type` and the custom config serialization (e.g. `RayFunctionTask` /
`task_type="ray"`). Since `dataclasses.replace` preserves `type(self)`, setting
`plugin_config` through `override()` left a plain `AsyncFunctionTaskTemplate` with
`task_type="python"` and no custom config on the wire.

Look the plugin class up in the same registry `TaskEnvironment.task()` uses, and rebuild
the overridden task as that class. `task_type` is dropped from the copied fields so the
plugin's own default applies. Overriding the config of a task that is already the plugin
class keeps the class and just replaces the config.

Also update the ray example to configure the plugin via `override()`.

fix: serialize concurrent code-bundle download/extract to prevent worker startup crashes in clustered tasks (#1370)

## Issue
Tracks the following Issue on Linear:
[ENG26-1039](https://linear.app/unionai/issue/ENG26-1039/clustered-task-environments-integration-test-failing)

## Motivation

Clustered (JobSet) tasks launch nproc_per_node separate a0 processes per
pod via torchrun, and each one independently runs download_bundle into
the same destination directory. The concurrent downloads and tar
--overwrite extractions race with each other, intermittently crashing
workers at startup (tar: <file>: Cannot open: No
such file or directory); each crash burns a JobSet restart, which is
what has been failing test_clustered_failure_cascade in the scheduled
integration tests ("jobset failed due to reaching max number of
restarts").

  ## Summary

- download_bundle now serializes download+extract per bundle behind an
exclusive flock (dest/.<basename>.lock), with a completion marker
(.extracted / .done) as the "ready" signal — the archive's existence
alone is not trusted, since it appears on disk before extraction
finishes.
- Downloads land atomically via mkstemp + os.replace, fixing the
non-atomic fsspec fallback that could expose a half-written tgz/pkl to a
peer process.
- The lock waits without a timeout and is never unlinked; the kernel
releases it if the holder dies, and the next waiter redoes the work (no
marker → re-download).
Where locking is unavailable (no fcntl, read-only destination) behavior
degrades to the previous semantics.
- The pkl branch gets the same protection (previously a peer could
gzip.open a half-written pkl). No new dependencies; public signature
unchanged.

 ## Test Plan

- New tests/flyte/code_bundle/test_download_bundle.py (11 tests): happy
path, marker fast-path, lock-wait, stale partial archive, corrupt bundle
retry, same-process and multi-process concurrency, degraded mode,
marker-write failure, pkl branch, cross-bundle non-contention.
- The multi-process test reproduces the production race against the
pre-fix code (fails 3/3 with the same tar collision) and passes with the
fix: git stash && uv run python -m pytest
tests/flyte/code_bundle/test_download_bundle.py::test_multi_process_concurrency
vs. unstashed.
- Full unit suite passes (make unit_test); only pre-existing unrelated
failure (test_keyring_store).
- End-to-end: 5/5 consecutive examples/clustered/failure_cascade.py runs
succeeded on playground canary with the fixed wheel baked into the image
and a CI-sized bundle (1863 files, 38 MB, --copy-style all), each
exercising crash → JobSet restart → completion with no tar errors.

docs: correct with_uv_project's install args and reset_root_logger, in Google style (#1493)

Replaces **#1302** and **#1316**, closed rather than rebased. Both
corrections are still valid — I re-verified each against today's code
before reopening them — but both were written in Sphinx `:param` style,
and `main` has **none left**: `838b41f4` (#1376, "strip inert
reStructuredText from docstrings") converted those files to Google
style. 60–70 `:param` lines on each old branch, zero on target. That is
a rewrite, not a conflict.

Two independent corrections, one commit each.

## 1. `with_uv_project` — the args feed `uv sync`, not pip

Three parameters were documented "for pip install". They never reach
pip. All three uv-project templates in `docker_builder.py` run:

```
uv sync --active --inexact $PIP_INSTALL_ARGS
```

and `$PIP_INSTALL_ARGS` is `get_pip_install_args()` — where `index_url`,
`extra_index_urls`, `--pre` and `extra_args` end up. That helper's name
is presumably why the docstring reads as it does; it is shared with the
layers that genuinely do call pip.

It matters because the accepted flags differ. `uv sync` takes
`--only-group`, which pip has no equivalent for, and rejects plenty pip
accepts — so a reader following this docstring reaches for the wrong
flag set. The docstring now gives that example.

## 2. `reset_root_logger` — documented backwards, in both places

```
_initialize.py   "By default, we clear out root logger handlers and set up our own."
_run.py          "If true, the root logger will be preserved and not modified by Flyte."
```

They disagree with each other and both disagree with the code. The
default is `False`, and `False` clears nothing; `True` is what replaces
the root handlers. So the first states the wrong default, and the second
**inverts the flag** — a reader wanting to keep their own root handlers
would set the exact flag that destroys them.

Both now describe what `initialize_logger` does: `True` replaces the
root handlers with Flyte's (JSON when `log_format` is `json`, else Rich
or plain console); the default `False` leaves them and wraps each so
third-party lines routed through root still carry run and action
context.

Also documents `FLYTE_RESET_ROOT_LOGGER=1`, which enables it and was
mentioned nowhere.

## Verification

`check-docstrings` clean · 433 tests · `make fmt` idempotent · ruff
clean on all three files.

fix: add V5E to TPUType so TPU v5e is reachable (#1548)

## Why

TPU v5e is wired up everywhere except the type that gates the
constructor.

`ACCELERATOR_DEVICE_MAP` already carries its node label, right next to
the two generations that do work:

```python
"V5E": "tpu-v5-lite-podslice",
"V5P": "tpu-v5p-slice",
"V6E": "tpu-v6e-slice",
```

and `_resources.py` already defines the slice shapes and a branch to
validate them:

```python
V5EParts = Literal["1x1", "2x2", "2x4", "4x4", "4x8", "8x8", "8x16", "16x16"]
...
elif partition is not None and device == "V5E":
    if partition not in get_args(V5EParts):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid partition for V5E: ...")
```

But `TPUType` listed only two of the three:

```python
TPUType = Literal["V5P", "V6E"]
```

So `TPU()` rejected the device at its first guard, the `elif device ==
"V5E"` branch below it was unreachable, and `V5EParts` was exported and
documented but unusable:

```python
TPU(device="V5E", partition="2x2")
# ValueError: Invalid TPU type: V5E. Must be one of ('V5P', 'V6E')
```

## What confirms the direction

Nothing downstream needed changing. Building the device directly — going
around the constructor — already serialized correctly before this patch:

```
Device(device="V5E", device_class="TPU", quantity=1, partition="2x2")
  -> gpu_accelerator { device: "tpu-v5-lite-podslice" partition_size: "2x2" device_class: GOOGLE_TPU }
```

which is structurally identical to what V5P and V6E produce. The whole
stack already handles v5e; only the literal was blocking it. That rules
out the other possible reading — deleting `V5EParts` and the dead branch
— since that would contradict `ACCELERATOR_DEVICE_MAP` at the layer that
actually talks to the backend.

## What changed

- `V5E` added to `TPUType`
- `V5EParts` admitted in the `partition` type hint (previously `V5PParts
| V6EParts | None`)
- `V5EParts` given the docstring its two siblings already have
- `V5E` named in the `Args:` example, which listed only `"V5P", "V6E"`

The previously-dead partition validation now actually runs:

```python
TPU(device="V5E", partition="3x3")
# ValueError: Invalid partition for V5E: 3x3. Must be one of ('1x1', '2x2', ...)
```

V5P and V6E are untouched, and an unknown device is still rejected.

## Tests

`test_tpu_all_types_with_partitions` is extended with three V5E cases
alongside the existing V5P/V6E ones, plus three new tests:

- `test_tpu_v5e_is_a_valid_type`
- `test_tpu_invalid_partition_v5e` — covers the branch that could not
previously execute
- `test_tpu_v5e_serializes_to_the_v5e_node_label` — pins
`tpu-v5-lite-podslice`

All six fail on `main` and pass with this change.

## Checks

- `make fmt` — clean
- `make mypy` — `Success: no issues found in 870 source files`
- `make check-docstrings` — `523 files clean`
- `codespell` — clean
- `make unit_test` — no new failures

feat: Apple Silicon accelerator for the devbox

`flyte.Resources(gpu="AppleSilicon")` (or `gpu=flyte.APPLE_SILICON()`) on a devbox started with
`flyte start devbox --apple-silicon` runs the task or app natively on the Mac, so its code can use
the Metal GPU directly (`torch.device("mps")`, MLX). A devbox container is a Linux VM with no Metal,
so the workload's entrypoint is handed to a host-side bridge, which runs it in a cached uv
environment built from the image's pip packages; the container streams its logs, mirrors its exit
code, forwards aborts and proxies an app's port.

- `--apple-silicon` is opt-in, because workload code runs outside any sandbox; it binds every devbox
  port to 127.0.0.1. A paused Apple Silicon devbox restarts its bridge on resume.
- Per-workload HMAC tokens (`as1.<workload>.<mac>`) minted by the backend from the devbox's bridge
  secret.
- `FLYTE_APPLE_SILICON_EXECUTION=container` keeps the workload in its container and gives it a
  host MLX model server (`mlx_lm.server`) over an OpenAI-compatible endpoint instead.
- Named errors (AppleSiliconNotAvailableError, AppleSiliconDaemonStartFailedError, ...) so a workload
  that cannot get the GPU fails with the reason instead of falling back to the CPU.
- `flyte get devbox` lists the bridge and every Apple Silicon workload; `flyte delete devbox` stops it.
- `flyte[apple-silicon]` extra (mlx-lm).
- Examples: examples/accelerators/apple_silicon_train.py (PyTorch on mps),
  apple_silicon_serve.py (Hugging Face model on mps in an AppEnvironment), and
  apple_silicon_proof/ (a runbook that proves the code runs on the Apple GPU).

feat(plugins): pydantic BaseModel batteries for typesafe-ai (#1609)

Follow-up to #1604. `ask()` already accepted a dataclass battery, a
single question type, or a mapping of them; it now also accepts a
**pydantic `BaseModel`**, so the answers land in a model you can
validate and pass around like any other.

## What actually needed changing

Transport already worked. A model holding `Choice[Intent]` round-trips
through the Pydantic transformer with the enum member and calibration
intact:

```
flyte transformer   Pydantic Transformer
flyte round-trip    ('Triage', <Intent.REFUND: 'refund'>, 'Choice')
compile_questions   BatteryError: ... is not a question    <- the only gap
```

So this is just the battery compiler learning to read pydantic fields:

- `Field(description=...)` → the question, which reads naturally
- `json_schema_extra={"question": ..., "criteria": ...}` → carries what
a description cannot, and overrides it
- `Annotated` metadata and enum docstrings behave exactly as on a
dataclass
- a required non-question field is rejected with the same message as the
dataclass path

Detection is duck-typed (`model_fields` + `model_validate`), so the
plugin still never imports pydantic.

## How this differs from Pydantic AI

[Pydantic AI's TypeSafe
integration](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/models/typesafe/) puts the
**question** in the field type — a `bool` is a yes/no question, a
`Literal` a pick-one, an `IntEnum` a rubric — and returns plain values
with the calibration alongside in `response.provider_details`.

This plugin puts the **answer** in the field type. A field is
`Choice[Intent]`, not `Intent`, so confidence and the full distribution
travel *with* the value: into the model, through validators, and across
Flyte task boundaries, with no side channel to thread through.
`examples/pydantic_battery.py` shows a `model_validator` acting on the
calibration directly — the case that gets awkward when it lives in a
separate response object.

Neither shape is better in the abstract; the README says when to reach
for each.

## Also here

One commit re-applies a type-checker fix to `examples/typesafe_ai/`.
`Score(criteria=...)` and `Choice(criteria=...)` are annotated with
invariant `list`/`dict`, so a `list[str]` literal is not assignable.
These only fail once `typesafe-sdk` is installed and the checkers can
see the real signatures — CI does not install it, which is why the
examples looked clean on #1602. Runtime was always fine.

## Testing

- 38 plugin tests, 7 of them new: compilation from pydantic fields, each
metadata source and its precedence, the required-field rejection,
`ask()` returning a populated model, a task-boundary round-trip, and
validators acting on the answers
- `make fmt`, `make mypy` (896 files), `make ty`, `check-docstrings`,
`codespell` clean
- The new example runs end to end against a live cluster: `route=review
intent=refund (p=1.00) severity=BLOCKING@2.6 refund_requested=0.99
conflicted=False`

fix: skip files that vanish before being added to code bundle (#1195)

## Problem

The code bundle file list (`ls`) is computed by walking the source tree,
but a file can disappear between listing and `tar.add` stat-ing it —
most commonly a transient lock file (e.g. `.codegraph/codegraph.lock`).
This raised a raw `FileNotFoundError` in `tarfile.gettarinfo` that
aborted the entire deploy.

Sentry: **FLYTE-SDK-52** — `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or
directory: '.../.codegraph/codegraph.lock'` (culprit `tarfile in
gettarinfo`, via `_packaging.create_bundle`).

## Fix

Wrap `tar.add` in a `try/except FileNotFoundError` that logs a warning
and skips the vanished file. A file disappearing mid-bundle is an
environment race, not an SDK bug, and shouldn't abort the whole deploy —
the rest of the bundle is still produced.

## Tests

- `test_create_bundle_skips_files_that_vanish_before_add` — a file
present in the list but missing on disk is skipped; the bundle is still
produced with the remaining files.

fixes FLYTE-SDK-52

fix: don't report an exhausted upload retry as an SDK crash (FLYTE-SDK-7N, FLYTE-SDK-7P) (#1553) ## Why `_put_signed_url_with_retry` (`src/flyte/remote/_data.py`) PUTs the code bundle — and tracked-run metadata — to a signed object-store URL. It keeps its own retry table, and every entry in it means *"the store is unhealthy right now, send it again"*: ```python if put_resp.status_code in [408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504] or _is_retryable_store_error(...): ``` plus, in the `except` arm, `httpx.TimeoutException / NetworkError / OSError`. When every attempt loses to the same condition, both arms raise `RuntimeSystemError`. **They were then reported inconsistently:** | half | how it fails | cause chain | reached Sentry? | |---|---|---|---| | transport (`httpx.ReadError`, timeouts, …) | `raise RuntimeSystemError(...) **from e**` | terminates in an httpx error | **no** — `_is_transient_network_error` filters it (it names `FLYTE-SDK-36` for this exact leg) | | HTTP status (502/503/500/…) | `raise RuntimeSystemError(...)` | **empty** — it is reacting to an `httpx.Response`, there is no exception to chain | **yes**, as an SDK crash | Same outage, same exhausted retries, opposite treatment. The filter never had anything to match on, because the failure the SDK is reporting was never an exception in the first place. Reproduced on `main` — an nginx `502` on every attempt: ``` raised: RuntimeSystemError code=UploadFailed __cause__: None _is_user_error (True == filtered from Sentry): False <-- leaks ``` and the sibling, for contrast: ``` TRANSPORT half -> code=UploadFailed cause=ReadError _is_user_error (filtered?): True <-- already fine ``` ## Impact `FLYTE-SDK-7N` (4 events, rel 2.6.5) and `FLYTE-SDK-7P` (6 events, rel 2.6.10) — both `Failed to upload …​ after 3 retries: status 502:`, one from `flyte run`, one straight from `_upload_with_retry`. 10 events of "the object store's gateway was down for four consecutive attempts" filed as Python-SDK crashes. **Update (2026-09-11):** `FLYTE-SDK-8C` (2 events, rel 2.7.2, first seen today) is the same leak on a different status — `Failed to upload … after 3 retries: status 503:` with an S3 `SlowDownPlease reduce your request rate.` body. 503 is in the retry table this filter keys off, so it is already covered by the change as written; no code change was needed to pick it up. Worth noting that the store asking us to slow down is about as clear a "not an SDK bug" as this class gets. Nothing in them is actionable in Python: the SDK asked for the object to be stored, retried on the schedule it advertises, and got a transient failure every time. ## What changed The exhaustion path gets its own error code, and `_sentry` filters on it. - `_data.py`: both exhaustion sites now raise `_RETRIES_EXHAUSTED_CODE` (`"UploadRetriesExhausted"`) instead of `"UploadFailed"`. Both, not just the leaking one — they are the same outcome, and a reader finding two different codes on two branches of one retry loop would be right to be confused. The transport half's filtering is unchanged either way (its cause chain still does the work). - `_sentry.py`: `_is_exhausted_upload_retry` joins the chain walk in `_is_user_error`. Keyed on the error **code**, not the message, so it cannot drift with wording. The code is read via `sys.modules.get("flyte.remote._data")` rather than imported: only that module raises this error, so if it was never imported no exception can carry the code — and a capture never drags in httpx/aiofiles/the remote client just to compare a string. ## Deliberately narrow - `"UploadFailed"` — a status the retry table **never** retries, e.g. a 403 on a signed URL — keeps reporting. - `"UploadUrlExpired"` keeps reporting. - This is strictly the **object-store PUT leg**. A 500 on the *control-plane RPC* leg arrives as a `ConnectError` and is untouched — `FLYTE-SDK-64` (276 events, `SelectCluster` → `Internal Server Error`) is real backend signal and still reports. There is a test pinning that. I tested the predicate across the whole unresolved corpus before writing it (71 issues / 1789 events): exactly `7N` and `7P` match, both `status 502`. Nothing else in the corpus is silenced. ## Tests `tests/flyte/test_sentry.py` — these drive the **real** retry loop to exhaustion rather than hand-constructing the error: - `test_capture_exception_skips_upload_that_exhausted_its_retries` — the production bug; also asserts `__cause__ is None`, which is *why* it leaked - `test_capture_exception_skips_upload_that_exhausted_its_retries_on_transport` — the two halves must not diverge again - `test_capture_exception_still_reports_a_non_retryable_upload_failure` — 403 still reports - `test_exhausted_upload_filter_ignores_other_system_errors` — guards the `FLYTE-SDK-64` class explicitly - `test_exhausted_upload_filter_tracks_the_code_data_actually_raises` — pins the premise, so renaming the constant in `_data` can't silently switch the filter off `tests/flyte/remote/test_upload_retry.py` — `test_exhausted_transient_status_gets_its_own_error_code`, `test_exhausted_transport_failure_shares_the_exhausted_code`, `test_non_retryable_status_keeps_the_plain_upload_failure_code`. Reverting only the wiring (keeping the symbols defined, so imports still resolve) fails 3 of them, including the capture test; the guard tests pass either way by design. ## Checks - `make fmt` — clean - `make mypy` — `Success: no issues found in 870 source files` - `ty check` on both changed files — `All checks passed!` - `make check-docstrings` — `523 files clean` - `pytest tests/` — 5712 passed; the 24 failures are pre-existing and reproduce identically on clean `origin/main` (local minio/sandbox and Docker dependencies) --- Sentry issues are not mirrored into GitHub issues for this repo (issues are disabled on `flyteorg/flyte-sdk`), so the trailers reference the Sentry short IDs: fixes FLYTE-SDK-7N fixes FLYTE-SDK-7P fixes FLYTE-SDK-8C - https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/?query=FLYTE-SDK-7N - https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/?query=FLYTE-SDK-7P - https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/?query=FLYTE-SDK-8C Signed-off-by: Haytham Abuelfutuh Signed-off-by: fiedlerNr9

fix(code-bundle): rebuild after source changes (#1508)

Fixes flyteorg/flyte#7923

Bug: `build_code_bundle` memoizes only its arguments → long-lived
processes reuse stale source after files are edited

### Summary

`build_code_bundle` and `build_code_bundle_from_relative_paths` are
wrapped in `@alru_cache`. The cache key contains function arguments such
as `from_dir`, `copy_style`, and `additional_files`, **but it does not
contain the selected files or their contents**.

In a long-lived process, the first `run()` builds and caches a
`CodeBundle`. If source files are then edited and the task is run or
forked again with the same bundling arguments, `alru_cache` returns the
original bundle before the working tree is scanned again.

The later run therefore executes the pre-edit source without rebuilding
the bundle or emitting a warning.

### Impact

- `run()` → edit source → `fork()` can execute the original source
instead of the edited source.
- Agent debugging loops, interactive sessions, and other long-lived
processes can silently retry stale code.
- The file-listing and content-digest code is never reached on an
argument-cache hit, so the existing content-addressed cache cannot
detect the edit.
- `skip_cache=True` does not provide a complete guarantee because
repeated calls using the same `skip_cache=True` arguments can themselves
be memoized.

### Root cause

`src/flyte/_code_bundle/bundle.py` memoizes the entire bundling
operation:

```python
@alru_cache
async def build_code_bundle(
    from_dir: Path,
    *,
    copy_style: CopyFiles = "loaded_modules",
    skip_cache: bool = False,
    additional_files: tuple[str, ...] = (),
) -> CodeBundle:
    ...
```

The same applies to the explicit-path builder:

```python
@alru_cache
async def build_code_bundle_from_relative_paths(
    relative_paths: tuple[str, ...],
    from_dir: Path,
    *,
    skip_cache: bool = False,
) -> CodeBundle:
    ...
```

The content-sensitive portion of the operation runs inside the memoized
function:

```python
files, digest = list_files_to_bundle(
    from_dir,
    True,
    *ignore,
    copy_style=copy_style,
    additional_files=additional_files or None,
)
```

On an `alru_cache` hit, execution returns before `list_files_to_bundle`
or `list_relative_files_to_bundle` can recompute the digest.

The bundler already has a content-addressed persistent cache after file
discovery:

```python
cached = _read_bundle_cache(digest)
if cached:
    hash_digest, remote_path = cached
    return CodeBundle(
        tgz=remote_path,
        destination=extract_dir,
        computed_version=hash_digest,
        files=files,
    )
```

This change removes the outer argument-only memoization while preserving
the digest-backed persistent cache. Each invocation now scans and hashes
the current source state; unchanged source still reuses the existing
uploaded bundle and skips compression and upload.

Regression tests modify a source file between calls made with identical
arguments and verify that:

- the new tarball contains the edited source;
- `computed_version` changes;
- both code-bundle builders detect edits without callers invoking
`cache_clear()`.

agents plugin (#1221) Run agents written with existing agent SDKs: OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Mistral Agents, and Google ADK, on Flyte as the durable orchestration runtime underneath. You keep writing agents in each framework's own idioms; Flyte provides replay, automatic retries / self-healing, per-tool containerized execution (CPU/GPU, caching), cross-run memory and observability. No agent loop is reimplemented. ## Packages Five co-located packages on a shared core: | Package | Underlying SDK | | --- | --- | | `flyteplugins-agents-core` | shared contract (no SDK) | | `flyteplugins-agents-openai` | OpenAI Agents SDK | | `flyteplugins-agents-claude` | Claude Agent SDK | | `flyteplugins-agents-mistral` | Mistral Agents (`mistralai` 2.x) | | `flyteplugins-agents-google` | Google ADK | ## The shared model Every adapter exposes the same surface: `function_tool` + `run_agent` and follows the same division of labor, so the call shape is identical across SDKs: - The agent run is a Flyte `@env.task`: the durable parent (`retries=` = self-healing, `report=True` = the agent timeline in the report). - Each tool is a Flyte task, invoked as a durable child action (its own container/resources, retries, caching) via `function_tool`. - Each model turn is recorded for replay by tracing the seam below the SDK's own loop (`durable=True`), so a crashed or retried run replays completed turns instead of re-calling (and re-billing) the model. Where the SDK runs its loop in a subprocess (Claude), durability is the SDK's own session-resume instead. - Cross-run memory via `memory_key`, backed by a durable keyed `MemoryStore`. The rule: if the SDK owns the loop, we run its loop and trace the seam beneath it. Agent maps to a task, each tool maps to a task, each model turn maps to a trace. ## What you get - Crash-and-resume: a crash mid-run replays completed model turns and cache-hits the tool calls on retry with no rework, no re-billing. - Tools as first-class Flyte actions: each tool runs in its own container with its own resources and caching, and fans out in parallel. - Observability: a per-run timeline (assistant turns, tool calls/results, token-usage summary) rendered into the task report. - Cross-run memory: continue a conversation across separate runs and workers with a shared `memory_key`. - Human-in-the-loop: gate a tool on `flyte.new_condition` -- a durable suspend that survives restarts, for approvals or for a customer sharing details mid-conversation. - Native multi-agent: each SDK's own handoff / sub-agent pattern (OpenAI handoffs, Claude subagents, ADK transfer, Mistral handoffs) runs durably on Flyte. *Attempt 1* *Attempt 2 (after the crash)* --------- Signed-off-by: Samhita Alla

fix(debug): ssh sessions exit 1 on images with a /bin/false passwd shell (Spark) (#1491)

## Problem

SSH-into-task against a Spark task connects and authenticates, but every
session exits 1 with no output — even `ssh flyte-debug true` — and PTY
logins close immediately.

`apache/spark-py`'s `entrypoint.sh` synthesizes a passwd entry for the
anonymous uid with a no-login shell:

```
185:x:185:0:anonymous uid:/opt/spark:/bin/false
```

`SshServer._handle_session` seeds `SHELL` from `pwd.getpwuid(...)`, so
every session exec'd `/bin/false -c <cmd>`.

## Fix

`_is_login_shell()` rejects `false` / `nologin` / `true` (and
non-executable paths); the passwd shell is only used when it passes,
otherwise fall back to `bash`, then `sh`.

## Verification

- Reproduced on dogfood-1 (real Spark driver pod `<run>-a0-0-driver`):
before the fix `ssh flyte-debug 'echo CONNECTED; id'` → exit 1, nothing
printed. With the fixed wheel baked into the image: prints `CONNECTED`,
`uid=185(185)`, `SHELL=/usr/bin/bash`, lands in the code dir; `ssh -tt`
PTY session works.
- Unit test for `_is_login_shell` in `tests/flyte/test_ssh_debug.py`;
file passes, ruff clean.
- `examples/plugins/spark_ssh_debug.py` is the repro used (takes an
optional config path).

docs: convert Sphinx field lists in docstrings to Google-style sections

The API-reference generator parses Sphinx field lists, but this SDK has no
Sphinx, so `:param x:` renders verbatim in an IDE tooltip, in `help()`, and
anywhere else a docstring is read as text. Google sections read as prose
everywhere and are the convention the rest of the SDK already uses.

  :param x:            -> Args:, entries indented beneath the header
  :type x: T           -> folded in as "x (T): ..."
  :return: / :returns: -> Returns:
  :rtype: T            -> folded in as "Returns:\n    T: ..."
  :raises E:           -> Raises:

1248 :param, 245 :return, 22 :raises, 3 :rtype and 2 :type fields across 105
files. Entries sit one level under the header and continuation lines one level
further: the parser leaves a section at the first non-empty line back at base
indentation, so renaming the header alone would leave the section unparsed and
every description dropped.

Six malformed fields are repaired on the way, each of which was losing a
parameter outright:

  _context.py       three `:param: name desc` entries, which collapsed onto a
                    single parameter literally named "param"
  _core.py          a bare `:param` with no name and no text, which rendered
                    as a parameter named "param"
  bigquery/task.py  `:param google_application_credentials:` indented one space
                    deeper than its siblings, so it read as a continuation of
                    the entry above it
  _packaging.py     type-first fields (`:param Text identifier:`), whose
  io.py             parameter name came out as "Text identifier"
  lazy_module.py
  pkce.py
  file_handling.py

Verified by running the generator's own docstring parser over every docstring
before and after: extracted parameters 2277 -> 2278 (the bare `:param` is gone
and the malformed names now resolve), return docs 387 -> 393, raises 51 -> 51,
and no description lost anywhere. Prose is unchanged; 21 lines were re-wrapped
where the added indent crossed the 120-column limit.

Docstrings only: every changed file AST-diffs clean against the previous commit
with docstrings normalised to a placeholder.

feat(env): add enable_fuse_mount flag to Environment + serializer injection

Mounting FUSE inside a task container needs three things on the pod:
- the /dev/fuse character device mounted in via hostPath
- the primary container marked privileged with CAP_SYS_ADMIN
- volume_mount the device into the primary container

Previously, plugins shipping FUSE-backed types (flyteplugins-union's
Volume) carried a `volume_pod_template()` helper that built this by
hand, forcing every consumer to wire it explicitly:

    env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(name=..., pod_template=volume_pod_template(), ...)

That's both repetitive and conflicts with user-supplied pod_templates
(can't merge two PodTemplates cleanly). Move the capability into the
SDK as a single declarative flag:

    env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(name=..., enable_fuse_mount=True, ...)

Implementation:

* `enable_fuse_mount: bool = False` on `Environment` (base class), so
  both `TaskEnvironment` and `AppEnvironment` inherit it.
* Propagated to `TaskTemplate` via `TaskEnvironment.task()`.
* New `pod_template_with_fuse_mount(pt)` helper in `flyte._pod` that
  takes any user-supplied PodTemplate (including None) and returns a
  copy with the FUSE bits merged in. Idempotent on repeated apply;
  preserves existing volumes, sidecars, and security_context fields.
* Injected at serialization time in `task_serde.py` and `app_serde.py`
  via `_resolve_pod_template(task)` — string/named PodTemplates emit a
  warning (server-side resolved, can't merge) and fall through.

Examples ported: bench.py, volume_example.py, volume_cold_fork.py now
use `flyte.TaskEnvironment(enable_fuse_mount=True, image=with_volume_deps(...))`
instead of the explicit volume_pod_template plumbing.

artifacts: the declaration protocol returns Metadata | None

The protocol annotated `get_artifact_metadata() -> Metadata` while its own
docstring said None means "publish nothing", `convert.py` and
`Artifact.create` both branch on `is not None`, and the reference implementer
(flyteplugins-union's Volume) returns None whenever a volume has no declared
artifact identity. So every correct implementation contradicted the signature,
and a type checker would have flagged the one real user of this protocol.

Now `Optional[Metadata]`, with the reason in the docstring: None is a normal
answer, not an error -- a type participates while a given instance declares
nothing. `ArtifactWrapper.get_artifact_metadata` keeps the narrower `Metadata`,
since a wrapper is only ever built around metadata and never returns None.

Two follow-ons:

  * `_declares_artifact` was typed `-> Any`, which hid the question. It is now
    `Optional[Callable[[], Optional[Metadata]]]`, so callers see at the call
    site that the getter can answer None.
  * dropped the `not isinstance(obj, type)` guard still duplicated at the
    `ensure_artifactable` call site -- the helper rejects classes itself now,
    and the point of moving it there was to have one answer rather than two.

Behaviour unchanged; the None path was already covered by
`test_none_metadata_not_declared_and_flag_unset`. `ty check` clean,
`make check-docstrings` clean (523 files), ruff check and format clean,
136 artifact tests pass.

feat(recovery): make action names stable across code changes (#1373)

Action names previously folded in a hash of the full serialized TaskSpec
(code-bundle URI, image, resources), so any code edit renamed every
action and recovery re-ran the whole workflow. Names now fold in only
position, inputs, and per-task code identity (task name + interface hash
+ discovery_version, computed with the auto cache policy even when
caching is disabled), so recovery can reuse completed actions across
code changes while an edited task's own function body still triggers a
re-run. Trace actions hash the traced function body so edited traces
re-execute instead of replaying, and call-sequence counters are keyed by

This pull request refactors and extends the logic for converting CLI
parameter values to Python types in the Flyte CLI, with a focus on
better handling of complex types such as dataclasses, lists, dicts, and
special Flyte IO types (`File`, `Dir`, `DataFrame`). The main
improvements include more robust type unwrapping, recursive conversion
of nested structures, and support for Pydantic models.

Type handling and conversion improvements:
* Introduced `_unwrap_field_type` to recursively resolve underlying
types, especially for handling `Optional`/`Union` types, ensuring
correct type conversion throughout the code.
* Refactored blob parameter conversion: replaced
`_make_string_blob_converter` with `_convert_blob_value`, which now
supports direct conversion of `File`, `Dir`, and `DataFrame` objects,
and integrates with Pydantic models.
* Added `_convert_blob_collection_elements` and
`_convert_blob_fields_in_value` to recursively convert elements in
lists, dicts, and dataclasses, ensuring nested structures are properly
handled.

Dataclass and collection instantiation:
* Implemented `_instantiate_dataclass` to recursively construct
dataclass instances from dictionaries, including handling of nested
dataclasses in lists and dicts.
* Updated the main `convert` method to use the new recursive conversion
and instantiation logic for lists, dicts, and dataclasses, improving
correctness and flexibility for complex parameter types.

Other improvements:
* Added import of `DataFrame` from `flyte.io` to support new conversion
logic.

These changes make parameter parsing more robust and extensible,
especially for workflows using complex/nested types and Flyte-specific
IO objects.

runtime: start downloading the inputs while the task module imports

load_inputs ran only after the controller was created and the task module
imported, and on a fresh pod it paid the object store's first-use cost
(store construction, credentials, connection) on top of the download:
0.22s measured in a task pod for a 9 KB inputs.pb, 0.33s from a laptop-ish
host. The runtime now starts the download on a background thread as soon
as storage is configured (prefetch_inputs), and load_inputs takes the
result, falling back to downloading if the prefetch failed. max_bytes is
still enforced.

Measured on the agent-workspace task (import its module, then load its real
inputs, 10 alternating fresh processes): min 0.941s -> 0.889s, median
1.047s -> 1.008s; the prefetch completes before the import does. The
saving is bounded by obstore's from_url holding the GIL (~0.1s, CPU).

fix: run/serve a file whose absolute path is outside the current directory

`flyte run /abs/path/task.py` and `flyte serve /abs/path/app.py` fail whenever the
path is not under the current directory:

    Error invoking command: '/abs/path/task.py' is not in the subpath of '/home/me'

`TaskPerFileGroup.__init__` and `AppPerFileGroup.__init__` shorten an absolute
filename for display with a bare `filename.relative_to(Path.cwd())`, which raises
`ValueError` for any path that has no relative spelling under the cwd.

The listing half of the same feature already gets this right: `FileGroup.files`
guards the identical conversion with `is_relative_to` and deliberately keeps
absolute paths for files it cannot spell relatively. So the two halves disagree,
and `flyte run <dir-outside-cwd>` walks straight into it -- `files` hands the
group an absolute path by design, and the group then rejects it.

Hoist that guarded conversion into `common.relative_to_cwd` and use it at all
three sites. The shortening was only ever cosmetic: `ObjectsPerFileGroup.objs`
loads the module through `spec_from_file_location(..., self.filename)` and
`os.path.abspath`, both of which take an absolute path, and `_module.py` already
catches the `ValueError` when a file is not under the source dir.

Repro'd end to end before and after on all three entry points (`flyte run FILE`,
`flyte run DIR`, `flyte serve FILE`). A relative `../` path was never affected --
`is_absolute()` is false, so the branch never ran -- and that stays true.

Not Sentry-evidenced: `InvokeBaseMixin.invoke` converts the `ValueError` into a
`click.ClickException`, which `_sentry._is_user_error` filters, so the crash
never reaches Sentry even though the command is unusable. Same standing as #1537.

Of the seven tests, the two `*_accepts_a_path_outside_the_current_directory` ones
fail on unpatched code with the exact production `ValueError`; the other five are
regression guards that pass on both sides by design, pinning the behaviour this
change must not alter (in-cwd paths still shorten, relative paths still pass
through, and `FileGroup` still lists outside paths as absolute).

rs_controller: support condition actions and decoupled start/wait

The Rust SDK (flyte-sdk-rs) consumes this crate as an rlib and needs to wait
on condition (signal) actions. The wire protocol and the backend are already
in place -- flyteidl2 generates ConditionAction, Action.spec::Condition,
ActionUpdate.value and ActionPhase::Paused -- but this crate models only Task
and Trace and discards ActionUpdate.value, so a signalled value never reaches
a caller. All changes here are additive; task and trace behavior is unchanged.

action.rs
- ActionType::Condition, plus Action.condition and Action.condition_output.
- Action::from_condition, mirroring from_trace's bytes convention. Phase is
  Unspecified rather than Succeeded: a trace is recorded after the fact, but a
  condition is launched and resolved later, and a terminal phase at birth would
  fire completion before any value arrived.
- merge_update now captures ActionUpdate.value. Un-gated on action type,
  because a cache entry created by new_from_update is typed Task until a later
  submit repairs it; gating would drop the value of an already-signalled
  condition on a retry.
- new_from_update captures the value too, for when the watch stream delivers an
  update before the local submit registers the action.
- merge_from_submit adopts action_type and the type-specific spec. Without
  this, a condition whose update arrived first would stay typed Task with no
  spec, and launch_task would find nothing to enqueue.
- is_action_successful() treats Recovered as success-equivalent, so callers stop
  either testing phase == Succeeded (which mistreats a recovered action) or
  inverting Failed (which also swallows Aborted and TimedOut). is_action_paused()
  names the not-terminal condition wait. Both exposed to Python as is_successful
  / is_paused, alongside condition_output_bytes.

core.rs
- Condition arms in build_actions_spec and launch_task's spec check. The legacy
  QueueService arm returns a clear error instead: the backend has no condition
  support there, so an enqueue would be silently dropped.
- submit_action is split into start_action (enqueue, return) and
  wait_for_action (await terminal), with submit_action as their composition.
  This is what allows a condition to be created early -- so it is visible and
  its webhook fires -- and awaited later, possibly elsewhere in the task. It
  mirrors the pure-Python controller's start/wait split.
- The trace wait bound is now an explicit match over action type rather than an
  equality test, so a future action type has to choose its policy. Conditions
  take the unbounded wait deliberately: they are bounded server-side by
  ConditionAction.timeout, which arrives as a TIMED_OUT update.

informer.rs
- Completion receivers are parked by action name (completion_waiters) so a wait
  can be claimed by a caller that did not submit the action; previously the
  receiver lived only on submit_action's stack. A oneshot send buffers, so a
  completion that fires before the receiver is claimed is not lost.
- The completion channel is only registered on first submit, so resubmitting an
  action no longer orphans an existing waiter.

Adds the crate's first tests that run without a live control plane (the
existing informer test needs one on localhost:8090): seven cases covering value
capture on both paths, the early-update ordering repair, Recovered as terminal
and successful, and which phases keep a waiter waiting.

fix: wrap any user-module import exception as ModuleLoadError (#1168)

## Problem

User modules can raise arbitrary third-party exceptions at **import
time** that don't inherit from `RuntimeError` / `ImportError` / etc. The
clearest example: `google.api_core.exceptions.RetryError` (parent:
`Exception`) is raised when a user's module-top-level code calls Google
Secret Manager and gcloud credentials have expired. The SDK's import
loop only catches a narrow tuple — `(ImportError, SyntaxError,
NameError, AttributeError, TypeError, ValueError, KeyError,
RuntimeError)` — so anything else escapes and lands in Sentry as if it
were an SDK bug.

PRs #1094 / #1134 / #1146 widened that tuple incrementally. Time to
finish the job: anything raised inside
`importlib.import_module(<user-module>)` is, by definition, an error in
the user's code or its third-party imports.

## Fix

Widen both `except` clauses in `src/flyte/_utils/module_loader.py`
(file-path branch and directory branch) from the explicit tuple to plain
`except Exception`. Wrap as `flyte.errors.ModuleLoadError` (a
`RuntimeUserError` already filtered by
`flyte/_sentry.py:_is_user_error`) so deploy surfaces an actionable
error and Sentry stops receiving user import-time crashes.

## Closes

- [FLYTE-SDK-39](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/FLYTE-SDK-39/) —
`google.api_core.exceptions.RetryError: Timeout of 60.0s exceeded`
raised from the user's `gsm_secrets.set_secrets_as_dict_gcp_flyte`
during user-module import (expired gcloud creds — `gcloud auth
application-default login`).

`fixes FLYTE-SDK-39`

## Tests

- Added a test that a user module raising a non-RuntimeError `Exception`
subclass at import time is captured as a load failure (or re-raised as
`ModuleLoadError` for the file-path branch).

Send the resolved artifact version for artifact-bound app parameters (#1400)

> [!NOTE]
> **Unblocked.** flyteorg/flyte#7808 is merged and shipped in
**`flyteidl2` 2.0.40**, which this PR now pins. The skip guard that let
the assertion test pass silently against older releases has been
removed, so the full suite runs unconditionally.

## Why are the changes needed?

An app parameter bound to an `ArtifactValue` was sent to the control
plane as a **plain storage path**.

Materializing an `ArtifactValue` collapses it to the `File` or `Dir` the
artifact stores, which drops the artifact identity. So a deployed app
recorded only *"some blob at this path"* — nothing tied it back to the
artifact it came from, and nothing could answer "which apps consume this
artifact?"

This is sharpest when the user pins no version:

```python
Parameter("model", ArtifactValue(name="my-model"))   # no version
```

`materialize()` resolves this to whatever is latest **at deploy time**.
That is the correct resolution semantic, but it was then thrown away —
so there was no record of which version the app actually got, and the
app spec described a reference that had already moved on.

## What changes were proposed in this pull request?

**1. `ArtifactValue` remembers what it resolved to.**

`materialize()` now records the resolved artifact on a `PrivateAttr`,
exposed read-only as `resolved_version_id`. It is `None` before
materialization. This reuses the existing `Artifact.artifact_version_id`
property, the same one `_run.py` already uses for run inputs.

**2. `translate_parameters` sends it as `artifact_id`.**

Parameters with a resolved artifact are sent as an artifact reference
rather than the path they materialized to. The ids are collected from
the **declared** parameters, not the materialized ones — materialization
is precisely what discards the identity, so reading the materialized
list back would find nothing.

**3. Drive-by correctness fix.**

`_materialize_parameters_with_delayed_values` awaited the delayed value
a second time after already resolving it:

```python
value = await param.value.get()        # resolve #1, used only for the assert
assert isinstance(value, (...))
_parameters.append(replace(param, value=await param.value.get()))   # resolve #2
```

`_DelayedValue.get()` is not cached — it calls `materialize()` every
time — so every delayed value was resolved **twice**, and an unpinned
artifact could pick up two *different* versions across the two calls.

This is load-bearing for the change above, not just tidiness: the second
resolution would overwrite `resolved_version_id` with a version
different from the value actually sent, so the app would report lineage
against a version it was not running.

## How was this patch tested?

```
$ pytest tests/flyte/app/runtime/test_app_serde.py tests/user_api_apps/test_artifact_value.py
61 passed
```

Nothing skipped — this is against the real released `flyteidl2==2.0.40`.

Added coverage:
- `test_materialize_records_resolved_version_id` — the resolved version
is captured, including the unpinned case where it is only known after
resolution.
- `test_translate_parameters_sends_artifact_id_instead_of_path` — an
artifact-bound parameter serializes to `artifact_id`, not
`string_value`.
- `test_translate_parameters_without_artifact_ids_is_unchanged` —
non-artifact parameters are untouched, guarding the existing path.

```python
import asyncio
import typing
from pathlib import Path

from distributed import Client
from flyteplugins.dask import Dask, Scheduler, WorkerGroup

    .with_env_vars({"UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE": "0"})
    .with_workdir("/root")
    .with_apt_packages("wget")
    .with_pip_packages("dask[distributed]")
    .with_source_folder(Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent / "plugins/dask", "./dask")
    .with_env_vars({"PYTHONPATH": "./dask/src:${PYTHONPATH}", "hello": "world2"})
)

dask_config = Dask(
    scheduler=Scheduler(resources=Resources(cpu="1", memory="1Gi")),
    workers=WorkerGroup(number_of_workers=4, resources=Resources(cpu="1", memory="1Gi")),
)

task_env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(
    name="hello_dask", resources=Resources(cpu=(1, 2), memory=("400Mi", "1000Mi")), image=image
)
dask_env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(
    name="dask_env",
    plugin_config=dask_config,
    image=image,
    resources=Resources(cpu="1", memory="1Gi"),
)

@task_env.task()
async def hello_dask():
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    print("Hello from the Dask task!")

@dask_env.task
async def hello_dask_nested(n: int = 3) -> typing.List[int]:
    print("running dask task")
    t = asyncio.create_task(hello_dask())
    client = Client()
    futures = client.map(lambda x: x + 1, range(n))
    res = client.gather(futures)
    await t
    return res

if __name__ == "__main__":
    flyte.init_from_config("../../config.yaml")
    run = flyte.run(hello_dask_nested, n=3)
    print("run name:", run.name)
    print("run url:", run.url)
    run.wait(run)

    action_details = flyte.remote.ActionDetails.get(run_name=run.name, name="a0")
    for log in action_details.pb2.attempts[-1].log_info:
        print(f"{log.name}: {log.uri}")
```

fix(runtime): surface load-time errors in task UI instead of empty message

A task that fails while *loading* -- e.g. a top-level `ModuleNotFoundError`
because a dependency is in the local env but missing from the image -- crashes
in `_download_and_load_task`, which runs before the `contextual_run` wrapper
that writes the error document (error.pb). With no error.pb, the backend has
nothing to display, so the task UI shows only an empty:

    [primary] terminated with exit code (1). Reason [Error]. Message:
    .

and the real ModuleNotFoundError (with the diagnostics load_task already
builds) is buried at the very bottom of the task logs.

Wrap the load step in `load_and_run_task`: on failure, convert the exception to
an error document and upload_error() it to the task's output path before
re-raising, so the actual reason shows up in the UI's Message field. The
re-raise preserves the non-zero exit.

Example: add async training with periodic eval and early stopping example

Add examples/ml/async_train_eval.py demonstrating a common ML pattern
where a long-running training task runs concurrently with periodic
evaluation rounds that can trigger early stopping on convergence.

How it works:
- A training task runs in the background via asyncio.create_task,
  writing JSON checkpoints (epoch + loss) to a shared File location
  after each epoch, and returning the final checkpoint on completion.
- The orchestrator loops through evaluation rounds, using
  flyte.durable.sleep.aio (crash-resilient) between each round. The
  sleep is raced against the training task via asyncio.wait so that
  training completion or failure is detected immediately.
- Each eval round reads the latest checkpoint and launches a batch
  inference task that checks if loss is below a convergence threshold.
- On convergence: training is cancelled and the pipeline returns early.
- On training failure: any in-progress eval is cancelled and the
  exception propagates.
- On training completion: a final eval is run against the checkpoint
  returned by the training task.

All tuning knobs (epochs, epoch duration, convergence threshold, eval
interval, max eval rounds) are exposed as parameters with defaults.

fix: don't report a disk quota as an SDK crash (FLYTE-SDK-8D) (#1578)

## What

Filter `OSError(EDQUOT)` — "Disk quota exceeded" — out of Sentry,
alongside the `ENOSPC` that has been filtered since FLYTE-SDK-32.

## Why

```
OSError: [Errno 122] Disk quota exceeded
  culprit: tarfile in copyfileobj
  release: 2.7.2
```

`create_bundle` writes the code-bundle tarball to local disk during
`flyte deploy`. On a filesystem that rations space **per user** rather
than running out of it globally, that write fails with `EDQUOT` instead
of `ENOSPC` — the usual shape on NFS, and on the shared or managed home
directories common in HPC and university clusters.

It is the same condition and the same remedy as disk-full: free some
space, or get the quota raised. Neither is something the SDK can do
anything about, and `ENOSPC` was filtered on exactly that reasoning. The
only reason `EDQUOT` still reports is that it is a different number.

## The change

```python
_USER_ENVIRONMENT_OSERROR_ERRNOS: frozenset[int] = frozenset(
    code for code in (errno.ENOSPC, getattr(errno, "EDQUOT", None)) if code is not None
)
```

The guarded lookup is not decoration. `EDQUOT` does not exist on Windows
— CPython's `errnomodule.c` defines these constants under `#ifdef` — so
a direct `errno.EDQUOT` would raise `AttributeError` at **import** of
`flyte._sentry` there, which would be a considerably worse bug than the
one being fixed. And where it does exist its value is not portable: 122
on Linux, 69 on macOS and the BSDs. Both sides of the comparison come
from the same machine, so looking it up is also the only correct way to
match.

## Why only this errno

Tested the predicate across the whole corpus first: 73 unresolved issues
contain exactly four `OSError`-family events, with errnos 98
(`EADDRINUSE`, PKCE bind — covered by #1199), 2 (`FileNotFoundError`,
FLYTE-SDK-8B), no-errno (`libgomp.so.1` missing in a user image), and
this one. Adding `EDQUOT` silences FLYTE-SDK-8D and nothing else.

The neighbouring errnos are deliberately left out, and the docstring
says why: `EACCES`, `EPERM` and `EROFS` can equally mean the SDK wrote
somewhere it should not have, and `EMFILE` / `ENFILE` would hide a
file-descriptor leak of our own.

## Tests

Three tests in `tests/flyte/test_sentry.py`: the direct `EDQUOT`, the
same through a `RuntimeSystemError` cause chain (how the bundle writer
wraps it), and a guard that the errno set still contains `ENOSPC`, holds
only ints, and excludes `EACCES` / `EPERM` / `EMFILE` — which also pins
the Windows-safe construction.

`tests/flyte/test_sentry.py`: 82 passed. `make fmt`, `ruff check`,
`mypy`, `ty check` and `make check-docstrings` all clean.

fix(image): always install the local wheel for with_local_v2()

PythonWheelHandler emitted the force-install step (--no-deps --no-index
--reinstall) *before* the dependency-resolution step. When the local
wheel can't be fully resolved during the dependency step -- e.g. a dev
wheel pins a dependency version that isn't published yet -- uv backtracks
and installs the stable PyPI release instead, silently swapping a
with_local_v2() build back to the released package.

Swap the order so the dependency step runs first and the force-install
step runs last. --no-index + --reinstall then guarantees the exact local
wheel is the final state, regardless of what the resolver picks for the
package itself. Dependencies still come from the index, and packages not
on PyPI (local plugin wheels) keep resolving via --find-links /dist.

Add a unit test asserting the force-install step is emitted after the
dependency step.

fix(image): only default to the localhost registry for local builds

Images were given localhost:30000 (flyte devbox's registry) when they were
defined, whenever the endpoint named localhost. A remote builder reached
through a localhost endpoint (unibox, a port-forward to a cluster) was then
sent localhost:30000/<name>, and the backend prefixed its own repository:
localhost:30000/onebox/localhost:30000/<name>: invalid reference format.
For a remote build localhost is the build pod, not this machine, anyway.

Images now get only a configured registry when they are defined
(_get_configured_registry). The localhost fallback stays in
_get_push_registry, which the build applies for local builds only; a
missing builder now resolves to "local" there, as _get_builder does, so
devbox's local builds keep pushing to localhost:30000.

Add InferencePipeline: 3-stage async pipeline for batch inference

InferencePipeline wires together preprocessing, batched GPU inference
(via DynamicBatcher), and postprocessing with proper thread pool dispatch
and backpressure — so users only define three functions:

  preprocess_fn  (per-item, sync or async, optional executor)
  inference_fn   (batched, async — the DynamicBatcher process_fn)
  postprocess_fn (per-item, receives original input + result)

Key design decisions:
- No new abstraction for batching — reuses DynamicBatcher internally
- Bounded asyncio.Queue between preprocess and batcher for backpressure
- Supports both sync and async stage functions (auto-detected)
- Sync stages can be dispatched to a ThreadPoolExecutor
- postprocess_fn receives the original raw item alongside the inference
  result so it has full context (filename, metadata, etc.)
- Streaming via async generator (run) or batch collect (run_all)
- Exposes underlying batcher + stats for monitoring/tuning

This pattern emerged from the embed_wikipedia and multimodal-retrieval
examples, where every GPU inference use case independently wired the
same load → preprocess → batch-infer → postprocess pipeline. The
abstraction eliminates that boilerplate while keeping full control over
DynamicBatcher tuning knobs (cost budgeting, batch size, timeouts).

feat: Apple Silicon accelerator: run devbox tasks and apps on the Mac's GPU (gpu="AppleSilicon") (#1685)

## Why

A devbox container on a Mac is a Linux VM. Linux has no Metal, so code
in a devbox task or app could never use the Apple Silicon GPU:
`torch.device("mps")` and MLX don't exist there.

With this PR, `flyte.Resources(gpu="AppleSilicon")` runs the workload
**natively on the Mac**. Your code uses the GPU the way `gpu="A100:1"`
code uses CUDA on a cluster: `torch.device("mps")`, `mlx`, and your own
models.

Depends on flyteorg/flyte#8181, which adds the IDL and backend: it
routes `APPLE_SILICON` pods to the host bridge and rejects them on
backends without one. The console change is unionai-oss/flyte2-ui#42.

## What

- **API**:
- `gpu="AppleSilicon"` (`"AppleSilicon:1"` is also accepted) or the
equivalent `gpu=flyte.APPLE_SILICON()`, with the `APPLE_SILICON` device
class. It is serialized by its wire value, so it works with the current
`flyteidl2` release.
  - The Mac's packages are the image's pip packages.
  - `AppleSilicon:2` is rejected, since the Mac has one GPU.
- **One flag**: `flyte start devbox --apple-silicon`. This runs workload
code outside any sandbox, so it is opt-in.
- The flag starts the host bridge and publishes every devbox port on
`127.0.0.1` only, so nothing else on the network can submit workloads.
- Without it, Apple Silicon workloads fail up front with
`APPLE_SILICON_NOT_AVAILABLE`, and the message says how to fix it.
- Resuming a paused Apple Silicon devbox (`flyte start devbox`) restarts
its bridge without the flag. Host runs are listed in `flyte get devbox`,
and `flyte delete devbox` stops the bridge.
- **Host bridge** (`flyte._internal.apple_silicon`): listens on
127.0.0.1 only and accepts a per-workload HMAC token
(`as1.<workload>.<mac>`) minted by the backend.
- The container's `a0`/`fserve` entrypoint hands its own invocation to
the bridge.
- The bridge runs the invocation in a cached `uv` environment built for
macOS, with in-cluster endpoints rewritten to the devbox's host ports.
State lives in `~/.flyte/apple-silicon`.
- The container streams the host process's log, mirrors its exit code,
forwards aborts, and for apps forwards its port.
- **Container mode (opt-out)**:
`env_vars={"FLYTE_APPLE_SILICON_EXECUTION": "container"}` keeps the
workload in its container. It calls a host-side `mlx_lm.server` (choose
the model with `FLYTE_APPLE_SILICON_MODEL`) through an injected
`OPENAI_BASE_URL`. `pip install 'flyte[apple-silicon]'` installs mlx-lm;
without it the bridge falls back to `uvx`.
- **Named errors** instead of a silent CPU fallback, all with
`APPLE_SILICON_*` codes: `AppleSiliconNotAvailableError`,
`AppleSiliconHostExecFailedError`, `AppleSiliconDaemonStartFailedError`,
`AppleSiliconDaemonOOMError`, `AppleSiliconModelNotFoundError`,
`AppleSiliconBridgeUnreachableError`. Setup failures that would fail the
same way again aren't retried.
- **Pods and revisions:** each request names its pod. Replicas of an app
revision share one host process, torn down when the last pod lets go; a
rollout's new revision gets its own (the backend scopes app workload ids
per spec revision). A task's run belongs to the pod that started it.
- **Examples**:
- `examples/accelerators/apple_silicon_train.py`: a task that trains a
PyTorch CNN on `mps` and returns its metrics and weights.
- `examples/accelerators/apple_silicon_serve.py`: an `AppEnvironment`
that loads a Hugging Face model onto `mps` and serves it.
- `examples/accelerators/apple_silicon_proof/`: a proof task and app,
plus a runbook (with checks you can run yourself and a negative control)
showing the code ran on the Apple GPU.
- `examples/accelerators/apple_silicon_fanout.py`: fans out N GPU tasks
at once and measures how they share the one GPU.

## Testing

- `tests/flyte/apple_silicon`: the bridge, the daemon supervisor, and
host execution end to end with stand-in entrypoints. They cover:
- env forwarding and rewrites, exit codes, and the app port forward,
plus a regression test that the port stays closed until the host app
listens;
- tokens, named errors, `flyte.APPLE_SILICON()`, and serialization of
the default and opt-out modes;
- the `--apple-silicon` flag, why it can't be enabled on a given host,
and resuming a paused devbox (including refusing one whose ports are
reachable from the network).
- With `tests/user_api` and `tests/cli/test_devbox.py`, 905 tests pass.
`make mypy`, `make check-docstrings`, `ruff format --check` and `ruff
check` are clean.
- Live, on an M5 Max devbox built from flyteorg/flyte#8181:
- `apple_silicon_train.py` trained on `mps:0` (3 epochs, 98.4–98.9% test
accuracy, about 6–7 s), and the weights uploaded to the devbox object
store.
- A `gpu=flyte.APPLE_SILICON()` task ran as Darwin arm64 with `mps`
available.
  - `apple_silicon_serve.py` served on `mps:0`, fp16, at 84–97 tokens/s.
- The proof passed all five checks as a task and as an app: Darwin
arm64; Apple M5 Max (Metal, 40 cores); 13.4 vs 1.6 TFLOPS on `mps` vs
CPU; 36.5 vs 1.6 on MLX; 91–95% GPU utilization vs 24–30% idle.
- Container mode: the task ran in Linux and got its answer from the
host's `mlx_lm.server`.
- Started without `--apple-silicon`, the devbox failed the task with
`APPLE_SILICON_NOT_AVAILABLE`. Pausing an Apple Silicon devbox and
resuming it without the flag brought the bridge back.

## Review fixes (latest push)

A full review of the stack found these; each now has a regression test
in `tests/flyte/apple_silicon/test_robustness.py`:

- App revisions and replicas no longer share (and tear down) one host
process; a second pod can't take over a task's run.
- `flyte delete/stop devbox` only signals a process confirmed to be the
bridge, so a stale pid file can't kill an unrelated process (or crash on
a root-owned pid).
- FastAPI, webhook and fixed-port command apps work on the host (the
host prefers the app's declared port; the built-in servers use
`get_port()`).
- A host process that fails to launch fails the workload instead of
hanging; process groups are always cleaned up; shutdown is parallel.
- Logs are drained to the last line, never split mid-line, and start
fresh per run.
- Only Kubernetes-injected service variables are dropped (not the user's
`DB_PORT`); container-only paths and CUDA settings stay behind;
requirements files (`-r`, continuation lines), uv/poetry/PEP 723
dependencies and pip index options carry over.
- `--apple-silicon` requires `uv`; `--gpu` can't be combined with it; a
failed start stops the bridge; resuming checks the devbox's secret still
matches; an empty secret is never trusted.
- `flyte get devbox` escapes workload text and no longer creates state;
`RemoteTask.override` keeps the Apple Silicon settings.

Re-verified end to end on the M5 Max devbox: training, the proof task,
the HF app, a 4-way fan-out, a FastAPI app, an app redeploy (old
revision torn down, new one serving, no pod restarts), container mode,
and pause/resume.

## Known limits

- **A backend older than flyteorg/flyte#8181 can't reject Apple Silicon
workloads.** It treats `APPLE_SILICON` as an NVIDIA GPU, and the pod
stays Pending. This happens with the published `flyte-devbox` image
until #8181 ships, so use a devbox image built from it (`--image`).
- Only Python packages carry over to the Mac (no apt packages, other
image contents, local wheels or a project's own code), and k8s-mounted
secrets aren't available there.
- Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps the network out, not other software on the
Mac: the devbox API is unauthenticated.
- Dev mode (`FLYTE_DEV`) isn't wired up.
- Re-deploying an app with an unchanged spec can leave `flyte.serve`
waiting after "Deployed App". This is pre-existing and not specific to
Apple Silicon.
- When a run fails before it starts, `flyte run`'s "failed in state"
line shows an empty message, though `flyte get run` has the full one.
This is pre-existing.

docs: backtick literals that were rendering as prose, and check for it (#1487)

Flag names, values and file names in help text and docstrings were
written three ways — `'local'`, `--recursive`, and `` `local` `` — and
only the third renders as monospace.

The CLI reference shows the effect inside a single table row: the
**Option** column is monospaced and the **Description** column beside it
is not, for the same flag.

## This is drift, not a distinction

```
CLI help strings:  31 backticked spans   vs   52 single-quoted tokens
help strings using both styles:  0
```

Zero mixing means no author ever drew a considered line — each picked a
style and kept to it. Backticks were already the majority.

## What changed

**51 literals across 17 files.** Quoted tokens and phrases become code
spans, and so do bare `--flags`:

```diff
- help="MCP transport. 'stdio' speaks JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout and ignores --port/--mcp-mount-path."
+ help="MCP transport. `stdio` speaks JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout and ignores `--port`/`--mcp-mount-path`."

- help="Image builder to use for building images. Defaults to 'local'."
+ help="Image builder to use for building images. Defaults to `local`."
```

Both halves of `--port`/`--mcp-mount-path`, and **every** item of
*"Accepts ISO dates, `now`, `today`, or `now - 1 day`"* — a rule that
converted only single words would have left that sentence inconsistent
**with itself**, which is worse than the uniform inconsistency it
replaces.

## Deliberately out of scope

Each measured rather than assumed:

feat(slack): interactivity, slash commands, notify helpers, and hitl-backed approvals (#1540)

## Why

Internal Slack agents like
[Cally](https://github.com/unionai/unionai-agents/tree/main/cally) and
[Nodey](https://github.com/unionai/unionai-agents/tree/main/nodey) run
hand-rolled slack_bolt servers and hand-rolled outbound API calls. This
PR closes the gaps that keep them off the plugin, in three layers.

## 1. Receive everything Slack sends (`_provider.py`)

The provider only parsed Events API JSON; interactivity payloads (Block
Kit buttons, shortcuts, modals) and slash commands arrive form-encoded
and 400'd. Now:

- a block action registers as `block_actions.<action_id>` (Cally's
`send_to_customer`), a shortcut as its `callback_id`, a slash command as
`command.<name>` (Nodey's `/hi-nodey`)
- full Slack JSON (`actions`, `container`, `message`, `response_url`)
rides in `event.payload`
- interactions dedupe per click (`action_ts`), redeliveries are no-ops;
commands key on `trigger_id`
- `handshake()` answers the `ssl_check` probe; `verify()` unchanged (v0
HMAC signs raw bytes for all three shapes)
- new `events.Interaction` / `events.Command` constants; runnable
`examples/slack_interactions.py` with `--local` signed replay

## 2. Send messages (`notify`)

Nodey ships a fifty-line `send_notification` task of raw `requests`;
Cally re-implements posting per handler. `notify` provides
`post`/`update`/`delete` (bot token via `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`),
`respond(response_url)` which needs **no token** (the zero-setup way for
a launched task to answer the click that launched it), and a deployable
`notify.env` + `send` task so only one environment holds the token.

## 3. Approvals on core `new_condition` (`approval`)

The pattern both agents build by hand — post buttons, pause, resume on
click — becomes:

```python
decision = await approval.request.aio("C0DEPLOYS", "Deploy release-42 to prod?")   # in a task
approval.register(app_env)                                                        # in the webhook app
```

`request` parks the run on a core `flyte.new_condition`; the clicked
button carries the run, action, and condition names, so the webhook
handler resolves it with `flyte.remote.Condition.get(...).signal(...)` —
no configuration on the app side — then swaps the buttons for a
"*approve* — decided by @who" line. Same mechanism the GitHub plugin's
review gate uses. Because it's an ordinary condition, the prompt is
**also** answerable from the Flyte UI, so an approval nobody clicks in
Slack is never stuck, and `timeout=` is the core contract
(`ConditionTimedoutError`). No extra install needed.

## Ergonomics

- **`on_event(..., action=...)`** (core `_app.py`): the user-defined
half of an event — a button's `action_id`, a command's name — is your
vocabulary, not Slack's, so no constant can spell it.
`on_event(events.Interaction.BLOCK_ACTIONS, action="approve_deploy")`
and `on_event(events.Command, action="/deploy")` now compose it; an
`EventType` class means its `ANY`, and a leading `/` is dropped. Raw
qualified strings still work.
- **Typed payload views** (`payloads`): nested TypedDicts over
`event.payload` so
`payloads.block_actions(event)["actions"][0]["value"]` autocompletes.
Casts, not validation.
- Handler `event` args annotated `event: WebhookEvent` throughout
examples and docs.

## Validation

- 24 slack tests pass, including the shared provider conformance
harness; 51 core webhook tests pass
- `notify` tested against an `httpx.MockTransport`; the decision handler
against events built by the real parser (including condition lookup args
and the already-signaled/timed-out case)
- end-to-end through `WebhookAppEnvironment`: signed Cally/Nodey-shaped
deliveries dispatch correctly, unsigned refused 401, JSON Events API
path unchanged
- ruff + pre-commit (fmt/mypy/ty/uvlock) clean; the deprecated
`flyteplugins-hitl` plugin is left untouched by this branch

## Notes

Slack expects interactivity/command acks within 3s; the README says to
do nothing slower than `run_once.aio` in handlers. A follow-up worth its
own PR: an early-ack option in the core webhook framework.

Add `flyte backfill <trigger>` for scheduled triggers

Expands a cron or fixed-rate trigger's schedule across a window, shows exactly
which runs it would create, and on approval launches a driver run that creates
them from inside the cluster (so a long backfill does not depend on the client
staying connected, and the work is observable and abortable like any run).

De-duplication is the point of the naming. A backfilled slot is created the way
the scheduler creates a real fire -- addressed by TriggerName, named by the
deterministic slot hash, and marked schedule-sourced -- so a slot that already
ran is recognised and skipped, and re-running the same backfill is a no-op.
`--force` salts the name into a separate namespace to re-run those slots.

The run-name hash mirrors the scheduler's runName() exactly: FNV-1 (not FNV-1a)
64-bit over org:project:domain:task:trigger plus unpadded wall-clock fields,
rendered as unpadded hex. Expected values in tests/backfill/test_naming.py were
generated by running the Go implementation; cron expansion is likewise pinned
against robfig/cron v3, the parser the scheduler uses.

Import build/deploy, the dataframe engine and JSON-schema tooling on first use (#1637)

Every task pod imports `flyte` (and, through plugins, `flyte.io`) before
running user code, and it was paying for machinery a running task never
uses.

## What changes
- **`flyte/__init__`:** `build`, `ImageBuild`, `deploy` and
`build_images` resolve on first use via module `__getattr__` (PEP 562)
instead of importing `_build`/`_deploy` eagerly.
- **`flyte.io`:** `DataFrame` and `PARQUET` load on first use. `File`
and `Dir` don't need the structured-dataset engine. Importing
`DataFrame` still registers its transformer, as before.
- **`TypeEngine.lazy_import_transformers`:** imports the dataframe
engine only if it's already imported (any `DataFrame` annotation does
that), or if pandas or pyarrow is. Those are the only cases where its
handlers can apply.
- **`mashumaro.jsonschema`** (about 85ms) is only needed to describe a
dataclass's schema. `PydanticSchemaPlugin` is built on first use and is
still importable by name.
- **`markdown_it`** is imported where markdown is rendered.

## Measured
Alternating fresh processes on a loaded host; minimum of 8 runs, except
the last row (6):

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `import flyte` | 0.893s | 0.622s |
| `import flyte; import flyteplugins.union.io` | 0.553s | 0.427s |
| Import a real agent-workspace task module and convert its real inputs
| 0.928s | 0.769s |

In a task pod, the runtime's own Stopwatch put `load_task_from_resolver`
at 0.59s for that task. This is the part of it that's flyte's.

## Compatibility
Public names are unchanged. One difference: `from flyte import *` now
resolves the lazy names on demand, which imports `_build`/`_deploy` as

feat(slack): give SlackClient both a sync and an async call form

Wraps the 13 client methods with flyte's @syncify, matching how the SDK
itself exposes Run.listall, flyte.run and flyte.serve. Each method now has
two forms: `client.foo(...)` blocks, `await client.foo.aio(...)` does not.

- Adds __enter__/__exit__ so the blocking form is actually usable. They run
  __aenter__/__aexit__ on syncify's background loop -- the same loop the
  syncified methods run on -- so the httpx.AsyncClient is created and used
  on a single loop.
- Internal self-calls use .aio(). The blocking form would deadlock when
  called from syncify's own loop thread.
- The MCP tool bridge uses .aio(). `await getattr(client, name)(...)` would
  otherwise raise TypeError on the returned value, and would stall the MCP
  server's event loop for the duration of every tool call.
- Tests, examples and READMEs use .aio() on async paths, and document both
  forms plus when not to reach for the blocking one.

The syncified client type-checks clean: mypy resolves methods to
SyncFunction[...] and the error count on the package is unchanged.

fix(webhooks): read the signature header ClickUp and Linear actually send

`ClickUpProvider` looked for `X-Clickup-Signature` and `LinearProvider` for
`X-Linear-Signature`. Neither product sends those. ClickUp signs with
`X-Signature` and Linear with `Linear-Signature`, so `verify` found no header,
returned False, and `WebhookAppEnvironment` raised 401 before `parse` ever ran.
With `require_signature=True` — the default — both integrations rejected every
genuine delivery.

The test suite could not see it. Each plugin's `SAMPLE_DELIVERY` signs with the
same wrong header its `verify` reads, so the conformance round trip verified
against itself and passed. The per-plugin `_parse` helpers also built signature
headers that `parse` ignores entirely, which spread the wrong name without
testing anything.

So each provider now gets a test asserting the literal wire header, which is
the one thing the self-consistent round trip cannot check, and `_parse` no
longer fabricates headers it does not use.

`_CREDENTIAL_HEADERS` in the shared conformance helper needed the new names
too. That set gates the hostile-credential check by header name and `continue`s
on anything unlisted, so a rename silently turned the check off for that
provider rather than failing — the same way the round trip hid the bug itself.
It now asserts that it matched a header.

GitHub (`X-Hub-Signature-256`) and Slack (`X-Slack-Signature`) were verified
correct against their docs and are untouched. Jira's `X-Webhook-Token` is the
plugin's own shared-token stand-in, since Jira Cloud does not sign webhooks.

Refs: https://developer.clickup.com/docs/webhooksignature
Refs: https://linear.app/developers/webhooks

fix(map): abort in-flight child tasks on failure, early exit, and cancellation

`flyte.map` could leave child actions running after a child failed or the
caller was cancelled, keeping the parent run active indefinitely.

- MapAsyncIterator.aclose() now also cleans up the default concurrency=0
  path, and cancelled tasks are awaited so their CancelledError handler can
  abort the remote action.
- `_map` closes its iterator in a `finally`.
- `map.aio()`, sync `flyte.map()`, and `collect()` close their inner
  iterators so early exit and cancellation reach that cleanup.
- syncify's iterate_in_loop / iterate_in_loop_sync close the generator on
  the background loop when the consumer stops, waiting for a cancelled
  in-flight `__anext__` to unwind first.
