feat(plugins): add flyteplugins-nextflow to run Nextflow pipelines on Flyte (#1622)

## Summary

Adds `flyteplugins-nextflow`, which runs a
[Nextflow](https://www.nextflow.io/) pipeline inside a Flyte task. The
whole pipeline becomes one Flyte run, with one child action per Nextflow
task.

The executor itself is [nf-flyte](https://github.com/unionai/nf-flyte),
a Nextflow plugin published to the [Nextflow plugin
registry](https://registry.nextflow.io/plugins/nf-flyte) (version
0.1.0). It submits each Nextflow task as a raw container action, and
Flyte's copilot stages the task's files. This package is the Flyte side:
it builds the image the Nextflow head runs in, and launches Nextflow
with everything nf-flyte needs.

```python
import flyte
from flyte.io import Dir
from flyteplugins.nextflow import nextflow_image, run_nextflow

env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(name="nextflow", image=nextflow_image())

@env.task
async def demo() -> Dir:
    return await run_nextflow("nf-core/demo", revision="1.2.0", profile="test", outdir="results")
```

## What's included

- `nextflow_image()`: an image with a JRE, a pinned Nextflow version
(default `25.10.6`) and nf-flyte (default `0.1.0`, from the registry, or
a local plugin zip for development). `nf-amazon` and `nf-cloudcache` are
installed at build time, not on every run.
- `run_nextflow(...)`, called from any task:
- writes the Nextflow config that loads nf-flyte and sets
`process.executor = 'flyte'`
- passes the current run and action to nf-flyte (`NF_FLYTE_RUN_NAME`,
`NF_FLYTE_PARENT_ACTION`), so task actions are created under the calling
action
- defaults the work directory to `nextflow-work` under the task's raw
data prefix, shared by all attempts of the task, so no bucket setup is
needed
- keeps Nextflow's resume state in the work dir (cloud cache, plus a
session ID derived from the work dir): a retried attempt resumes
automatically, and a fixed `work_dir` with `resume=True` resumes across
runs
- supports `revision`, `profile`, `params` (passed as a params file),
`outdir` (returned as a `Dir`), `config` (a file path or config text),
`report` (Nextflow's report, timeline and DAG rendered into the task's
Flyte report) and `extra_args`
- streams Nextflow's output into the task logs, and raises
`NextflowError` with the end of the output and of `.nextflow.log` on
failure
- forwards SIGTERM to Nextflow on cancellation, so it aborts its running
task actions
- in a local run (`flyte run --local`), leaves out nf-flyte and uses
Nextflow's own executors
- `examples/nf_core_demo.py` and a README

## Design notes

- Nextflow keeps control of retries (`errorStrategy`) and `-resume`;
nf-flyte turns Flyte retries off for task actions.
- Flyte caches task results: nf-flyte gives each task action a cache key
derived from the process script, container, environment, `bin` scripts
and inputs (not the Nextflow session), so a task finished in one run is
reused by the next.
- Process containers need only `bash`. They don't need Flyte, the AWS
CLI or anything else: copilot moves the data.
- The work directory can be on any object store both the head and Flyte
can read (S3, GCS or Azure); the default always is.
- `nextflow_image()` doesn't check that a local plugin zip exists. The
task module is imported again inside the pod, where the zip isn't
present; a missing zip fails the image build instead.

## Known limitation

Pipelines whose tasks produce many or large output files can run copilot
out of memory on Flyte releases up to v2.0.51. The fixes are
flyteorg/flyte#8149 (bounded upload concurrency, merged) and
flyteorg/flyte#8185 (stow bump to stream uploads from disk, open);
they'll be in the next Flyte release. This package doesn't need to
change for them.

## Testing

- Unit tests (`plugins/nextflow/tests`, 19 tests) run `run_nextflow`
against a fake `nextflow` executable. They check the command line, the
generated config, params, env vars, the default `outdir` and `work_dir`,
resume on retry, reports, cancellation and error reporting.
- `nextflow plugin install nf-flyte@0.1.0` on Nextflow 25.10.6 (the
image's install step) installs the plugin from the registry.

fix: surface actionable error when docker is missing for image build (#1064)

## Summary
- `DockerImageBuilder._ensure_buildx_builder` shells out to
`subprocess.run(["docker", "buildx", "version"])` and only catches
`CalledProcessError`. If docker isn't installed at all, the call raises
`FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'docker'`,
which bubbles all the way up to Sentry as an unhandled SDK crash.

user-facing error type the CLI already special-cases) with a message
that tells the user docker isn't on PATH, links the install
instructions, and points at the remote builder as the no-local-docker
escape hatch.

version pin fires only on exactly that version
- `flyte.TriggeredArtifact` sentinel binds the triggering artifact's
value to one task input (the artifact-trigger analogue of
`TriggerTime`); other inputs keep their registered defaults, offloaded
exactly as schedule triggers do today
- Serde emits `TriggerAutomationSpec(TYPE_ARTIFACT,
ArtifactTrigger{artifact_name, version, input_arg})` with the sentinel
key as `input_arg`, validated against the task interface; no kickoff
context key is emitted — the backend fire step (leaseworker plugin)
injects the real literal into the offloaded inputs
- Cross-validation at construction: at most one sentinel, sentinel
requires `OnArtifact`, `TriggerTime` rejected on artifact triggers
- `flyte get trigger` / rich repr render `on artifact: name@version ->
input`
- Runnable example: `examples/triggers/artifact_trigger.py`

**CI will fail on the new serde tests until a flyteidl2 release carries
it and the pin is bumped** — developed against a local wheel build.

fix: sync remote methods, clearer CLI errors, image Python warning, MCP tenant pinning (#1691)

## Summary

A batch of SDK usability fixes.

Several remote methods were plain `async def` while the rest of the
remote API is syncified, so sync code got an un-awaited coroutine back.
They now use a new `syncify_compat` decorator
(`Syncify.awaitable_compat`): a sync call returns the value, `.aio()`
works as usual, and a direct call inside a running loop still returns an
awaitable but warns once per call site. This covers
`Action.details()`/`wait()`, the
`inputs`/`outputs`/`*_literals`/`typed_*` methods on `ActionDetails` and
`RunDetails`, `Artifact.to_python()`/`coerce_to_literal()` and
`Trigger.get_details()`. In-repo async callers now use `.aio()`.

CLI fixes:
- A value like `False` after a boolean flag gets a hint that boolean
inputs are flags.
- Subcommand usage errors are no longer wrapped in "Error invoking
command" and keep the `--help` pointer.
- A root option placed after the subcommand gets an explanation and the
corrected command line.
- `flyte get` tables keep short columns intact on narrow terminals.
- `flyte update trigger` reports "active" or "inactive" instead of
"deactivate".

`Image.from_debian_base()` without `python_version` logs a one-time
warning naming the inferred version (skipped inside task and app
containers). SDK-internal defaults pass the version explicitly, so they
don't warn.

`flyte-mcp` could pick up a project's `.flyte/config.yaml` over
`FLYTECTL_CONFIG` and act on that tenant silently. It now takes
`--config`/`FLYTE_MCP_CONFIG` and `--endpoint`/`FLYTE_MCP_ENDPOINT`,
logs the resolved config and endpoint to stderr at startup, warns when
the config came from the working directory or its repo, and `whoami`
reports `config_file`.

## Compatibility

Code that does `await details.outputs()` and similar keeps working with
a `DeprecationWarning`; direct awaiting will be removed later. In
Jupyter (which runs a loop), calling these without `await` still returns
an awaitable. Type checkers will flag the old `await x.method()` form.

## Tests

New unit tests cover the syncified methods and the deprecated path, the
CLI hints and table layout, the trigger message, the image warning and
`flyte-mcp` config resolution. Format, lint, mypy, ty, docstring and CLI
docs checks pass. `make unit_test`: 6309 passed, 1 failed
(`test_retrieve_degrades_when_keyring_not_installed`, which also fails

jsonl plugin (#728)

This PR adds jsonl (json lines) file and directory types, backed by
`orjson` for fast serialization and optional `zstd` compression.

```bash
pip install flyteplugins-jsonl

# For Arrow RecordBatch support
pip install 'flyteplugins-jsonl[arrow]'
```

### `JsonlFile`

A single JSONL file. Inherits from `flyte.io.File` so it works with
remote storage, upload/download and the Flyte type engine out of the
box.

```python
from flyteplugins.jsonl import JsonlFile

env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(
    image=flyte.Image().from_debian_base().with_pip_packages("flyteplugins-jsonl")
)

# Async read
@env.task
async def process(f: JsonlFile):
    async for record in f.iter_records():
        print(record)

# Async write
@env.task
async def create() -> JsonlFile:
    f = JsonlFile.new_remote("data.jsonl")
    async with f.writer() as w:
        await w.write({"key": "value"})
    return f

# Sync write
@env.task
async def create_sync() -> JsonlFile:
    f = JsonlFile.new_remote("data.jsonl")
    with f.writer_sync() as w:
        w.write({"key": "value"})
    return f
```

### `JsonlDir`

A directory of sharded JSONL files (`part-00000.jsonl`,
`part-00001.jsonl`, etc.). Inherits from `flyte.io.Dir`. Supports
automatic shard rotation on write and transparent cross-shard iteration
on read.

```python
from flyteplugins.jsonl import JsonlDir

# Write with automatic sharding
@env.task
async def create() -> JsonlDir:
    d = JsonlDir.new_remote("output_shards")
    async with d.writer(max_records_per_shard=10_000) as w:
        for i in range(50_000):
            await w.write({"id": i})
    return d

# Read across all shards
@env.task
async def process(d: JsonlDir):
    async for record in d.iter_records():
        print(record)
```

fix: expose ca_cert_file_path and insecure_skip_verify in init_from_api_key (#1438)

## Problem

Users behind corporate TLS-intercepting proxies (MITM proxies that
re-sign traffic with a private corporate CA) get:

```
httpcore.ConnectError: [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate
```

when authenticating via `flyte.init_from_api_key()` and then making any
remote call (the failure surfaces on the OAuth token refresh POST).
`flyte.init()` already supports `insecure_skip_verify` and
`ca_cert_file_path`, but `init_from_api_key` hardcoded
`insecure_skip_verify=False` and exposed neither parameter — so API-key
users had no way to supply a corporate CA bundle.

## Fix

Add `insecure_skip_verify: bool = False` and `ca_cert_file_path: str |
None = None` to `init_from_api_key` and forward them to the underlying
`init.aio(...)` call (`insecure` remains hardcoded to `False`). Defaults
are unchanged, so existing behavior is preserved.

```python
import flyte

flyte.init_from_api_key(ca_cert_file_path="/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt")
```

The docstring notes that if both options are set, `insecure_skip_verify`
takes precedence (matching the behavior of `_resolve_tls_ca_cert` and
`get_async_authenticator`, which check `insecure_skip_verify` first).

## Tests

- `tests/flyte/test_init_from_api_key.py`: new tests asserting the TLS
defaults (`insecure_skip_verify=False`, `ca_cert_file_path=None`) and
that explicitly passed values are forwarded to `init.aio`, with
`insecure` still `False`.
- `tests/user_api/test_init_api_key.py`: async (`.aio`) equivalents of
the same assertions.
- Full run of `tests/flyte/test_init_from_api_key.py`,
`tests/user_api/test_init_api_key.py`, and
`tests/cli/test_api_key_with_config.py`: 20 passed. `ruff check`/`ruff
format`, mypy, and ty all pass.

fix: map disk to ephemeral-storage and skip shm in pod_spec_from_resources

`pod_spec_from_resources` walks every field of `Resources` and looks each one
up in an unguarded dict. That dict is still keyed on `ephemeral_storage`, the
flytekit v1 name for the field now called `disk`, and has no entry for `shm`
at all -- so any `Resources` setting either one raised `KeyError` instead of
producing a pod spec:

    pod_spec_from_resources(requests=Resources(cpu=1, disk="10Gi"))  # KeyError: 'disk'
    pod_spec_from_resources(requests=Resources(cpu=1, shm="2Gi"))    # KeyError: 'shm'

The function is public API (exported from `flyte.extend`) and the Ray plugin
calls it for every head/worker group that sets resources, so a Ray task asking
for ephemeral disk failed before submitting anything.

The serde path already settles what both fields mean, so the mapping is not
ambiguous: `_get_disk_resource_entry` sends `disk` to
`ResourceName.EPHEMERAL_STORAGE`, and `get_proto_extended_resources` surfaces
`shm` as `ExtendedResources.shared_memory` mounted at /dev/shm -- a volume, not
a container resource key.

Key `disk` to `ephemeral-storage`, drop the stale `ephemeral_storage` entry,
and skip fields the map has no entry for, which leaves `shm` out of container

bit trickier so I don't want to do that now. The issue is that while we
can do the upload, it's harder to construct the entire literal. The

column information as well as the storage format, the latter of which

happens). I don't think we should we should make the user declare the

alongside the existing fuse/curl deps.

fix(image): strip _BASE_REGISTRY on clone() of SDK base image

When a user derives from Image.from_debian_base() — via .clone(name=...)
or any with_*() chain — the clone inherited _BASE_REGISTRY
("ghcr.io/flyteorg"), a registry the user doesn't own. The clone should
have registry=None: a user-owned derivative whose push target is
determined by the build system, not by the SDK's registry constant.

clone() rule (condition 3 only):
  parent_registry = None if self.registry == _BASE_REGISTRY else self.registry
  registry = registry or parent_registry

This is clean because _get_default_image_for() now builds the base image
with registry=None during construction (so internal clone() calls never
trigger the strip), then stamps _BASE_REGISTRY explicitly at the end —
consistent with the existing object.__setattr__ pattern used for `tag`.

  from_debian_base().clone(name="ci") → registry=None
  .clone(registry="myreg", name="x")  → registry="myreg" (explicit wins)

Signed-off-by: machichima <nary12321@gmail.com>

Cache cluster-aware clients per value, not per event loop (#1634)

## Problem

Running any tracked workflow prints a warning from `async_lru`:

```
async_lru/__init__.py:369: AlruCacheLoopResetWarning: alru_cache detected event loop
change and auto-cleared stale entries. This is safe but unusual outside of tests
(pytest-anyio, etc.).
```

Traced from `flyte run --tracked hello.py main`:

```
flyte/_persistence/_remote_reporter.py:730  loop.run_until_complete(self._process_batch(batch))
flyte/_persistence/_remote_upload.py:97     await dataproxy.create_tracked_run_upload_location(req)
flyte/remote/_client/controlplane.py:451    client, cluster = await self._resolve_with_cluster(...)
async_lru/__init__.py:259                   self._check_loop(loop)   -> AlruCacheLoopResetWarning
```

`alru_cache` stores the `asyncio.Task` it created for each key, so every
entry is bound to
the loop that produced it. async_lru >= 2.3.0 notices when the same
cache is used from a
second loop, clears it, and warns. Flyte legitimately drives one
`ClientSet` from several
loops in a single process — the CLI's `asyncio.run` loop, the syncify
background loop, the
controller thread, the tracked-run reporter thread — so the reset fires
during ordinary
runs: the CLI resolves a dataproxy client on its own loop, then the
reporter thread
resolves one on its loop while uploading inputs.

Besides the user-visible noise, each crossover discarded entries that
were perfectly
reusable, costing an extra `SelectCluster` round trip plus session
build. The cached values
are pyqwest-backed clients that carry no event-loop state (the default
clients in a
`ClientSet` are already shared across loops by design), so sharing them
is safe — only
alru's task-shaped entries were not.

## Change

- `flyte._utils.async_cache.ThreadSafeCache`: a small LRU memo (default
`maxsize=128`, same
as alru's default) that stores an async factory's resolved *value*,
never its task, so one
instance serves every event loop and thread in the process. The mapping
is guarded by a
`threading.Lock`; the factory runs outside the lock on a miss, and only
successful results
are stored, so a failed resolution is never cached and the next call
retries.
- `_ClusterAwareService` now owns one `ThreadSafeCache` per instance,
and the six
cluster-aware `_resolve*` methods in `controlplane.py` route through it
with an explicit
per-method key instead of `@alru_cache`. Side benefit: caches are per
service instance
  rather than keyed on `self` inside a decorator that outlives it.
- `async_lru` drops out of the `cli_run` and `runtime` import profiles.

**Trade-off:** unlike `alru_cache`, concurrent misses for the same key
are not collapsed
onto one in-flight call — each resolves independently and the last
result wins. This only
happens on a cold cache, `SelectCluster` is idempotent, and it keeps the
cache free of
loop-bound tasks. The old "concurrent resolve issues one SelectCluster"
test was replaced
accordingly (see below).

`alru_cache` is still used by `ImageBuildEngine` and the Snowflake
plugin; nothing in this
path exercises those from two loops, and their tests depend on alru's
`.cache_clear()`, so
they are left as-is.

## Test plan

- 6 new cases in `tests/utils/test_async_cache.py` for
`ThreadSafeCache`: memoization,
reuse across a loop change with no warning, sharing across threads,
failures not cached,
  LRU eviction, and per-instance isolation.
- `tests/flyte/remote/test_cluster_aware_dataproxy.py`:
  - `test_concurrent_resolve_for_same_key_is_deduplicated` replaced by
`test_resolve_reuses_cached_client_across_calls` (sequential calls issue
one
    `SelectCluster`) and `test_concurrent_resolves_all_succeed`.
- New `test_resolve_cache_survives_event_loop_change`: resolving the
same request under
two `asyncio.run` calls issues one `SelectCluster` and emits no warning.
- `tests/utils` + `tests/flyte/remote`: 802 passed, also with
`-W error::async_lru.AlruCacheLoopResetWarning`. mypy clean on the
changed files.
- Full suite: 6452 passed; the only 2 failures
(`test_keyring_store::test_retrieve_degrades_when_keyring_not_installed`,
`test_int_image_builder::test_real_build`) fail identically on `main`
(local env: keyring
  installed / no container registry).
- Manual, against a hosted org with async_lru 2.3.0:
- `main`: `flyte run --local --tracked hello.py main` prints
`AlruCacheLoopResetWarning`.
- This branch: 3 runs with `PYTHONWARNINGS=always` — all succeed, run is
tracked, no warning.

GPU faults are catchable typed exceptions (#1524)

# Why

The backend now classifies GPU faults into the failure a task reports:
the error code names the fault (GpuXidError, GpuFallenOffBus,
GpuEccUncorrectable, GpuRowRemapPending, GpuNvlinkError, GpuGspError),
the message leads with the driver's own sentence, and ExecutionError
carries a typed gpu_fault with the Xid, severity, GPU UUID and node.
Until now the SDK converted all of that into a generic runtime error, so
a parent task could only string-match on the code. This makes GPU faults
catchable as typed exceptions.

# What

- flyte.errors gains GPUFaultError, carrying fault_kind, fault_code,
fault_name, severity, gpu_uuid, gpu_index, node, pci_bus_id and process,
plus xid and sxid properties that answer only for the matching kind,
since Xid and SXid share a numbering space but not a meaning. Two
leaves, GPUFaultUserError and GPUFaultSystemError, keep the error kind
honest: the backend files a user-severity Xid (an out-of-bounds access
in the workload's own kernel) as USER and a critical hardware fault as
SYSTEM, and a single class would have to lie about kind for one of them.
except flyte.errors.GPUFaultError catches both.
- The error conversion selects the GPU classes on an exact match of the
six backend codes, ahead of the existing substring branches, and
tolerates server-prefixed codes. Fields fill only from the typed
gpu_fault; a failure carrying none leaves every fault attribute at None,
with the raw message untouched. The message is prose, not a contract, so
nothing parses it — the backend that classifies a fault always attaches
the typed data, since the two shipped together.
- The docstring states the semantics plainly: user-severity Xids arrive
on the task's own retry budget, while critical hardware faults are
retried by the platform without charging that budget, so user code sees
those only after platform policy gives up.

```python
try:
    result = await train(shard)
except flyte.errors.GPUFaultError as e:
    if e.severity == "USER":
        raise  # the workload's own kernel is at fault
    result = await train(shard)
```

# Tests

31 tests in the conversion suite: ruff, mypy and ty clean; the touched
test modules pass 187 tests total.

fix: cap mcp below 2.0 in the mcp extra (#1377)

## Summary

`pip install flyte[mcp]` is currently broken. **mcp 2.0.0** (released
2026-07-28) removed
`mcp.server.fastmcp`, which `FlyteMCPAppEnvironment` imports, and the
extra asked for
`mcp>=1.26.0` with no upper bound — so any fresh install resolves to a
version this code cannot
use, and the server dies at import.

The failure is easy to misdiagnose. `_create_mcp_server` catches the
`ImportError` and re-raises
`"mcp is not installed. Please install 'flyte[mcp]'"` — but it *is*
installed, just incompatible.
Chasing that message leads to the packaging, not the version.

## Repro (before this change)

```
$ uv pip install "flyte[mcp]==2.5.18b0"
 + mcp==2.0.0
$ python -c "from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP"
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp.server.fastmcp'
```

With the cap, `mcp` resolves to 1.29.0, the import succeeds, and a
`FlyteMCPAppEnvironment`
constructs normally.

## Change

`mcp>=1.26.0,<2` in the `mcp` extra, and the same in the `dev` group so
CI resolves what the
extra actually ships. Same shape as the existing `connectrpc<0.11` cap
directly above it.

Supporting mcp 2.x is a migration rather than a rename — `mcp.server`
was reorganised
(`apps`, `connection`, `caching`, …) — so it needs its own change before
this cap moves. Worth
tracking separately.

## Impact

Anyone installing `flyte[mcp]` since 2026-07-28, and any container image
that resolves the extra
at build time. Three of our deployed MCP apps crash-looped on exactly
this.

## Testing

`tests/flyte/ai/mcp` + contextvar tests → 426 passing. Plugin lockfiles
re-locked, since the root
`pyproject.toml` changed.

fix(controller): guard against None responses in informer watch loop (#1080)

When gRPC deserialization fails, grpc._common._transform() logs the
exception and returns None instead of raising. In the informer's watch
loop this caused an AttributeError on resp.control_message, which
crashed the loop and triggered a retry/backoff cycle. During that
backoff window the trace-action completion event was never received, so
wait_for_action_completion() blocked forever.

Two fixes:
1. _informer.py: skip None responses with a warning so the stream stays
alive and can receive the real completion update on the next message.
2. _core.py: add a 60-second timeout on wait_for_action_completion() for
trace actions only (task actions may run for hours). On timeout we fire
the completion event ourselves so the caller is unblocked even if the
server update was genuinely missed. The timeout is configurable via
_F_TRACE_COMPLETION_TIMEOUT.

docsy: correct Image.from_base() WORKDIR guidance (#1413)

## Summary

`Image.from_base()`'s docstring recommends a fix that cannot work, and
cites a docs section that does not exist. Both render into the generated
API reference, so the SDK reference and the Bring Your Own Image guide
currently give contradictory instructions for the same failure.

## The broken advice

Current text tells users that hardened non-root bases

> commonly need a `` .with_commands(["chmod 0755 /root && chown
<uid>:<gid> /root"]) `` layer

That command fails the build. `.with_commands()` runs as the base
image's declared `USER`, and a non-root user can neither `chmod` nor
`chown` a root-owned path (it needs `CAP_CHOWN`):

```
chmod: changing permissions of '/root': Operation not permitted
```

Replaced with the approach that does work, `.with_workdir()` pointed at
a path the declared `USER` already owns, plus an explicit note on why a
commands layer cannot repair it.

## The stale section reference

The docstring says *"See the **Base image USER requirements** section"*.
The guide's heading is **"Base image USER and WORKDIR requirements"**.

## Why they drifted

Ordering. This docstring shipped in #1071 on 2026-05-20, two days after
the docs page replaced the chmod workaround with `.with_workdir()`
(unionai-docs `aa4fb7d32`, 2026-05-18). The docstring carried the
superseded advice forward.

(`7ad3ec84`)
- `.with_commands()` runs as the declared `USER`: no `llb.User` override
in the builder's `command.go`
- Guide heading at `bring-your-own-image.md:148`; the "Operation not
permitted" warning at `:273`

format --check` clean

Upgrade pydantic-monty to 1.0.0 (#1642)

## Summary

Moves the sandbox runtime from `pydantic-monty==0.0.22` to `1.0.0`.

- **Limit key rename.** Monty 1.0 renamed `max_duration_secs` to
`max_feed_duration_secs` and rejects unknown limit keys at checkout, so
every sandbox execution failed against it. `_limits` now passes the new
key.
- **Sleep budget.** 1.0 lets sandbox code call `time.sleep` /
`asyncio.sleep` and excludes sleeps from the execution clock. A snippet
with `timeout_ms=500` could sleep for the full 10 s per-call cap.
`_limits` now sets `max_total_sleep_secs` to the same value as the
timeout, so an over-budget sleep raises `TimeoutError` immediately.
- **No clock, no entropy.** 1.0 gives sandbox code the worker's clock
and OS entropy by default, so the same code and inputs could take
different paths on each run. Both are now routed to the host, which
never answers: `time.time()`, `time.monotonic()`, `datetime.now()`,
`date.today()`, unseeded `random` and `os.urandom()` raise
`RuntimeError: ... is not supported in this environment` inside the
sandbox. `time.sleep`, date arithmetic and explicitly seeded `random`
still work.
- **OS calls in the bridge.** 1.0 surfaces OS calls to `feed_start`
callers as function snapshots. The bridge took them for unknown tools,
so `time.sleep` failed with a host `RuntimeError` in any code that had
tools attached. It now waits out sleeps and declines every other OS
call, which raises at the offending line in the sandbox.
- **`ORCHESTRATOR_SYNTAX_PROMPT`.** No longer forbids `str.format()`,
which 1.0 supports, and tells the model there is no clock: take dates as
inputs.
- **Pins.** `sandbox` extra, dev group, `MONTY_REQUIREMENT`, `uv.lock`
and the plugin lockfiles.

Sandbox examples that failed on a remote cluster for reasons unrelated
to Monty are fixed too:

- `sandboxed_tasks.py`: the environment had no `flyte[sandbox]` image,
and the code-string environment was missing `depends_on=[env]`.
- `dynamic_code.py`: missing `depends_on=[env]` ("Environment
'dynamic-demo' not found in image cache").
- `opaque_io.py`: `orchestrate_etl` awaited tool calls, which the
sandbox rejects. The workers are `async def`, so the synchronous calls
carry `# type: ignore`.
- `orchestrator.py`: the docstring claimed `await` works inside the
sandbox; it does not.
- `sales_agent.py`: the system prompt showed `await` on tool calls.
- `mle_orchestrator_agent.py`: `claude-sonnet-4-20250514` returns 404;
switched to `claude-sonnet-4-6`.

## Sandbox behaviour after this change, compared with 0.0.22

- `str.format()`, `eval` and `exec` now work.
- `time.sleep` / `asyncio.sleep` now work, bounded by `timeout_ms` in
total and 10 s per call.
- `import time` and `import random` now succeed, but only sleeping and
explicitly seeded `random` are usable; the clock and unseeded randomness
raise.
- `os.getcwd()` returns `/`.
- The timeout message reads "feed time limit exceeded".
- File, network, `os.environ` and `os.system` access are still blocked,
and memory, recursion and timeout limits still fire.

## Testing

- **Unit tests:** `tests/flyte/sandbox/test_runtime.py` (new) covers the
limit keys, timeout enforcement, the sleep bound, and clock/entropy
refusal with and without tools; `test_bridge.py` covers OS-call
handling. `tests/flyte/sandbox` and `tests/flyte/ai` pass (735 tests).
- **Local mode:** every task in `code_string`, `sandboxed_tasks`,
`orchestrator` and `dynamic_code` returns the expected value through
Monty, matching a 0.0.22 baseline on `main`.
- **Remote (demo tenant):** every Monty-backed example was run with an
image carrying Monty 1.0.0 and this branch's wheel, **before** the
clock/entropy and bridge commit was added; that commit has unit-test
coverage only.
- `code_string`, `orchestrator`, `sandboxed_tasks`, `dynamic_code`,
`remote_tasks`: all tasks pass.
  - `opaque_io`: 4 of 6 pass (see below).
- `codemode/durable_agent`, `agents/codemode_durable_task_agent`,
`agents/flyte_agent/code_mode_agent`,
`genai/mle_agent/mle_orchestrator_agent`: pass.
- Apps `codemode/chat_app` and `agents/codemode_durable_agent_ui`:
deployed and answered a chat request through the sandbox.

## Known issues, not addressed here

- `opaque_io.file_pipeline` and `dir_pipeline` fail because a `dict`
output containing a `File`/`Dir` cannot be serialized. Same on `main`
with 0.0.22.
- `sales_agent.py` builds its image with `install_flyte=False` +
`flyte[sandbox]` from PyPI + the local wheel. Until this pin is
released, that yields the new SDK on Monty 0.0.22 and every sandbox call
fails with `unknown limits key 'max_feed_duration_secs'`. It works with
Monty 1.0.0 forced into the image.
- Upgrading `flyte` while keeping an old `pydantic-monty` produces that
same `ValueError`; there is no version check in the lazy import.
- With tools attached, `asyncio.gather` over several sleeps waits for
them one after another instead of overlapping.
- `io_types_agent.py` and `mle_tool_builder_agent.py` still use the
retired `claude-sonnet-4-20250514` model id.

fix(artifacts): send the run's org/project/domain on a task-side artifact's source (#1625)

## Summary
`Artifact.create` from inside a task built its source as a
`TaskActionSource` whose `RunIdentifier` carried only the run name,
leaving org/project/domain for the server to inherit. The artifact
service validates those as required, so every task-side publish failed:

```
validation error:
 - spec.source.task_action.action.run.org: must be at least 1 characters [string.min_len]
 - spec.source.task_action.action.run.project: must be at least 1 characters [string.min_len]
 - spec.source.task_action.action.run.domain: must be at least 1 characters [string.min_len]
```

Seen on every seal of a Union Volume that publishes as an artifact
(flyteplugins-union >= 0.12), hourly and at finalize, for a whole day on
the demo tenant.

## Why the SDK, not the server
The old docstring said scope is "left for the server to inherit", and
the artifact service's handler (`applySource` in unionai/cloud
`artifacts/pkg/server/service_v2.go`) does accept empty scope and
inherit the artifact's. But the request never reaches it:
`common.RunIdentifier` validates org/project/domain as `string.min_len =
1`, and `TaskActionSource.action` is required, so protovalidate rejects
an empty scope first — the error above is protovalidate's. The backend's
own path (the action-state replicator) always sends a full
`ActionIdentifier`. Relaxing the shared `RunIdentifier` rule would
loosen every RPC that takes one, so the SDK sends what it knows.

## Changes
- `_current_task_source` fills the run's org/project/domain from the
running action, falling back to the artifact's own scope for any the
action lacks (an artifact can only reference an action in its own
org/project/domain). `Artifact.create` passes that scope in.
- The service only accepts a source in the artifact's own
org/project/domain, so a task publishing into another project sends
**no** source rather than failing the publish (with empty scope it would
have been recorded as an action in the artifact's project, which it is
not).
- It uses `task_action` rather than `action`: inside a `@trace` step,
`action` is the trace's pseudo-action, not the task that is running.

## Tests
`tests/flyte/test_artifact_source_scope.py` (new): no source outside a
task; the running action's scope is sent; the artifact's scope fills
what the action lacks; a traced step still names the real task;
publishing into another project sends no source. Passes with the
neighbouring artifact suites (37 tests); ruff clean.

Signed-off-by: Alex Wu <c.alexwu@gmail.com>

Add `flyte run hello` and `flyte serve hello`, first steps that need no files (#1496)

## Why

The first thing a new Flyte user has to do today is write a file. Before
they have any feel for what a task or an app looks like, they need a
`TaskEnvironment`, a decorator, a `main`, and a guess at how to invoke
it. That is a lot of blank page for someone who just wants to see the
thing work once.

These two commands remove the blank page. They need nothing in the
current directory, and each one prints the path to the source it just
ran or served, so the next step is `cp` rather than "now write your own
from the docs."

```bash
flyte run hello             # run the example workflow on the configured cluster
flyte run --local hello     # ...or on this machine
flyte serve hello           # serve the example app on the configured cluster
flyte serve --local hello   # ...or on this machine
```

## What's here

**`flyte run hello`** runs the quickstart workflow — a `flyte.map` over
a small task, averaged:

```python
env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(name="hello")

@env.task
def worker(x: int) -> int:
    return 2 * x + 5

@env.task
def main(x_list: list[int] = list(range(10))) -> float:
    results = list(flyte.map(worker, x_list))
    return sum(results) / len(results)
```

Task inputs are exposed as CLI options, so `flyte run --local hello
--x_list '[1, 3]'` works the same way it does for a user's own file.

**`flyte serve hello`** serves a minimal FastAPI app: an `index.html`
landing page pointing at `/docs`, plus `/hello`, `/line/{x}`, `/mean`,
and `/health` to poke at. It uses `FastAPIAppEnvironment`, so the
`/docs` link shows up in the UI automatically.

**Neither command needs a configured endpoint to be useful.** With no
endpoint, each prints an explanation and falls back to local execution
rather than failing — the point is that the very first command a user
types does something.

## How it works

The SDK carries the two examples as source strings, writes them to a
per-user scratch directory, and imports them from there. That
indirection is load-bearing: the code bundle resolves a task or app
through its module's location on disk, so an example living inside the
installed package would not be shippable to the cluster. Writing it out
first means the remote path works exactly like a user's own file — and
it also means the printed path is a real file they can copy.

Each example gets its own subdirectory, because the bundle is rooted at
the example's directory and would otherwise pick up its sibling. The
app's `index.html` is not a Python module, so it ships via
`include=("index.html",)` rather than through module tracing.

## Not on `flyte deploy`

An earlier revision of this PR added `flyte deploy hello-world-task` and
`flyte deploy hello-world-app`. Those are removed here. Deploying an
example the user didn't write leaves them at a step with nothing on the
other side of it — `run` and `serve` both end in something to look at,
and `deploy` doesn't. `_deploy.py` is byte-for-byte back to where it
started.

## A macOS path bug worth calling out

The first real remote run of `flyte run hello` failed with:

```
'/var/.../flyte-hello-<user>/task/hello.py' is not in the subpath of
'/private/var/.../flyte-hello-<user>/task'
```

`copy_code_bundle_to_context` resolves the root directory it is handed,
then takes each loaded module's `__file__` relative to it.
`tempfile.gettempdir()` returns a path under `/var`, which on macOS is a
symlink to `/private/var` — so the module kept the unresolved spelling,
the root got the canonical one, and every file in the bundle looked like
it lived outside the root. It reproduced on `flyte serve hello` too.

Resolving the scratch root fixes both sides at once, and `materialize()`
resolves as well so a caller-supplied directory can't reintroduce the
mismatch. Guarded by a test that runs the real bundling function for
both examples; it fails with exactly the error above if the fix is
reverted.

Worth noting this was invisible to the local paths — only the remote
bundle takes a file relative to the resolved root.

## Testing

- 29 tests in `tests/cli/test_hello.py`; the full `tests/cli` suite
passes (462 tests).
- The FastAPI app's endpoints are covered via `TestClient`, and
separately by an actual local `flyte.serve` run against uvicorn — `/`,
`/docs`, `/hello`, `/line/{x}`, `/mean`, `/health` all verified over
real HTTP.
- `flyte run --local hello` verified from an empty directory: `14.0`,
and `9.0` with `--x_list '[1, 3]'`.
- `flyte run hello` verified against a live cluster: bundles, uploads,
and the run succeeds with `o0=14.0` — matching the local result.
- Code bundles verified by dry run: `hello.py` for the task,
`hello_app.py` + `index.html` for the app.
- `flyte gen docs --type json` regenerated and checked with
`maint_tools/check_cli_json.py` — `flyte run hello` and `flyte serve
hello` are present, and `flyte deploy` has no static subcommands.
- ruff, mypy, and ty are clean.

**Not verified:** `flyte serve hello` against a live cluster. It shares
the bundling path that the remote `flyte run hello` now exercises end to
end, and its local serving is verified against real uvicorn, but the
deploy-and-activate round-trip is worth a manual check before merge.

Export the backend's platform env vars into the Slurm job

A native task exited 2 with `Missing option '--run-base-dir'`. That option
is required by `a0` and its only other source is the `_U_RUN_BASE`
environment variable, which the backend injects directly into the pod spec
on Kubernetes (leaseworker/lifecycle/context.go) rather than putting it in
the TaskTemplate. A connector therefore only ever sees it through
`TaskExecutionMetadata.environment_variables` -- which this plugin was
discarding, along with ACTION_NAME, RUN_NAME, _U_ORG_NAME and the
endpoint-discovery pair _U_EP_OVERRIDE / _U_INSECURE.

Merge them into the job environment, ordered so task config still wins over
platform vars, which win over whatever the template carries.

Only the deployed path was affected: for local runs the executor's
`_render_task_template` passes `--run-base-dir` on the command line instead,
and passes no TaskExecutionMetadata at all, so the merge is a no-op there.

feat(io): add File.copy_to / File.copy_to_sync + use in Volume.fork cold path

File.copy_to performs a single-file copy to a destination URI:
- same protocol (S3, GCS, local, etc.) → native server-side copy via
  fsspec's _cp_file (S3 CopyObject, GCS rewrite, shutil.copyfile);
- cross-protocol → stream copy through a local temp.
Bytes preserved, so the returned File inherits name / format / hash /
hash_method from self. Named copy_to (not copy) to avoid colliding with
Pydantic v2's BaseModel.copy.

Volume.fork cold path now uses File.copy_to instead of downloading to
local meta_dir + re-snapshotting + uploading. For S3-backed Volumes
this is one CopyObject — no bytes traverse the pod. For a 1-2 GB Redis
dump.rdb, cold fork drops from network-bound (~30-60s) to ~constant
(~100ms). Live path unchanged.

The cold-fork dst_path is generated under the active raw_data root via
ctx.raw_data.get_random_remote_path, matching how commit() places the
index after upload.

[Feature] Add task git repo host uri when deploying task (#335)

## Changes
We will store flyte task git repo host url in the backend when sending a
deploy request request to the run service. The url will be respond in
the GetTaskDetails api.

How the url is defined:
1. If task code file is under git repo and the git tree is clean, the
url will be suffixed with line number.
2. If task code file is under git repo and the git tree is not clean,
the url will only points to the code file in remote repo.
3. If task code file is not under git repo, the url will not be sent to
the backend.
4. The SDK will choose origin as default remote. If origin remote does
not exist, the SDK will sort remotes alphabetically and choose the first
one.

feat(errors): make backend-classified GPU faults catchable

The backend now classifies GPU and NVSwitch faults into the ExecutionError
it hands the SDK: the code becomes one of the gpufault codes, the driver's
own sentence is prepended to the message, and the fault travels as typed
data on ExecutionError.gpu_fault. Until now all of that arrived as an
opaque RuntimeUserError or RuntimeSystemError, so a task that lost a GPU
could not tell that apart from any other failure.

Add a GPUFaultError family and select it from those codes. One except
clause catches every GPU fault, and the xid, severity, gpu_uuid, node and
device attributes are there to branch on. The concrete errors keep the
kind the backend chose, GPUFaultUserError for a fault the workload caused
and GPUFaultSystemError for one that condemned the hardware, which is also
what decides whose retry budget paid for it.

Attributes come from the typed fault where the failure carries one and
from the prepended sentence otherwise, so a failure from a backend that
predates the typed field still names the Xid. Reading them never fails the
conversion: an unreadable message costs the details, not the error.

fix: make flyte start devbox work on Windows (FLYTE-SDK-79, FLYTE-SDK-7B)

`flyte start devbox` carried three POSIX-only assumptions. On Windows each one
crashed the CLI with an exception that reads like an SDK bug:

- `_KUBE_DIR = Path("/tmp/.kube")` has no meaning on Windows, where it resolves
  to the drive-relative `\tmp\.kube` and `mkdir` fails with
  `OSError: [WinError 123] ... syntax is incorrect` (FLYTE-SDK-79). Derive the
  directory from `tempfile.gettempdir()` instead. As a side benefit this also
  gives each user their own directory on shared Linux hosts, where a single
  `/tmp/.kube` owned by another user is exactly what the chown fallback below
  exists to work around.

- `KUBECONFIG` is a path *list* that kubectl splits on the platform separator.
  Joining with a hardcoded `:` makes kubectl split `C:\Users\...` on its drive
  letter, so neither file loads and `kubectl config view --flatten` exits 1.
  Use `os.pathsep`.

- Recovering from that failure reached for `os.getuid()`/`os.getgid()`, which do
  not exist on Windows, so the recovery attempt itself raised
  `AttributeError: module 'os' has no attribute 'getuid'` and buried the real
  kubectl error (FLYTE-SDK-7B). The chown is only meaningful where POSIX uids
  exist; elsewhere, report the original kubectl failure.

While here, the two `subprocess.CalledProcessError`s that could escape
`_merge_kubeconfig` -- from the `docker exec ... chown` and from the retried
flatten -- are now `click.ClickException`s carrying kubectl's own stderr, so
users see what went wrong instead of a traceback.

Give artifacts an explicit kind discriminator

Nothing on an artifact said what it was. "This is a model" had to be inferred
from two optional, independent signals, neither of which is reliable:

- The shape of the attr key set written by create_model_metadata. Any unrelated
  artifact could carry the same keys, and nothing says they mean "model".
- Card type. Optional even for models -- flyte.prefetch.hf_model only attaches a
  card when the HuggingFace repo had a README, so a prefetched model frequently
  has no card at all.

Add one reserved attr, flyte.io/kind, stamped at creation and read back through
a typed Artifact.kind property returning "model" | "data" | "generic".

The key is namespaced because user_metadata is documented as user-supplied: a
bare "kind" would collide with an attr a user legitimately owns, and quietly
misclassify their artifact. Nobody arrives at "flyte.io/kind" by accident, so
writing it by hand is treated as deliberate and wins over the kind= field;
create_model_metadata overrides both, matching how its other keys already behave.

kind lives in metadata rather than a typed proto field on purpose. The set of
kinds is still open, and an enum would have to be widened through an IDL release
before a producer could even write a new value. The key is narrow enough to be
promoted to a typed ArtifactInfo field later and backfilled, without touching
producers -- which is not true in the other direction.

Artifact.kind falls back to card.type so artifacts published before this change
still classify, and returns "generic" rather than None when there is no signal:
unlabelled and not-a-model are the same answer to the caller.

Reading is only through the property, never user_metadata directly, so the
storage can move without breaking callers.

feat(extras): Volume.mount(read_only=True)

Add a ``read_only`` knob to ``Volume.mount``. When enabled, the FUSE
mount is brought up with juicefs ``--read-only`` so writes return EROFS
and the writeback queue isn't engaged. The metadata engine still starts
(Redis loads the index) but no chunks ever upload.

Use case: expose a prior Volume's state read-only — multiple readers
can attach to the same index, no concurrent-writer hazards.

feat(extras): receive SaaS webhooks, at flyte.extras.webhooks (#1512)

First of a stack that replaces the six per-product integration plugins
(#1502–#1507) with the parts that are genuinely Flyte's. Structured like
`plugins/agents`: **core holds the contract, each product is its own
thin package.**

**Stack:** this → github → slack → linear → clickup → jira → examples.
Each PR's diff is just its own package.

## What core owns

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `WebhookAppEnvironment` | One app: a dashboard and a verified receiver
at `/webhook/{provider}`, for whichever providers it is handed |
| `Provider` | The contract a product plugin implements |
| `WebhookEvent` | The normalized event every provider parses into |
| `run_once` | Launch a run once per event key, returning the run that
covers it either way |
| `EventType` | Base for the typed event constants each plugin ships |
| verification primitives | `constant_time_equals`, `hex_hmac_sha256`,
`json_body`, `lower_headers` |
| `testing.assert_provider_conforms` | The conformance check every
plugin runs |

A product plugin owns only what is specific to it — usually under 150
lines. Core is tested against a **stub provider**, so it depends on no
product package.

## Two decisions worth reviewing

**Identity lives on a run label, never a name.** `run_once` launches
only when no run carrying the same `dedupe` label is live or succeeded;
when one is, it returns that run with `created=False` rather than
launching a second or raising, so a handler can answer "already handled"
and link to it. Names race against concurrent launches and cap how many
runs one key can ever have, so the control plane assigns them. It is
async-first behind `@syncify` — the blocking form stalls an app's event
loop, and webhook senders time out in seconds. A test asserts four
concurrent launches overlap; against a blocking implementation it
measures 0.81s instead of 0.42s and fails.

**`constant_time_equals` compares bytes.** `hmac.compare_digest` raises
`TypeError` on `str` operands containing non-ASCII, and these headers
come off the wire — ASGI hands Starlette raw bytes which it decodes
latin-1, so a crafted header would turn a clean 401 into a 500. Writing
it once here is the main argument for a shared core.

## The conformance harness

Each product plugin ships `SAMPLE_DELIVERY`, a real payload. The harness
signs and replays it, so `verify` and `parse` are checked against an
actual payload rather than against each other — without one, every other
check is vacuous.

It earned its keep during development twice:

- It caught that **Jira's shared token is not bound to the request
body**, unlike the four HMAC providers. That is inherent to an unsigned
webhook, not a bug, so `signed=False` now opts out of the body-tampering
check *and* makes the dashboard say the product does not sign.
- It caught **a hole in itself**: the hostile-header check sent a bare
non-ASCII value, which GitHub and Slack reject on their scheme prefix
before reaching the comparison — leaving the check vacuous for exactly
the two providers it mattered most for. Hostile values now preserve the
prefix, and a `str`-based `compare_digest` fails conformance as
intended.

I verified it discriminates by injecting three regressions (plain `str,
Enum` constants, a `str` comparison, a constant that no longer matches
the parser); each one fails with a specific message.

## Notes

No new dependencies land in `flyte`: the shared core lives in
`flyte.extras.webhooks` behind the same soft-import pattern the other
`flyte.extras` apps use, and each product plugin ships its own provider.

46 core tests plus each plugin's suite. `make fmt`, `make mypy` (864
files), `make ty`, ruff, and codespell pass.

The caveat from the review that prompted this: the parsers still encode
payload-shape assumptions I cannot verify without live accounts. That
surface is much smaller now — the six API clients and their ~213 field
assumptions are gone — and `SAMPLE_DELIVERY` pins what remains, but one
real pass per product is still the thing that would confirm it.

fix: don't crash when devbox unpause loses the paused-state race (FLYTE-SDK-6W)

`flyte start devbox` checks `docker ps --filter status=paused` and then runs
`docker unpause` as two separate docker calls. If the container leaves the
paused state in between (a concurrent unpause, a daemon restart, the container
exiting), docker fails with "container not paused" and the `check=True` call
raised a raw `CalledProcessError` out of `launch_devbox`, which is wrapped in
`@_sentry.capture_errors` — so a local state race got reported as an SDK crash.

Every other docker invocation in this module already goes through
`_run_docker()`, which turns failures into a user-facing `ClickException`;
`pause`/`unpause` were the two that were missed.

- `_resume_container()` treats "not paused" as a lost race and returns False so
  `launch_devbox` falls through to the normal start path, and converts any other
  unpause failure into a `ClickException` carrying docker's stderr.
- `stop_devbox` routes `docker pause` through `_run_docker`.

Add `flyte run hello-world`, a first workflow that needs no files

Getting a first workflow running meant writing a file before you could run
anything. `flyte run hello-world` removes that step: the SDK carries the source
of a small quickstart-style example, writes it to a per-user scratch directory,
and runs it.

The example is materialized and imported from that file rather than shipped as
an importable module inside the package, because the code bundle resolves a task
through its module's location -- a task whose module lives in site-packages is
not something the remote side can load. `run_args.root_dir` is pointed at the
scratch directory for the same reason, so the bundle contains exactly
`hello_world.py`. The printed path is a real file the user can copy into a
project of their own.

Someone running their first workflow may not have a cluster yet, so with no
endpoint configured the run falls back to local and says so rather than failing
on a connection the user was never told they needed.

`flyte gen docs` walks `flyte run` for its non-file subcommands only; the
allowlist there is now a named set that includes hello-world, so the command a
newcomer most needs is in the CLI docs.

refactor(errors): parse the GPU fault sentence only when asked to

The conversion read the fault attributes out of the failure message
whenever the failure carried no typed fault. That made a promise the SDK
cannot keep: the sentence is prose the GPU health daemon happens to write
today, nothing stops it changing, and a user who saw exc.xid filled in
once would reasonably expect it to stay filled in.

So the conversion now reads the typed fault and nothing else. The code
still selects GPUFaultUserError or GPUFaultSystemError exactly as before,
and a failure with no typed fault on it converts to the same exception
with its fault attributes left at None.

The parser moves to flyte.errors.parse_gpu_fault_message, where it is a
helper a caller reaches for deliberately. It returns the keyword
arguments GPUFaultError takes, or None when it can read nothing, and its
docstring says plainly that the format is not a contract and that this
exists for backends predating the typed field. GPUFaultError's docstring
now states the guarantee too: the typed exception and its fields appear
when the platform classified the fault, and where it did not, the same
failure arrives as a generic runtime error, so user code must not depend
on this exception firing.

fix: walk exception cause chain in Sentry user-error filter (#1078)

## Summary

`_upload_single_file` (and other call sites) wrap the underlying
`ConnectError` / `AuthenticationError` / `RuntimeError("SelectCluster
failed ...")` in a `RuntimeSystemError("Failed to get signed url ...")`.
The outer `RuntimeSystemError` is not in `_is_user_error`'s set, so even
though the chained cause is a user-facing problem (expired refresh
token, expired device code, IDP rejection, transport timeout), the
wrapped exception lands in Sentry as an unhandled SDK crash.

Two changes:

1. **`_iter_cause_chain`** — walk `__cause__` / `__context__` with a
`seen` set and a depth cap of 16 (cycle-safe, won't spin even if a
downstream bug wires a cycle).
2. **`_is_user_error`** — classify against the cause chain rather than
just the outermost exception, and add `AuthenticationError` /
`AccessTokenNotFoundError` (`flyte.remote._client.auth.errors`) to the
user-error set. This also makes the existing `DeploymentError` /
`ImageBuildError` / `InitializationError` / click filters robust to
wrapping further up the stack.

## Sentry issues

These all share the same outer title (`RuntimeSystemError: Failed to get
signed url for ...`) but the chained cause varies — this PR filters them
all out at the Sentry boundary:

- [FLYTE-SDK-2A](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7475986722/) — cause:
`AuthenticationError`/`RuntimeError(invalid_grant ... refresh token
expired)`
- [FLYTE-SDK-2P](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7479057871/) — cause:
`AuthenticationError(device code has expired)`
- [FLYTE-SDK-29](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7475758083/) — cause:
`TimeoutError` / `ConnectError(Request timed out)`
- [FLYTE-SDK-31](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7483511296/) — cause:
`ConnectTimeout`

`FLYTE-SDK-2H` (cause: server-side validation `project_id.organization
length must be at least 1`) is **not** classified as a user error by
this change — it's a config gap on the user's side but the SDK should
produce a clearer error before hitting the server. Tracked separately.

## Test plan

- [x] New tests in `tests/flyte/test_sentry.py`:
- wrapped `AuthenticationError` 3-deep chain (the exact shape from
FLYTE-SDK-2P) is filtered
  - wrapped `AccessTokenNotFoundError` is filtered
  - wrapped `DeploymentError` (via `__cause__`) is filtered
- unrelated `RuntimeError` still goes to Sentry (no regression on real
crashes)
  - cycle in `__cause__` chain doesn't hang `_iter_cause_chain`
- [x] All 13 sentry tests pass
- [x] `make fmt` clean
- [x] Commit signed (`-s`)

Remove multi-tenant central mode from the MCP server (#1391)

Central mode is being retired — stdio and per-tenant deployments replace
it. A single deployment that resolved a different Flyte tenant per
request was the only reason `_tenancy.py` existed, so the module goes
with it.

## Removed

- `src/flyte/ai/mcp/_tenancy.py` (918 lines) and
`tests/flyte/ai/mcp/test_tenancy.py`
- `tests/flyte/ai/mcp/test_mcp_cli_central.py`
- `FlyteMCPAppEnvironment`: the `central_mode` and
`allowed_endpoint_suffixes` fields, `CENTRAL_MODE_ENV_VAR`, the
`__post_init__` central guards, `_require_host_allowlist`, and the
central branches in `_starlette_middleware` (which now always takes the
passthrough-auth path) and `_starlette_lifespan_startup`
- `flyte-mcp` CLI: `--central`, `--allowed-endpoint-suffixes`,
`_central_mode_default`, `_host_allowlist_configured`, and the four
central validation branches
- The `TestCentralMode` and `TestCentralModeRequiresHostAllowlist`
suites, plus the now-unneeded `allowed_hosts=CENTRAL_HOSTS` arguments

`allowed_endpoint_suffixes` came out alongside `central_mode`: it was
only ever consumed by `CentralTenantMiddleware`, so it is dead once
`_tenancy.py` is gone.

## Kept deliberately

- **`init_config_context` and `_context_init_config`** in
`_initialize.py`. Added for central mode, but
`FlyteMCPAppEnvironment._scoped` uses it for per-call project/domain
scoping on *every* tool — stdio and per-tenant deployments both depend
on it. `tests/flyte/test_init_config_context.py` stays too. The comments
citing central mode as the motivating example were reworded to describe
the scoping use that remains.
- **`allowed_hosts` / `allowed_origins` and the transport-security
wiring** (`FLYTE_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS` / `_ORIGINS`,
`_transport_security_settings`). DNS-rebinding protection is worth
having on any HTTP deployment. Only the central-mode *requirement* that
one be configured is gone; the fields, env vars, and opt-in behaviour
are unchanged.
- All 32 tools, `ToolAnnotations`, `read_only`, `resolve_tools`, the
tool registry, the search timeout, the list ordering fix, and the
`mcp<2` cap.

`resolve_scope` now raises a plain `pass them as tool arguments or set
FLYTE_MCP_PROJECT/FLYTE_MCP_DOMAIN` error instead of the multi-tenant
one.

feat(slack): parse interactivity payloads and slash commands

The Slack provider only understood Events API JSON, but a real Slack app
receives two more delivery shapes on the same signing scheme: interactivity
payloads (Block Kit actions, shortcuts, modals -- form-encoded JSON under a
`payload` field) and slash commands (form-encoded fields). Internal agents
like Cally (`@app.action("send_to_customer")`) and Nodey (`/hi-nodey`)
could not move onto the plugin without them: those deliveries failed in
`parse` with a 400.

- parse() now sniffs form-encoded bodies and normalizes both shapes: a
  block action registers as `block_actions.<action_id>`, a shortcut as its
  callback_id, a slash command as `command.<name>`; the full Slack JSON
  (actions, container, message, response_url) rides in event.payload
- interactions dedupe per click via action_ts/trigger_id, so a Slack
  redelivery is a no-op but two clicks of one button are two events
- handshake() answers the `ssl_check` probe Slack sends to interactivity
  and slash-command URLs, so those Request URL fields verify themselves
- new events.Interaction and events.Command constants; README documents
  pointing all three Request URLs at the same /webhook/slack route

Verified end to end through WebhookAppEnvironment with signed
Cally/Nodey-shaped deliveries: dispatch, dedupe keys, 401 on unsigned,
and the JSON Events API path unchanged.

artifacts: validate parents client-side (at most 32, non-empty, typed)

`Metadata.parents` documented "up to 32" and nothing enforced it, so an
over-long list surfaced as a server rejection after the upload rather than a
ValueError where the caller can act on it. `MAX_PARENTS = 32` now mirrors the
service limit on `parent_artifacts` (flyteorg/flyte#7972), checked in
`Metadata.__post_init__` and again in `parents_to_pb2`, so the imperative
`Artifact.create(parents=...)` path gets the same checks without going
through a Metadata.

While there: an empty version string was accepted and would have produced a
keyless parent with no version -- rejected now -- and an entry of the wrong
type raises TypeError at declaration rather than deep in serialization.

[Fix] Image Cache bug when python version different between local and remote (#163)

## Description

When the image has the version that's different from local env (e.g. use
python 3.10 image but use 3.12 in local env), the remote execution will
fail as it cannot find the image.

## Changes

Exclude python version when creating image identifier hash. Change the
structure of look up table into nested. Below is the example:

```sh
{'rRtF_Uo8Wabpz3pMlhjELA': {'3.10': '356633062068.dkr.ecr.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/union/playground:flyte-7a4ec1d4c17a82d32086f976606d13ab'}}
```

If the running env use different environment (e.g. 3.11), which is not
in the look-up table, it will fall back to the first image, i.e. "3.10",
in the dict

fix(examples): repair the volume examples against flyteplugins-union 0.10.9

All four Volume examples failed on a real cluster. Three classes of rot,
plus two defects the verification runs surfaced.

**Hardcoded /workspace.** The default mount path is now per-volume
(`_default_mount_path()` keys off the volume name), so an explicit
`mount_path="/workspace"` in one task and a bare `mount()` in the next
landed in different directories:

    FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/workspace/hello.txt'

Every task now reads and writes under the `Path` that `mount()` returns.
In bench.py that means threading `root` into the workload functions; in
volume_recover.py the `mounted` bool is gone — `root: Optional[Path]`
does double duty as the mount-once flag.

**Version pin.** `flyteplugins-union>=0.4.0` -> `>=0.10.9`, in both the
PEP 723 header and `with_pip_packages`.

**allow_fuse() -> allow_volumes().** The surrounding comments described
the old in-process mount path (smarter-devices/fuse, CAP_SYS_ADMIN); a
brokered mount needs neither, so the comments and the Prereqs docstrings
now describe the CSI mount broker instead.

**bench.py's index-size probe was silently dead.** It stat'd
`/var/lib/flyte-volume/index.db`, which no longer exists, so
`index_bytes` was 0.0 for every cell. It now pins `meta_dir` on
`mount()` and stats that — the verification run reports real numbers
again (1.37 MB for metadata_burst, 156 KB for fork_burst).

**volume_recover.py was OOMKilled at memory="1Gi".** The first clean run
took three attempts, not two: the intentional crash after epoch 2, then
an OOMKilled (exit 137) on the resume, and only the third attempt
finished. With `retries=2` that is one bad break from failing outright.
Raised the three demos to cpu="1", memory="4Gi" — the mount client
(JuiceFS plus its metadata store) and the memory-backed staging emptyDir
that allow_volumes() attaches both draw on the pod limit. The re-run
took exactly two attempts, the only failure being the simulated crash.

gcsfuse_example.py is untouched: it is plain GKE gcsfuse CSI, not the
Volume plugin, and its MOUNT_PATH is already used consistently.

Note for anyone reproducing: `with_local_v2()` bakes whatever wheel is
already in `dist/` rather than rebuilding from `src/`, so run `make dist`
first. A stale wheel there is what produced the original failure —
`ImportError: cannot import name 'run_sync_in_thread'` — because the
baked SDK predated #1472's rename while the working tree did not.

Every example run end-to-end on prima-mente, all SUCCEEDED:

docs: reset_root_logger was documented backwards in both places

Two docstrings, disagreeing with each other and with the code:

  _run.py         "If true, the root logger will be preserved and not modified by Flyte."

fix: pin plugin wheel version via SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION on release (#1067)

## Summary

- The plugin-pypi release job was producing wheels with PEP 440 **local
version identifiers** (e.g.
`flyteplugins_papermill-2.3.0b1.dev0+gc32c0adb8.d20260513`) that PyPI
rejects with a 400 error.
- Root cause: `uv run python -m build --wheel --installer uv` triggers
`uv sync`, which re-resolves dependencies and rewrites the plugin's
`uv.lock`. For plugins that pull `flyte` from PyPI (e.g. `mlflow`,
`papermill`) the lockfile changes, dirtying the working tree. Plugins
with `[tool.uv.sources] flyte = { path = "../../", editable = true }`
(e.g. `ray`, `spark`) re-resolve to a byte-identical lock and stay clean
— which is why those uploads succeeded.
- A dirty parent tree causes `setuptools_scm` (configured with `root =
"../../"` in each plugin) to bump to the next dev version and append a
local segment, which PyPI then refuses.
- Fix: on release events, export
`SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION=<tag-version>` so `setuptools_scm`
returns the exact tag version regardless of working-tree state. This
mirrors the `SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION_FOR_FLYTE` fix already
applied to the main `flyte` package in the prior PR.

## Test plan

- [ ] Push a pre-release tag (e.g. `v2.3.0b1`) and confirm `mlflow` and
`papermill` wheels are built and uploaded to PyPI with the clean tag
version.
- [ ] Verify all other plugin uploads still succeed.

examples/apps: make WebSocket handshake header limits configurable (#1557)

## Overview

The WebSocket upgrade is a plain HTTP request, and both the ASGI server
and the `websockets` library cap how large its headers may be. Behind an
auth proxy that injects large headers (e.g. large IdP tokens or
forwarded session cookies) the handshake can exceed those caps and fail
with HTTP 431 — the WebSocket never connects and the app doesn't fully
render.

This exposes those caps as env vars in the two app examples,
**defaulting to the underlying library defaults so behavior is
unchanged**. A deployment that hits the ceiling can raise the limits
without editing the example.

## Changes

- **`examples/apps/websocket/fastapi_websocket.py`** — pass a
`uvicorn.Config` and `env_vars`:
- `UVICORN_H11_MAX_INCOMPLETE_EVENT_SIZE` → uvicorn/h11 whole-request
cap (unset → uvicorn's default, 16 KiB)
  - `WEBSOCKETS_MAX_LINE_LENGTH` → per-header-line cap (default 8 KiB)
  - `WEBSOCKETS_MAX_NUM_HEADERS` → header-count cap (default 128)
- **`examples/apps/basic_app.py`** (Streamlit) — the two `websockets`
caps via `env_vars`, same defaults. Streamlit's `/_stcore/stream`
upgrade runs through the same library.

Defaults are the pre-existing library values, so unset env vars
reproduce today's behavior exactly.

## Test Plan

- Both files `py_compile` clean.
- Verified end-to-end against a live app-serving deployment: with the
caps unset the WebSocket handshake 431s behind the auth proxy; setting
the env vars lets `/ws` (FastAPI) and `/_stcore/stream` (Streamlit)
complete the upgrade and the app renders.

fix: add V5E to TPUType so TPU v5e is reachable (#1548)

## Why

TPU v5e is wired up everywhere except the type that gates the
constructor.

`ACCELERATOR_DEVICE_MAP` already carries its node label, right next to
the two generations that do work:

```python
"V5E": "tpu-v5-lite-podslice",
"V5P": "tpu-v5p-slice",
"V6E": "tpu-v6e-slice",
```

and `_resources.py` already defines the slice shapes and a branch to
validate them:

```python
V5EParts = Literal["1x1", "2x2", "2x4", "4x4", "4x8", "8x8", "8x16", "16x16"]
...
elif partition is not None and device == "V5E":
    if partition not in get_args(V5EParts):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid partition for V5E: ...")
```

But `TPUType` listed only two of the three:

```python
TPUType = Literal["V5P", "V6E"]
```

So `TPU()` rejected the device at its first guard, the `elif device ==
"V5E"` branch below it was unreachable, and `V5EParts` was exported and
documented but unusable:

```python
TPU(device="V5E", partition="2x2")
# ValueError: Invalid TPU type: V5E. Must be one of ('V5P', 'V6E')
```

## What confirms the direction

Nothing downstream needed changing. Building the device directly — going
around the constructor — already serialized correctly before this patch:

```
Device(device="V5E", device_class="TPU", quantity=1, partition="2x2")
  -> gpu_accelerator { device: "tpu-v5-lite-podslice" partition_size: "2x2" device_class: GOOGLE_TPU }
```

which is structurally identical to what V5P and V6E produce. The whole
stack already handles v5e; only the literal was blocking it. That rules
out the other possible reading — deleting `V5EParts` and the dead branch
— since that would contradict `ACCELERATOR_DEVICE_MAP` at the layer that
actually talks to the backend.

## What changed

- `V5E` added to `TPUType`
- `V5EParts` admitted in the `partition` type hint (previously `V5PParts
| V6EParts | None`)
- `V5EParts` given the docstring its two siblings already have
- `V5E` named in the `Args:` example, which listed only `"V5P", "V6E"`

The previously-dead partition validation now actually runs:

```python
TPU(device="V5E", partition="3x3")
# ValueError: Invalid partition for V5E: 3x3. Must be one of ('1x1', '2x2', ...)
```

V5P and V6E are untouched, and an unknown device is still rejected.

## Tests

`test_tpu_all_types_with_partitions` is extended with three V5E cases
alongside the existing V5P/V6E ones, plus three new tests:

- `test_tpu_v5e_is_a_valid_type`
- `test_tpu_invalid_partition_v5e` — covers the branch that could not
previously execute
- `test_tpu_v5e_serializes_to_the_v5e_node_label` — pins
`tpu-v5-lite-podslice`

All six fail on `main` and pass with this change.

## Checks

- `make fmt` — clean
- `make mypy` — `Success: no issues found in 870 source files`
- `make check-docstrings` — `523 files clean`
- `codespell` — clean
- `make unit_test` — no new failures

fix: include FlyteIgnore in default code-bundle ignores (#1162)

## Motivation

Large git-tracked assets (e.g. git-lfs files) were being swept into code
bundles even when listed in .flyteignore, bloating bundles on flyte
run/flyte deploy with copy_style="all". PR #1098 added a FlyteIgnore
class (and a default_ignores constant) precisely to exclude git-tracked
files, but it was never wired into build_code_bundle's fallback ignore
set — which still used only StandardIgnore + GitIgnore, so .flyteignore
had no effect on tracked files. This completes that fix.

 ## Summary

- Add FlyteIgnore to the default ignore tuple in build_code_bundle
(_code_bundle/bundle.py), so .flyteignore patterns now exclude all
matching files, including git-tracked ones.
- Reuses the FlyteIgnore mechanism introduced in PR #1098 — this change
connects it to the actual bundler fallback used by flyte run/flyte
deploy, which previously passed no ignores.
- Add a regression test exercising the default ignore path with a
tracked file under .flyteignore.

 ## Test Plan

- uv run python -m pytest
tests/flyte/code_bundle/test_build_code_bundle.py
tests/flyte/code_bundle/test_ignore.py → 34 passed, no regressions.
- New test test_build_code_bundle_default_ignores_respect_flyteignore:
creates main.py, a tracked tests/images/big.bin, and a .flyteignore with
tests/images/, then bundles with copy_style="all" and no explicit
ignores; asserts main.py is present and tests/images/big.bin is excluded
(fails without this change).

feat(cli): add --version to flyte run (#1575)

## What

Adds `--version` to `flyte run`, passed through to
`flyte.with_runcontext(version=...)`.

## Why

- Python callers can set a run's version with
`with_runcontext(version=...)`. The CLI couldn't.
- `with_runcontext` raises `ValueError("Version is required when
copy_style is 'none'")` whenever `copy_style="none"` has no version. So
`flyte run --copy-style none` failed every time, in local mode too:
  ```
$ flyte run --local --copy-style none my_example.py my_task --name World
  ✕ Execution failed: Version is required when copy_style is 'none'
  ```

## Equivalence with the programmatic path

`flyte run <file> <task>` builds its runner with the same
`flyte.with_runcontext(...)` a Python caller uses, then calls
`run.aio(task, ...)`. This change passes `version=` into that call, so
`_Runner` receives exactly what `with_runcontext(version=...)` would
give it. Inside the runner, `version` is used the same way for both:

- **Remote runs of a local task** (`_build_task_spec_from_template`) and
**hybrid runs** (`_run_hybrid`) use `self._version or
code_bundle.computed_version` as the task version.
- **Local runs** (`_run_local`) use `"na"`, so `version` is ignored
there. The `copy_style="none"` check in `with_runcontext` still applies,
which is why local runs need it too.

Two details:

- **Both file-run call sites pass it**, the direct run and the TUI path.
Otherwise `--version` would silently do nothing in the TUI.
- **`deployed-task` does not use it.** `_run_remote` takes a fetched
task's version from the task itself (`task.pb2.task_id.version`), so
`--version` there would be silently ignored. It's rejected instead,
pointing to `env.task:version`. The check runs in
`TaskFiles.get_command`, before anything loads config or fetches the
task: `RunRemoteTaskCommand.get_params` contacts the backend before
`invoke` runs, so a check in `invoke` never fires when there is no
config. The second commit fixes that; CI caught it.

## Tests

Six new tests in `tests/cli/test_run.py`:
- the option exists;
- `from_dict` parses it;
- it's passed to `with_runcontext`, and defaults to `None`;
- `--copy-style none` fails without `--version` and succeeds with it,
through the real `with_runcontext`;
- it's rejected for `deployed-task`.

Results:
- `tests/cli`: 468 passed, both with a Flyte config and in a CI-like
environment with none.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check`: pass.
- `make check-docstrings`: clean.
- `flyte gen docs --type json | python maint_tools/check_cli_json.py`:
57 commands described, all keys present.

Also run by hand with this branch's CLI:
- `flyte run --local --copy-style none --version v1.0.0 my_example.py
my_task --name World` prints `Hello, World!`.
- The same without `--version` fails with the version error.
- `flyte run --version v1.0.0 deployed-task my_env.my_task` is rejected
with the `env.task:version` hint.

## Noticed, not changed

`flyte run` offers `--copy-style custom`, but `with_runcontext` always
rejects `"custom"` ("not yet supported through with_runcontext"), so
that choice can never succeed from the CLI.

actionable instruction to the user — it is not a crash report worth paging

DeploymentError and ImageBuildError so it stops flooding Sentry.

fix(logging): wrap pre-existing root-handler formatters with [run][action]

Restores parity with main's ContextFilter behavior: when
initialize_logger() is called with reset_root_logger=False (the
default), wrap any pre-existing root-handler formatter so
third-party log lines routed through root render with
[run][action]. Captures handlers registered before this call,
matching main's temporal limitation; the LogRecord factory still
stamps the attrs on every record so callers can format them
themselves for handlers added later.

ContextFormatter gains an `inner: logging.Formatter | None` kwarg.
When set, base formatting is delegated to the inner formatter
instead of ContextFormatter's own fmt string — this preserves the
original handler's layout while letting us prepend the prefix.

Also removes the unused register_log_context / unregister_log_context
machinery (no longer needed; users can stamp their own attrs
through their own formatters now that the factory exposes context).

  wrap path and idempotency on repeated init calls.

feat(webhooks): a provider brings its own secret

default_secret_env is now a class property on the provider, and
WebhookAppEnvironment mounts it. Wiring up an app no longer repeats the
environment variable the provider already knows:

    app_env = WebhookAppEnvironment(
        name="acme-webhooks",
        providers=[AcmeProvider()],
        image=...,
    )

Anything the caller does declare wins, which is how you point a provider at a
secret stored under a different key:

    secrets=[flyte.Secret("my-gh-key", as_env_var="GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET")]

Detection matches on the environment variable a secret actually lands as, not
on its key, so `secrets=["GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET"]` and an explicit as_env_var
both count as declared and neither produces a duplicate mount. Unrelated
secrets are kept alongside.

The module-level DEFAULT_SECRET_ENV constants are gone; the value lives on the
class that owns it, and instances still take a secret_env override.

Conformance now requires a plugin to declare default_secret_env and to default
to it, because the app mounting the value means a plugin that omits it hands
users an app with no secret and no error -- verified to fail loudly.

fix: reject unusable access tokens from external auth command (FLYTE-SDK-6Y)

An external_process authenticator uses the stdout of the configured command
verbatim as the bearer token. When that command is an interactive helper it can
exit 0 while printing a prompt instead of a token, e.g.

    Please visit this URL to authorize this application: https://accounts...

.strip() only removes the surrounding whitespace, so the interior newline
survives into 'Authorization: Bearer <prompt>'. connectrpc's pyqwest transport
then rejects the header with a bare ValueError: Invalid header value, raised far
from the real cause, wrapped as a SelectCluster RuntimeError and reported as an
SDK crash.

Validate the command output before it becomes a credential and raise
AuthenticationError with an actionable message instead. The output is not echoed
back, since it may contain a genuine token.

The bad token was also written to the keyring before it was ever used, so
affected users stayed broken on every subsequent run without ever re-running the
command. get_auth_headers now treats a cached token that cannot be sent as a
header as if there were no credentials, which lets the normal refresh path run
and surface the real error.

Also stop re-wrapping the non-zero-exit AuthenticationError in the generic
handler, and fix the debug log that joined the command string character by
character.
