feat(slack): interactivity, slash commands, notify helpers, and hitl-backed approvals (#1540)

## Why

Internal Slack agents like
[Cally](https://github.com/unionai/unionai-agents/tree/main/cally) and
[Nodey](https://github.com/unionai/unionai-agents/tree/main/nodey) run
hand-rolled slack_bolt servers and hand-rolled outbound API calls. This
PR closes the gaps that keep them off the plugin, in three layers.

## 1. Receive everything Slack sends (`_provider.py`)

The provider only parsed Events API JSON; interactivity payloads (Block
Kit buttons, shortcuts, modals) and slash commands arrive form-encoded
and 400'd. Now:

- a block action registers as `block_actions.<action_id>` (Cally's
`send_to_customer`), a shortcut as its `callback_id`, a slash command as
`command.<name>` (Nodey's `/hi-nodey`)
- full Slack JSON (`actions`, `container`, `message`, `response_url`)
rides in `event.payload`
- interactions dedupe per click (`action_ts`), redeliveries are no-ops;
commands key on `trigger_id`
- `handshake()` answers the `ssl_check` probe; `verify()` unchanged (v0
HMAC signs raw bytes for all three shapes)
- new `events.Interaction` / `events.Command` constants; runnable
`examples/slack_interactions.py` with `--local` signed replay

## 2. Send messages (`notify`)

Nodey ships a fifty-line `send_notification` task of raw `requests`;
Cally re-implements posting per handler. `notify` provides
`post`/`update`/`delete` (bot token via `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`),
`respond(response_url)` which needs **no token** (the zero-setup way for
a launched task to answer the click that launched it), and a deployable
`notify.env` + `send` task so only one environment holds the token.

## 3. Approvals on core `new_condition` (`approval`)

The pattern both agents build by hand — post buttons, pause, resume on
click — becomes:

```python
decision = await approval.request.aio("C0DEPLOYS", "Deploy release-42 to prod?")   # in a task
approval.register(app_env)                                                        # in the webhook app
```

`request` parks the run on a core `flyte.new_condition`; the clicked
button carries the run, action, and condition names, so the webhook
handler resolves it with `flyte.remote.Condition.get(...).signal(...)` —
no configuration on the app side — then swaps the buttons for a
"*approve* — decided by @who" line. Same mechanism the GitHub plugin's
review gate uses. Because it's an ordinary condition, the prompt is
**also** answerable from the Flyte UI, so an approval nobody clicks in
Slack is never stuck, and `timeout=` is the core contract
(`ConditionTimedoutError`). No extra install needed.

## Ergonomics

- **`on_event(..., action=...)`** (core `_app.py`): the user-defined
half of an event — a button's `action_id`, a command's name — is your
vocabulary, not Slack's, so no constant can spell it.
`on_event(events.Interaction.BLOCK_ACTIONS, action="approve_deploy")`
and `on_event(events.Command, action="/deploy")` now compose it; an
`EventType` class means its `ANY`, and a leading `/` is dropped. Raw
qualified strings still work.
- **Typed payload views** (`payloads`): nested TypedDicts over
`event.payload` so
`payloads.block_actions(event)["actions"][0]["value"]` autocompletes.
Casts, not validation.
- Handler `event` args annotated `event: WebhookEvent` throughout
examples and docs.

## Validation

- 24 slack tests pass, including the shared provider conformance
harness; 51 core webhook tests pass
- `notify` tested against an `httpx.MockTransport`; the decision handler
against events built by the real parser (including condition lookup args
and the already-signaled/timed-out case)
- end-to-end through `WebhookAppEnvironment`: signed Cally/Nodey-shaped
deliveries dispatch correctly, unsigned refused 401, JSON Events API
path unchanged
- ruff + pre-commit (fmt/mypy/ty/uvlock) clean; the deprecated
`flyteplugins-hitl` plugin is left untouched by this branch

## Notes

Slack expects interactivity/command acks within 3s; the README says to
do nothing slower than `run_once.aio` in handlers. A follow-up worth its
own PR: an early-ack option in the core webhook framework.

Bump certifi, uv and rustls-webpki for the emSign CA distrust (#1695)

## Why
The eMudhra/emSign CA private keys are compromised, so the root has been
pulled from CA bundles ([Python
advisory](https://discuss.python.org/t/information-for-python-users-regarding-emudhra-emsign-ca-certificate-security-incident/109576),
[RUSTSEC-2026-0382](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0382.html)).
Several of our pins still trust it.

## What changed
- **uv `0.8.13` → `0.13.4`** in the image builder template
(`docker_builder.py`). This is the main user-facing fix: this uv binary
is copied into every image the SDK builds, and it ships its own CA
roots. Also bumped the CI uv pins (`0.9.21` → `0.13.4`).
- **certifi → `2026.10.19`** in every `uv.lock` that contains it. Only
the certifi entry changes (re-locking with any uv version also rewrote
unrelated `exclude-newer` metadata, so I swapped the entry directly and
checked hashes against PyPI). Also added `certifi = "0 days"` to
`exclude-newer-package` so CA bundle updates aren't held back 5 days.
- **rs_controller:** `rustls-webpki` `0.103.13` → `0.103.16` and
`webpki-roots` `1.0.8` → `1.0.10`.

`flyte` itself doesn't pin certifi, so `pip install flyte` already pulls
in the fixed bundle. The lockfiles mainly affect CI and dev
environments.

uv 0.9 → 0.13 breaking changes reviewed against the template: `uv venv`
only runs when the venv doesn't exist and always passes `--python`, so
the `--clear` and default-Python changes don't apply.

## Testing
- `uv lock --check` passes on the root lock with both uv 0.13.4 and
0.9.28
- `cargo check --locked` in `rs_controller`
- `pytest tests/flyte/imagebuild tests/flyte/test_image.py`: 226 passed
- Built a multi-arch image locally with `DockerImageBuilder` (pushed to
a local registry) and checked inside it:
  - `uv --version` is `0.13.4` on both arm64 and amd64
  - `uv pip install` reaches PyPI over TLS
- certifi `2026.10.19` drops the distrusted emSign root (4 → 3 emSign
roots; the unaffected ones stay, as the advisory expects)

feat(controller): run a fork's code-overridden action from its own bundle

A fork can now patch the code of one task action: ActionInputOverridesData
names a replacement code bundle per action. When the parent's controller
enqueues such an action it keeps the name computed from its own copy of the
code (so the override key matches and recovery is skipped), then serializes
the child against the replacement bundle, so only that action and the actions
it launches run the patched code. The action skips the cache, whose version
comes from the parent's copy of the function, and is flagged as overridden so
the server accepts the enqueue. An override on a deployed (reference) task, or
from a parent without a source bundle, fails with a user error.

drop task_template from rerun; replaying with new code is fork

`task_template` existed on rerun solely to substitute local code for the
prior run's task spec: it selected the task source, supplied the native
interface when inputs were also changed, and backfilled ids on the freshly
built spec. All three go away with it, so rerun now always replays the
prior action's spec as-is and converts any changed inputs against the
interface guessed from that spec.

This removes `flyte run --rerun-from`, whose only implementation was
rerun(task_template=<local task>). Re-running a prior run with new code is
fork, reserved for flyteplugins-union.

The recover guard narrows accordingly: recover=True can now only collide
with changed inputs, since substituting code is no longer expressible.

fix: clamp Backoff.compute_delay to the cap instead of overflowing (#1544)

## Why

`Backoff` requires a `cap` whenever `factor > 1.0`, and says exactly
why:

```python
if self.factor > 1.0 and self.cap is None:
    raise ValueError("Backoff.cap is required when factor > 1.0 to prevent unbounded growth")
```

`compute_delay` then computed the unbounded product *before* comparing
it to that cap, so the growth the cap is there to prevent happened
anyway and overflowed the `timedelta` range:

```python
delay = self.base * (self.factor**n)      # overflows here
if self.cap is not None and delay > self.cap:
    return self.cap
return delay
```

Using the policy from the `RetryStrategy` docstring:

```python
b = Backoff(base=timedelta(seconds=10), factor=2.0, cap=timedelta(minutes=5))
b.compute_delay(20)   # 0:05:00  — capped, fine
b.compute_delay(43)   # OverflowError: days=1628906115; must have magnitude <= 999999999
```

The documented formula is `min(base * factor**n, cap)`, and `min`
against a 5-minute cap cannot exceed 5 minutes. The first failing index
is low enough to hit in practice — n=43 for the above, n=42 for
`base=30s, factor=2.0, cap=1h`.

## Impact

`RetryStrategy(count=100)` is a supported configuration (asserted in
`test_retry_strategy_high_count`), and the local controller calls
`compute_delay` once per attempt:

```python
# src/flyte/_internal/controllers/_local_controller.py:281
backoff = user_backoff.compute_delay(attempt_num - 1).total_seconds()
```

So a task with a high retry count and exponential backoff retried
normally for 43 attempts and then raised `OverflowError` on attempt 44 —
from inside the failure-handling path, so the retry loop itself is what
broke. The remaining ~56 attempts were lost, and the traceback pointed
at `timedelta` arithmetic with nothing to connect it to the retry
policy.

## What changed

`compute_delay` catches the overflow and returns the cap.
`__post_init__` guarantees a cap whenever `factor > 1.0`, and `factor ==
1.0` cannot overflow, so a cap is always present on that path; the bare
`raise` is defensive and unreachable.

Behaviour for every non-overflowing `n` is byte-for-byte unchanged — the
fix only adds a branch that previously raised.

fix(io): preserve zero-byte files in Dir/File downloads

A task returning a `flyte.io.Dir` silently dropped every zero-byte file on
download. `ObstoreParallelReader._chunks(size)` iterates `range(0, size, cs)`,
which is empty for a 0-byte object, so `_gen` emitted no `DownloadTask` for it,
no buffer was ever created, and the local file was never materialized. Upload
was unaffected (the object exists in the store and is even returned by
`obstore.list`), so directory round trips looked complete with no error signal.

Fix, scoped to the download path so the other `_chunks` caller (the model
loader, which intentionally skips zero-size tensors) is unchanged:
- `download_files._gen` emits a single `(0, 0)` chunk for zero-byte objects so
  the file is created via `_FileBuffer.new` (which touches it).
- `_worker` skips the `obstore.get_range_async` fetch and write when the chunk
  length is 0 (obstore rejects a zero-length `start == end` range request); the
  buffer is already complete, so the empty file is still finalized.

Adds a regression test covering a mixed 0-byte / non-empty directory download.

feat(artifacts): typed partitions on artifacts, partition-aware get/list/triggers (#1599)

> **CI is red until the IDL ships.** `ty` and the unit-test jobs resolve
`flyteidl2==2.0.48` from PyPI, which does not carry the messages this PR
uses (`DeclareArtifact`, `ListPartitionValues`,
`ArtifactPartitionSchema`, `Granularity.WEEK`). They come from
flyteorg/flyte#8056. Once that merges and a `flyteidl2` release is cut,
bump the pin here and the jobs go green; every other check passes today.
Verified locally against a build of that branch: 369 tests pass across
the artifacts, triggers, CLI and image suites.

Depends on flyteorg/flyte#8056 (IDL). Draft until a `flyteidl2` release
carries the new messages; the pin is relaxed to `>=2.0.45` so the branch
builds against a local wheel and must be bumped to that release before
merge.

## Why

Partitions become part of an artifact's identity in the registry instead
of reserved labels in free-form metadata. The SDK needs a natural way to
publish a partition and to ask for one: the latest version of a
partition, one version per partition over a range, and the values a
dimension has. The factory module in flyteplugins-union plans backfills
with these calls.

## What

- `flyte.artifacts.Metadata(partitions=...)`: a `date` is a daily time
partition, a `datetime` an hourly one, anything else a string partition;
`flyte.artifacts.TimePartition(value, granularity)` for week and month.
The mapping key is the partition key. Carried on `ProducedArtifact` for
`produces_artifacts` tasks.
- `flyte.remote.Artifact`: `partitions` and `time_partition` properties;
`Artifact.get(name, date=..., region=...)`; `Artifact.listall(name,
date=(lo, hi), latest_per_partition=True)`;
`Artifact.partition_values(name, key, **fixed)`; `Artifact.declare(name,
partitions={"date": date, "region": str})`; `Artifact.get_schema(name)`
returning `PartitionSchema`.
- Triggers: `OnArtifact(name, region="us")` and
`flyte.TriggeredPartition("date")` in `Trigger.inputs`.
- CLI: `flyte get artifact NAME --partition key=value` (also `key=a..b`,
`key=a,b`) and `--latest-per-partition`.
- Dev-mode task images bake a local `flyteidl2` wheel from `dist/` next
to the SDK wheel.

## Testing

The SDK does not verify a version against the registry's schema: keys
are the registry's business. A version published with keys the
artifact's schema does not name is stored as published and answers by
the keys it carries — compare `Artifact.get_schema(name)` against a
version's `partitions` to see a difference.

## Testing

New tests: `tests/flyte/test_artifact_partitions.py`,
`tests/flyte/remote/test_artifact_partitions.py`,
`tests/cli/test_get_artifact_partitions.py`, plus cases in the trigger
serde, triggers and produces-artifacts suites. Touched suites: 339
passed. Exercised end to end against a local control plane running the
matching artifact service: publish with partitions, get by partition,
latest-per-partition ranges, value listing, declare and redeclare, a
deliberate schema mismatch, and a factory materialization built on these
calls.

fix: accept dry_run in flyte.deploy, deprecate dryrun (#1573)

## Summary

`flyte.deploy` is the only public API that spells the dry-run flag
`dryrun`. Everything else uses `dry_run`:

| Call | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `flyte.deploy(...)` | `dryrun` | `dry_run` (`dryrun` deprecated) |
| `flyte.with_runcontext(...)` | `dry_run` | unchanged |
| `flyte.with_servecontext(...)` | `dry_run` | unchanged |
| `flyte.build(...)` | `dry_run` | unchanged |
| `flyte deploy` CLI | `--dry-run` / `--dryrun` | unchanged |

On 2.7.2, `flyte.deploy(env, dry_run=True)` raises `TypeError: deploy()
got an unexpected keyword argument 'dry_run'`. The user docs have
already tripped over this.

## Changes

- `flyte.deploy` now takes `dry_run: bool = False`.
- `dryrun` is still accepted as a deprecated keyword. It emits a
`FutureWarning` and maps onto `dry_run`. If both are passed, either one
being `True` requests a dry run, so disagreement errs toward not
deploying.
- The `flyte deploy` CLI now calls `flyte.deploy(dry_run=...)`, so it no
longer triggers the warning.
- Internal helpers (`apply`, `_deploy_task`, `DeploymentContext`, code
bundling) keep their `dryrun` names. Only the public signature changes.

### Why `FutureWarning` and not `DeprecationWarning`

`@syncify` runs the coroutine body on a background-loop thread, so the
warning can't be attributed to the caller's module. Under Python's
default filters, a `DeprecationWarning` raised there is silently
dropped. A plain-script check confirmed this: the `DeprecationWarning`
probe printed nothing, and the `FutureWarning` was shown.

## Tests

- New tests in `tests/flyte/test_deploy.py` check that `dry_run` is
forwarded to `apply` with no warning, that `dryrun` still works and
warns, and how the two combine when both are passed.
- `uv run pytest tests/flyte/test_deploy.py tests/cli`: all pass (35 and
462).
- `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy`, `ty check` and `make
check-docstrings` are clean on the changed files.

codegen plugin (#704)

LLM-driven single-file Python code generation plugin

- Adds `flyteplugins-codegen`, a plugin that uses LLMs to generate,
test, and iterate on single-file Python scripts inside isolated
sandboxes
- Supports two execution backends: LiteLLM mode (any model with
structured output support) and Claude Agent SDK mode (autonomous Claude
agent)

### AutoCoderAgent - the main entry point:
- Takes a prompt + optional samples/schema/constraints, generates a
Python script, writes pytest tests, builds a sandbox image, runs tests,
diagnoses failures, and iterates until tests pass
- `result.run()` / `result.as_task()` execute the generated code against
real data in an isolated container
- Supports data extraction from DataFrames and Files, auto-generates
Pandera schemas, and infers input/output types

```python
import flyte
from flyte.io import File
from flyte.sandbox import sandbox_environment
from flyteplugins.codegen import AutoCoderAgent

agent = AutoCoderAgent(model="gpt-4.1", name="summarize-sales", resources=flyte.Resources(cpu=1, memory="1Gi"))

env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(
    name="my-env",
    secrets=[flyte.Secret(key="openai_key", as_env_var="OPENAI_API_KEY")],
    image=flyte.Image.from_debian_base().with_pip_packages(
        "flyteplugins-codegen",
    ),
    depends_on=[sandbox_environment],  # Required
)

@env.task
async def process_data(csv_file: File) -> tuple[float, int, int]:
    result = await agent.generate.aio(
        prompt="Read the CSV and compute total_revenue, total_units and row_count.",
        samples={"sales": csv_file},
        outputs={"total_revenue": float, "total_units": int, "row_count": int},
    )
    return await result.run.aio()
```

### Agent mode (`backend=claude`):
- Runs an autonomous Claude agent that writes files, runs tests
(intercepted into sandboxes), and fixes issues
- Hooks checkpoint intermediate artifacts to named remote storage for
durable execution across retries

```python
agent = AutoCoderAgent(
    name="my-task",
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    backend="claude",  # Requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY as a Flyte secret
)

result = await agent.generate.aio(
    prompt="...",
    samples={"input": my_file},
    outputs={"result": str},
)
```

fix(storage): honor exclude on recursive parallel-reader downloads (#1610)

## Problem

`ObstoreParallelReader.download_files` only applies `exclude` on the
explicit-paths branch. The recursive branch (`obstore.list`) yields
every object unfiltered. It has behaved this way since the original
streaming PR (#387).

The vLLM and SGLang model-loader shims call `prefetch(...,
exclude_safetensors=STREAM_SAFETENSORS)`, which passes
`exclude=["*.safetensors"]` for a recursive download. The intent is to
fetch config and tokenizer files up front and stream the weights
directly into the GPU. Because the filter was skipped, every cold start
with `stream_model=True`:

1. downloaded all safetensors to `/tmp/flyte/model`, then
2. streamed the same weights from object storage again through
`SafeTensorsStreamer`.

## Impact measured (A/B)

`Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8` (31 GB) served by `VLLMAppEnvironment` on one
L40S (g6e.2xlarge), streaming on. Both apps used the same vLLM image and
args. "Fixed" adds one image layer that applies this patch to the
installed flyte 2.9.0.

| step | baseline | fixed |
|---|---|---|
| container start → weight fetch begins | 33s | 34s |
| **weights fetched and loaded onto the GPU** | **4m 46s** | **1m 00s**
|
| torch.compile | 68s | 69s |
| KV cache / CUDA graphs / warmup | ~86s | ~89s |
| **container start → serving** | **7m 55s** | **4m 13s** |

On the baseline pod, `/tmp/flyte/model` held all 68 `.safetensors` files
(29 GB), even though `FLYTE_MODEL_LOADER_STREAM_SAFETENSORS=true`. On
the fixed pod it held 23 MB: config, tokenizer and the index.

## Fix

Apply the existing `_keep` filter to recursive listings too. `_keep`
uses `Path.match`, so the string path from `obstore.list` is wrapped in
`pathlib.Path`.

## Tests

- Added `test_recursive_download_honors_exclude`. It **fails on `main`**
and passes with the fix.
- `tests/flyte/storage` and `tests/flyte/app` pass (251 passed, 2
skipped); ruff is clean.

fix(image): only default to the localhost registry for local builds (#1680)

## Problem

When the endpoint names `localhost`, images were given flyte devbox's
registry (`localhost:30000`) at the moment they were defined, before the
builder was known. Through a remote builder reached via a localhost
endpoint — unibox, or a port-forward to a cluster — the build target
became `localhost:30000/<name>`, and the backend's builder put its own
repository in front of it:

```
failed to push localhost:30000/onebox/localhost:30000/biotech-biopython:a8262555…: invalid reference format
```

For a remote build `localhost` is the build pod, not this machine, so
the guess is wrong there anyway. A remote builder picks its own
repository when an image names none.

## Change

- `_get_configured_registry()` returns only a configured registry
(init-time `image.registry`, ambient config, `FLYTE_IMAGE_REGISTRY`).
Images get this at construction (`from_debian_base`, the default image),
so without one configured they stay bare.
- `_get_push_registry()` keeps the localhost fallback, and the build
applies it only for local builds (the existing `_builds_locally`
branch). A missing builder now resolves to `"local"` there, as
`_get_builder` already does, so devbox's local builds still push to
`localhost:30000`.
- `remote_builder` is unchanged: it now receives a bare name unless a
registry is configured.

## Tests

- localhost endpoint + remote builder → `image.registry is None`, built
URI `my-app:…`
- localhost endpoint + local builder → `localhost:30000/my-app:…` at
build time
- configured registry → used at construction and by remote builds
- non-localhost endpoint → unchanged (bare, existing tests)

`tests/flyte/test_image.py` and `tests/flyte/imagebuild/` pass apart
from tests that need a `docker` binary, which fail identically on `main`
in this environment; the two existing
`test_build_applies_configured_push_registry_to_preinit_image` /
`test_build_hard_errors_without_push_registry` tests, which failed on
`main` here because a `None` builder skipped the local-build branch, now
pass. ruff and mypy clean on the changed files.

ENOSPC has been filtered as a user environment problem since FLYTE-SDK-32.
EDQUOT is the same condition reported by a different kind of filesystem --
the usual shape on NFS, and on the shared or managed home directories common
in HPC and university clusters. The user has to free space or get their quota
raised either way; neither is something the SDK can fix.

EDQUOT is looked up with a guarded getattr rather than referenced directly:
it does not exist on Windows, and where it does exist its value is not
portable (122 on Linux, 69 on macOS and the BSDs).

Kept to those two errnos. EACCES, EPERM and EROFS can equally mean the SDK
wrote somewhere it should not have, and EMFILE / ENFILE would hide a file
descriptor leak of our own, so those stay reported.

feat: populate RunSpec.related_to on rerun and in-container flyte.run (#1279)

## Why

The backend added `RunSpec.related_to` (field 15,
`flyteidl2.common.RunIdentifier`): an optional, set-at-creation pointer
to the single parent run this run was derived from (re-run, recover,
clone, or explicit provenance). This PR makes the SDK populate it
automatically at CreateRun time.

## What

Two implicit provenance sources, both resolved by a new
`_Runner._resolve_related_to` helper and stamped in `_apply_overrides`:

1. **Rerun** — every rerun surface (`flyte rerun`, `flyte run
--rerun-from`, `flyte.rerun`, `with_runcontext().rerun()`) converges on
`_Runner.rerun`; the new run points at the run being rerun. The source
id comes from the fetched `action_details.pb2.id.run`, with a fallback
to the `run_name` argument when the fetched id is empty.
2. **In-container `flyte.run`** — when a run is created from inside a
running remote task (`TaskContext.is_in_cluster()`), the new run points
at the invoking run (`flyte.ctx().action`). Local and hybrid executions
are excluded; in a rerun the explicit source wins over the ambient task
context.

### Gating & scope rules

- **Descriptor-gated, silent skip**: the published flyteidl2 (2.0.26)
doesn't ship the field yet. Unlike `recover` — explicitly
user-requested, so its absence raises — implicit provenance silently
skips with a debug log, so reruns keep working on older builds.
- **Same-scope, complete-id only**: per the proto contract `related_to`
is scoped to the new run's org/project/domain, and all four
`RunIdentifier` fields are server-required (buf.validate `min_len=1`).
The resolver stamps only when the source scope (empty fields inherited
from the init config) equals the new run's target scope and the id is
complete — a provenance pointer must never fail run creation.
- **Rerun base-copy path**: the field is unconditionally cleared before
stamping, so a rerun-of-rerun overwrites the inherited grandparent
pointer, and a cross-scope rerun (e.g.
`with_runcontext(project="other").rerun(...)`) clears it rather than
propagating a wrong-scope pointer.

### Tests

- New `tests/flyte/test_related_to.py`: resolver rules (ctx detection,
mode gating, explicit-source precedence, scope mismatch, empty-org,
cfg-scope leniency) — runs on any flyteidl2 build.
- `test_run_runspec_chars.py` / `test_rerun.py`: wire-level tests gated
on `RunSpec.DESCRIPTOR.fields_by_name` — they skip on 2.0.26 and were
verified to pass against the generated protos that ship the field
(stamping, overwrite, clear, name fallback). Two inverse-gated tests pin
the silent no-op on old builds and flag when the gate becomes obsolete.
- `_init_for_testing` gains an `org=` parameter (stamping requires a
non-empty org); existing tests init without org and are unaffected — the
RunSpec snapshot oracle stays byte-for-byte identical.

### Notes for reviewers

- **Backend caveat**: if the server stamps `related_to` itself, a rerun
performed with an *old* SDK fetches the base spec carrying field 15 as
an unknown field, which `CopyFrom` preserves and `ClearField` cannot
touch — the backend should treat client-sent `related_to` at create time
as advisory.
- Follow-ups deliberately out of scope: explicit
`with_runcontext(related_to=...)`, provenance for trigger-created runs.

docsy: add `flyte gen docs --type json` and record plugin provenance at registration (#1470)

Adds a machine-readable output mode to the CLI doc generator, and stops
the generator guessing which plugin provided a command. **The markdown
path is untouched** — generated output is byte-identical apart from the
line documenting the new option.

This is the flyte-sdk half of moving the Hugo-specific rendering of the
CLI reference into the docs repo, where that knowledge belongs. **It is
also a question**, see the end.

## The guess that needs to stop

`get_plugin_info` decides provenance from a command's `__module__`:

```python
if not cmd or not cmd.callback:
    return False, None
module = cmd.callback.__module__
```

A `click.Group` that only dispatches to subcommands has no callback, so
the module is never consulted. `flyte fork` is exactly that shape, and
it shipped into the **open-source** CLI reference — a command requiring
a plugin install and a Union backend, documented for readers who have
neither (#1463 fixed the symptom).

`__module__` describes where code was *written*. The question is what
*shipped* it, and the answer is already in hand at registration time:

```python
for ep in entry_points(group="flyte.plugins.cli.commands"):
    command = ep.load()
    _stamp_distribution(command, ep)   # ep.dist.name
```

So `_plugins.py` records it and `get_command_distribution()` reports it.
No inference anywhere.

## Inheritance is not optional

Only **35** plugin commands are entry points. Four more are defined
*inside* a plugin's own group and carry no stamp:

```
flyte explore volume · flyte undelete cluster · flyte undelete cluster-pool · flyte undelete queue
```

Attributing by entry point alone reports those as core — the same defect
from the other side, and one the `__module__` guess happened to get
right. So provenance inherits from the nearest stamped ancestor. A
plugin subcommand attached to a *core* group (`flyte get api-key`) keeps
its own stamp and is not laundered back to core by its parent.

**Verified against `flyteplugins-union` 0.8.1:** the 39 commands the
JSON reports as plugin-provided are exactly the 39 the renderer gates to
the union variant. No difference in either direction.

## What the JSON says, and what it deliberately does not

```json
{ "path": "flyte create api-key", "name": "api-key", "is_group": false,
  "distribution": "flyteplugins-union",
  "help": "...", "arguments": [{"name": "name", "required": true}],
  "options": [{"opts": ["-p","--project"], "secondary_opts": [], "type": "text",
               "default": null, "help": "Project to which this applies."}] }
```

It reports what the CLI **is**. It takes no view on who should see what
— audience is a decision for the documentation that consumes this, not a
property of the CLI. So there is no grouping by variant, only a
per-command label; and help text is normalised with `inspect.cleandoc`
(undoing click's indentation, an artefact of how the string was written)
but otherwise verbatim: no escaping, no code fencing, no markup.

## Tests

`_gen.py`'s walker has never had a test. That is tolerable while it
lives here — a rename breaks it in the same PR, in front of the person
making the change — and stops being tolerable once anything outside
depends on its output. **Both private types it matches by class-name
string** (`TaskFiles`, `RemoteTaskGroup`) are now pinned, with a failure
message explaining why the walker cares.

20 tests: stamping including the callback-less group that started this;
inheritance in both directions; the emitted shape; help left
unmarked-up; JSON-safe defaults with the build directory stripped; and
the walker declining to descend into `RemoteTaskGroup` or to enumerate a
`FileGroup`'s files.

`tests/cli`: **419 passed**. `ruff check`/`format` clean.
`check-docstrings`: 492 files clean.

## What we would like to know

This is docs-pipeline plumbing, so it is ours to maintain — but the JSON
is a contract between your repo and ours, and that is a request, not a
fait accompli:

1. **Are you willing to treat `--type json` as stable-ish?** Not frozen,
but not reshaped without a heads-up. If not, we should know before
building on it.
2. **Does anything outside our pipeline consume `flyte gen docs --type
markdown`?** We found only `Makefile:115`. If it is genuinely internal,
a later PR would narrow that mode to plain Markdown and move the Hugo
shortcodes out of this repo entirely.
3. **Anything you would rather see in the payload** while it costs
nothing to change?

Happy to adjust the shape to whatever is easiest for you to live with.

fix: validate the Literal-typed fields of artifacts.Metadata at construction

`Metadata.__post_init__` validated `parents` carefully -- length, per-element
type, empty strings -- and said nothing about its other fields. `kind` is
declared `Kind = Literal["model", "data", "generic"]`, but nothing enforces a
Literal at runtime, so `Metadata(name="m", kind="Model")` was accepted, stamped
into `attrs` under the reserved `flyte.io/kind` key, and written to the wire.

`Artifact.kind` then re-checks membership on the way out and falls back to
"generic", which is right for artifacts published by older SDKs or other
writers -- but it means a typo on the write side is discarded in silence. The
artifact is misclassified permanently, nothing raises at either end, and
`Artifact.listall(kind="model")` never returns it.

`name` had the mirror-image gap: `Artifact.create` has always rejected a falsy
name, while the declarative path (`artifacts.new(obj, Metadata(name=""))`)
reached `ProducedArtifact` with an empty one.

Validate both at construction, and share the `kind` check with
`Artifact.create(kind=)` and `Artifact.listall(kind=)` -- the same reason
`_validate_parents` is already shared between the declarative and imperative
paths. The allowed set is derived from the `Kind` alias with `get_args`, so the
check cannot drift from the type.

feat: asyncio.run() works in sync tasks; sync-task calls from async must use .aio (#1472)

Two related changes to how sync tasks and sync-task calls behave.

## 1. `asyncio.run()` now works inside sync tasks

Sync task bodies used to run inside a hidden coroutine on a per-call
helper event loop (`run_sync_with_loop`, from #565). That loop was never
usable — `asyncio.run()` raised "cannot be called from a running event
loop" — it just made the thread look async. Sync bodies now run as plain
sync code on a dedicated daemon thread (`run_sync_in_thread`).
`asyncio.run()` and third-party sync wrappers (e.g. pydantic_ai
`run_sync`) work there now.

## 2. Calling a sync task from async code requires `.aio`

```python
@env.task
def child() -> str: ...

@env.task
async def parent() -> str:
    return child()              # raises SyncTaskCallInAsyncContextError
    return await child.aio()    # correct
```

A blocking call from async code parks the event loop that also runs the
controller failure watch. If the actions service goes down, the process
can never observe it and the pod hangs forever. It now raises
immediately with the fix in the message.

## What breaks

- **Blocking sync-task calls from async code** now raise. Migrate to
`await task.aio(...)`. (In-repo callers updated: one test, two
examples.)
- **Sync task bodies no longer see a running event loop** —
`asyncio.get_running_loop()` raises there. Nothing in-repo relied on it;
the agents plugin bridge doesn't depend on it (docstring updated).
- **`flyte._utils.asyncify.run_sync_with_loop` → `run_sync_in_thread`**
(private; papermill and docker_builder callers updated — plugin releases
should pair with this SDK version).

Sync → sync calls, `flyte.map`, sandbox orchestrators, and syncify-based
sync APIs (`download_sync`, `storage.*`, `flyte.run`) are unaffected:
they never used the caller's loop.

## Verified on a real cluster

Remote run on demo with this branch baked into the image:
https://demo.hosted.unionai.cloud/v2/domain/development/project/ketan/runs/ukf2hnfjhtrpvpbc4dqc
— sync body sees no running loop, `asyncio.run()` returns, sync→sync
blocking call works, `await leaf.aio()` from async works, and a blocking
call from an async body raises `SyncTaskCallInAsyncContextError` with
the `.aio` hint.
`tests/flyte/test_sync_tasks.py::test_sync_task_through_runtime_taskrunner`
covers the same through the real runtime entrypoint (local runs don't go
through taskrunner).

## Companion

`flyteplugins-union` is the only external importer of the renamed
helper: unionai/flyteplugins-union#100 adopts `run_sync_in_thread` with
an `ImportError` fallback, so it loads on both SDK versions.

## Tests

`tests/flyte/test_sync_call_guard.py` (raises from async, `.aio` ok,
sync→sync ok, end-to-end local run),
`tests/flyte/utils/test_asyncify.py` updated for the new semantics. Full
sweep: 4577 passed; 3 environment-dependent failures reproduce without
this diff.

Record serving facts at prefetch, and make the prefetch task registerable (#1405)

## Why are the changes needed?

Union's deploy path reads a `flyte.io/serving` attr off a model artifact
to decide which GPUs it fits on and which engines can load it. **Nothing
wrote that key.** Searching every branch of this repo for it returns no
producer at all, so every model published through the SDK arrived
without it and could not be deployed — a consumer that has existed for a
while, against a producer that never did.

Prefetch is the right place to fix that: it already downloads
`config.json`, and it already receives per-file sizes from the Hub that
it was throwing away.

Separately, `hf_model` builds its environment at call time and ships the
task as a cloudpickle bundle. That is the right shape for a notebook and
the wrong one for a control plane — a console button has no Python
process to run — so there is no way to start a prefetch other than from
Python.

## What changes were proposed in this pull request?

1. **Record serving facts at prefetch.** `_serving_facts` derives what
sizing needs — weight bytes, dtype, layer and head geometry, context
length, architectures, sharding — and `_wrap_as_model_artifact` stamps
it as versioned JSON. Everything is read from the Hub's metadata rather
than from the weights, so the same derivation works before a byte is
downloaded.

2. **Add a registered prefetch task.** `flyte/prefetch/_deployable.py`
declares the same work as an ordinary task, addressable by name and
version, so a backend can bind it to a run in the user's own project —
the shape the remote image builder's `build-image` task already uses.
Both paths call `store_hf_model_task`, so there is one implementation
with two ways to reach it.

### Three details worth reviewing

- **`architectures` is written as a list.** It was being comma-joined
into a scalar, which deserializes as one bogus architecture name and
fails every engine-support lookup.
- **GPT-2-family configs spell their geometry
`n_layer`/`n_head`/`n_embd`**, which transformers reconciles through
each config class's `attribute_map`. Reading the raw JSON sees the
original names, so a missed alias silently zeroes the KV-cache term —
and that *under*-estimates VRAM, the direction that OOMs a deploy rather
than merely wasting a GPU.
- **The registered task is `prefetch.hf_model`, not
`prefetch-hf-model`.** `TaskEnvironment` prefixes task names with the
environment's name; `build-image` keeps its bare name only because it is
a `ContainerTask`.

Deriving the facts is best-effort on purpose: a model that cannot be
measured is still a perfectly good artifact, so a failure publishes
without facts rather than failing a download that may have taken an
hour.

No `HF_TOKEN` secret is attached to the registered environment. Public
repos need none, and naming a secret that does not exist wedges the pod
in `CreateContainerConfigError` with no HuggingFace error to read — an
opaque failure in exactly the first-run case. Callers supply a token per
run instead.

## How was this patch tested?

Against the live Hub: `Qwen3-0.6B` (751M params, 1.5 GB bf16, GQA at 8
KV heads), `Qwen3-32B` (65.5 GB across shards), `gpt2` (legacy config
names, and ships both `.bin` and `.safetensors` without
double-counting), and `bert-base` (no `head_dim` or `kv_heads`, absorbed
by the consumer's fallbacks).

End to end on a local Union backend: the registered task imports
`hf-internal-testing/tiny-random-LlamaForCausalLM`, publishes an
artifact carrying `kind=model` and the facts blob, and the deploy
service then reports it deployable with a populated recommendation.

Unit tests cover the derivations offline, against fixtures rather than
the live Hub: the geometry fields including the GPT-2 aliases and the
nested `text_config`, `architectures` staying a list, absent
`head_dim`/`num_key_value_heads` reported as 0 rather than guessed, the
dtype table and its 2-byte fallback, and both unstreamable verdicts (no
safetensors, and a failed listing — which must degrade rather than
raise). One test pins that the facts land as a single attr key holding
compact JSON rather than ~15 flat attrs, which is what keeps the control
plane's GIN index at one entry for the whole blob.

`_deployable` had no tests; its registered name — the entire contract
for a non-Python caller — is now pinned, along with the
empty-string-means-unset convention, the opt-in secret and the image
override. Its "not imported at the `flyte` level" claim is checked in a
subprocess, because this test session has already imported the module
and an in-process check would always pass.

Adding the raw config to `_lookup_huggingface_model_info`'s return
changed it from a 2-tuple to a 3-tuple, which broke the four existing
tests that unpack it. They now assert on the config as well.

```
$ pytest tests/flyte/prefetch tests/cli
397 passed
```

`ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy src/flyte/prefetch/` and
`check-docstrings` are all clean. Importing `flyte` pulls in no new
modules — `_deployable` stays lazily imported.

## Check all the applicable boxes

- [ ] I updated the documentation accordingly.
- [x] All new and existing tests passed.
- [x] All commits are signed-off.

## Out of scope

Sharded prefetch through the registered task — it needs vLLM, a CUDA
toolchain and GPUs at prefetch time, so it belongs in its own
environment. Revision pinning also stays out: `hf_model` has no
`revision` parameter and always resolves the latest commit, which
becomes the artifact version.

Support local app serving (#628)

# Summary
This PR implements local app serving for AppEnvironment, enabling
developers to serve Flyte apps on localhost for rapid local development
and testing. It introduces a symmetry with the existing
`flyte.with_runcontext(mode="local") ` pattern by adding
`flyte.with_servecontext(mode="local")` for apps.

Key changes:
- New `_LocalApp` class and local serving infrastructure in `_serve.py`
(server-decorator, command/subprocess, and FastAPI-based apps)
- `AppEnvironment.endpoint` now transparently resolves to localhost when
the app is served locally
`ephemeral_ctx` / `ephemeral_ctx_sync` context managers on both
_LocalApp and remote App for scoped activate/deactivate lifecycle
- `_LocalApp` `activate` and `deactivate` methods mirror the methods in
remote `App` object.
- `activate`: if the server is not running locally, starts it, and
optionally waits for the server to be active.
  - `deactivate`: stop the server locally
- `--local` flag on the flyte serve CLI command
- Signal handler and atexit cleanup to ensure child processes are torn
down on `Ctrl-C` or process exit
- 6 example scripts and comprehensive unit tests

extras: public model streamer; vLLM "flyte-streaming" load format

SafeTensorsStreamer (flyte.app.extras._model_loader) is reachable only
through VLLMAppEnvironment / SGLangAppEnvironment, driven by env vars read
at import. Its one public method runs an asyncio.Runner, so it raises
inside a running event loop -- every async task body -- and a reusable
task cannot use it in an alru_cache'd bootstrap.

flyte.extras.model_streamer exposes it (torch stays a lazy import, so
flyte.extras and the import profile are unchanged):

- ModelStreamer: async stream(), a thread-backed stream_sync() that works
  from any thread (bounded hand-off, errors re-raised, clean early stop),
  state_dict(), load_into() for any nn.Module built on meta with
  empty_weights() (assign semantics, re-ties HF tied weights, strict
  check), download_metadata() for config/tokenizer.
- load_hf_model(): transformers model built on meta, weights streamed onto
  the device, base_model_prefix reconciled like from_pretrained.

flyteplugins-vllm gains flyteplugins.vllm.model_streamer: load_format
"flyte-streaming", registered in every vLLM process through the
vllm.general_plugins entry point (engine core and TP workers included) and
configured through model_loader_extra_config instead of env vars;
engine_args() builds the LLM kwargs. Verified against vLLM 0.26.0: plugin
discovery registers it, the default loader's extra-config check sees only
its own keys, and get_all_weights streams every tensor from a thread with
a running loop.

Examples: examples/ml/batch_inference_streamed.py (the
batch_inference_saturate pattern with the model streamed into the GPU) and
examples/ml/embed_streamed.py (load_hf_model).

  so writes return at local-disk speed and chunk uploads run in the
  background. Drained on ``commit()`` (umount). If the pod dies before

  storage.

fix(logging): include log level in console log lines

Console log records were formatted with `fmt="%(message)s"`, so lines
emitted through the plain StreamHandler carried no severity (WARNING/
DEBUG/...). This is the path taken by reusable container tasks: they run
in-cluster, where get_rich_handler() returns None, so the rich handler
(which renders the level in its own column) is never used and the level
was dropped entirely.

Add a shared DEFAULT_CONSOLE_FORMAT = "%(levelname)s %(message)s" and
point every console ContextFormatter call site at it. The rich and JSON
handlers already emit the level, so they're left unchanged to avoid
double-printing it.

Import build/deploy, the dataframe engine and JSON-schema tooling on first use

A task pod imports flyte (and through a plugin, flyte.io) before running
any user code, and paid for machinery a running task never touches:
- flyte/__init__ eagerly imported _build and _deploy (image building,
  deployment) — now resolved on first use via module __getattr__ (PEP 562).
- flyte.io imported the structured-dataset engine to export DataFrame and
  PARQUET (~0.2s with its handlers); File and Dir do not need it. DataFrame
  and PARQUET now load on first use; importing them still registers the
  transformer as before.
- TypeEngine.lazy_import_transformers imported that engine unconditionally
  on the first transformer lookup. It now does so only if the engine is
  already imported (any DataFrame annotation imports it) or pandas/pyarrow
  are, i.e. whenever its handlers could apply.
- mashumaro.jsonschema (~85ms) is only needed to describe a dataclass's
  schema; PydanticSchemaPlugin is now built on first use (still importable
  by name). markdown_it is imported where markdown is rendered.

Measured (alternating fresh processes on a loaded host, minimum of 8):
  import flyte                               0.893s -> 0.622s
  import flyte; import flyteplugins.union.io  0.553s -> 0.427s
  import an agent task module + convert its real inputs
                                              0.928s -> 0.769s (min of 6)
Public names are unchanged; tests check that light imports skip the heavy
modules and that the lazy names still resolve.

fix: show distinct sys.modules keys in duplicate-env error message (#1074)

## Summary
- When the same file gets loaded twice under different import paths (the
classic src/ layout dual-import scenario), `_check_duplicate_env` told
the user the env was *"imported twice under different module names
('multi_status' and 'multi_status')"* — the two displayed names were
identical, defeating the entire purpose of the message.
- Root cause: `_find_env_module` returned the module object, and the
error formatter read `module.__name__`. But when the SDK's path-based
loader creates a module via
`importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(file_path.stem, ...)`, both
module objects end up with the *same* `__name__` (the file stem), even
though they sit at different `sys.modules` keys.
- Switch `_find_env_module` to iterate `sys.modules.items()` and return
the `(key, module)` tuple. The error message now uses the sys.modules
keys — the distinguishing import paths the user can actually act on.

## Sentry issues
Fixes [FLYTE-SDK-2S](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7481668212/)
(`ValueError: Environment 'multi_status_demo' ... imported twice under
different module names ('multi_status' and 'multi_status')`)

## Test plan
- [x] New regression test
`test_check_duplicate_env_dual_import_shows_distinct_sys_modules_keys`
constructs two modules that intentionally share `__name__` but sit at
different sys.modules keys (the exact shape from the Sentry crash) and
asserts the error message shows both distinct keys
- [x] All existing `_check_duplicate_env` / dual-import tests still pass
- [x] `make fmt` clean

fix: don't report a disk quota as an SDK crash (FLYTE-SDK-8D) (#1578)

## What

Filter `OSError(EDQUOT)` — "Disk quota exceeded" — out of Sentry,
alongside the `ENOSPC` that has been filtered since FLYTE-SDK-32.

## Why

```
OSError: [Errno 122] Disk quota exceeded
  culprit: tarfile in copyfileobj
  release: 2.7.2
```

`create_bundle` writes the code-bundle tarball to local disk during
`flyte deploy`. On a filesystem that rations space **per user** rather
than running out of it globally, that write fails with `EDQUOT` instead
of `ENOSPC` — the usual shape on NFS, and on the shared or managed home
directories common in HPC and university clusters.

It is the same condition and the same remedy as disk-full: free some
space, or get the quota raised. Neither is something the SDK can do
anything about, and `ENOSPC` was filtered on exactly that reasoning. The
only reason `EDQUOT` still reports is that it is a different number.

## The change

```python
_USER_ENVIRONMENT_OSERROR_ERRNOS: frozenset[int] = frozenset(
    code for code in (errno.ENOSPC, getattr(errno, "EDQUOT", None)) if code is not None
)
```

The guarded lookup is not decoration. `EDQUOT` does not exist on Windows
— CPython's `errnomodule.c` defines these constants under `#ifdef` — so
a direct `errno.EDQUOT` would raise `AttributeError` at **import** of
`flyte._sentry` there, which would be a considerably worse bug than the
one being fixed. And where it does exist its value is not portable: 122
on Linux, 69 on macOS and the BSDs. Both sides of the comparison come
from the same machine, so looking it up is also the only correct way to
match.

## Why only this errno

Tested the predicate across the whole corpus first: 73 unresolved issues
contain exactly four `OSError`-family events, with errnos 98
(`EADDRINUSE`, PKCE bind — covered by #1199), 2 (`FileNotFoundError`,
FLYTE-SDK-8B), no-errno (`libgomp.so.1` missing in a user image), and
this one. Adding `EDQUOT` silences FLYTE-SDK-8D and nothing else.

The neighbouring errnos are deliberately left out, and the docstring
says why: `EACCES`, `EPERM` and `EROFS` can equally mean the SDK wrote
somewhere it should not have, and `EMFILE` / `ENFILE` would hide a
file-descriptor leak of our own.

## Tests

Three tests in `tests/flyte/test_sentry.py`: the direct `EDQUOT`, the
same through a `RuntimeSystemError` cause chain (how the bundle writer
wraps it), and a guard that the errno set still contains `ENOSPC`, holds
only ints, and excludes `EACCES` / `EPERM` / `EMFILE` — which also pins
the Windows-safe construction.

`tests/flyte/test_sentry.py`: 82 passed. `make fmt`, `ruff check`,
`mypy`, `ty check` and `make check-docstrings` all clean.

Adds a new `flyteplugins-llamacpp` plugin for serving GGUF models with
[llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp)'s `llama-server`
behind Flyte Apps, adapted from `internal-union-apps/llm-service` and
following the existing vllm/sglang plugin structure.

- **`LlamaCppAppEnvironment`**: OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`/v1`) +
embedded Web UI. Serves weights from object storage (`model_path` as
remote path / `RunOutput` / `ArtifactValue`, downloaded and mounted) or
straight from a Hugging Face GGUF repo (`model_hf_path` → `--hf-repo`,
downloaded by llama-server at startup). Supports speculative decoding
via `draft_model_path` / `draft_model_hf_path` (→ `--model-draft` /
`--hf-repo-draft`), with tuning through `extra_args`.
- **`llama-cpp-fserve` shim** (console script): the GGUF filename inside
a mounted directory is unknown at deploy time, so the shim rewrites
`--model-dir`/`--draft-model-dir` into concrete
`--model`/`--model-draft` paths at startup (first-shard aware for
sharded models) and execs `llama-server`.
- **`build_llama_cpp_image`**: llama.cpp has no GPU pip wheel, so the
default image compiles `llama-server` from source with CUDA 12.8 and the
embedded SvelteKit Web UI (Node build), keeping the internal app's
stub-linking and base64 RUN-script workarounds. Knobs: `cuda_arch` (fat
binaries), `repo`/`ref` pinning, and `cuda=False` for a CPU-only image.

Not carried over from the internal app: the preset catalog, subdomain
derivation, and deployment-config machinery (internal concerns, not
plugin API).

CI needs no changes: unit tests, lint, and publish workflows
auto-discover plugins.

## Test plan

- [x] 39 unit tests (`make unit_test_plugins` with
`FLYTE_PLUGIN=plugins/llamacpp`): env validation, argv construction, HF
vs mounted weights, draft models, shell quoting, `clone_with`, and shim
GGUF resolution.
- [x] ruff check/format clean; pre-commit (mypy, ty) passed.
- [ ] Deploy smoke test on a live cluster.

feat(github): form-encoded deliveries, GitHub App installation tokens, installation events (#1541)

Follow-up to #1540 (Slack): the same exercise for the GitHub plugin —
study how the internal agents actually use GitHub, and close the gaps in
`flyteplugins-github` that would block them (or any similar agent) from
adopting it.

## What the agents actually do with GitHub

- **Cally** (`oncall_agent/github_app.py`) holds no PAT: it
authenticates as a GitHub App and mints 1-hour installation tokens for
read-only clones, with a `GH_TOKEN` fallback and a
degrade-to-`None`-with-a-logged-reason contract. Its chat app
(`opencode_chat/mint_gh_token.py`) carries a **verbatim copy** of that
logic, with a docstring noting the copy exists because "the two projects
ship as separate code bundles and share no package."
- **Nodey** (`node_changer_agent.py::get_github_app_token`) is a **third
copy** of the same minting flow — with the app id and installation id
hardcoded and no error handling — feeding clones, pushes, and `gh pr
create`.
- **Engy** (`webhook_app.py`) runs the one hand-rolled GitHub webhook
receiver: `issue_comment.created` carrying a `/swe_agent fix` command,
plus `issues.labeled`. Its setup instructions have to warn users to
switch the webhook's content type to `application/json` — because
GitHub's *Add webhook* form **defaults** to
`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, which naive receivers (and this
plugin, until now) choke on.

## Gaps closed

1. **Form-encoded deliveries.** `parse()` only accepted JSON bodies; a
webhook left on GitHub's default content type wraps the JSON in a
`payload=` form field and every delivery would have failed. `parse` now
sniffs and unwraps both shapes into the same `WebhookEvent` — same
`qualified_type`, same dedupe key — so a redelivery on the other content
type is still a redelivery. `verify` already covered both, since the
HMAC signs the raw body.
2. **GitHub App installation tokens** (`[auth]` extra, PyJWT[crypto]).
`mint_installation_token()` + `clone_url()` replace the three per-agent
copies: env-var configuration (`GITHUB_APP_ID` /
`GITHUB_APP_INSTALLATION_ID` / `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`),
explicit-argument override, `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` fallbacks for
one-secret-at-a-time migration, and Cally's degrade-to-`None` contract
so half-configured deployments keep working unauthenticated instead of
crashing.
3. **`Installation` / `InstallationRepositories` event constants.**
Every GitHub App webhook receives these unconditionally, and all three
agent deployments authenticate as Apps; they normalize with no resource
and dedupe per delivery.

## Deliberately not done

- No `workflow_job` / `deployment_status` / `status` constants — no
agent touches them; raw strings still work if one ever does.
- No slash-command-style parsing: engy's `/swe_agent fix` trigger is
just an `issue_comment` body, which the existing normalization already
carries verbatim in `event.payload` (verified by a test modeled on
engy's exact trigger payload).
- No PyGithub wrapping beyond the existing review gate — unchanged
plugin boundary, now stated as "the parts every GitHub agent otherwise
duplicates."

## Validation

- `uv run --frozen pytest tests/ -q` — 41 passed (new: form-encoded
parity with the engy-shaped `/swe_agent fix` payload,
signature-over-form-body, rejection of a form body with no `payload`
field, installation-event dedupe, and Cally's
JWT-verifies/fallback/outage/clone-URL matrix against a real RSA key
with the HTTP seam monkeypatched).
- `python examples/github_webhooks.py --local` now also replays the
sample delivery form-encoded and prints it landing on the identical
dedupe key.
- `uvx ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean; conformance test
unchanged and passing.

connector, Enroot for the compute nodes, object storage for the job -- and
how to read a failure from the generated sbatch script.

Glob already recurses into subdirectories via pathlib.Path.glob — patterns
like Glob("**/*.bed") or Glob("./**/*") collect files at any depth, while a
plain Glob("*") stays single-level. This behavior was undocumented and
untested.

- Document globstar support in the Glob docstring, the create() outputs
  docstring, and the lists/globs example.
- Add 4 tests to TestUnpackOutputs covering recursive matching, the ./**/*
  form, shallow default behavior, and directory exclusion.

No production behavior change.

Move the connector's output upload off the GetTask RPC

`get` was doing the transfer inline, which cannot work: GetTask has a deadline --
`defaultTimeout`, 10s unless a deployment raises it, and no deployment does -- and
a connector-side upload reads over SSH and writes to object storage on the
connector's bandwidth. Measured from the connector pod on a real cluster, the SSH
read alone runs at 6.4 MB/s, so the 10s budget covers roughly 60 MB one-way,
below the 100 MB ceiling this plugin documents as its default.

Past that the deadline cancels the call mid-transfer, the platform records a sync
failure and polls again, the next poll starts the transfer from the beginning,
and after maxSystemFailures the task fails as infrastructure trouble without ever
reporting why. A large output would have looped and then failed opaquely.

The transfer now runs as a task on the connector's own event loop, which the
RPC's cancellation does not reach, and `get` reports RUNNING with a message
naming the outputs until it finishes. Reporting SUCCEEDED any earlier would hand
a downstream task a URI with nothing behind it.

Details that matter more than the mechanism:

Outputs the job uploaded itself stay inline. That work is a bounded existence
check, and deferring it would cost every script task an extra poll interval for
nothing.

The transport cache is per job, so a repeat poll joins the transfer already in
flight rather than starting a second copy of it. A finished result is kept for
half an hour so a late poll is answered from it, then forgotten -- the connector
is long-lived and sees every job, so this cannot grow without bound.

`delete` cancels a transfer in flight. An aborted task should not leave the
connector still moving its bytes.

The "attach to the running job" hint is now gated on the Slurm job's own phase
rather than the reported one, since there is no allocation to attach to while the
connector is uploading. Caught by watching the poll sequence, not by a test.

Tests poll to a terminal phase the way the platform does, which is a truer shape
than the single call they used before.

fix: correct broken uvx invocations in MCP examples

The local-setup commands in both MCP examples did not work, in three separate
ways. Each one fails for anyone who copies it.

1. `uvx --with "flyte[mcp]" flyte-mcp` resolves the package from the *command
   name* (`uvx <cmd>` is shorthand for `uvx --from <cmd> <cmd>`), and `flyte-mcp`
   is a real but unrelated third-party package on PyPI. Following the example
   installed and ran someone else's MCP server, with flyte[mcp] attached only as
   an extra dependency. Use --from, as the neighbouring line already did.

2. The commands did not pass `--transport stdio`, so a client launching them as a
   stdio subprocess got a streamable-HTTP server writing to a port instead.

3. `uvx --from . flyte-mcp` omits the `[mcp]` extra, so the repo-checkout path
   exited with "mcp is not installed. Please install 'flyte[mcp]'". Now
   `uvx --from ".[mcp]" flyte-mcp`.

Verified by running the corrected invocation end to end: it completes an MCP
initialize handshake and returns the expected tool list.

Also documents that MCPAppEnvironment.run_stdio_async delegates to FastMCP's
method of the same name, which reads as self-recursion at a glance.

timeout during a long image build -- the caller saw the stream end, treated
the action as finished, and read a still-running phase as a failure
(remote_builder raises ImageBuildError on a build that is fine).

TCP keepalive does not hold such a connection open (the probes carry no data)
and pyqwest exposes no HTTP/2 PING knob, so reconnect on the client instead.
The stream is idempotent -- the server re-sends current state -- so the watch
now re-establishes it until the action is done. Backoff resets whenever a
stream delivers an update and doubles to 30s only while streams keep ending
empty. CANCELED and non-retryable errors behave as before.

docs(examples): browser-use agent powered by Lightpanda (#1351)

Adds `examples/agents/lightpanda_browser_agent.py` — an agent that
browses the live web through [Lightpanda](https://lightpanda.io), a
headless browser engine written in Zig. It speaks CDP (so Playwright
drives it unchanged) but ships as a single static binary with no
rendering stack, which makes it light enough to install *into the task
image* rather than run as a separate browser service.

### What it shows

- **Browser in the task image.** `with_apt_packages(...)` +
`with_commands(...)` install the Lightpanda binary at build time, so
each browser tool is a durable `@browser_env.task` running in its own
container, separate from the lightweight chat-UI app. Follows the
existing `flyte_agent/agent_chat_ui.py` pattern (parent entrypoint task
+ `passthrough_auth=True`).
- **Five tools:** `read_page`, `extract_links`, `extract_elements`
(CSS), `evaluate_on_page` (JS escape hatch), and `read_pages` — a
concurrent multi-page read, since Lightpanda serves one page per CDP
connection and parallelism comes from opening several.
- **An A/B switch:** `LIGHTPANDA_MODE=cloud` drives Lightpanda Cloud
over `wss://` instead of the in-container binary, no other code change.
Every tool returns `elapsed_ms` and `engine` so the two are comparable.
- **`--check`** exercises the whole browser path locally against live
sites, no cluster needed.

### Verified

Deployed and run on a live cluster — the agent browsed `lightpanda.io`
and reported real in-pod timings from `read_pages`: **1236 ms wall vs
1917 ms serial** across two pages.

Two non-obvious runtime details are handled and commented, since neither
is documented upstream:

- The page that arrives with a CDP connection cannot be navigated — it
hangs until timeout. The context is reused (a second one is rejected)
but the page must be freshly created.
- Entering `async_playwright()` per tool call spawns a Node driver and
cost ~3 s/call; hoisting it to a per-container handle took calls from
3266 ms to 137 ms.

Also worth knowing for anyone copying the image recipe:
`ca-certificates` is mandatory or every HTTPS navigation fails with
`PeerFailedVerification`, and `playwright install` is *not* needed since
we connect over CDP rather than launching a browser.

### Caveats

Lightpanda has no renderer, so screenshots and PDFs are impossible — the
agent's instructions tell it to say so rather than pretend. It is Beta
software; the image pulls the `nightly` release asset, which you may
want to pin for anything long-lived.

explicitly handle discriminator + oneOf for pydantic Unions (#1202)

This pull request refactors the logic for generating attribute lists
from dataclass JSON schemas, improving the handling of `$ref` references
and discriminated unions in Pydantic-generated schemas. It also updates
dependency recency exclusion for the `flyte` package.

### Schema processing improvements

* Refactored the order of handling for `$ref` references and
discriminated unions in
`generate_attribute_list_from_dataclass_json_mixin`, ensuring that
non-dict property values and discriminated unions with both
`discriminator` and `oneOf` are handled before `$ref` logic. This makes
the type inference more robust and fixes edge cases with Pydantic v2
schemas.
* Moved the `$ref` handling block to after the checks for non-dict
property values and discriminated unions, restoring and improving the
previous logic for nested models and custom types.

### Dependency management

* Added `flyte = "0 days"` to the `[tool.uv.exclude-newer-package]`
section in `pyproject.toml`, ensuring that the latest `flyte` package
releases are picked up immediately, similar to other Flyte-related
packages.

feat(slack): interactivity, slash commands, notify helpers, and hitl-backed approvals (#1540)

## Why

Internal Slack agents like
[Cally](https://github.com/unionai/unionai-agents/tree/main/cally) and
[Nodey](https://github.com/unionai/unionai-agents/tree/main/nodey) run
hand-rolled slack_bolt servers and hand-rolled outbound API calls. This
PR closes the gaps that keep them off the plugin, in three layers.

## 1. Receive everything Slack sends (`_provider.py`)

The provider only parsed Events API JSON; interactivity payloads (Block
Kit buttons, shortcuts, modals) and slash commands arrive form-encoded
and 400'd. Now:

- a block action registers as `block_actions.<action_id>` (Cally's
`send_to_customer`), a shortcut as its `callback_id`, a slash command as
`command.<name>` (Nodey's `/hi-nodey`)
- full Slack JSON (`actions`, `container`, `message`, `response_url`)
rides in `event.payload`
- interactions dedupe per click (`action_ts`), redeliveries are no-ops;
commands key on `trigger_id`
- `handshake()` answers the `ssl_check` probe; `verify()` unchanged (v0
HMAC signs raw bytes for all three shapes)
- new `events.Interaction` / `events.Command` constants; runnable
`examples/slack_interactions.py` with `--local` signed replay

## 2. Send messages (`notify`)

Nodey ships a fifty-line `send_notification` task of raw `requests`;
Cally re-implements posting per handler. `notify` provides
`post`/`update`/`delete` (bot token via `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`),
`respond(response_url)` which needs **no token** (the zero-setup way for
a launched task to answer the click that launched it), and a deployable
`notify.env` + `send` task so only one environment holds the token.

## 3. Approvals on core `new_condition` (`approval`)

The pattern both agents build by hand — post buttons, pause, resume on
click — becomes:

```python
decision = await approval.request.aio("C0DEPLOYS", "Deploy release-42 to prod?")   # in a task
approval.register(app_env)                                                        # in the webhook app
```

`request` parks the run on a core `flyte.new_condition`; the clicked
button carries the run, action, and condition names, so the webhook
handler resolves it with `flyte.remote.Condition.get(...).signal(...)` —
no configuration on the app side — then swaps the buttons for a
"*approve* — decided by @who" line. Same mechanism the GitHub plugin's
review gate uses. Because it's an ordinary condition, the prompt is
**also** answerable from the Flyte UI, so an approval nobody clicks in
Slack is never stuck, and `timeout=` is the core contract
(`ConditionTimedoutError`). No extra install needed.

## Ergonomics

- **`on_event(..., action=...)`** (core `_app.py`): the user-defined
half of an event — a button's `action_id`, a command's name — is your
vocabulary, not Slack's, so no constant can spell it.
`on_event(events.Interaction.BLOCK_ACTIONS, action="approve_deploy")`
and `on_event(events.Command, action="/deploy")` now compose it; an
`EventType` class means its `ANY`, and a leading `/` is dropped. Raw
qualified strings still work.
- **Typed payload views** (`payloads`): nested TypedDicts over
`event.payload` so
`payloads.block_actions(event)["actions"][0]["value"]` autocompletes.
Casts, not validation.
- Handler `event` args annotated `event: WebhookEvent` throughout
examples and docs.

## Validation

- 24 slack tests pass, including the shared provider conformance
harness; 51 core webhook tests pass
- `notify` tested against an `httpx.MockTransport`; the decision handler
against events built by the real parser (including condition lookup args
and the already-signaled/timed-out case)
- end-to-end through `WebhookAppEnvironment`: signed Cally/Nodey-shaped
deliveries dispatch correctly, unsigned refused 401, JSON Events API
path unchanged
- ruff + pre-commit (fmt/mypy/ty/uvlock) clean; the deprecated
`flyteplugins-hitl` plugin is left untouched by this branch

## Notes

Slack expects interactivity/command acks within 3s; the README says to
do nothing slower than `run_once.aio` in handlers. A follow-up worth its
own PR: an early-ack option in the core webhook framework.

Add a third benchmark arm so "could System 2 fill that schema itself?" is measurable

The with/without comparison in examples/typesafe_ai could not answer its own
strongest counter-argument. It varied three things at once — who answers the
atomic questions, whether the verdict is composed in code or in a prompt, and
whether the pipeline may abstain — so a win for Jev was unattributable between
them, and several scoring choices leaned the same way.

Add `system2_structured`: System 2 answers exactly the battery Jev answers,
against exactly the criteria Jev is given, and runs through the same derive(),
the same confidence gate, the same tools and the same prose prompt. Both composed
arms call one shared `_compose_and_finish` rather than two copies, so nothing
downstream of the battery can drift and confound the comparison. The matrix now
supports two independent readings: with-Jev vs structured isolates the answerer,
structured vs without isolates what moving composition into Python is worth with
the model held fixed.

Level the specification and the scoring:

- Criteria parity. Jev's battery carries NoulCriteria(true/false), full label and
  tool descriptions and every severity tier; System 2 previously got bare label
  keys and one-line questions, so it was graded against a rubric it had never
  seen. Both System 2 arms now get the same material via _battery_spec().
- temperature=0 for every System 2 call, so the decision-stability metric
  measures the model rather than the gateway's default sampler.
- Lenient boolean counting, with the strict count reported beside it as a
  "format gap" — a signal answered "yes" instead of true is a decoder quirk, not
  a failure to analyse the input.
- SYSTEM2_BATTERY_MAX_TOKENS 4096 -> 8192, and finish_reason/stop_reason is now
  captured, so a battery truncated at the ceiling is no longer scored the same as
  one the model declined to answer.
- New `coverage` metric. `success` demands four fields at once and an abstention
  produces none of them, so an arm that escalates everything scored 0% while
  doing exactly what it was designed to do.

Two asymmetries are kept deliberately and flagged in the report: the structured
arm runs the verify pass through System 2 and is billed for it rather than
looking cheaper for skipping work, and the two gates are not the same quantity —
Jev's confidence is calibrated, the LLM's is self-reported, which makes their
routing split a calibration test rather than an accuracy one.

logic_check.py gains a second offline proof: a perfect System 2 answer sheet
derives the identical label, tool and routing tier as a perfect Jev battery on
all 36 cases, including mixed boolean spellings. Without it a lossy adapter could
handicap the challenger and the benchmark would confirm its own hypothesis.

The published results table is marked stale — every change above moved the
baseline it was measured against, and it has no third-arm column.

feat: add user-facing logger as flyte.logger  (#1027)

## Motivation
Users couldn't see task logs because flyte.logger pointed to the
internal SDK logger (WARNING default), silently dropping user log calls.
The internal and user-facing loggers needed to be separated.

 ## Summary                                                             
- Added user_logger in _logging.py ("flyte.user", INFO default, no
[flyte] prefix) and exported it as flyte.logger
- Internal SDK logger stays private in _logging.py, imported directly
via from flyte._logging import logger in SDK code
- Added --user-log-level CLI flag and USER_LOG_LEVEL env var to control
user log level independently of -v
- Threaded user_log_level through init_from_config → init →
_initialize_logger → initialize_logger so the CLI flag survives
  re-initialization
                                        
## Test Plan
                                                                      
  - `uv run pytest tests/user_api/test_logging.py -v`
  - Manual verification with examples/basics/user_logging.py:
### INFO visible, DEBUG suppressed
`flyte run --local examples/basics/user_logging.py process --name hello
--iterations 3`
                                                                      
  ### DEBUG visible
`flyte --user-log-level debug run --local
examples/basics/user_logging.py process --name hello --iterations 3`

  ### Structured JSON output
`flyte --log-format json run --local examples/basics/user_logging.py
process --name hello --iterations 3`

fix: auto-size multipart parts for File uploads (from_local_sync + hashed from_local)

File.from_local_sync uploaded via raw fs.open(remote, "wb"), and File.from_local
with a HashMethod streamed through storage.put_stream with the writer's fixed
10 MiB buffer. On obstore-backed filesystems each buffer becomes one multipart
part, so a single file was capped at ~97.6 GiB (10,000-part S3 limit) -- the
same class of bug #1462 fixed for Dir.from_local_sync, at 2x the threshold.

- File.from_local_sync (no hash / precomputed hash): syncify(storage.put),
  which auto-sizes the part per file. Mirrors Dir.from_local_sync (#1462).
- put_stream gains size_hint=; when the hinted size would exceed the part
  limit at the default buffer, chunk_size is scaled up. Smaller streams are
  untouched.
- New _upload_hashed helper shared by from_local and from_local_sync (via
  syncify) so both hashed paths pass the file size as size_hint.

DataFrame is intentionally left alone: its encoders write through
pandas/pyarrow file-likes with no size known up front, and a single >97 GiB
in-memory parquet frame is not a realistic path today.

fix: raise InvalidImageNameError for unknown image ref in deploy

When a user references an image name in a TaskEnvironment that isn't declared
in their config, `_build_images` raised a bare `ValueError`. During
`flyte deploy`/`flyte run` this is captured and leaks into Sentry as if it were
an SDK crash (FLYTE-SDK-4C), even though it's a user-config mistake.

Raise the purpose-built `InvalidImageNameError` (a `RuntimeUserError`) instead.
This is already filtered by `flyte/_sentry.py:_is_user_error` and gives the user
a clearly-typed, actionable error. The existing test is updated to assert the
typed exception (the message assertions are unchanged).

A "<model> shared" device requests time-sliced (or MPS) capacity, a
share of one physical GPU on a node pool that advertises the shared
accelerator for that model, so several tasks can run on the same GPU at
once. A plain "<model>" request never lands on such a pool. A shared
device takes no partition, and it works in the Resources string form too
(gpu="T4 shared:1"). The SDK sends the device name as written. The
shared names keep the space, unlike the underscore device names, because
the backend accelerator mapping uses that spelling. These devices need a
backend whose accelerator mapping includes the shared names, which comes
with flyteorg/flyte#8163 (https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte/pull/8163).

Three short examples are added under examples/accelerators. Each one
only sets the GPU request, and the backend's accelerator and partition
node selectors do the rest.

- mig_slice.py runs a task on one 1g.24gb slice of an RTX PRO 6000.
- mig_mixed.py runs two 1g.24gb tasks and one 2g.48gb task, which fit on
one GPU under the MIG strategy mixed with the all-balanced layout.
- gpu_shared.py runs three tasks that share one T4 through gpu="T4
shared:1".

Make action watch resilient to transient stream interruptions

The run/action watch rode a single server stream and treated any end of
that stream as authoritative: a ConnectError(CANCELED) was swallowed, a
clean close was indistinguishable from completion, and transport errors
like pyqwest.StreamError ("Error reading content", FLYTE-SDK-6H)
propagated and killed the wait. Proxies and load balancers reset
long-lived HTTP/2 streams routinely, so waiting on a slow action (e.g. a
remote image build) could crash mid-wait or silently return while the
action was still running - which the image builder then misreported as
"Build failed" even though the linked run was green.

ActionDetails.watch now re-subscribes with exponential backoff on
transient failures (CANCELED/UNAVAILABLE/DEADLINE_EXCEEDED,
OS-level connection drops and timeouts, pyqwest.StreamError) and on
clean closes before a terminal phase. Only consecutive failed
subscriptions count against the reconnect budget - any delivered update
resets it - so long watches survive periodic proxy resets indefinitely
while an unreachable backend still fails fast. The generator now only
ends at a terminal phase or raises, which fixes every caller of
run.wait/Action.wait including the remote image builder.

This pull request introduces a robust retry mechanism for file uploads
in the `src/flyte/remote/_data.py` module. The main improvement is the
addition of an exponential backoff strategy for handling transient
network and server errors during file uploads, replacing the previous
single-attempt upload logic. This enhances reliability, especially in
unstable network conditions.

* Added a new `_upload_with_retry` async function that uploads files
using exponential backoff and retries on transient network errors and
retryable HTTP status codes (408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504). This
function logs retries and raises a `RuntimeSystemError` if all attempts
fail.
* Introduced a custom `_RetryableUploadError` exception and a helper
function `_is_retryable_status_code` to distinguish between retryable
and non-retryable HTTP errors.

**Integration with file upload flow:**

* Updated the `_upload_single_file` function to use `_upload_with_retry`
instead of directly uploading the file in a single attempt, ensuring all
uploads benefit from the new retry logic.
* Refactored header preparation and removed redundant file open/close
logic in `_upload_single_file`, delegating the upload responsibility to
the new retry-enabled function.
