feat(cli): add --recover (rerun) and --recover-from (run) (#1237)

Adds the recovery surface to the CLI and un-gates it end to end
(ENG26-830).

```bash
# Recover from the run being rerun (fetched code, reuse its succeeded actions):
flyte rerun ul56wcvgqrb9vzhzz5l2 --recover

# Recover a fresh run with NEW local code from a prior run:
flyte run main.py main --recover-from ul56wcvgqrb9vzhzz5l2

# Force named actions to re-execute even though they succeeded in the source run:
flyte rerun ul56wcvgqrb9vzhzz5l2 --recover --force-rerun-action a3 --force-rerun-action a7
```

Both map to `with_runcontext(recover=...)`: `--recover` (bool) recovers
from the run being rerun; `--recover-from <run>` (string) recovers a
fresh `run()` from a named prior run. Recovery reuses the prior run's
succeeded actions and re-runs only what failed or changed (remote-only;
`--local` is rejected). `--force-rerun-action` (repeatable, maps to
`with_runcontext(recover_force_rerun_actions=[...])` →
`RunSpec.recover.force_rerun_actions`) forces named actions to
re-execute anyway; a listed parent re-enqueues its children (list them
too to force the whole subtree), unknown names are ignored.

Since the original draft:

- Merged main (#1236 landed there and evolved: `related_to` provenance,
`run_base_dir`, image-cache seeding).
- Reworked to the wire contract that actually merged in
flyteorg/flyte#7615: a recovery run is `RunSpec.relation = {related_to:
<run>, relation_type: RELATION_TYPE_RECOVER}`; `RunSpec.recover` carries
only optional extras (`force_rerun_actions`) and stays unset. There is
no `Recover.run_id`.
- Bumped flyteidl2 to 2.0.28 (pyproject, rs_controller pyproject +
Cargo, uv.lock), which opens the runtime gate — the
`NotImplementedError` path only triggers on older flyteidl2 builds.
- Treat `ACTION_PHASE_RECOVERED` (10) as terminal/success everywhere
phases are classified: python controller (`Action.is_terminal`, covering
both watch snapshot and live updates), rust controller
(`is_action_terminal` + crate bump — 2.0.27 dropped/panicked on unknown
phase 10), `Run.wait()`/`watch` done-checks, `flyte.models.ActionPhase`,
and TUI display. Without this, recovered children never resolve and the
run hangs re-opening `WatchForUpdates` (reproduced on devbox
2026-07-16). On resolution the child's `output_uri` points at the source
run's outputs and is consumed as-is.
- Skew-tolerant phase handling: bindings that predate
`ACTION_PHASE_RECOVERED` (e.g. a stale task-image venv) no longer kill
the run — the wire value (10) is used as a `getattr` fallback, and
phase-name rendering goes through a helper that never raises on unknown
enum values.

Recovery never reads the global cache — `overwrite_cache` /
`cache_lookup_scope` are orthogonal.

Needs the actions-service recovery logic (ENG26-828) for end-to-end
behavior.

fix(ci): run twine outside the project venv when publishing plugins

twine 7.0.0 does `from packaging import errors`, and `packaging.errors`
only exists in packaging >= 26.2. The plugin publish jobs installed twine
into a bare venv (getting packaging 26.2), then ran `uv run python -m
build`, which syncs the *project* environment. Because twine is not a
project dependency, its `packaging>=26.2` constraint is dropped and
packaging is downgraded to whatever the plugin's own dep tree resolves
to (26.0 for several plugins). The subsequent `uv run python -m twine
upload` then fails with:

    ImportError: cannot import name 'errors' from 'packaging'

18 of 34 plugin publish jobs failed this way; the rest happened to
resolve packaging to 26.2 on their own.

Use `uvx twine upload` so twine runs in its own isolated tool
environment and a project sync can no longer downgrade its dependencies.

Updates `urllib3` from 2.6.3 to 2.7.0
Release notes

Sourced from urllib3's releases.

2.7.0

🚀 urllib3 is fundraising for HTTP/2 support

urllib3 is raising ~$40,000 USD to release HTTP/2 support and ensure long-term sustainable maintenance of the project after a sharp decline in financial support. If your company or organization uses Python and would benefit from HTTP/2 support in Requests, pip, cloud SDKs, and thousands of other projects please consider contributing financially to ensure HTTP/2 support is developed sustainably and maintained for the long-haul.

Thank you for your support.

Security

Addressed high-severity security issues. Impact was limited to specific use cases detailed in the accompanying advisories; overall user exposure was estimated to be marginal.

  • Decompression-bomb safeguards of the streaming API were bypassed:

    1. When HTTPResponse.drain_conn() was called after the response had been read and decompressed partially. (Reported by @​Cycloctane)
    2. During the second HTTPResponse.read(amt=N) or HTTPResponse.stream(amt=N) call when the response was decompressed using the official Brotli library. (Reported by @​kimkou2024)

    See GHSA-mf9v-mfxr-j63j for details.

  • HTTP pools created using ProxyManager.connection_from_url did not strip sensitive headers specified in Retry.remove_headers_on_redirect when redirecting to a different host. (GHSA-qccp-gfcp-xxvc reported by @​christos-spearbit)

Deprecations and Removals

  • Used FutureWarning instead of DeprecationWarning for better visibility of existing deprecation notices. Rescheduled the removal of deprecated features to version 3.0. (urllib3/urllib3#3763)
  • Removed support for end-of-life Python 3.9. (urllib3/urllib3#3720)
  • Removed support for end-of-life PyPy3.10. (urllib3/urllib3#4979)
  • Bumped the minimum supported pyOpenSSL version to 19.0.0. (urllib3/urllib3#3777)

Bugfixes

  • Fixed a bug where HTTPResponse.read(amt=None) was ignoring decompressed data buffered from previous partial reads. (urllib3/urllib3#3636)
  • Fixed a bug where HTTPResponse.read() could cache only part of the response after a partial read when cache_content=True. (urllib3/urllib3#4967)
  • Fixed HTTPResponse.stream() and HTTPResponse.read_chunked() to handle amt=0. (urllib3/urllib3#3793)
  • Updated _TYPE_BODY type alias to include missing Iterable[str], matching the documented and runtime behavior of chunked request bodies. (urllib3/urllib3#3798)
  • Fixed LocationParseError when paths resembling schemeless URIs were passed to HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen(). (urllib3/urllib3#3352)
  • Fixed BaseHTTPResponse.readinto() type annotation to accept memoryview in addition to bytearray, matching the io.RawIOBase.readinto contract and enabling use with io.BufferedReader without type errors. (urllib3/urllib3#3764)

Adds an opt-in capability flag so `import flyte` and async local task execution
work in constrained runtimes with no thread support (notably Pyodide/WASM in the
browser). Two import-time blockers are addressed:

- syncify started a background event-loop thread at import time. Add
  `flyte._utils.runtime_env.background_loop_disabled()` (auto-on under
  `sys.platform == "emscripten"`, overridable via `FLYTE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_LOOP`).
  When enabled, no thread is started: `.aio()` runs coroutines directly in the
  caller's running loop, and the blocking sync API raises a clear error.

  `storage/_storage.py`, breaking `import flyte.storage`. Guard it with the
  existing `HAS_X` idiom; `_is_obstore_supported_protocol` returns False without
  it, so local/file:// IO falls back to plain fsspec. Same guard in
  `_parallel_reader.py`.

Async-only by design: sync tasks, conditions, cloud-URI IO, and DataFrame types
remain unsupported in this mode.

feat(artifacts): typed partitions on artifacts, partition-aware get/list/triggers (#1599)

> **CI is red until the IDL ships.** `ty` and the unit-test jobs resolve
`flyteidl2==2.0.48` from PyPI, which does not carry the messages this PR
uses (`DeclareArtifact`, `ListPartitionValues`,
`ArtifactPartitionSchema`, `Granularity.WEEK`). They come from
flyteorg/flyte#8056. Once that merges and a `flyteidl2` release is cut,
bump the pin here and the jobs go green; every other check passes today.
Verified locally against a build of that branch: 369 tests pass across
the artifacts, triggers, CLI and image suites.

Depends on flyteorg/flyte#8056 (IDL). Draft until a `flyteidl2` release
carries the new messages; the pin is relaxed to `>=2.0.45` so the branch
builds against a local wheel and must be bumped to that release before
merge.

## Why

Partitions become part of an artifact's identity in the registry instead
of reserved labels in free-form metadata. The SDK needs a natural way to
publish a partition and to ask for one: the latest version of a
partition, one version per partition over a range, and the values a
dimension has. The factory module in flyteplugins-union plans backfills
with these calls.

## What

- `flyte.artifacts.Metadata(partitions=...)`: a `date` is a daily time
partition, a `datetime` an hourly one, anything else a string partition;
`flyte.artifacts.TimePartition(value, granularity)` for week and month.
The mapping key is the partition key. Carried on `ProducedArtifact` for
`produces_artifacts` tasks.
- `flyte.remote.Artifact`: `partitions` and `time_partition` properties;
`Artifact.get(name, date=..., region=...)`; `Artifact.listall(name,
date=(lo, hi), latest_per_partition=True)`;
`Artifact.partition_values(name, key, **fixed)`; `Artifact.declare(name,
partitions={"date": date, "region": str})`; `Artifact.get_schema(name)`
returning `PartitionSchema`.
- Triggers: `OnArtifact(name, region="us")` and
`flyte.TriggeredPartition("date")` in `Trigger.inputs`.
- CLI: `flyte get artifact NAME --partition key=value` (also `key=a..b`,
`key=a,b`) and `--latest-per-partition`.
- Dev-mode task images bake a local `flyteidl2` wheel from `dist/` next
to the SDK wheel.

## Testing

The SDK does not verify a version against the registry's schema: keys
are the registry's business. A version published with keys the
artifact's schema does not name is stored as published and answers by
the keys it carries — compare `Artifact.get_schema(name)` against a
version's `partitions` to see a difference.

## Testing

New tests: `tests/flyte/test_artifact_partitions.py`,
`tests/flyte/remote/test_artifact_partitions.py`,
`tests/cli/test_get_artifact_partitions.py`, plus cases in the trigger
serde, triggers and produces-artifacts suites. Touched suites: 339
passed. Exercised end to end against a local control plane running the
matching artifact service: publish with partitions, get by partition,
latest-per-partition ranges, value listing, declare and redeclare, a
deliberate schema mismatch, and a factory materialization built on these
calls.

Clarify rerun and recover behavior (#1452)

This pull request refactors the recovery and rerun logic in the Flyte
runner, simplifying the API and clarifying the responsibilities of
recovery versus rerun. The main changes remove support for recovery in
non-remote modes, eliminate the ability to recover from arbitrary runs
using `run()`, and make recovery an explicit option of `rerun()` only.
The API for forcing rerun of specific actions during recovery is also
updated and clarified.

**Recovery and Rerun Refactoring:**

* Removed `recover` and `recover_force_rerun_actions` parameters from
the `with_runcontext()` and runner constructor APIs. Recovery is now
only supported via the `rerun()` method in remote mode.
(`src/flyte/_run.py`)
* Refactored the `rerun()` method to accept new `recover` and
`force_rerun_actions` parameters, making recovery an explicit choice and
disallowing code or input changes during recovery (except via a private
hook for plugins). (`src/flyte/_run.py`)
* Removed the ability to substitute new code or recover from arbitrary
runs using `run()`; rerun always uses the prior run's code, and recovery
is now strictly a rerun concern. (`src/flyte/_run.py`)

**Provenance and Internal Logic Updates:**

* Updated internal logic to cleanly separate "rerun" and "recover"
provenance, and to ensure that recovery always replays the original
run's code and inputs. (`src/flyte/_run.py`)
* Updated `_apply_overrides` to accept `force_rerun_actions` directly,
and removed now-obsolete recovery resolution logic.
(`src/flyte/_run.py`)

These changes clarify the intended usage of rerun and recovery, reduce
complexity in the runner API, and improve error handling and
documentation for users.

feat(plugins): add crewai, langgraph, langchain, pydantic_ai, and hermes agent plugins (#1297)

## Summary

Add five new Flyte agent adapter plugins following the established
pattern from existing adapters (OpenAI, Claude, Google, Mistral):

- **flyteplugins.agents.crewai** — CrewAI agent adapter
- **flyteplugins.agents.langgraph** — LangGraph agent adapter
- **flyteplugins.agents.langchain** — LangChain agent adapter
- **flyteplugins.agents.pydantic_ai** — Pydantic AI agent adapter
- **flyteplugins.agents.hermes** — Hermes agent adapter (template SDK)

## Each plugin includes

- `pyproject.toml` (+ tracked `uv.lock`) with framework-specific
dependencies
- `__init__.py` exporting `tool` and `run_agent` (langgraph also exports
`ai_node`/`tool_node`)
- `_run.py` with SDK-specific `run_agent` implementation
- `_tools.py` with `@tool` decorator stacking on `@env.task` and
producing the framework's **native tool type** (crewai `BaseTool`,
LangChain `StructuredTool`, pydantic-ai callable tool)
- `_memory.py` — cross-run conversation persistence over a keyed
`MemoryStore`
- `_durable.py` — model-turn record/replay via `durable_step` (parity
with the openai adapter)
- `examples/` with custom_agent, durable_agent, memory, and multi_agent
demos
- `tests/` with conformance, tool, memory, durability, and run tests

## Key design decisions

- **Standardized `run_agent` signature** across all adapters: `tools`,
`model`, `instructions`, `durable`, `observability`, `memory_key` —
enforced by `flyteplugins.agents.core.testing.assert_adapter_conforms`
- **Native tool attachment**: each `*_custom_agent.py` example attaches
`@tool`-wrapped tasks using the framework's own convention
(`Agent(tools=[...])` for crewai/pydantic-ai/hermes,
`create_agent(model, tools, ...)` for langchain, user-built `StateGraph`
for langgraph); `run_agent(agent=...)` and `run_agent(tools=...)` are
mutually exclusive
- **LangGraph devex**: users build the `StateGraph` themselves;
`ai_node(model, tools)` (durable model turns) and `tool_node(tools)`
(durable tool-call child actions) are the Flyte-durable building blocks,
wired with `tools_condition` into the standard tool-calling loop
- **Memory**: `run_agent(memory_key=...)` loads/saves the conversation
to a path-addressed JSON slot in the keyed `MemoryStore` using
framework-native serialization (`ModelMessagesTypeAdapter`,
`messages_to_dict`, role/content transcripts); best-effort so memory
never breaks a run
- **Durability**: per-model-turn record/replay via `durable_step` —
`FlyteModel` (pydantic-ai, incl. prebuilt agents via `Agent.override`),
`DurableChatModel` (langchain), a durable `LLM` provider subclass
(crewai), `ai_node` (langgraph); hermes records at run granularity
(template SDK, no per-turn hook). Prebuilt agents that own their inner
model keep their own turns non-durable (documented); tool calls stay
durable regardless

## Compatibility

All adapter code is verified against the pinned framework versions:
crewai 1.15 (`BaseTool` + `kickoff_async`), pydantic-ai 2.9
(`Agent(tools=...)`, `result.output`), langchain 1.3 (`create_agent`;
`AgentExecutor`/`create_tool_calling_agent` are gone), langgraph 1.2
(`StructuredTool` + `MessagesState`).

## Testing

94 tests passing across the five adapters (plus the shared
`assert_adapter_conforms` harness). Run with:

```bash
uv run pytest plugins/agents/{crewai,langgraph,langchain,pydantic_ai,hermes}/tests/
```

GPU faults are catchable typed exceptions (#1524)

# Why

The backend now classifies GPU faults into the failure a task reports:
the error code names the fault (GpuXidError, GpuFallenOffBus,
GpuEccUncorrectable, GpuRowRemapPending, GpuNvlinkError, GpuGspError),
the message leads with the driver's own sentence, and ExecutionError
carries a typed gpu_fault with the Xid, severity, GPU UUID and node.
Until now the SDK converted all of that into a generic runtime error, so
a parent task could only string-match on the code. This makes GPU faults
catchable as typed exceptions.

# What

- flyte.errors gains GPUFaultError, carrying fault_kind, fault_code,
fault_name, severity, gpu_uuid, gpu_index, node, pci_bus_id and process,
plus xid and sxid properties that answer only for the matching kind,
since Xid and SXid share a numbering space but not a meaning. Two
leaves, GPUFaultUserError and GPUFaultSystemError, keep the error kind
honest: the backend files a user-severity Xid (an out-of-bounds access
in the workload's own kernel) as USER and a critical hardware fault as
SYSTEM, and a single class would have to lie about kind for one of them.
except flyte.errors.GPUFaultError catches both.
- The error conversion selects the GPU classes on an exact match of the
six backend codes, ahead of the existing substring branches, and
tolerates server-prefixed codes. Fields fill only from the typed
gpu_fault; a failure carrying none leaves every fault attribute at None,
with the raw message untouched. The message is prose, not a contract, so
nothing parses it — the backend that classifies a fault always attaches
the typed data, since the two shipped together.
- The docstring states the semantics plainly: user-severity Xids arrive
on the task's own retry budget, while critical hardware faults are
retried by the platform without charging that budget, so user code sees
those only after platform policy gives up.

```python
try:
    result = await train(shard)
except flyte.errors.GPUFaultError as e:
    if e.severity == "USER":
        raise  # the workload's own kernel is at fault
    result = await train(shard)
```

# Tests

31 tests in the conversion suite: ruff, mypy and ty clean; the touched
test modules pass 187 tests total.

`n = await submit_and_wait_for_action(action)` but then passed the local
`action` stub (built by `Action.from_task`) to `handle_action_failure`,
instead of the observed final state `n`.

On a first attempt this is harmless: the sub-action does not yet exist in
the state store, so the informer's submit-before-observe ordering makes the
stub the cached object, and `merge_state` lands the error on it.

On a parent recovery the sub-action already exists in a terminal FAILED
state, so the watch observes it first via `Action.from_state` (which holds
the error) and `merge_in_action_from_submit` only copies submit metadata --
it never writes phase/err back onto the stub. The stub stays
`err=None, phase=None`, so `handle_action_failure` produces
`RuntimeSystemError("UnableToConvertError", "Error in task ...: None")`,
masking a recoverable USER error as a SYSTEM error and driving a parent
retry loop.

Fix: pass `n` (the observed/cached final state) at both call sites. Adds a
regression test reproducing the recovery race and updates
`test_submit_task_with_error`, which had asserted the buggy fallback message.

Updated HashMethod approach (#105)

New approach to the `HashMethod` concept from flytekit.

## HashMethod
In `flytekit`, users could annotate output types of tasks with
`HashMethod(...)` where the `...` was a lambda function that would be
computed and then added into the `hash` field of the Flyte Literal
message. This `hash` field was then used in _downstream_ tasks to
compute the cache key for discovery (i.e. whether to run the task or
read from cache).

### New approach
A couple things:
* The fact that hashes were computed during outputs makes a lot less
sense in the dynamic v2 approach. Users can take the output of a Task,
and modify the contents completely, before submitting it again to the
next task. There's no easy way to know if an object has been touched and
if so meaningfully so the system can't reasonably know if a hash value
computed or provided at output time is still relevant.
* In many instances, the inputs to cache-enabled Tasks will not be
outputs of other tasks. A parent task can generate inputs, and
immediately pass them downstream.

so we're moving hash computation to the input side now. However, since
this concept was really only ever useful in flytekit for FlyteFile,
FlyteDirectory, and StructuredDataset types, this pr adds this
functionality directly on the types instead of relying on the
`typing.Annotated` approach. Also this only contains the change for File
and Dir so far - DataFrame to be added later.

### Changes
* Removed the old HashMethod object and removed the calculate hash
function in the type engine.
* Added a new HashMethod protocol with a standard PrecomputedValue
implementation if you just want to provide a value.
* Updated constructors for File/Dir to take this object, either as is,
or as a str in cases where I/O isn't relevant (e.g.
`from_existing_remote`).
* Added I/O classes that capture and scan bytes as they are
written/read.
* Updated the File class to have both hash and hash_method and Dir to
just have hash. The reason for not adding hash_method yet to Dir is just
because the storage layer would need a much bigger change to support the
scan and hash updating approach used for Files. We will add this to Dir
in the future if there is demand, or maybe remove from File if we find
it's never used.
* Update cache key generation to respect Literals with a hash value,
including cases where the Literal is a container type that has literals
underneath that have hash values. (Also, this change to only look at the
literals rather than the whole Inputs object is needed as we added more
fields to the Inputs object (like context)).

Cache cluster-aware clients per value, not per event loop

`alru_cache` stores the `asyncio.Task` it created for each key, so every entry
is bound to the loop that produced it. async_lru >= 2.3.0 notices when the same
cache is used from a second loop, clears it, and emits
`AlruCacheLoopResetWarning`.

Flyte drives one `ClientSet` from several loops in a single process, so that
reset fires during ordinary runs. A tracked run is the easy repro: the CLI
resolves a dataproxy client on the `asyncio.run` loop, then the tracked-run
reporter thread resolves one on its own loop while uploading inputs, and the
user sees

  async_lru/__init__.py:369: AlruCacheLoopResetWarning: alru_cache detected
  event loop change and auto-cleared stale entries.

Besides the noise, each crossover threw away entries that were perfectly
reusable, costing an extra SelectCluster round trip and session build. The
cached values are pyqwest-backed clients that carry no event-loop state, so
sharing them across loops is safe — only alru's task-shaped entries were not.

Add `loop_agnostic_async_cache`, which memoizes the resolved value in
per-instance state so every loop shares it, and keeps only the in-flight tasks
per loop. Concurrent callers on a loop still collapse onto a single call,
failures are still not cached, and the shared call is shielded so one caller's
cancellation doesn't cancel it for the others. Use it for the six cluster-aware
`_resolve*` methods.

feat(types): support IntEnum and parameterized dataclasses as task types

Two types that Flyte could carry but did not.

**IntEnum.** The enum wire format is already the member *name* — `to_literal`
writes `python_val.name`, `to_python_value` does `expected_python_type[name]` —
so member values never had to be strings. Two guards were all that rejected an
IntEnum. They are replaced by a check that states the real rule: a member needs a
name that addresses it again. `Flag`/`IntFlag` therefore stay rejected, now with
a reason, because a composite member such as `READ|WRITE` has a `.name` but
`Perm["READ|WRITE"]` raises `KeyError`.

**Parameterized dataclasses.** `Choice[Intent]` is a generic *alias*, so
`dataclasses.is_dataclass()` and `dataclasses.fields()` both reject it. Such a
type fell through every branch of `get_transformer` and landed on pickle,
silently. A `_dataclass_class()` helper resolves the alias to its origin for
structural checks while leaving the alias itself for mashumaro, which needs it to
bind the type variable — applied in `get_transformer`, `assert_type`,
`to_python_value` and `from_binary_idl`.

Note one intended consequence: a generic dataclass holding a payload mashumaro
cannot encode used to "work" via that pickle fallback and now fails exactly as
its non-generic equivalent always has. A test pins both forms to the same error.

Also hardens two pre-existing rough edges on the lines involved: an empty enum
reported `IndexError` from inside a comprehension, and `issubclass()` was called
on a value that need not be a class.

(bugfix) Overrides not applied to pods (#1173)

## Problem

`TaskDetails.override(resources=...)` applied the container resource
override **only when the task template had a `container` field**.
Pod-template tasks (multi-container environments — e.g. the
code-execution sandbox) carry the primary container's resources inside
the `k8s_pod.pod_spec` Struct and have **no** `template.container`, so
the override was silently skipped. Only `extended_resources` (the GPU
accelerator *type* → nodeSelector/toleration) was set.

Result: a per-run `override(resources=Resources(gpu="L4:1"))` produced a
pod with the accelerator nodeSelector but **no `nvidia.com/gpu`
request**, so it scheduled without a GPU. cpu/memory overrides were
dropped the same way.

This was found via the unionai-sandbox GPU notebook override path
(follow-up to #1170, which fixed the accelerator-type half of the same
`override`).

## Fix

When the template uses `k8s_pod`, apply the resource override to the
**primary container inside the pod_spec Struct**, mirroring the build
path (`task_serde._get_k8s_pod`): convert the override to k8s resource
maps via `_sanitize_resource_name` and replace the primary container's
`resources` (full replacement, matching
`template.container.resources.CopyFrom`). The primary container is
located by `_PRIMARY_CONTAINER_NAME_FIELD` (with a single-container
fallback); other containers are left untouched.

## Tests

- `test_gpu_override_on_pod_template_sets_container_request` — GPU
override populates the primary container's `requests` (cpu/memory/gpu)
and the accelerator type; sidecar untouched.
- `test_override_does_not_mutate_original_pod_template` — override
returns a new `TaskDetails` without mutating the source.
- Existing container-path override tests still pass (67 passed in
`test_task.py` + `test_pod_template.py`).

feat(rerun): support new inputs alongside --recover, in the CLI and the API

`flyte rerun` had no way to change inputs at all, and `rerun(..., recover=True)`
rejected changed inputs outright (pointing at fork). Both now work together.

- `flyte rerun <run> --input KEY=VALUE` (repeatable): values are converted
  against the source task's interface, fetched from the platform since rerun
  never uses local code. Composes with --recover, --action-name, everything else.
- `flyte.rerun(..., inputs={...})` / `with_runcontext(...).rerun(...)`: an
  explicit inputs dict alongside the existing **kwargs form. The dict is also
  the only way to reach a task input whose name collides with a rerun argument.
  Passing the same input both ways is an error.
- recover + changed inputs is allowed. The new run starts from the changed
  inputs while still reusing the source run's succeeded actions, so a warning
  points out that recovered actions keep the outputs they produced under the
  original inputs, and that force_rerun_actions is how to re-execute them.
- Partial input changes now merge onto the source run's inputs instead of
  failing with "missing required inputs": only the changed inputs are converted
  and overlaid on the prior literals. A full set of new inputs still skips the
  source-input fetch entirely, which keeps it working as the escape hatch when
  those inputs are gone from storage. Unknown input names are rejected up front
  rather than silently dropped.

FlyteLiteralConverter.convert now takes an optional click context, so a value
can be parsed outside click's option parsing. Code substitution stays fork's
job; only inputs moved.

feat(config): add named profiles selected with --profile

A config file may declare a top-level `profiles:` mapping. Under a profile,
every switch is looked up at `profiles.<name>.<switch>` and falls back to the
top-level `<switch>`, so the top level acts as defaults shared by every
profile:

    admin:
      endpoint: dns:///default.example.com
    task:
      project: research
    profiles:
      prod:
        admin: {endpoint: dns:///prod.example.com}
        task:  {domain: production}

    $ flyte --profile prod run ...

This lands in `ConfigFile._get_from_yaml`, the single chokepoint every config
read funnels through, so all of `config/_internal.py` becomes profile-aware
without touching the per-section `auto()` methods. A file with no `profiles:`
key reads exactly as before.

Selection is `--profile` or `FLYTE_PROFILE`. `FLYTE_*` environment variables
still override the file, matching how `AWS_PROFILE` behaves. Requesting a
profile the file does not declare raises `ProfileNotFoundError` rather than
falling back to the defaults and talking to the wrong control plane. The
`ConfigFile` cache is keyed by path *and* profile; sharing one entry across
profiles would silently return the wrong file.

Also:

- `flyte create config --profile NAME` merges into `profiles.<name>` instead
  of replacing the file, so profiles accumulate.
- `flyte get profiles` lists what a file declares and marks the active one.
- `flyte.use_profile` / `aio_use_profile` scope a profile to a `with` block:
  they read it, build a client, and install it as the active config for the
  current context only, leaving the process-wide config from `flyte.init()`
  untouched so concurrent callers are unaffected. They default to the file
  the session was initialized from rather than re-running the default search,
  which would let a switch land in a different discoverable file. Tested
  across the syncify thread boundary, since `flyte.run` inside such a block
  relies on the caller's context being copied to the loop thread.
- `Config.source` is recorded as `source_config_path` when no explicit path
  was passed, so later readers can find the file actually used.
- Fix `_apply_hook_to_subcommand` invoking `original_command.callback()` at
  registration time, which ran the wrapped command during plugin discovery.
  This broke subcommand hooks for any plugin, not just new ones.

Have the connector move a script's outputs by default

Declared outputs made the script do its own upload -- `aws s3 cp` to a URI it
was handed -- which asks the node for tooling and credentials it may not have,
and made the awkward path the only path.

`FLYTE_OUTPUT_<NAME>` is now a local path by default. The script writes an
ordinary file and the connector streams it to object storage afterwards, over
the SSH connection it already holds, chunked through `storage.put_stream` so
nothing is buffered whole: the connector pod has 100Mi of ephemeral storage
and is polling every other job at the same time. A declared Dir is walked and
each file streamed to the matching key.

Above roughly 100MB it warns and uploads anyway. Refusing would throw away a
finished job for a transfer that does work, just less well -- two hops instead
of one, through a shared pod, on the connector's bandwidth rather than the
cluster's. The warning names the fix: `output_upload="job"` hands the script
the URI so it uploads directly, which is what a large artifact wants.

Verified against a live cluster: `stat` on a 3MB file and on a missing path,
a nested directory walk, and a chunked read whose sha256 matches the source.

PodTemplate capability helpers (allow_fuse / allow_nested_sandboxing, from_spec) + fix GPU accelerator in override() (#1170)

Two changes:

## 1. PodTemplate capability helpers

Image-style chainable methods for requesting pod privileges without
hand-writing Kubernetes security contexts:

```python
pt = flyte.PodTemplate.from_spec(my_v1_pod_spec)        # wrap an existing pod spec
pt = flyte.PodTemplate().allow_fuse()                   # /dev/fuse + SYS_ADMIN + privileged
pt = my_pt.allow_nested_sandboxing()                    # bwrap prerequisites: SYS_ADMIN + AppArmor unconfined + allowPrivilegeEscalation=false
pt = my_pt.allow_fuse(privileged=False).allow_nested_sandboxing()  # composable on clusters that permit /dev/fuse unprivileged
```

Helpers are pure augmentors with tested laws: never mutate the input,
idempotent, additive over user-set fields
(sidecars/volumes/securityContext preserved), order-free where
composable, stamp `flyte.org/capability-<name>` annotations for
auditability, and raise loudly on conflicting pre-set security posture
(e.g. `allow_fuse()` after `allow_nested_sandboxing()`).

## 2. Fix: `task.override(resources=...)` dropped the GPU accelerator

`TaskDetails.override` only copied `container.resources` and never set
`task_template.extended_resources`, so
`task.override(resources=flyte.Resources(gpu="L40s:1"))` produced a pod
with no accelerator nodeSelector/toleration and scheduled on a non-GPU
node. Now mirrors the build path (`get_proto_extended_resources`),
clearing the field when the replacement has no extended resources.
Enables per-run GPU overrides.

## Test plan
- `tests/user_api/test_pod_template.py`: 51 tests — `from_spec`
resolution rules, parametrized augmentor-law suite over all three grant
variants, conflict and both-order composition tests
- `tests/flyte/remote/test_task.py`: GPU override sets
`gpu_accelerator.device == "nvidia-l40s"`; cpu-only re-override clears
`extended_resources`
- Full sweep: 662 passed (user_api + remote + task/app/resources serde)

```python
import typing

import flyte

# TaskEnvironments provide a simple way of grouping configuration used by tasks (more later).
env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(name="hello_world", resources=flyte.Resources(memory="250Mi"))


# use TaskEnvironments to define tasks, which are regular Python functions.
@env.task
def fn(x: int) -> typing.Any:  # type annotations are recommended.
    slope, intercept = 2, 5
    return slope * x + intercept


# tasks can also call other tasks, which will be manifested in different containers.
@env.task
def main(x_list: list[int]) -> typing.Any:
    x_len = len(x_list)
    if x_len < 10:
        raise ValueError(f"x_list doesn't have a larger enough sample size, found: {x_len}")

    y_list = list(flyte.map(fn, x_list))  # flyte.map is like Python map, but runs in parallel.
    print("y_list:", y_list)
    y_mean = sum(y_list) / len(y_list)
    return y_mean


if __name__ == "__main__":
    flyte.init_from_config()  # establish remote connection from within your script.
    run = flyte.run(main, x_list=list(range(10)))  # run remotely inline and pass data.

    # print various attributes of the run.
    print(run.name)
    print(run.url)

    run.wait(run)  # stream the logs from the root action to the terminal.

```

feat: add Action.get_report to pull reports from actions inside a run (#1352)

## Summary

`Run.get_report()` (added recently) only fetches the HTML report for a
run's **root** action. This PR adds **`Action.get_report()`**, letting
you pull the report artifact for **any action nested inside a run**
(e.g. a child task invoked by the root task), using that action's own id
and latest attempt.

- **`Action.get_report(attempt=None, expires_in=1h)`** — requests a
signed download link from the data proxy for the action's
`ARTIFACT_TYPE_REPORT`, downloads it, and returns the HTML string.
Defaults to the latest attempt. Raises a clear error naming the action
and run when no report exists.
- **`Run.get_report()`** now delegates to its root action's
`get_report()`, removing the duplicated data-proxy/download logic (and
the now-unused imports in `_run.py`).

## Usage

```python
run = flyte.run(make_report, name="world")
run.wait()

# Root action report (unchanged)
root_html = run.get_report()

# Report from a specific action inside the run
for action in flyte.remote.Action.listall(for_run_name=run.name):
    if action.task_name == child_report.name:
        child_html = action.get_report()
```

## Tests

- Updated the 4 existing `Run.get_report` tests (patch targets moved to
the `_action` module since the logic moved there).
- Added 2 tests for `Action.get_report`: a nested action fetches its own
report by its own id/latest attempt, and the error message references
the action and run.
- Full remote suite: **474 passed**.

## Example

Updated `examples/remote_management/get_report.py` to a root task that
invokes a child task (both `report=True`), then fetches both the root
report and the child action's report.

**Verified live** against the demo cluster: the run succeeded, and the
two downloaded HTML files each contained only their respective action's
content (root → "Hello, world!", child → "Child report for world").

fix: skip symlinks pointing outside source when bundling code (#1063)

## Summary
- `create_bundle` and `ls_relative_files` computed the arcname / hash
path via `Path(ws_file).resolve().relative_to(source.resolve())`.
`resolve()` follows symlinks, so a symlink inside the source dir that
points outside the source dir (e.g. `.venv/bin/python` ->
`/usr/bin/python3.10`) crashes with `ValueError: '/usr/bin/python3.10'
is not in the subpath of '<source>'`, aborting the entire deploy at
code-bundle time.
- Switch both call sites to `os.path.relpath` against the **absolute**
(non-resolved) source path. `abspath` still normalizes ".." components
(the property the original `resolve()` was added to preserve, per the
comment) but doesn't follow symlinks, so the arcname reflects the file's
position inside `source` rather than the symlink target's location.
- As a defensive fallback, `create_bundle` now skips and logs a warning
for any path that still lands outside `source` after normalization,
rather than letting one stray entry abort the whole bundle.

Fixes [FLYTE-SDK-2E](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7476727356/)

`test_create_bundle_skips_symlinks_pointing_outside_source` constructs
the exact symlink-outside-source shape from the Sentry crash and asserts
the bundle succeeds

fix: mirror sys.path entries reached through a symlinked root

`local_sys_paths_env` compares each `sys.path` entry against a *resolved*
root:

```python
root_dir_abs = Path(root_dir).resolve()
value = ":".join(
    f"./{Path(path).relative_to(root_dir_abs)}"
    for path in sys.path
    if Path(path).is_relative_to(root_dir_abs)
)
```

The entries themselves are never resolved. Both writers record them with
`abspath`, which normalizes but does not follow symlinks --
`_initialize.py:352` for the root itself and `_load_module_from_file` for
a loaded module's directory. So whenever the root is reached through a
symlink the two spellings never match: on macOS `/tmp` is a symlink to
`/private/tmp`, so the root resolves to `/private/tmp/proj` while
`sys.path` still carries `/tmp/proj/pkg`.

Nothing raises. `is_relative_to` guards the `relative_to`, so the entry
is simply dropped and `_F_SYS_PATH` ships empty. The task or app then
loses the path it needed and fails inside the container with a
`ModuleNotFoundError` on a sibling import -- the failure this env var
exists to prevent. A repro shows it drops the entry under *both*
spellings of the root, so passing the real path does not avoid it.

This is the silent half of the path-containment bug FLYTE-SDK-7E (#1441)
fixes for the code bundle, at a site that PR does not touch. Take the
same approach it uses in `_rebase_under_source`: a literal subpath is
kept as-is, and only a path that is not a literal subpath is resolved.
That ordering matters -- resolving everything would follow a symlink
that legitimately points outside the root (`.venv/lib` is the canonical
case) and drop it, which is why `create_bundle` keeps those unresolved.

Also fold the third copy of this logic, `_run.py:492`, into the shared
helper. #1539 extracted `local_sys_paths_env` out of `_deploy.py` and
added an `app_serde.py` caller, but left the `flyte run` copy inline, so
it carried the same bug independently.

Entries are now de-duplicated: with the fix, `/tmp/proj/pkg` and
`/private/tmp/proj/pkg` can both be present and rewrite to one relative
path.

No Sentry issue: the failure is a silent drop on the client, and the
resulting `ModuleNotFoundError` happens in the container, outside the
four `capture_exception` extents.

Refuse the clock and entropy in the sandbox; handle sleeps in the bridge (#1643)

## Summary

Follow-up to #1642, which was merged before this commit was pushed. The
description of #1642 already describes this behaviour; this PR is the
code for it.

- **No clock, no entropy.** Monty 1.0 gives sandbox code the worker's
clock and OS entropy by default, so the same code and inputs could take
different paths on each run. Both are now routed to the host, which
never answers: `time.time()`, `time.monotonic()`, `datetime.now()`,
`date.today()`, unseeded `random` and `os.urandom()` raise
`RuntimeError: ... is not supported in this environment` inside the
sandbox. `time.sleep`, date arithmetic and explicitly seeded `random`
still work.
- **OS calls in the bridge.** Monty 1.0 surfaces OS calls to
`feed_start` callers as function snapshots. The bridge took them for
unknown tools, so `time.sleep` failed with a host `RuntimeError` in any
code that had tools attached. It now waits out sleeps and declines every
other OS call, which raises at the offending line in the sandbox.
- **`ORCHESTRATOR_SYNTAX_PROMPT`.** No longer lists `time` and `random`
as importable, and tells the model there is no clock: take dates as
inputs.
- **`examples/sandbox/orchestrator.py`.** The docstring claimed `await`
works inside the sandbox; it does not.

## Testing

- `tests/flyte/sandbox/test_runtime.py` covers clock and entropy
refusal, seeded `random`, date arithmetic and sleeping, each with and
without tools attached. `test_bridge.py` covers OS-call handling.
- `tests/flyte/sandbox` and `tests/flyte/ai` pass (735 tests).
- 34 sandbox probes give the same result with and without tools. The
sleep budget from #1642 still holds through the bridge path: a 2 s sleep
under `timeout_ms=500` fails immediately.
- `hash()`, set order and `id()` are identical across separate
processes.
- Not run on a remote cluster; the demo runs for #1642 predate this
commit.

## Known limitation

With tools attached, `asyncio.gather` over several sleeps waits for them
one after another instead of overlapping (0.9 s instead of 0.3 s for
three 0.3 s sleeps).

Raise a cause-specific timeout error when a sub-action times out (#1626)

## Problem

When a sub-action ends `TIMED_OUT`, both remote controllers
(`_controller.py`, `_r_controller.py`) raise a generic
`TaskTimeoutError` before reading the sub-action's error. The parent
cannot tell *which* `flyte.Timeout` bound fired.

Reproduced on dogfood with a B300 child (no B300 nodes) and
`max_queued_time=1m`. The server recorded `timed out waiting for
resources: queued_timeout of 1m0s exceeded`, but the parent got only:

```
flyte.errors.TaskTimeoutError code='TaskTimeoutError': Action 4o8tbl7myeu62maq5qqxgj18z timed out, raising exception in current Action a0
```

## Change

- `flyte.errors`: new `MaxQueuedTimeExceededError`,
`MaxRuntimeExceededError` and `DeadlineExceededError`, all subclasses of
`TaskTimeoutError`, so existing `except TaskTimeoutError` handlers keep
working.
- `convert.convert_timeout_error` maps the server code to one of these:
`QUEUED_TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED`, `MAX_RUNTIME_EXCEEDED` or
`DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`. A missing or unknown code (older backends write a
bare `TIMED_OUT`) falls back to the base `TaskTimeoutError`. The server
message is appended to the error text.
- Both controllers use it.
- Example: `examples/retries_timeout/queued_timeout_b300.py`.

## Backend dependency

The leasor already writes `QUEUED_TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED` and
`DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`. The leaseworker, which enforces queued_timeout
after dispatch and also enforces max_runtime, wrote a bare `TIMED_OUT`
until unionai/cloud#18796. Before that lands, the post-dispatch case
still yields the base `TaskTimeoutError`, which is the same behavior as
today.

## Tests

- Parametrized `test_submit_task_timed_out_raises_cause_specific_error`
covers all three codes, a bare `TIMED_OUT`, and no error.
- `tests/flyte` + `tests/internal` pass apart from two failures
unrelated to this change:
`test_keyring_store::test_retrieve_degrades_when_keyring_not_installed`
(also fails on main) and `test_int_image_builder::test_real_build` (real
Docker build).
- E2E on dogfood with the patched leaseworker: pending.

feat(image): add Image.from_pixi_script()

The pixi counterpart to `from_uv_script`: describe an image with the PEP 723
block at the top of a script, but resolve it with pixi so the environment can
pull conda packages (`[tool.pixi.dependencies]`) alongside PyPI ones.

Pixi has no `install --script`. The only commands that materialize a script's
environment are `pixi run --script`, which runs the script, and they place the
environment in a rattler cache directory that the build cache mount discards.
So a `PixiScript` layer is lowered into the equivalent `pixi.toml` workspace
manifest and installed through the existing, tested `PixiProject` path — the
same shape as `UVScript` lowering to `PipPackages`/`UVProject`. Both the local
docker builder and the remote builder pick it up for free.

The translation keeps the whole `[tool.pixi]` table verbatim, so tables flyte
does not model (target, feature, environments, activation) still reach pixi.
`requires-python` becomes the environment's python unless
`[tool.pixi.dependencies].python` states one, and PEP 723 `dependencies` become
`[pypi-dependencies]`.

A workspace manifest, unlike a script, must state its channels and platforms:
channels default to conda-forge (what pixi assumes for a script) and platforms
come from the image's own platforms, so a script that declares neither builds
correctly for whatever it is built for. A script that declares fewer platforms
than the image needs now fails in `validate()` with an actionable message
rather than partway through the pixi install.

A sidecar lock from `pixi lock --script` (`<script>.pixi.lock`) validates
against the generated manifest, so it is installed with `--locked`.

The layer hashes the generated manifest rather than the script body, so editing
a script's code reuses the built image and editing its dependencies rebuilds it.

feat(debug): SSH-into-task debug over WebSocket (#1230)

## SSH-into-task debug over WebSocket (pod side)

Adds an `_F_E_SSH` debug mode — a real-ssh sibling to the existing
browser code-server `_F_E_VS` path. On the `a0` entrypoint it starts an
`sshd` bound to `127.0.0.1:2222` and an in-process **WebSocket→sshd
bridge** on the routed debug port (`:6060`), so a developer can attach
plain `ssh`, `scp`/`rsync`, or **VS Code Remote-SSH** to a running task
pod.

Enabled via the `_F_E_SSH` env var (the SSH public key is injected via
`_F_SSH_PK`), e.g. through `flyte.with_runcontext(env_vars=...)`. This
PR is the **pod-side server only**; the matching desktop client is
provided separately.


### What's here
- **`Sshd`** class — daemon lifecycle: locate / best-effort apt-install
the binary, generate the host key, write `authorized_keys` + a minimal
key-only `sshd_config`, `start()` (asyncio subprocess) / `wait(timeout)`
/ `stop()`.
- **`WsBridge`** class — readiness endpoint + WebSocket↔sshd bridge:
`start()`/`stop()`; handles concurrent connections, ping/pong keepalive,
and serializes frame writes under a lock.
- key-only sshd with `internal-sftp` (VS Code Remote-SSH) and
`AllowTcpForwarding` (`ssh -L` / debugpy).
- stages the code bundle and writes `.vscode/launch.json` + a `python -m
pdb` helper; interactive shells land in the code dir.
- async-first throughout; `sys.exit()` after a max-uptime ceiling.

### Tests
`tests/flyte/test_ssh_debug.py` (19): WS frame roundtrip
(masked/large/oversize), RFC6455 accept key, `Sshd`
config/keys/`find_binary`, `WsBridge` start/stop, and an **end-to-end
WS→sshd bridge echo**. ruff clean.

### Verified on cluster
Built the wheel, launched a debug run, resolved the route, then `ssh` →
landed a root shell in `/home/flyte` with the task code present
(connected first attempt).

Signed-off-by: Ketan Umare <kumare3@users.noreply.github.com>

Fail the task when a declared output is missing, instead of hanging

Reported from a real run: a script with its output-writing line removed left the
task on "Waiting on resources" while the connector logged the error every poll.

Raising out of `get` was the bug. An exception there becomes an RPC error, and
the platform's resource cache treats that as a sync failure: it keeps the item,
leaves the phase at PhaseResourcesCreated -- which renders as waiting -- and
retries. After SyncFailureCount passes MaxSystemFailures (5 by default) it
becomes PhaseSystemFailure, a *system* failure, attributed to infrastructure
rather than the task, retried on the platform's own budget, and reported without
the message that says what to change. A script that forgot to write its output
was being treated as connector flakiness.

`get` now catches OutputCollectionError -- raised for a missing declared output
and for one too large to carry -- and returns Resource(phase=FAILED) with the
explanation. Same text, but it lands on the task, immediately, once.

The distinction is what makes this right, so it is a named exception rather than
a blanket try/except. A missing output is deterministic and the author's to fix.
A storage or transport error may be transient, so it still escapes `get` and
keeps the retry-then-system-failure semantics that suit it; blaming the user's
script for a 403 the connector hit would be worse than the hang. Both directions
are now tested.

Because the phase is set before the FAILED branch, the stderr tail is appended
here too -- usually the reason the script did not write the output.

Verified against the reported scenario: phase FAILED, outputs None, message
carrying the job state, the log paths and the explanation.

feat(remote): route run uploads to the run's queue pool (#1671)

## Summary

Builds on #1700 (run-time routing of the code bundle and inputs via
`flyte._upload_queue`). This PR now carries only what #1700 does not
cover, all on top of the same `upload_queue(...)` context:

- **`UploadInputsRequest.queue`**: when an upload queue is set,
`upload_inputs` and `upload_trigger` name it on the request, so a
control plane that proxies the upload writes the inputs to that queue's
pool. Feature-detected on the descriptor; takes effect once a flyteidl2
release includes flyteorg/flyte#8148.
- **Trigger uploads routed by queue**: `upload_trigger` now uses the
queue-aware resolver, and `offload_trigger_inputs(queue=...)` uploads
inside `upload_queue(queue)`.
- **`flyte deploy --queue`** / `flyte.deploy(queue=...)`: each
environment's effective queue is the override, else its own queue, else
the task's. The code bundle is uploaded once per distinct queue, each
task is serialized against the bundle for its queue, and each trigger's
offloaded inputs go to (and its RunSpec records) the trigger's queue.
- **Rerun / run-from-trigger**: when the run's queue differs from the
source run's or trigger's queue, the stored inputs are read back and
uploaded again via the new queue instead of reusing a URI in another
pool's bucket. Same queue keeps reusing it.

Ref RUN-70. Related: flyteorg/flyte#8148 (IDL), flyteorg/flyte#8088 /
unionai cloud SelectCluster `queue_id`.

## Compatibility with #1714

#1714 routes the image-build run to the run's queue by adding `queue=`
to `build_images` / `_build_images` / `_build_image_bg`. This PR does
not touch those functions or their callers in `_run.py`, so the two
compose. For `flyte deploy`, #1714's per-build `queue=` can take each
environment's effective queue computed here.

`_upload_single_file`'s generic `except Exception` branch wrapped the
underlying error with a static message — `f"Failed to get signed url for

docsy: hf_model docstring documents CLI flags as Python parameters

The `hf_model()` docstring describes an API the function does not have. Its
example passes `accelerator="A100:8"`, which is not a parameter at all, and its
Args block documents six names that do not exist in the signature -- `cpu`,
`mem`, `disk`, `gpu`, `shm`, `wait` -- while omitting two that do:
`raw_data_path` and `resources`.

The six are exactly the flags on `flyte prefetch hf-model`
(`--cpu/--mem/--disk/--gpu/--shm/--wait`), which the CLI folds into a single
`Resources(...)` before calling this function. So the docstring was written
against the CLI's surface and never updated when the Python API consolidated
them. `accelerator=` is a third spelling matching neither.

This is not cosmetic. Anyone copying the example gets a TypeError, and anyone
reading Args to size a sharding run reaches for `gpu=`, which also does not
exist -- the accelerator goes in `Resources(gpu=...)`. The example is the more
likely path, since it is the only one showing sharding, and sharding is the
case that actually needs an accelerator.

Fixed by documenting what the signature has:

  - the example now passes `resources=flyte.Resources(cpu=..., memory=...,
    disk=..., gpu="A100:8")`
  - Args documents `resources` and `raw_data_path`, notes that the default
    carries NO accelerator (so sharding needs it set explicitly), and points
    at the CLI's separate flags so the two surfaces are reconcilable
  - `raw_data_path` wording taken from the CLI flag's own help text

Also corrected an overstatement in the same docstring: "the repo's README is
attached as the model card" is conditional. The README fetch is wrapped in a
try/except that logs "No README.md file found", and the card is only built
`if card_md`, so a repo without one yields no card.

Verified: the docstring example now parses as valid Python and its call
matches the released signature; ruff check and ruff format both clean.

fix: report a missing file in an image definition as the user error it is

`ImageBuildEngine.build` asks `image_exists()` for the image tag before it
calls `image.validate()`, and computing that tag hashes the files the image
definition names. So a user who points `with_uv_project(uvlock=...)` at a
file that is not there gets a bare

    FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '.../does-not-exist.lock'

raised from inside `filehash_update`, and reported to Sentry as an SDK crash.

`UVProject.validate()` has had a clear message for exactly this mistake since
it was written -- "UVLock file ... does not exist" -- along with
`PoetryProject`, `PixiProject` and `UVScript`. None of them ever get to run on
this path, because the unguarded read in `update_hash()` always fires first.

Ask the layer to diagnose itself when a hash-time read fails, and rewrite the
error only when it actually objects. A read that fails while the layer
considers its own definition fine is not a mistake in the image spec, so it
keeps its original exception and stays reportable.

fixes FLYTE-SDK-8B

Add code_mode option to `Agent`, add `call_handler` to `@tool` decorator (#1179)

This pull request updates the codebase to standardize how conversational
agent memory is handled and passed between calls, and clarifies agent
usage patterns. The main change is the replacement of the `history`
parameter with `memory` in all `Agent.run` and related method calls,
reflecting a more functional and explicit approach to agent memory
management. Documentation and example agents are updated to match this
new pattern, and the agent-with-memory example is simplified to
demonstrate the new, stateless memory handling.

**Standardization of Agent Memory Handling**

- All invocations of `Agent.run` and `Agent.run.aio` now use a `memory`
parameter instead of `history`, both in code and documentation. This
clarifies that memory (including conversation transcripts and artifacts)
is explicitly passed in and out, rather than being attached to the agent
or handled implicitly.

**Documentation and Example Updates**

- The `agent_with_memory.py` example and its documentation are rewritten
to show functional memory passing: the caller is responsible for
loading, passing, and saving the memory store, and tools are stateless.
The example now uses a simple `current_time` tool and omits the previous
note-taking tools for clarity.

**New Example Added**

- A new example, `code_mode_agent.py`, is added to demonstrate an agent
in "code mode," where the LLM generates Python code to orchestrate Flyte
tasks. This example showcases parallel data fetching, aggregation, and
report rendering, all using the updated memory handling approach.

Add support for pushing and pulling private images in the remote builder (#252)

This pull request adds support for using private base images when
building and running Flyte tasks, allowing users to specify registry
secrets for authentication. The main changes introduce a new workflow
for handling private registries, update the `Image` class to accept and
propagate registry secrets, and ensure secrets are used during image
build and runtime. The example demonstrates how to use these features.

**Support for private image registries:**

* Added an example (`examples/image/private_base_image.py`) showing how
to build and run a Flyte task using a private base image, including
instructions for creating and using a registry secret.
* Updated the `Image` class (`src/flyte/_image.py`) to accept a
`registry_secret` parameter in relevant methods (`from_debian_base`,
`from_uv_script`, `clone`) and propagate it internally for use during
image build/pull.

rs_controller: support condition actions and decoupled start/wait (#1401)

## Why

The Rust SDK ([flyte-sdk-rs](https://github.com/unionai/flyte-sdk-rs))
consumes this crate as an rlib, and needs to wait on **condition
(signal) actions** so a Rust task can pause for a human approval or an
external callback.

The wire protocol and the backend already support this — `flyteidl2`
generates `ConditionAction`, `Action.spec::Condition`,
`ActionUpdate.value` and `ActionPhase::Paused`, and the actions service
resolves conditions today. The gap is entirely in this crate: it models
only `Task` and `Trace`, and `merge_update` reads `output_uri` but never
`value`, so a signalled value can never reach a caller.

The pure-Python remote controller already implements conditions end to
end; this is a port of that behavior into the Rust crate, not a new
design.

**Everything here is additive. Task and trace behavior is unchanged.**

## What changed

**`action.rs`**
- `ActionType::Condition`, plus `Action.condition` and
`Action.condition_output`.
- `Action::from_condition`, following `from_trace`'s bytes convention.
Phase is `Unspecified`, not `Succeeded` — a trace is *recorded* after
the fact, but a condition is *launched* and resolved later, and a
terminal phase at birth would fire completion before any value arrived.
- `merge_update` captures `ActionUpdate.value`. **Un-gated on action
type**, because an entry created by `new_from_update` is typed `Task`
until a later submit repairs it — gating would drop the value of an
already-signalled condition on a retry.
- `new_from_update` captures the value too, for when the watch stream
delivers an update before the local submit registers the action.
- `merge_from_submit` adopts `action_type` and the type-specific spec.
Without this, a condition whose update arrived first stays typed `Task`
with no spec, and `launch_task` finds nothing to enqueue.
- `is_action_successful()` treats **`Recovered`** as success-equivalent,
so callers stop either testing `phase == Succeeded` (which mistreats a
recovered action) or inverting `Failed` (which also swallows
`Aborted`/`TimedOut`). `is_action_paused()` names the non-terminal
condition wait. Both exposed to Python as `is_successful` / `is_paused`,
with `condition_output_bytes`.

**`core.rs`**
- `Condition` arms in `build_actions_spec` and `launch_task`'s spec
check. The legacy `QueueService` arm returns a clear error instead — the
backend has no condition support there, so an enqueue would be silently
dropped.
- `submit_action` is split into `start_action` (enqueue, return) and
`wait_for_action` (await terminal), with `submit_action` as their
composition. This is what allows a condition to be created early — so it
is visible in the console and its webhook fires — and awaited later,
possibly elsewhere in the task. Mirrors the Python controller's
start/wait split.
- The trace wait bound is now an explicit `match` over action type
rather than an equality test, so a future action type must choose its
policy. Conditions deliberately take the unbounded wait: they are
bounded server-side by `ConditionAction.timeout`, which arrives as a
`TIMED_OUT` update.

**`informer.rs`**
- Completion receivers are parked by action name so a wait can be
claimed by a caller that did not submit the action; previously the
receiver lived only on `submit_action`'s stack, which is the one thing
that made decoupled start/wait impossible. A `oneshot` send buffers, so
a completion that fires before the receiver is claimed is not lost.
- The completion channel is registered only on first submit, so
resubmitting an action no longer orphans an existing waiter.

## Tests

Adds the crate's first tests that run **without a live control plane**
(the existing informer test needs one on `localhost:8090`, which is
presumably why CI does not run `cargo test`):

```
cargo test --lib action::
```

Seven cases: value capture on both paths, the early-update ordering
repair, `Recovered` as terminal *and* successful, unsuccessful terminal
phases, and which phases keep a waiter waiting.

## Verification

- `cargo build`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo
+nightly fmt --check` — all clean.
- `cargo test --lib action::` — 7 passed.
- The downstream Rust SDK builds and its full suite (26 tests) passes
against this branch via its path dependency.
- Python consumers are unaffected: `_r_controller.py` constructs
`Action` only through the two `from_*` staticmethods with keyword
arguments and never reads `action_type`, and the new `ActionType`
variant is additive on an `eq_int` pyclass.

Not verified against a live cluster — that needs the Rust SDK side,
which is the follow-up.

## Note

`rs_controller/Cargo.lock` is left untouched, though it is stale: it
pins `flyteidl2 2.0.32` while `rs_controller/Cargo.toml` declares
`=2.0.37`, so any build rewrites it. That drift predates this change, so
it seemed better left out of this diff than swept in.

fix: preserve run start time during local execution (#1605)

## Summary

Local tasks reset `run_start_time` when they start, so a parent and its
delayed child report different kickoff times within the same run. A
retry also gets a new timestamp.

Forward the existing run timestamp through local dispatch. This uses the
existing field and runtime argument; it adds no API and does not change
the remote or experimental controllers.

Related to https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/pull/1100.

## Testing Done

The supported Python local runner reproduces this on current main and
release 2.8.1. No TaskContext objects or timestamp fields are assigned
by the reproducer.

| Source | Parent and child timestamps | Exit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current main | Different | 1 |
| 2.8.1 | Different | 1 |
| Current main with fix | Equal | 0 |
| 2.8.1 with the same runtime patch | Equal | 0 |

<details>
<summary>Reproducer and raw output</summary>

I used Python 3.12.9 with each checkout's locked runtime dependencies.
Save as `public_clock_probe.py`:

```python
import asyncio
import json
import flyte

env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(name="local-clock")

@env.task
async def child() -> str:
    return str(flyte.ctx().run_start_time)

@env.task
async def parent(delay: float) -> tuple[str, str]:
    started = str(flyte.ctx().run_start_time)
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return started, await child()

flyte.init(local_tracked=False)
outputs = flyte.with_runcontext(mode="local", disable_run_cache=True).run(parent, delay=0.05).outputs()
print(json.dumps({"parent_start": outputs[0], "child_start": outputs[1]}, sort_keys=True))
assert outputs[0] == outputs[1], "run_start_time changed within one managed run"
```

```bash
export FLYTE_DISABLE_SENTRY=true
export _F_USE_RUST_CONTROLLER=0
python public_clock_probe.py
```

fix: filter DeploymentError/ImageBuildError from Sentry

These two error types are explicitly defined as `RuntimeUserError`
subclasses in `flyte/errors.py` -- they are raised at deploy/build time
to feed an actionable, user-facing message back through the CLI (bad
trigger schema, image push permission denied, etc.). They are not SDK

fix: raise InitializationError when auth-config endpoint returns HTML

The unauthenticated AuthMetadataService config fetch (get_public_client_config /
get_o_auth2_metadata) is the first call the SDK makes against a configured endpoint.
When that endpoint serves an HTML body instead of protobuf -- a misconfigured address
(web console / login URL) or a proxy/ingress that doesn't forward gRPC/Connect traffic
-- connectrpc raises ConnectError(UNKNOWN, "invalid content-type: 'text/html';
expecting 'application/proto'"). This leaked into Sentry wrapped as
RuntimeSystemError("Upload failed ...") even on the latest SDK, masking a clear user
misconfiguration as a system bug.

RemoteClientConfigStore.get_client_config now catches the content-type ConnectError and
re-raises it as InitializationError("InvalidEndpoint", "user", ...) with an actionable
message. InitializationError is in the _is_user_error allowlist, so the wrapped chain is
filtered from Sentry; other ConnectError codes still propagate unchanged.

Adds unit tests for the new behavior and a Sentry-filter test for the wrapped chain.

fixes FLYTE-SDK-5N

Adds examples/genai/vllm_lmcache: several single-replica vLLM workers that
share KV cache through LMCache (L0 GPU, L1 pinned CPU, L2 a shared Valkey),
behind a FastAPI router that keeps its routing index in the same Valkey.

known prompt prefix, then the least-loaded worker. It skips overloaded
owners, retries the next candidate on failure, and falls back to round-robin
when Valkey is unavailable. bench.py compares routing modes and measures an
L2 fetch against recompute.

fix: wrap docker buildx CalledProcessError as ImageBuildError (#1082)

## Summary

Two related fixes in `flyte/_internal/imagebuild/docker_builder.py`:

1. **`_build_from_dockerfile`** had no try/except around
`subprocess.run(..., check=True)`, so a non-zero `docker buildx build -f
Dockerfile` exit propagated the raw `subprocess.CalledProcessError`
straight up to the caller — and into Sentry as an unhandled SDK crash.
2. **`_build_image`** already wrapped the same case, but raised a plain
`RuntimeError("Failed to build image: ...")`. `RuntimeError` is not in
`_is_user_error`'s filter set, so even though docker rejecting the
user's Dockerfile/context is purely user-facing feedback, each
occurrence landed in Sentry as a crash.

Both call sites now wrap the failure as `ImageBuildError`, which is
already filtered from Sentry via `_is_user_error` (#1052). The chained
`CalledProcessError` is preserved via `raise ... from e` so the
diagnostic information remains available.

## Sentry issues
- Fixes [FLYTE-SDK-34](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7487857254/)
(`CalledProcessError: Command '['docker', 'buildx', 'build', '-f', ...]'
returned non-zero exit status 1.`) — escaped from
`_build_from_dockerfile`
- Fixes [FLYTE-SDK-2R](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7481358912/)
(`RuntimeError: Failed to build image: Command '['docker', 'buildx',
'build', '--tag', ...]' returned non-zero exit status 1.`) — escaped
from `_build_image`

docs: strip inert reStructuredText from docstrings, convert NumPy sections to Google style

The SDK has no Sphinx (no conf.py, no .rst sources, no dependency), so the
reStructuredText in its docstrings is inert markup. It renders verbatim in
the published API reference, in IDE tooltips, in help() and in Jupyter.

Roles (464 across src/ and plugins/) become plain code spans. The tilde is
dropped and the fully-qualified name kept, so the docs site links them
automatically:

    :class:`~flyte.io.Dir`  ->  `flyte.io.Dir`

A bare name is qualified only when it resolves to a public export on the
referencing module's own package chain (or, for the handful of cross-package
references, to a path checked against the published linkmap). Module-private
symbols stay bare rather than acquire a path that does not import. Bare
methods and attributes are written in dotted Class.member form when the
enclosing class actually defines them.

Literal-block markers (81) become fenced blocks with an explicit language.
The trailing :: was rendering as a stray double colon, and the indented
block that followed became a code block with no language, which is why part
of the API reference had no syntax highlighting. No CSS change could have
fixed that; the blocks genuinely had no language.

RST directives (8) -- .. warning::, .. code-block::, .. autosummary::,
.. currentmodule:: -- become plain prose or fenced blocks.

NumPy sections (11, across 8 files) become Google style. The API-reference
generator parses Google sections and Sphinx field lists only; it has no
NumPy support, so a Parameters section was dropped outright and every
Description cell in the rendered parameter table came out empty while the
source held full prose for each parameter. flyte.ai.agents.agent.Agent is
the reference case: 11 parameters, all documented, all rendering blank.
After conversion the generator's own parser extracts all 11 with
descriptions.

Prose is preserved verbatim throughout; only markup changes. Two factual
corrections were made where the docstring disagreed with the code:
flyte.app.extras' module example named a FastAPIAuthMiddleware class that
does not exist (the class is FastAPIPassthroughAuthMiddleware), and
lazy_module's example imported from flytekit rather than flyte.

feat: make MCP transport="stdio" actually serve stdio (#1319)

## Problem

`MCPAppEnvironment` accepts `transport="stdio"` and validates it, but
never implements it. `__post_init__` builds the Starlette app and sets
`_server = self._starlette_app_server` for *every* transport value, so
`"stdio"` silently serves streamable-HTTP:

```python
env = FlyteMCPAppEnvironment(name="x", transport="stdio", tool_groups=["run"])
env._server.__name__        # -> '_starlette_app_server'
env._starlette_app is None  # -> False
```

The `flyte-mcp` CLI had no `--transport` flag either, so the only way to
reach that path was to build the environment by hand.

The practical consequence: there was no way to run a Flyte MCP server
for clients that launch it as a subprocess, which is how most MCP
clients (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) prefer to run a local server.
Anyone following the "local MCP" path got an HTTP server on `:8080` and
had to attach to it separately.

## Changes

### 1. Real stdio support

- **`transport="stdio"` builds no HTTP surface** — no Starlette app, no
`/health`, no links. `mcp_mount_path` is unused.
- **New `run_stdio()` / `run_stdio_async()`** on `MCPAppEnvironment`.
- **`_server` is deliberately left unset for stdio.** `flyte.serve()`
runs the server on a background thread and then polls an HTTP health
check (`_LocalApp.is_active()` GETs `http://host:port/health`), so it
can never host a process-bound stdio stream. Leaving `_server` unset
makes `serve()` fail fast rather than hang forever waiting on a health
check that will never pass.
- **`flyte-mcp --transport {stdio,sse,streamable-http}`**, default
`streamable-http` (unchanged).
- **stdout protection under stdio.** stdout is the JSON-RPC channel, and
the CLI `click.echo`s progress during setup (corpus cache,
clone/download). One stray byte breaks the client's first parse, so
setup-phase stdout is redirected to stderr. The redirect covers setup
only — `stdio_server()` re-wraps `sys.stdout.buffer` at call time, so
leaving it active would have sent the entire protocol to stderr.
- **`--requires-auth` warns under stdio**, where it has no effect: the
server talks only to the process that launched it and runs with the
caller's own credentials.
- **Drive-by:** the HTTP startup banner printed `{mount_path}/mcp` even
for `sse`, sending sse users to a nonexistent path. It now matches the
transport.

### 2. Fix three broken `uvx` invocations in the MCP examples

Separate from stdio, and worth reviewing on its own — every local-setup
command in `examples/mcp/` was broken:

- **`uvx --with "flyte[mcp]" flyte-mcp` runs the wrong package.** `uvx
<cmd>` is shorthand for `uvx --from <cmd> <cmd>`, so the package is
resolved from the *command name* — and
[`flyte-mcp`](https://pypi.org/project/flyte-mcp/) is a real, unrelated
third-party project on PyPI ("MCP server exposing Flyte V2 SDK
knowledge"). Anyone following our own examples installed and ran
**someone else's MCP server**, with `flyte[mcp]` attached only as an
extra dependency. The adjacent line in the same docstring already used
`--from` correctly, so this was a slip rather than intent.
- **Missing `--transport stdio`** — the commands are presented as stdio
setup but would start an HTTP server.
- **`uvx --from . flyte-mcp` omits the `[mcp]` extra**, so the
repo-checkout path fails immediately with `ModuleNotFoundError: mcp is
not installed`. Found by actually running it; now `uvx --from ".[mcp]"
flyte-mcp`.

## Usage

```bash
flyte-mcp --transport stdio --tool-groups run,task
```

```jsonc
// MCP client config
{ "mcpServers": { "flyte": { "command": "uvx",
  "args": ["--from", "flyte[mcp]", "flyte-mcp", "--transport", "stdio"] } } }
```

## Testing

`tests/flyte/ai/mcp/test_mcp_app_environment.py` gains a
`TestStdioTransport` class that drives a **real** `initialize` →
`tools/list` → `tools/call` session over in-memory streams (asserting
the tool actually returns `"pong"`), plus assertions that the HTTP
transports are unmodified and that `run_stdio_async()` rejects non-stdio
transports.

Verified manually end-to-end by speaking JSON-RPC to the CLI over a
pipe:

```

fix: retry a stalled upload instead of failing it (FLYTE-SDK-5F)

S3 answers a PUT whose body stopped arriving with `400 RequestTimeout`
("Your socket connection to the server was not read from or written to
within the timeout period. Idle connections will be closed."). 400 is
otherwise the canonical "your request is malformed, retrying will not
help" status, so `_classify`'s status table sent it straight down the
fatal branch: the upload failed on the first stall, with no retry, and
surfaced as a RuntimeSystemError carrying S3's raw XML.

The store means the opposite. `RequestTimeout` sits in the AWS SDKs'
standard retryable set precisely because re-sending the PUT is the
documented remedy.

FLYTE-SDK-5F is a mixed group: 24 of its 39 events are the expired-URL
403 the rest of this branch addresses, but 6 are this stall, which the
lifetime change does not touch. Match the store's own `<Code>` element
rather than widening the status table, so a genuine malformed-request
400 still fails fast. `ExpiredToken` shares the status and keeps its
own unretried branch -- a dead signature stays dead.

feat(app): add cluster to pin an app to a specific cluster (#1570)

## Summary

Adds a `cluster` field to `AppEnvironment` and a `cluster` argument to
`serve()`, setting app `Spec.cluster` so a user can **pin a serving app
to a named cluster** instead of load-balancing across a `cluster_pool`.

Motivation: today app placement is `cluster_pool` →
first-healthy-cluster-that-pulls (non-deterministic, no capacity
awareness). Users who need a serving app on a *specific* cluster (e.g.
the one with a particular accelerator) had no way to express it.

## Behavior
- `cluster` and a **non-default** `cluster_pool` are **mutually
exclusive** — raises `ValueError` at `AppEnvironment` construction and
in `serve()`.
- When `cluster` is set, the serialized `Spec` sends an **empty
`cluster_pool`** so the control plane sees an unambiguous pin.
- `cluster` unset → unchanged behavior (pool placement; empty pool →
default pool).

## Depends on
flyteorg/flyte#8018 (adds `app.Spec.cluster` to `flyteidl2`). The
control plane honors the pin (leases only to the named cluster) and
validates mutual exclusion.

Document that connector-side upload needs the connector's own storage access

Found by running the script example on a real GKE data plane: the upload failed
with 403 storage.objects.create denied, after the job had already succeeded.

The cause is structural, not a misconfiguration. output_upload="connector" makes
the connector pod write to the run's output prefix, which a connector otherwise
never does -- it talks to its remote system and nothing else. So the dataplane
chart gives the backend cloud identity to union-system, webhook, dataproxy and
fluent-bit, but not to flyteconnector, whose serviceAccount.annotations default
to {}. Every existing GCP and AWS data plane therefore fails this default until
someone annotates that service account.

Worth being plain about: this makes the easy path the one that needs a
deployment change, while output_upload="job" needs none. The default still earns
its place -- a node with no cloud client and no credentials can still produce
outputs -- but the prerequisite has to be unmissable, and it was not documented
at all.

artifacts: one protocol, not two — drop the unused _flyte_metadata declaration

Review feedback asked why declaration needed a second protocol when `Artifact`
already existed. It did not. `Artifact` declared `_flyte_metadata: Metadata`,
and a runtime_checkable protocol's `isinstance` checks data members as well as
methods, so `isinstance(plugin_volume, Artifact)` was False -- which is what
pushed me to add a separate method-only protocol rather than question the
member.

The member was dead. It appears once as a protocol annotation and six times on
`ArtifactWrapper` itself (slots, __init__, the __getattr__ guards, the getter);
nothing ever read it *through* the protocol type. Deleting the annotation costs
nothing, `ArtifactWrapper` still carries the attribute, and one protocol then
serves both shapes:

                          duck type   wrapper
  with _flyte_metadata      False       True
  without it                True        True

So `ArtifactMetadata` is gone and `Artifact` is the single method-only protocol
used for declaration. The two guards alongside `isinstance` stay: a class
satisfies a method-only protocol exactly as its instances do, and a
non-callable attribute of the right name satisfies it too.
