Env-var control of in-cluster auth mode (ExternalCommand without EAGER_API_KEY) (#1536)

## Problem

A customer does not want the control plane issuing eager API keys to
their task pods. They mint their own, more narrowly scoped tokens and
want the SDK to authenticate with `ExternalCommand`, which we already
support and prototyped with them.

`init_in_cluster` resolved credentials in this order:

1. an explicit `api_key=` argument
2. a mounted config file, if the pod has `UCTL_CONFIG` /
`FLYTECTL_CONFIG` set
3. the injected `_UNION_EAGER_API_KEY` / `EAGER_API_KEY`

So the only way to opt out of the injected key was to mount a config
file. There was no env-var-only route — even though every credentials
config entry already derives an env var (`admin.authType` →
`FLYTE_ADMIN_AUTHTYPE`).

Two things were also quietly broken along the way, and both had to be
fixed for the env-var route to work end to end.

## What this does

A task pod can now carry:

```
FLYTE_AUTH_TYPE=ExternalCommand
FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND="/usr/local/bin/mint-token --audience flyte"
```

and authenticate by running that command, with no API key issued to it
at all.

- `FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND` takes a shell-quoted command line, or a JSON
array when an argument contains spaces. Its stdout is the access token,
re-run on refresh.
- **Setting `FLYTE_AUTH_TYPE` disables the injected-key fallback
outright** rather than layering on top of it, so a cluster still
injecting a key mid-migration cannot have the two silently disagree.
- The endpoint still comes from the injected `_U_EP_OVERRIDE`, and now
also accepts `FLYTE_ADMIN_ENDPOINT` — dropping the API key drops the
endpoint it used to decode to.
- `FLYTE_AUTH_PROXY_COMMAND` is picked up independently of the auth
type.
- An explicit `api_key=` argument still wins, and logs that it is
ignoring the env vars instead of doing so quietly.
- `ExternalCommand` with no command raises at init, rather than
deferring to an `AuthenticationError` on the first RPC that names
neither env var.

The entries are read via `ConfigEntry.read()` with no config file, which
consults only the environment. That deliberately keeps the pod off
`resolve_config_path`, whose `git rev-parse` subprocess is wasted work
in a task pod.

## Two bugs fixed on the way

**`FLYTE_ADMIN_COMMAND` was unusable even on the existing config-file
path.** `ConfigEntry` applied no transform to env values, so a
`list`-typed entry came back as the raw string and
`asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(*self._cmd)` spread it *one argument per
character*. Same shape for the proxy command and scopes. YAML already
yields a list and is unaffected; the new transforms are idempotent on
that path.

**`create_remote_controller` accepted `command` and threw it away.** It
took `command`, `proxy_command`, `http_proxy_url` and `client_config`
and never forwarded them to `ControllerClient`. Since `init_in_cluster`
builds the SDK client and the controller from the same kwargs,
`auth_type="ExternalCommand"` would have authenticated the client
correctly while leaving the controller holding the auth mode with
nothing to run — surfacing only as `AuthenticationError: Command cannot
be empty for command authenticator` on the controller's first RPC. The
controller is what enqueues and watches child actions, so eager tasks
would have failed at the point of spawning work rather than at init.

`rpc_retries` is deliberately still not forwarded there: the controller
has never installed the retry interceptor, and adding it would change
retry behavior rather than fix a drop.

## On the env var names

These names are normally *derived*, not chosen: `get_env_name()` does
`FLYTE_{SWITCH_UPPERCASED}`, so `admin.authType` →
`FLYTE_ADMIN_AUTHTYPE`. That spelling leaks flyte-1 `flyteadmin` naming
into something a customer has to type into a pod spec, and
`read_from_env`'s docstring already called the scheme provisional.

Renaming outright would cost more than the wart. The scheme's one real
virtue is that env var and config key are derivable from each other both
ways; changing 2 of the 11 `admin.*` entries leaves no rule, just a
lookup table with exceptions. The derived names are also public surface
predating this feature — they are what the config-file path has always
used.

So the preferred name is now explicit rather than implicit.
`YamlConfigEntry` takes an `aliases` tuple checked ahead of the derived
name; `get_env_name()` reports the preferred one (docs, error messages)
and `env_names()` gives the precedence order.

| setting | preferred | still accepted |
|---|---|---|
| `admin.authType` | `FLYTE_AUTH_TYPE` | `FLYTE_ADMIN_AUTHTYPE` |
| `admin.command` | `FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND` | `FLYTE_ADMIN_COMMAND` |
| `admin.proxyCommand` | `FLYTE_AUTH_PROXY_COMMAND` |
`FLYTE_ADMIN_PROXYCOMMAND` |

Nothing that worked before stops working. When two names for one setting
disagree the higher-precedence one wins and the conflict is logged
rather than dropped silently — that ambiguity is how a migration goes
wrong quietly; identical values are not reported.

Scoped deliberately to the three auth entries this feature documents.
`FLYTE_ADMIN_ENDPOINT` keeps its derived name, since the endpoint is a
platform setting rather than an auth one. Renaming the rest of the
`admin.*` family is the scheme-wide change the code comment anticipates
and wants its own discussion.

## Known gap

The opt-in Rust controller (`_F_USE_RUST_CONTROLLER=1`) reads the
injected API key directly and does not honor these vars. Anyone on it
cannot drop the key yet. Called out in the `init_in_cluster` docstring.

## Testing

- 18 new tests in `tests/user_api/test_init_in_cluster_env_auth.py`
covering parsing (shlex, JSON array, quoted args), precedence (explicit
auth type beats the injected key; explicit `api_key` beats the env vars;
no env vars means unchanged legacy behavior), the endpoint fallback, the
loud-failure case, the controller forwarding, and the alias mechanism
(preferred name wins, derived name still honored, conflicts reported,
non-aliased entries unchanged).
- Verified end to end that the env vars produce an
`AsyncCommandAuthenticator` which runs the command and returns its
stdout as the token.
- Full suite failure set is byte-identical before and after this change.
`ruff` and `mypy` clean.

Note for reviewers running tests inside a Flyte task pod:
`_U_EP_OVERRIDE` and `_UNION_EAGER_API_KEY` are live in that environment
and leak into several tests, including a pre-existing one in
`test_init_in_cluster_fallback.py`. Unset them for a clean run.

contain lists

When users accidentally pass a list instead of a tuple to Layer fields

test(cli): smoke-check the JSON output against the real command tree

`make cli-docs-gen` is the only thing that runs the doc generator against the
live CLI rather than against commands a test constructed, and it covered only
`--type markdown`. The new mode had unit tests and no end-to-end run at all.

That distinction is the whole value of this target. The unit tests build their
own click objects, so they cannot see the failures that exist only on the real
tree: a walk that stopped descending because a private type it matches by class
NAME was renamed, or a genuine command whose default does not serialise. Both
yield a generator that exits 0 and emits a plausible, wrong document.

So the target now also runs `--type json` and pipes it through a check that
asserts something, rather than just exiting 0 as the markdown half does: valid
JSON, every command carrying every key, the root command present, and a command
count above a floor set far below the real one to catch a collapse without
needing an edit whenever a command is added.

Verified to fail on each: malformed output, a collapsed walk, and a missing key.
Passes on the real tree at 55 commands core and 94 with flyteplugins-union
installed.

feat(github): add flyteplugins-github (webhooks + review_pr gate) (#1513)

Part of the webhook plugin stack. Requires #1512
(`flyteplugins-webhooks-core`), which is this PR's base — the diff here
is just this package.

Receive GitHub webhooks in Flyte.

## What it implements

The `Provider` contract from core: which environment variable holds the
secret, how to verify a delivery, how to parse one into a
`WebhookEvent`, plus typed constants for every event GitHub sends.

**Verification:** HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body (`X-Hub-Signature-256`).

Answers GitHub's `ping` automatically, so a green check in *Recent
Deliveries* means the app is reachable.

Comment and review events fold the comment id into `resource_id`, so two
comments on one issue are two events rather than a redelivery of the
first — the bug that prompted this whole restructure.

## Conformance

Runs the shared `assert_provider_conforms`, which replays this plugin's
`SAMPLE_DELIVERY` — a real GitHub payload — through `verify` and `parse`
rather than trusting them to agree with each other. It also asserts the
verifier returns False rather than raising on a hostile header, that
event constants render as wire values rather than enum names, and that
the sample parses to something the constants actually spell.

7 tests. `make fmt`, `make mypy`, `make ty`, ruff, and codespell pass.

## What it does not do

Call the GitHub API. Use `PyGithub` directly from your tasks — the
recipes are in the examples PR at the end of this stack. This plugin
owns only the part that is Flyte's: authenticating an inbound delivery
and turning it into a run.

feat(config): add named profiles selected with --profile

A config file may declare a top-level `profiles:` mapping. Under a profile,
every switch is looked up at `profiles.<name>.<switch>` and falls back to the
top-level `<switch>`, so the top level acts as defaults shared by every
profile:

    admin:
      endpoint: dns:///default.example.com
    task:
      project: research
    profiles:
      prod:
        admin: {endpoint: dns:///prod.example.com}
        task:  {domain: production}

    $ flyte --profile prod run ...

This lands in `ConfigFile._get_from_yaml`, the single chokepoint every config
read funnels through, so all of `config/_internal.py` becomes profile-aware
without touching the per-section `auto()` methods. A file with no `profiles:`
key reads exactly as before.

Selection is `--profile` or `FLYTE_PROFILE`. `FLYTE_*` environment variables
still override the file, matching how `AWS_PROFILE` behaves. Requesting a
profile the file does not declare raises `ProfileNotFoundError` rather than
falling back to the defaults and talking to the wrong control plane. The
`ConfigFile` cache is keyed by path *and* profile; sharing one entry across
profiles would silently return the wrong file.

Also:

- `flyte create config --profile NAME` merges into `profiles.<name>` instead
  of replacing the file, so profiles accumulate.
- `flyte get profiles` lists what a file declares and marks the active one.
- `flyte.use_profile` / `aio_use_profile` scope a profile to a `with` block:
  they read it, build a client, and install it as the active config for the
  current context only, leaving the process-wide config from `flyte.init()`
  untouched so concurrent callers are unaffected. They default to the file
  the session was initialized from rather than re-running the default search,
  which would let a switch land in a different discoverable file. Tested
  across the syncify thread boundary, since `flyte.run` inside such a block
  relies on the caller's context being copied to the loop thread.
- `Config.source` is recorded as `source_config_path` when no explicit path
  was passed, so later readers can find the file actually used.
- Fix `_apply_hook_to_subcommand` invoking `original_command.callback()` at
  registration time, which ran the wrapped command during plugin discovery.
  This broke subcommand hooks for any plugin, not just new ones.

fix(auth): act on the device-polling review

Four review comments, all correct.

**A non-JSON 5xx now keeps the poll alive.** The previous change only swapped
the exception type: a 502 with an HTML body stopped raising JSONDecodeError and
started raising AuthenticationError, which poll_token_endpoint re-raises, so the
login still died on one bad gateway response. get_token now raises a typed
AuthenticationTransientError for a 5xx or 429 carrying no OAuth error code, and
the poll loop rides it out. It subclasses AuthenticationError so the refresh and
client-credentials callers, which have nothing to retry with, are unchanged.
A 4xx with no error code still fails immediately -- that is the request being
wrong, not the upstream faltering -- and there is now a test pinning each side.

**The regression test asserted the opposite of its own name.** It was called
test_non_json_error_body_does_not_kill_the_poll, its docstring said the login
must not abort, and then it asserted that AuthenticationError was raised on the
first response. The handler's second, successful response was never reached, so
the test passed precisely because the bug was present. It now asserts the token
comes back and the handler was called twice; it fails against the previous
implementation, which is what makes it a regression test.

**The poll deadline is measured on a monotonic clock.** datetime.now() meant an
NTP step or a manual clock change could end the loop early or run it past
expires_in.

**The verification URI is parsed and rebuilt rather than concatenated.** The
fallback for a server that sends no verification_uri_complete appended
"?user_code=..." unconditionally, so a verification_uri that already carried a
query produced a second "?" -- an unusable URL, read off a screen and typed by
hand. _verification_uri_with_code merges into the existing query and keeps any
fragment after it.

fix(remote-builder): translate PythonWheels → CopyConfig + Commands

`flyteidl2.imagebuilder.PythonWheels` only declares `dir` / `options` /
`secret_mounts` — there's no `package_name` field today. The SDK's
remote-builder serializer at remote_builder.py:262 sets
`PythonWheels(... package_name=layer.package_name, ...)`, which the
proto-generated message rejects with:

  Protocol message PythonWheels has no "package_name" field.

Consequence: any image with a `PythonWheels` layer
(`Image.with_local_v2()`, `Image.with_local_v2_plugins(...)`, or any
caller that adds the layer directly) blows up at image-build time on
the remote builder. The local docker builder is unaffected because
it reads `package_name` straight off the Python dataclass.

This was a known gap — the wheel-changes commit (1cdbd6bb) literally
says "Will need to update the remote builder as well." Until the
proto + the server-side builder gain a real `package_name` field, we
can sidestep the proto entirely by emitting the equivalent local
docker-builder behavior using existing wire-compatible messages:

  CopyConfig{src=<staged wheel dir>, dst=/<dir_name>}
  Commands{cmd=[
      "pip install ... --find-links /<dir_name> --no-deps --no-index
       --force-reinstall <package_name>",
      "pip install ... <package_name>",
  ]}

The two pip invocations mirror exactly what
`docker_builder.PythonWheelHandler` runs locally:

  1. Install the wheel WITHOUT deps from --find-links (--no-index
     guarantees we never reach PyPI for the package itself).
  2. Install dependencies normally (pip resolves the dep tree from
     PyPI for everything except the package we just baked).

feat(artifacts): let a caller declare which outputs of a task are artifacts (#1608)

Stacked on #1599 (typed artifact partitions).

## Why

Code that composes other people's tasks — the artifact factory first —
has had no way to make a task's outputs into artifacts without changing
the task. Its only option was to call `CreateArtifact` itself after the
task returned. That path records a caller-asserted source (on the
devbox, every factory-built artifact points at the factory's own action
rather than the build that made it), mints random versions, and
publishes even when the task failed.

## What

`flyte.artifacts.produces(...)` lets the caller declare which outputs of
the task it calls are artifacts:

```python
with flyte.artifacts.produces(o0=Metadata(name="events", partitions={"date": day, "region": "us"})):
    await clean.override(produces_artifacts=True)(raw=raw)
```

The task is unchanged. Its declared outputs are published through the
existing path, exactly as if it had returned `flyte.artifacts.new(...)`:
leaseworker extraction on success, `created_by` and `source` stamped by
the control plane, `<run>-<action>-<attempt>` versions, and
`AlreadyExists` on replay. No IDL or backend change.

- **Transport.** Declarations ride on the child action's
`Inputs.context` under a reserved key, `_u_produced_artifacts`,
alongside the existing kickoff-time key. Reserved keys are filtered out
of `Inputs.context`, so a declaration applies to the one action it was
made for and never reaches the actions that task spawns.
`get_custom_context()` hides it.
- **Caching.** Context is not part of the cache key, so declaring
changes neither caching nor sub-action naming.
- **Output conversion.** Emits a `ProducedArtifact` for each declared
slot and fills in the literal type. If the task also wraps that output,
the caller wins for name, version, partitions and parents, and the
task's description, card and attrs fill in what the caller left empty. A
declaration for an output the task doesn't have fails the task with a
message naming both.
- **`TaskDetails.override(produces_artifacts=...)`.** Added for remote
task refs, since that flag is what lets the platform extract a task's
artifacts. Local task templates already had it.
- The artifacts module docstring no longer says mismatched partition
keys are flagged.

## Testing

- New `tests/flyte/test_produced_artifact_declarations.py` (13 tests):
declarations reach the child and not the grandchild;
`get_custom_context` hides the key; concurrent calls under
`asyncio.gather` keep their own declarations; no-op outside a task; bad
declarations fail in the caller; only declared slots are produced, with
the literal type filled in; caller-wins merge; unknown slot is an error;
the remote override sets the template flag.
- `pytest -k "artifact or partition or trigger or context or convert or
taskrunner"`: 742 passed.
- `make fmt`, `make lint`, `make check-docstrings` clean. `make ty`
reports only the existing diagnostics in `examples/`.

fix(bundle): skip ruff import analysis when ruff is too old (#1641)

## Problem

ruff is an optional aid for `--copy auto` bundling: when present, `ruff
analyze graph` adds lazily and `TYPE_CHECKING`-imported local modules to
the code bundle. A missing ruff is handled quietly at debug level, but
an old ruff passes the `shutil.which` check, fails on `ruff analyze
graph --type-checking-imports`, and gets its whole usage text logged as
a warning on every remote submit:

```
[flyte] WARNING 'ruff analyze graph' exited with 2: error: unexpected argument '--type-checking-imports' found
  tip: to pass '--type-checking-imports' as a value, use '-- --type-checking-imports'
Usage: ruff check <FILES|--fix|...>
```

Reported with ruff 0.3.4 on flyte 2.7.2. The run itself is fine,
bundling falls back to `sys.modules`.

## Change

- `_ruff_is_available()` now checks `ruff --version` and skips the
analysis when ruff is older than 0.14.6. ruff is not run in that case; a
single one-line warning is logged instead:

  ```
[flyte] WARNING ruff 0.3.4 is too old for code bundle import analysis
(needs >= 0.14.6); lazily imported local modules may be left out of the
bundle. Upgrade ruff to fix.
  ```

- 0.14.6 is the first release whose `analyze graph` accepts
`--type-checking-imports` (probed: 0.14.5 rejects it, 0.14.6 accepts it;
`analyze graph` itself does not exist in 0.3.x).
- The check is cached per process, so the version probe (about 15ms) and
the warning happen once.
- If the version cannot be determined, ruff is skipped with a debug log,
same as a missing ruff.
- The remaining non-zero-exit warning from `ruff analyze graph` keeps
only the first line of stderr, so it can never dump usage text.

ruff stays optional; no dependency is added.

## Testing

- New unit tests: old ruff is not run and warns once across two bundles,
version parsing, failed version probe, one-line failure warning.
- `pytest tests/flyte/code_bundle`: 103 passed.
- End to end with a real ruff 0.3.4 on PATH: two `ls_files` calls print
the one-line warning once and bundle from `sys.modules`.

build: type-check all examples with mypy and ty; add ty make target + pre-commit hook (#1298)

## Why are the changes needed?

`make mypy` only checked `src/` plus two hand-picked example files
(`examples/basics/hello.py`, `hello_v2.py`), so type regressions in the
other ~500 example scripts — the SDK's primary user-facing documentation
— went unnoticed, and several SDK typing gaps forced users into
unannotatable code. This PR makes the entire tree (`src/` + `examples/`)
pass **both mypy and ty**, and enforces it on every commit.

Baseline before this change: **548 mypy errors** and **1059 ty
diagnostics** across the tree.

## What changes were proposed in this pull request?

### Tooling
- `make mypy` now checks `src/ examples/`; new `make ty` target checks
the same scope; both run as prek pre-commit hooks.
- `[tool.mypy]`: `explicit_package_bases` + `mypy_path = ["src"]` so
example scripts with recurring filenames (`main.py`, `app.py`, ...)
resolve to unique module names in one invocation.
- `[tool.ty.rules]`: `unresolved-import` ignored (same policy as mypy's
`ignore_missing_imports` — examples import optional heavy deps like
torch/sklearn); unused-ignore-comment rules disabled in both directions
since the tree is checked by two checkers; fixed two stale rule names
(`possibly-unbound-*` → `possibly-missing-*`) that ty had renamed and
were **silently not applying**.
- ty added to the dev dependency group, with an `exclude-newer-package`
override (ty releases outpace the repo's 5-day recency cutoff).

### SDK — typing-only, no runtime or user-facing API changes
- `File`/`Dir` generic `T` now defaults to `Any` (PEP 696):
`File(path=...)` and `File.new_remote()` type-check without an
annotation on the assignment target (~150 errors).
- `File.open()` gains mode-based overloads (`"rb"` → readable handle,
`"wb"` → writable). The overloads live on a plain method returning
`AbstractAsyncContextManager` delegating to the `@asynccontextmanager`
generator, because neither mypy nor ty matches overloads through that
decorator (~170 errors across both checkers).
- `AppEnvironment.on_startup`/`server`/`on_shutdown` accept sync **or**
async callables — matching their documented behavior and the
`iscoroutinefunction` dispatch in `_serve.py` — and preserve the
decorated function's type.
- `AsyncConnector` is now `Generic[M: ResourceMeta]` with a default, so
subclasses can parameterize (`AsyncConnector[MyJobMetadata]`) and narrow
`create`/`get`/`delete`/`get_logs` honestly. `metadata_type` corrected
to `type[M]` (every real connector assigns a class; internal code calls
`.decode` on it), and `get_logs` is typed to permit the async-generator
form the connector server already documents and handles. Unparameterized
subclasses type-check exactly as before.
- ~280 further ty diagnostics fixed across 84 src files (casts, narrowed
annotations, TYPE_CHECKING imports). 28 justified `# ty: ignore[rule]`
comments remain, each marking a documented checker limitation.

### Examples (~470 fixes across ~180 files)
- Recurring honest patterns: `flyte.ctx()` None-guards, coroutine-list
annotations, `BaseException` filtering after
`gather(return_exceptions=True)`.
- `Runner.run` is now honestly typed `-> Run` in every mode: hybrid mode
(test-only) wraps its natively computed outputs in the same inline Run
wrapper local mode uses, instead of returning raw task outputs. This
removed the `R | Run` union that would otherwise have required `assert
isinstance(run, Run)` narrowing at ~75 example call sites.
- Renamed `examples/plugins/polars` → `polars_examples`: the directory
shadowed the real polars package in ty's module resolution, producing 72
false diagnostics.
- Only 4 `# ty: ignore` comments across all examples.

### Real bugs the checkers caught (fixed here)
- Missing `@syncify` on `CodeModeAgent.run` — `agent.run.aio(...)` call
sites would `AttributeError` at runtime.
- `typing.NotRequired` import that crashes on Python 3.10 (project
floor).
- A stray `flyte.g` statement (AttributeError when run).
- A custom image builder example returning `str` where the
`ImageBuilder` protocol requires `ImageBuild`.
- Shadowed FastAPI `app` variables (serve handles overwriting the ASGI
app), deprecated `datetime.utcnow()`, and a `gpu_memory_utilization`
kwarg silently dropped by pydantic.

### Known follow-ups (deliberately not fixed — behavior-change
constraint)
- `src/flyte/cli/_tui/_remote/_screens.py:767-772` reads nonexistent
proto fields (`pb2.id`/`pb2.task_template`), so that TUI panel always
hits its error fallback; likely intended fields noted in a comment.
- `src/flyte/storage/_remote_fs.py:148` — dead code path awaits a
syncify sync wrapper.
- Protocol/stub drift in `remote/_client/_protocols.py` worked around
with ~7 casts.

### API behavior changes (intentional)
- `flyte.run(...)` / `with_runcontext(...).run(...)` now returns a `Run`
in **every** mode. Hybrid mode (test-only) previously returned the
task's raw outputs; it now wraps them in the same inline Run wrapper
local mode uses (`wait()` no-op, `outputs()` serves the values).
- `flyte.ctx()` now always returns a `TaskContext`. Outside a task it
returns a **falsy null context** (`NULL_TASK_CONTEXT`) whose fields are
all `None`, instead of `None` itself — so task code reads
`flyte.ctx().action` without None-guards. Detect task execution with
truthiness (`if flyte.ctx():`). **Compat note:** code using identity
checks (`flyte.ctx() is None`) must switch to truthiness; all in-repo
call sites (src, plugins, examples, tests) were converted. One such site
— the log-record factory in `flyte/_logging.py` — initially slipped
through and hung any await on a `DynamicBatcher` future whose
`process_fn` logged an error; fixed and covered by the
previously-hanging `test_error_propagation`.

## How was this patch tested?

- `make mypy` — clean (810 files)
- `make ty` — clean
- `make unit_test` — 4268 passed, 9 skipped
- bigquery / databricks / snowflake plugin suites (subclass
`AsyncConnector`) — 91 passed
- `File.open` read/write round-trip verified at runtime; `ruff
format`/`check` clean
- All pre-commit hooks (fmt, mypy, ty, uvlock) passed on commit

flyte serve: make Parameter more user-friendly (#914)

This pull request introduces several improvements and fixes to the
handling of application parameters in Flyte, especially around file and
directory parameters, explicit parameter typing, and deployment-time
validation. It also adds comprehensive tests to ensure correct behavior
when parameters change, including during app replacement and
serialization. The changes enhance usability, robustness, and error
reporting for users defining and serving parameterized applications.

**Parameter Handling and Validation Improvements:**

* The `Parameter` class now allows the `value` to be `None`, enabling
values to be supplied at serving time via `parameter_values` in
`flyte.with_servecontext`. The new `type` attribute allows explicit
parameter typing, and the documentation has been updated accordingly.
[[1]](diffhunk://#diff-a19db05b7e98eb861ff10ff6d60ed61dd27492ff35e8a3e4bbf7f8402e0b09d4L213-R215)
[[2]](diffhunk://#diff-a19db05b7e98eb861ff10ff6d60ed61dd27492ff35e8a3e4bbf7f8402e0b09d4L225-R228)
* Deployment-time validation in `SerializableParameter.from_parameter`
ensures that all parameters have a value before deployment, raising a
clear error if not.
* When an explicit `type` is provided, it overrides type inference, and
setting a `mount` for file/directory types automatically enables
downloading.
* A new helper, `_ensure_dest_writable`, checks that mount destinations
for parameters are writable and provides informative errors if not.
* The parameter synchronization logic in `sync_parameters` now handles
directory mounts for files more robustly and validates destination
writability.

**Testing Enhancements:**

* Extensive new tests verify that app specs are considered different
when parameters change (in value, name, or count), and that app
replacement triggers updates only when necessary.
[[1]](diffhunk://#diff-0fa0d8d33b0ed0445c5e99a8669ddee1989821c9780aea47297287717d7889abR73-R165)
[[2]](diffhunk://#diff-0fa0d8d33b0ed0445c5e99a8669ddee1989821c9780aea47297287717d7889abR463-R540)

Env-var control of in-cluster auth mode (ExternalCommand without EAGER_API_KEY) (#1536)

## Problem

A customer does not want the control plane issuing eager API keys to
their task pods. They mint their own, more narrowly scoped tokens and
want the SDK to authenticate with `ExternalCommand`, which we already
support and prototyped with them.

`init_in_cluster` resolved credentials in this order:

1. an explicit `api_key=` argument
2. a mounted config file, if the pod has `UCTL_CONFIG` /
`FLYTECTL_CONFIG` set
3. the injected `_UNION_EAGER_API_KEY` / `EAGER_API_KEY`

So the only way to opt out of the injected key was to mount a config
file. There was no env-var-only route — even though every credentials
config entry already derives an env var (`admin.authType` →
`FLYTE_ADMIN_AUTHTYPE`).

Two things were also quietly broken along the way, and both had to be
fixed for the env-var route to work end to end.

## What this does

A task pod can now carry:

```
FLYTE_AUTH_TYPE=ExternalCommand
FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND="/usr/local/bin/mint-token --audience flyte"
```

and authenticate by running that command, with no API key issued to it
at all.

- `FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND` takes a shell-quoted command line, or a JSON
array when an argument contains spaces. Its stdout is the access token,
re-run on refresh.
- **Setting `FLYTE_AUTH_TYPE` disables the injected-key fallback
outright** rather than layering on top of it, so a cluster still
injecting a key mid-migration cannot have the two silently disagree.
- The endpoint still comes from the injected `_U_EP_OVERRIDE`, and now
also accepts `FLYTE_ADMIN_ENDPOINT` — dropping the API key drops the
endpoint it used to decode to.
- `FLYTE_AUTH_PROXY_COMMAND` is picked up independently of the auth
type.
- An explicit `api_key=` argument still wins, and logs that it is
ignoring the env vars instead of doing so quietly.
- `ExternalCommand` with no command raises at init, rather than
deferring to an `AuthenticationError` on the first RPC that names
neither env var.

The entries are read via `ConfigEntry.read()` with no config file, which
consults only the environment. That deliberately keeps the pod off
`resolve_config_path`, whose `git rev-parse` subprocess is wasted work
in a task pod.

## Two bugs fixed on the way

**`FLYTE_ADMIN_COMMAND` was unusable even on the existing config-file
path.** `ConfigEntry` applied no transform to env values, so a
`list`-typed entry came back as the raw string and
`asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(*self._cmd)` spread it *one argument per
character*. Same shape for the proxy command and scopes. YAML already
yields a list and is unaffected; the new transforms are idempotent on
that path.

**`create_remote_controller` accepted `command` and threw it away.** It
took `command`, `proxy_command`, `http_proxy_url` and `client_config`
and never forwarded them to `ControllerClient`. Since `init_in_cluster`
builds the SDK client and the controller from the same kwargs,
`auth_type="ExternalCommand"` would have authenticated the client
correctly while leaving the controller holding the auth mode with
nothing to run — surfacing only as `AuthenticationError: Command cannot
be empty for command authenticator` on the controller's first RPC. The
controller is what enqueues and watches child actions, so eager tasks
would have failed at the point of spawning work rather than at init.

`rpc_retries` is deliberately still not forwarded there: the controller
has never installed the retry interceptor, and adding it would change
retry behavior rather than fix a drop.

## On the env var names

These names are normally *derived*, not chosen: `get_env_name()` does
`FLYTE_{SWITCH_UPPERCASED}`, so `admin.authType` →
`FLYTE_ADMIN_AUTHTYPE`. That spelling leaks flyte-1 `flyteadmin` naming
into something a customer has to type into a pod spec, and
`read_from_env`'s docstring already called the scheme provisional.

Renaming outright would cost more than the wart. The scheme's one real
virtue is that env var and config key are derivable from each other both
ways; changing 2 of the 11 `admin.*` entries leaves no rule, just a
lookup table with exceptions. The derived names are also public surface
predating this feature — they are what the config-file path has always
used.

So the preferred name is now explicit rather than implicit.
`YamlConfigEntry` takes an `aliases` tuple checked ahead of the derived
name; `get_env_name()` reports the preferred one (docs, error messages)
and `env_names()` gives the precedence order.

| setting | preferred | still accepted |
|---|---|---|
| `admin.authType` | `FLYTE_AUTH_TYPE` | `FLYTE_ADMIN_AUTHTYPE` |
| `admin.command` | `FLYTE_AUTH_COMMAND` | `FLYTE_ADMIN_COMMAND` |
| `admin.proxyCommand` | `FLYTE_AUTH_PROXY_COMMAND` |
`FLYTE_ADMIN_PROXYCOMMAND` |

Nothing that worked before stops working. When two names for one setting
disagree the higher-precedence one wins and the conflict is logged
rather than dropped silently — that ambiguity is how a migration goes
wrong quietly; identical values are not reported.

Scoped deliberately to the three auth entries this feature documents.
`FLYTE_ADMIN_ENDPOINT` keeps its derived name, since the endpoint is a
platform setting rather than an auth one. Renaming the rest of the
`admin.*` family is the scheme-wide change the code comment anticipates
and wants its own discussion.

## Known gap

The opt-in Rust controller (`_F_USE_RUST_CONTROLLER=1`) reads the
injected API key directly and does not honor these vars. Anyone on it
cannot drop the key yet. Called out in the `init_in_cluster` docstring.

## Testing

- 18 new tests in `tests/user_api/test_init_in_cluster_env_auth.py`
covering parsing (shlex, JSON array, quoted args), precedence (explicit
auth type beats the injected key; explicit `api_key` beats the env vars;
no env vars means unchanged legacy behavior), the endpoint fallback, the
loud-failure case, the controller forwarding, and the alias mechanism
(preferred name wins, derived name still honored, conflicts reported,
non-aliased entries unchanged).
- Verified end to end that the env vars produce an
`AsyncCommandAuthenticator` which runs the command and returns its
stdout as the token.
- Full suite failure set is byte-identical before and after this change.
`ruff` and `mypy` clean.

Note for reviewers running tests inside a Flyte task pod:
`_U_EP_OVERRIDE` and `_UNION_EAGER_API_KEY` are live in that environment
and leak into several tests, including a pre-existing one in
`test_init_in_cluster_fallback.py`. Unset them for a clean run.

fix: route Dir.download_sync through obstore-aware storage.get (#1320)

## Summary

Fixes
[ENG26-937](https://linear.app/unionai/issue/ENG26-937/bug-reading-a-dir-input-from-a-sync-task-via-dirdownload-sync-fails).

Reading a `Dir` input from a **sync** task via `Dir.download_sync()`
failed with `Object at location <dir-uri> not found`, even though the
directory and its files exist in object storage. The async equivalent,
`await Dir.download()`, on the same `Dir` worked.

### Root cause

`Dir.download_sync()` bypassed the SDK's obstore-aware `storage.get()`
and called the raw fsspec `fs.get(self.path, local_dest,
recursive=True)`. For obstore-backed filesystems (S3/GCS/ABFS), the
obstore backend resolves `recursive=True` on a directory prefix as a
**single-object GET** on that prefix, which 404s. The async
`Dir.download()` didn't hit this because it routes through
`storage.get()`, which detects obstore protocols and lists + downloads
the prefix contents.

### Fix

`download_sync` now mirrors the async path, running the obstore-aware
`storage.get()` synchronously via the existing `syncify` bridge:

```python
return syncify(storage.get)(self.path, local_dest, recursive=True)
```

The local-filesystem and `local_path is None` branches are unchanged.

## Tests

Added two `@pytest.mark.sandbox` regression tests in
`tests/flyte/io_types/test_dirs.py`:
- `test_download_dir_sync` — downloads an S3 dir to a target path,
asserting nested subdirectory contents arrive.
- `test_download_dir_sync_no_local_target` — downloads without a target
path.

Both were verified to **fail with the original `FileNotFoundError`**
when the fix is reverted and **pass** with it (run against a local minio
S3 backend).

## Reproduction example

Added `examples/basics/dir_download_sync_repro.py`, which builds a
multi-file `Dir` (with a nested subdirectory) in an async task and
downloads it from a **sync** task via `download_sync()` — the exact
scenario from the issue. It only manifests the bug against real object
storage; the docstring notes it must be run against a remote storage
config.

## Test plan

- [x] `test_download_dir_sync` /
`test_download_dir_sync_no_local_target` fail without the fix, pass with
it (minio S3)
- [x] Full non-integration io_types suite passes (54 tests)
- [x] Reproduction example fails without the fix, succeeds with it
- [x] ruff + mypy clean

perf(extras): drop hash_method on Volume index uploads (~100× faster)

Volume index uploads (fork, commit, migrate_metadata_engine) were passing
``hash_method=HashlibAccumulator.from_hash_name("md5")`` to
``File.from_local``. That routes through the streaming-hash path:

  AsyncHashingReader(aiofiles_handle) → storage.put_stream → async-for-bytes

But AsyncHashingReader's ``__aiter__`` delegates to the underlying aiofiles
handle, whose async iteration yields **lines** split on ``\n``. On binary
metadata indexes (Redis RDB or SQLite .db) ~1/256 bytes are 0x0A, so a
100 MB index produces ~400k tiny writes to the S3 obstore — observed
throughput ~234 KB/s (471s upload for 107 MB).

Volume indexes don't benefit from content-addressable cache keys: every
fork rewrites allocator counters so the snapshot is unique anyway, and
the consumer caches at the Volume level, not on the underlying File.
Removing the hash_method lets ``storage.put`` use native fsspec multipart
PUT — should bring the upload to single-digit seconds for ~100 MB.

fix: ClusteredTaskEnvironment registers empty custom via flyte deploy (#1598)

## Motivation

flyte deploy registered every ClusteredTaskEnvironment task with an
empty custom, so each run failed in the backend with
[BadTaskSpecification] invalid ClusteredTaskSpec: nil Struct Object
passed after ~34 minutes of retries. ClusteredTaskTemplate read its
settings back through the parent_env weakref, which copy.copy (used by
_deploy._with_local_sys_paths, on by default) and cloudpickle (notebook
bundles) both drop. The same copy also blanked TaskSpec.environment.name
for every deployed task since v2.5.14.

##  Summary

- ClusteredSettings: a frozen snapshot of the clustered fields built in
ClusteredTaskEnvironment.__post_init__ and carried on
_ClusteredPlugin.settings; custom_config/container_args read it instead
of parent_env, so custom and the --runtime=jax arg survive copy and
pickle. A settings-less marker (the in-container routing case) now
raises a clear RuntimeUserError if it ever reaches serialization instead
of registering {}.
- TaskTemplate.__copy__: a shallow copy keeps parent_env; the pickle
hooks are unchanged. Restores environment.name/description on deployed
specs (cloud persists the name and groups actions on it).
- _run.py: run-level _F_SYS_PATH is emitted only for ephemeral task
specs. For a deployed target (TaskDetails, base.task_spec_source ==
DEPLOYED, or the trigger-fire path) the registered spec already carries
the deploy-time value; re-sending the launcher's copy was the wrong
source and duplicated the key, which JobSet (a CRD with env as a
name-keyed map) rejects with a 422. Deployed reruns also strip the
inherited key.
- Tests: copy and cloudpickle round-trips keep custom/runtime flag; bare
marker fails loudly; clone_with rebuilds settings; deploy dry-run keeps
environment.name; _apply_overrides gate cases (ephemeral / deployed /
deployed base / ephemeral base / explicit).

tests/flyte/test_task_copy.py tests/flyte/test_run_runspec_chars.py

fix a few core bugs (#1282)

- Local cache deadlock: `LocalDB.initialize` held a `threading.Lock`
across an aiosqlite `await`, so two cached child actions dispatching at
once could wedge a local run. The async init now serializes on an
`asyncio.Lock` so a waiting coroutine yields the loop instead of
blocking it.
- `flyte.trace` no longer replays transient errors: a recoverable
failure inside a traced step was memoized and re-raised on every retry,
so the task could never self-heal. Recoverable errors now re-run; only
non-recoverable ones replay. This also fixes a crash where an errored
step recorded an empty output URI and `load_outputs` choked on it.
- Local cross-run memory: keyed `MemoryStore` memory didn't persist
across separate local runs because the per-run action name wasn't
stripped from the local raw-data root. Two local runs sharing a key now
resolve to the same store.
- int -> float tool args: passing an int like `42` where a `float` is
declared was rejected during input conversion (so the child action was
never created). It's now coerced, matching what we already do when
reading a `float` back. `bool` stays rejected.
- `Environment.depends_on` was aliased instead of copied when cloning an
environment, so `add_dependency` on one leaked into the other.

Resolve the scratch directory so remote runs can bundle the example

`flyte run hello` failed against a real cluster on macOS:

    '/var/.../flyte-hello-<user>/task/hello.py' is not in the subpath of
    '/private/var/.../flyte-hello-<user>/task'

`copy_code_bundle_to_context` resolves the root directory it is given, then takes
each loaded module's `__file__` relative to it. `tempfile.gettempdir()` returns a
path under `/var`, which on macOS is a symlink to `/private/var`, so the module
kept the unresolved spelling while the root got the canonical one and every file
in the bundle looked like it lived outside the root.

Resolving the scratch root fixes both sides at once: the module is imported from
the canonical path, so `__file__` and the root dir agree. `materialize()` resolves
too, so a caller-supplied directory cannot reintroduce the mismatch.

This affected `flyte serve hello` identically -- the new bundling test covers both.

Verified against a live cluster: the run now bundles, uploads, and succeeds with
the same output as the local run (14.0).

Configure the connection from the task config, not Helm values

Matching what Spark and the other backend plugins do: everything the
connector needs can come from the config object, leaving the data plane
values with nothing to carry but the connector image.

Most of this already worked. `ssh_private_key` names a Flyte secret, which
`to_custom_config` puts in `connection.secrets`; the backend resolves it
through the secret manager and hands the value to the connector
(flyte2 webapi/connector/plugin.go:177-191). Host, username and port are
plain config fields.

`known_hosts` was the exception, because it is a path on the connector and so
needed the deployment to mount a file. `known_hosts_secret` names a secret
holding the entries themselves instead: asyncssh reads bytes as known_hosts
content rather than a filename, so they can be passed straight through with
nothing written to disk. That removes the last reason for a volume.

The connector environment still exists and still wins where it is set. It is
the right model when one cluster serves every task -- a platform team
configures it once and tasks carry only scheduling options -- and it is what
stops a task redirecting the deployment's shared key at a host of its
choosing. The two compose: a connector with nothing set leaves everything to
the task config, which is also how local execution works.

docsy: strip inert reStructuredText from docstrings, and gate it in CI (#1376)

## What and why

`flyte-sdk` docstrings are written in reStructuredText, but this repo
**has no Sphinx** — no `conf.py`, no `.rst` sources, no dependency. So
every RST construct is inert markup that renders verbatim in the
published API reference, in IDE tooltips, in `help()`, in Jupyter `?`
and in LSP hovers.

Roughly 40% of it never reaches the docs site at all and is visible only
to SDK users in their editor, which is why this is fixed at source
rather than translated in the docs generator. A generator-side
translation would have made the docs look clean while every editor kept
showing the markup, and nothing would have signalled new ones arriving.
That is how it accumulated in the first place.

## Measured, before → after

| Class | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-reference roles (`` :class:`X` ``) | 464 | 0 |
| Trailing `::` literal-block markers | 81 | 0 |
| NumPy `Parameters` sections | 11 (8 files) | 0 |
| RST directives (`.. warning::`) | 8 | 0 |
| Sphinx field lists (`:param x:`) | 105 files | 0 |
| RST inline literals (` ``value`` `) | 2,602 | 0 |
| RST hyperlink targets, grid tables, footnotes | 2 + 1 table | 0 |

`make check-docstrings` reports **469 files clean**.

## Commits

1. **Sphinx field lists → Google `Args:` / `Returns:` / `Raises:`.** The
generator parses both, so nothing rendered wrong; this is about leaving
the SDK on one convention that also reads correctly in an editor.
2. **RST inline literals → Markdown code spans.** ` ``X`` ` renders
correctly only by accident, since a double backtick is also a valid
Markdown code span.
3. **The remaining RST constructs.** An RST grid table in `dataframe.py`
that rendered as garbage, a hyperlink target, overline/underline section
headers, and a malformed `:return is_ipython (bool):` field.
4. **The CI gate, widened**, plus the 919 literals the first pass
missed.

## The gate

`make check-docstrings` already rejected roles, `::` markers, NumPy
sections and directives. It now also rejects Sphinx field lists,
double-backtick literals, hyperlink targets, grid tables and footnote
references, and it is **fence-aware**, so an example that deliberately
shows RST is not flagged.

Every rule was negative-tested: a synthetic docstring containing one of
each construct is caught nine times over, and the same constructs inside
a fenced block are correctly ignored.

## What was verified, and how

The mechanical passes here have a nasty failure mode: they produce
output that looks right and a green run that changed nothing. Two such
bugs were caught during this work, neither visible in the diff.

- **`ast.col_offset` is a UTF-8 byte offset, not a character offset.**
Every docstring on a line containing a non-ASCII character resolved to
the wrong slice, and the splice guard turned that into a silent skip.
Every splice here is now asserted to round-trip through
`ast.literal_eval` before it is applied.
- **A file glob that missed a directory layout.** The first literal pass
used `plugins/*/src/`, which does not match the `plugins/*/*/src/`
layout of the 11 agent plugins, so 919 occurrences were silently
untouched while the pass reported success. Caught only because the CI
check scans both layouts.

So the checks are:

- **No documentation lost.** Every changed file was re-parsed with the
API generator's own docstring parser and the count of parameters
carrying a description compared before and after. It does not fall
anywhere; 1,347 → 1,349.
- **No code touched.** Every changed file was AST-compared against its
previous version with docstrings normalised to a placeholder. The only
non-docstring change in the whole PR is
`maint_tools/check_docstring_style.py` itself.
- **No syntax regressions.** The full tree compiles with `SyntaxWarning`
promoted to an error, catching things like an invalid `\ ` escape
introduced while rewriting a table.

## Scope

`src/` and every `plugins/*/src` and `plugins/*/*/src` tree.
**`examples/` and `tests/` are deliberately untouched.** Prose is
preserved verbatim; only markup changes.

Two exceptions, where the docstring contradicted the code:

- `_auth_middleware.py`'s module example imported
`FastAPIAuthMiddleware`, **which does not exist** — the class is
`FastAPIPassthroughAuthMiddleware`, so anyone copying that example got
an `ImportError`.
- `lazy_module.py`'s example imported from `flytekit`, a 1.x path.

Setext underlines that are valid Markdown headings are left alone, and
the gate does not reject them.

Ref: DOC-1322, DOC-1386.

fix: filter ConnectError(Unauthenticated/PermissionDenied/FailedPrecondition) from Sentry

The CLI's InvokeBaseMixin already treats these gRPC-style status codes as
user-config errors and converts them to ClickException. But other code
paths (e.g. capture_exception in cli/_run.py, the @capture_errors decorator
on deploy) hit Sentry before InvokeBaseMixin sees them — the outer
RuntimeSystemError they raise carries a cause chain that terminates in a
ConnectError, and the existing user-error filter never inspected that.

Extends _is_user_error to walk the cause chain looking for ConnectError
with codes the backend uses to signal user/config problems:
UNAUTHENTICATED, PERMISSION_DENIED, FAILED_PRECONDITION, INVALID_ARGUMENT,
NOT_FOUND, ALREADY_EXISTS. INTERNAL / UNAVAILABLE / UNKNOWN are
deliberately excluded — those indicate backend bugs or outages and
should still reach Sentry.

fix: clear error when the configured endpoint doesn't resolve (FLYTE-SDK-6Z) (#1387)

## Why

[FLYTE-SDK-6Z](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7656368628/) — a bare
`socket.gaierror: [Errno 8] nodename nor servname provided, or not
known` escaping `flyte deploy`:

```
flyte/cli/_deploy.py invoke
flyte/_initialize.py init -> _initialize_client
flyte/remote/_client/controlplane.py for_endpoint
flyte/remote/_client/auth/_session.py create_session_config
flyte/remote/_client/auth/_session.py _resolve_tls_ca_cert
flyte/remote/_client/auth/_session.py _bootstrap_ssl_from_server:102
socket.py create_connection -> getaddrinfo
```

With `insecure_skip_verify` enabled, `_bootstrap_ssl_from_server` opens
a plain socket to the configured endpoint to grab its certificate chain.
If the hostname doesn't resolve, the raw `gaierror` propagates all the
way out: the user sees an errno with no mention of *which* endpoint
failed or what to do, and Sentry records it as an SDK crash.

## What

- **`_bootstrap_ssl_from_server`** converts any `OSError` from the
connect into an `InitializationError` naming the `host:port` and
pointing at the usual causes (DNS, VPN, firewall), with the original
chained on `__cause__`. `InitializationError` is already in the Sentry
user-error set, so this also stops the report at the source. The
empty-cert-chain `RuntimeError` becomes an `InitializationError` too —
same "that endpoint isn't the control plane" shape (it still derives
from `RuntimeError`, so the existing test is unaffected).
- **`_is_transient_network_error`** now covers `socket.gaierror` /
`socket.herror` generally, so name-resolution failures on *any* path
stop being reported as crashes. These carry `EAI_*` / `h_errno` values
rather than errno values, so the existing
`_USER_ENVIRONMENT_OSERROR_ERRNOS` check could not reach them.

The hostname the SDK resolves always comes from user configuration, so a
lookup that fails is a stale endpoint, a VPN that isn't up, or a broken
resolver — never an SDK bug.

## Before / after

```
# before
gaierror: [Errno 8] nodename nor servname provided, or not known

# after
InitializationError: Could not reach endpoint [my-cluster.example.com:443] to retrieve
its TLS certificate chain: [Errno 8] nodename nor servname provided, or not known.
Check that the endpoint is correct and reachable from this machine (DNS, VPN, firewall).
```

## Tests

4 new tests, all verified failing on `main` and passing here:

- `test_dns_failure_raises_initialization_error` — `gaierror` becomes an
`InitializationError` naming the endpoint
- `test_connect_failure_preserves_cause` — original `OSError` stays on
`__cause__`, `kind == "user"`
- `test_capture_exception_skips_gaierror`
- `test_capture_exception_skips_gaierror_via_cause_chain`

fixes FLYTE-SDK-6Z

Scope the task-call sequence to the task context, not the controller (#1694)

## Problem

Sub-action names are `hash(parent action, inputs hash, task identity,
call seq[, group])`. The call sequence tells identical calls apart
(`foo(); foo(); foo()` → seq 1, 2, 3), and must restart at 1 on every
attempt so that a retry or recovery re-derives the same names and reuses
the completed children.

The counters lived on the controller, keyed by `{action}_{run}` and
cleared in `run_task`'s `finally`. unionai-reuse creates **one**
`RemoteController` per worker process and runs every action, and every
retry of an action, through it. All attempts of an action share that
key, so a retry only restarted at seq 1 if the previous attempt's
`clear()` had run, and run before the retry began. Three cases break
that, all reproduced in `test_reusable_sequencer.py` against `main`:

| Scenario on one shared controller | Retry's seqs on `main` |
|---|---|
| previous attempt's `finalize_parent_action` raises | `[4,5,6]`: new
names, children re-run |
| previous attempt cancelled (timeout/abort) while finalize is in flight
| `[4,5,6]` |
| two attempts of the same action overlap on one replica | `[4,5,6,1]`:
the old attempt's `clear()` resets the new one mid-run, so its 4th call
collides with its 1st |

Normal retries after a user error, and separate runs, were fine on
`main`. Different runs use different keys, and the run name isn't part
of the hash.

## Fix

- `TaskContext` carries a private `_call_counters` dict.
`convert_and_run` builds a new context per attempt (in unionai-reuse
too, and for local retries via `direct_dispatch`), so every attempt
starts from zero without any cleanup.
- `TaskContext.replace()` hands out fresh counters when `action` changes
(`@trace` scopes) and shares them otherwise (groups). Before, call sites
keyed on `tctx.action`, so **every existing action name is unchanged**
and recovery against old runs still matches.
- Controllers are the only readers/writers, via
`flyte._internal.controllers.next_call_seq(tctx, call_key)`.
- Removed `TaskCallSequencer`, its action-keyed map, and the
finalize-time `clear()`. This also stops counters for trace scopes
(never cleared) and the local controller (never cleared at all) from
piling up in long-lived processes.
- Local conditions build their id from `action` instead of
`task_action`, so a trace and its task waiting on the same condition no
longer collide. Outside a trace the id is unchanged, and the TUI still
nests the condition under the real task.

## Testing

- `tests/internal/controllers/test_reusable_sequencer.py` (new) drives
attempts through the real `run_task` on one shared controller: retry
after a user error, back-to-back runs, two different actions running at
once, finalize raising, cancellation during finalize, and overlapping
attempts. All pass now; the last three fail on `main`.
- `test_action_name_stability_gaps.py` covers `next_call_seq` directly,
including shared counters for groups and fresh counters for traces.
- Full suite: 6558 passed. The 6 failures also fail on a clean
`origin/main` (keyring, image build, docker) or are order-dependent
under xdist (`test_falls_back_to_name_without_source` passes when run
alone).
- **Remote, demo tenant.** Ran
`examples/reuse/sequencer_action_names.py` on an image built from this
branch with `make dist`. `main` runs in a reusable env with
`replicas=1`, so all attempts land in one process. It calls `foo()`
three times and then fails attempt 1:

  | Mode | Run | Attempt 1 | Attempt 2 | foo actions |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
| error |
[unbshkdqzhbhks4rpjhv](https://demo.hosted.unionai.cloud/v2/domain/development/project/ketan/runs/unbshkdqzhbhks4rpjhv)
| FAILED | SUCCEEDED | 3 |
| error |
[us6gr7w5rttdgqg7mx7q](https://demo.hosted.unionai.cloud/v2/domain/development/project/ketan/runs/us6gr7w5rttdgqg7mx7q)
| FAILED | SUCCEEDED | 3 |
| timeout |
[uplzp8kkgrzhlbtbzwds](https://demo.hosted.unionai.cloud/v2/domain/development/project/ketan/runs/uplzp8kkgrzhlbtbzwds)
| TIMED_OUT | SUCCEEDED | 3 |
| timeout |
[u98v7g8gbpt4bfq4kncj](https://demo.hosted.unionai.cloud/v2/domain/development/project/ketan/runs/u98v7g8gbpt4bfq4kncj)
| TIMED_OUT | SUCCEEDED | 3 |

In every run the retry reused attempt 1's children, and the foo names
are identical across all four runs. They also match the names from
earlier runs on the released SDK, which confirms existing names are
unchanged.

## Notes

- `flyte.ctx().attempt_number` reads `FLYTE_ATTEMPT_NUMBER`, which is
set once per process, so in a reused process it stays `0` on retries.
It's the same class of bug (per-process state outliving the action) and
isn't fixed here. The example works around it with a marker file in
storage.
- `rich.print(flyte.ctx())` shows `_call_counters={}`, because rich
ignores `repr=False`. It's cosmetic.

Signed-off-by: Katrina Rogan <katroganGH@gmail.com>

artifacts: declare via a get_artifact_metadata protocol (review feedback)

Two review comments from @kumare3, taken together.

**Naming.** `get_flyte_metadata` was vague in a codebase where everything is
Flyte; the method returns artifact metadata. Renamed to
`get_artifact_metadata`. The old spelling is still accepted for one release --
this is a duck-typed cross-repo contract (flyteplugins-union implements it),
and a rename with no alias fails silently: no import error, the value simply
stops being recognised as an artifact and publishes nothing.

**Protocol.** A `@runtime_checkable` protocol already existed (`Artifact`), but
detection could not use it: `Artifact` declares the data member
`_flyte_metadata`, and a runtime_checkable `isinstance` checks data members
too, so `isinstance(volume, Artifact)` is False for exactly the plugin volumes
the protocol exists to support. Measured, not assumed. So declaration now has
its own method-only protocol, `ArtifactMetadata`, which `Artifact` extends.

`isinstance` against it is the declarative check, and it replaces the getattr
sniff -- but it does not replace two guards, because it is weaker than it
looks in ways worth stating:

  * a *class* satisfies a method-only protocol exactly as its instances do, so
    the existing `not isinstance(obj, type)` guard still earns its place;
  * a non-callable attribute of the right name satisfies it too
    (`get_artifact_metadata = 42` passes `isinstance`), so the getter is
    confirmed callable.

Both are covered by tests, along with the old spelling and the reason
detection cannot use `Artifact`, so the next person to simplify this finds out
from a red test rather than from silently unpublished artifacts.

fix setting config image registry (#1392)

- Follow-up to https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/pull/1304

Fixes local image builds for images declared before
flyte.init_from_config().

Image.from_debian_base() can run at module import time before config is
loaded, leaving the image without a registry. The local builder then
failed with “no container registry is configured” even when
image.registry was set in the config file.

  Changes:
- Re-resolve the push registry at build time for local, registry-less
cloned images.
- Clone the image with the configured push registry before existence
checks/building.
  - Add a regression test for pre-init image declarations.
  
  
  **Before:**
  
  ``` python
  # hello.py

import flyte

env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(
    name="my_map_workflow",
    image=flyte.Image.from_debian_base().with_pip_packages("pandas"),
)


# use TaskEnvironments to define tasks, which are regular Python
functions.
@env.task
def fn(x: int) -> int:  # type annotations are recommended.
    slope, intercept = 2, 5
    print(slope * x + intercept)
    return slope * x + intercept


# tasks can also call other tasks, which will be manifested in different
containers.
@env.task(entrypoint=True)
def main(x_list: list[int] = list(range(10))) -> float:
    x_len = len(x_list)
    if x_len < 10:
        raise ValueError(
f"x_list doesn't have a larger enough sample size, found: {x_len}"
        )

    y_list = list(
        flyte.map(fn, x_list)
    )  # flyte.map is like Python map, but runs in parallel.
    y_mean = sum(y_list) / len(y_list)
    return y_mean


if __name__ == "__main__":
    flyte.init_from_config("jan-playground.yaml")
    run = flyte.run(main)
    print(run.url)
```

Let every default the plugin class redefines win, not just task_type

Plugin task classes redefine more than task_type: pytorch sets task_type_version=1 and
debuggable=False, ray/spark/dask set debuggable=True, and clustered sets
task_type_version=1. Excluding only task_type by name meant the rebuilt task carried the
old class's values for the rest.

Carry a field over unless the plugin class redefines its default and the task still holds
its own class default, in which case the plugin's default applies. A field the task set
away from its default is preserved. A field explicitly set to a value that is already its
class default is indistinguishable from one never set, so the plugin default wins there;
that limitation is covered by a test.

refactor(rerun): keep **inputs, and build CLI input options like `flyte run`

Two changes to how the new inputs are passed, following review:

- `rerun()` keeps its `**inputs` varkwargs on both surfaces; the explicit
  `inputs={...}` dict argument (and the duplicate-key check it needed) is gone.
  `FlyteLiteralConverter.convert` goes back to requiring a click context, since
  click does the conversion again.
- `flyte rerun` no longer takes `--input KEY=VALUE`. The source task's inputs
  are options, built from its interface with the same
  literal-type-to-click-type conversion `flyte run` uses, so `flyte rerun rxyz
  --n 10` reads like `flyte run ... --n 10`. `flyte rerun rxyz --help` lists
  them.

The interface is only discoverable once RUN_NAME has been read off the command
line, so RerunCommand parses in two passes: rerun's own options first (a
resilient parse that tolerates the not-yet-built input options), then the
interface fetch, then the real parse. Nothing left over from the first pass
means no input was passed, so the common case costs no extra round trip.

Unlike `flyte run`, no input option is required and none carries the task's
default: only what the user typed is forwarded (checked via the click parameter
source), because an input left out has to keep the source run's value. Booleans
get `--x/--no-x` for the same reason. An input whose name would shadow one of
rerun's own options is skipped rather than silently taking it over.

fix: filter transient network/timeout errors from Sentry

The `flyte deploy`/`flyte run` upload path (flyte.remote._data) reaches the
cluster service (SelectCluster) and then PUTs the bundle to a signed object
store URL. Both legs ride the user's network, so flaky links, VPN drops,
refused/reset connections and request timeouts surface as RuntimeSystemError
wrappers whose cause chain terminates in a timeout or transport-level
connection error. These are user-environment / transient-infra failures, not
SDK crashes, but they currently leak into Sentry as if they were SDK bugs.

Add `_is_transient_network_error`, walked over the existing cause chain in
`_is_user_error`, covering:
- builtin TimeoutError (asyncio/socket timeouts) and ConnectionError
  (refused/reset/aborted/broken-pipe)
- httpx.TimeoutException / httpx.NetworkError (the signed-URL PUT transport
  errors: ConnectTimeout, ReadTimeout, ReadError, WriteError, ConnectError, ...)
- httpx.RemoteProtocolError ("Server disconnected without sending a response")
  — the object store hangs up mid-PUT

Transient ConnectError status codes (DEADLINE_EXCEEDED / UNAVAILABLE) are
already classified by `_is_user_actionable_connect_error` (#1137), so they are
not duplicated here. INTERNAL / UNKNOWN ConnectError codes are deliberately
left reported — those can indicate real backend bugs worth tracking.

examples/apps: make WebSocket handshake header limits configurable

The WebSocket upgrade is a plain HTTP request, and both the ASGI server
and the `websockets` library cap how large its headers may be. Behind an
auth proxy that injects large headers (big IdP tokens or forwarded
session cookies) the handshake can exceed those caps and fail with HTTP
431, so the WebSocket never connects.

Expose those caps as env vars in the two app examples, defaulting to the
underlying library defaults so behavior is unchanged:

- fastapi_websocket.py: uvicorn/h11 request cap
  (UVICORN_H11_MAX_INCOMPLETE_EVENT_SIZE, unset -> uvicorn's 16 KiB) plus
  the websockets per-line (WEBSOCKETS_MAX_LINE_LENGTH, 8 KiB) and
  header-count (WEBSOCKETS_MAX_NUM_HEADERS, 128) caps.
- basic_app.py (streamlit): the two websockets caps.

A deployment can now raise these without editing the example.

fix File, Dir, DataFrame cli parsing with collections (#1214)

This pull request significantly enhances the Flyte CLI's support for
structured data types (such as `File`, `Dir`, and `DataFrame`) when
passing parameters via JSON, especially for dataclasses and collections.
It introduces robust recursive conversion of string paths within lists,
dictionaries, and nested dataclasses into their appropriate Flyte types,
ensuring a more seamless and type-safe CLI experience. Comprehensive
tests are also added to validate these behaviors.

### Core Improvements to Parameter Handling

* Refactored the `JsonParamType` in `src/flyte/cli/_params.py` to
recursively convert string paths in lists, dicts, and dataclasses to
proper `File`, `Dir`, and `DataFrame` objects, both for top-level and
nested structures. This includes handling optional types and unions, and
supports both path strings and structured dict formats.
* Added logic to handle remote DataFrame paths in local mode,
automatically inferring the format (CSV or Parquet) and creating a
`DataFrame` object accordingly.

### Testing Enhancements

* Introduced a comprehensive suite of tests in `tests/cli/test_run.py`
to verify:
- Conversion of lists and dicts of file/dataframe paths to Flyte
objects.
- Proper handling of dataclasses (including nested and optional fields)
with `File`, `Dir`, and `DataFrame` fields.
- Acceptance of both string and structured dict formats for these types.
- Support for local and remote paths, and for both CSV and Parquet
DataFrames.

These changes make the CLI parameter parsing much more robust and
user-friendly, especially for complex input types in Flyte workflows.

feat(logging): stamp run/action context via LogRecordFactory (#1038)

## Summary

Replaces the per-logger `logging.Filter` approach for context stamping
with a global `LogRecordFactory`. The factory runs on every `LogRecord`
regardless of which logger created it, so any user-defined logger
automatically picks up `run_name`, `action_name`, and
`is_flyte_internal` attributes — no per-handler filter wiring required.

This also fixes a latent bug in main: the old `ContextFilter` and
`FlyteInternalFilter` mutated `record.msg` in place, so a record passing
through multiple handlers could get its `[run][action]` and `[flyte]`
prefixes prepended multiple times. Stamping attributes on the record
(and rendering them at format time) sidesteps that entirely.

## What changed

- **LogRecordFactory** (`src/flyte/_logging.py`) — stamps the active
flyte action context on every record, lazily importing `flyte._context`
to avoid import-time cycles.
- **`ContextFormatter`** replaces `ContextFilter` +
`FlyteInternalFilter`. The `[flyte]` internal-prefix marker is now a
formatter flag (`internal_prefix=True`), so the same record can be
formatted by multiple handlers without prefixes compounding.
- **`ContextFormatter(inner=...)`** — optional kwarg to delegate base
formatting to an existing `logging.Formatter`. Used to wrap pre-existing
root-handler formatters without losing their layout.
- **`initialize_logger(reset_root_logger=False)`** now wraps each
existing root-handler formatter with `ContextFormatter(inner=existing)`,
preserving main's "third-party log lines through root get
`[run][action]`" behavior. Idempotent on repeated init calls. Same
temporal limitation as main: handlers added after `flyte.init()` won't
be wrapped, but the factory still stamps the attrs so callers can format
them themselves.
- **`get_rich_handler(internal_prefix=True)`** — opt-out parameter; the
user-logger call site passes `False` so user-emitted lines don't carry
the `[flyte]` marker even under rich logging.

## Behavior parity vs main

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `[run][action]` on flyte/flyte.user logs | ✅ | ✅ |
| `[run][action]` on third-party logs through root (when handler exists
at init) | ✅ (via filter) | ✅ (via formatter wrap) |
| `[run][action]` on third-party logs through root (handler added after
init) | ❌ | ❌ — but attrs still on record |
| `[flyte]` marker on flyte internal logs | ✅ | ✅ |
| Compounding prefixes when record passes through multiple handlers | ❌
(latent bug) | ✅ fixed |
| `record.run_name` / `action_name` available everywhere | partial | ✅
universal (factory) |

## Why this matters for users

`flyte.logger` and any child of `flyte.user` continue to work as before.
New: anyone using a stdlib logger (`logging.getLogger("myapp")`) outside
the flyte namespace also gets `run_name` / `action_name` /
`is_flyte_internal` stamped on every record by the factory — they just
need a formatter that references them (e.g.
`"[%(run_name)s][%(action_name)s] %(message)s"`).

## Example

`examples/basics/reuse_concurrent_logging.py` exercises three logger
configs with a reusable container running concurrent tasks, so log
output from multiple actions interleaves on a single stderr — each line
correctly prefixed by its own `[run][action]`:

1. `flyte.logger` — canonical user-facing logger.
2. `logging.getLogger("flyte.user.myapp")` — child of `flyte.user`,
inherits the formatter via propagation.
3. `logging.getLogger("myapp")` — fully independent logger with its own
handler that references the factory-stamped attrs in its format string.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/user_api/test_logging.py
tests/flyte/test_logging.py` passes (23 tests)
- [x] `test_user_logger_no_flyte_prefix` updated to check the formatter
flag instead of the removed `FlyteInternalFilter`
- [x] `test_user_logger_no_flyte_prefix_after_rich_init` — regression
test for rich-handler internal prefix bleeding into user logger
- [x] `test_initialize_logger_wraps_existing_root_handlers` — covers
wrap path + idempotency on repeated init
- [ ] Manual: run `examples/basics/reuse_concurrent_logging.py` against
a cluster and confirm all three worker variants emit
`[run][action]`-prefixed log lines on the shared reused container

add crash recovery, OOM escalation, and fanout aggregation to the sweep

The report task OOMKilled (137) on an org where one run alone carried 200k
fanned-out sleep actions (1.19M rows total held in memory, then json.dumps'd
into the HTML payload — far past the container limit).

- aggregate fanouts: identical leaf actions under one parent collapse into a
  counted row (cnt) with summed durations. Only actions that are nobody's
  parent aggregate — the run's full action set is listed first, so 'has
  children' is decidable — keeping drill-down intact while bounding memory
  and report size. The UI and both CSV exports are cnt-aware, and the tree
  shows a xN badge on aggregated rows.
- crash recovery via traces: the scope list, the run list, and each 50-run
  sweep batch are @flyte.trace checkpoints inside a collect_actions child
  task (retries=2), so retries replay completed steps. The run list is
  traced for correctness, not just speed: batch checkpoints slice it by
  index, so a re-listed set would misalign them.
- OOM escalation: the report task wraps collect_actions in try/except
  OOMError and re-runs it once at cpu=2/8Gi (the basics/oomer.py pattern);
  same-size retries can't fix a deterministic OOM, so it is not retried at
  the collect level.

fix: surface unpicklable deployments as ClickException (#1051)

## Summary

`apply()` derives the deployment version by piping the user's envs and
image cache through `cloudpickle.dumps`. If anything in the user's
task or environment is unpicklable (e.g. a captured
`sys.stdin`/`stdout` tty handle, an open file, a thread, or a lock),
cloudpickle raises `PicklingError`/`TypeError` and the raw stack ends
up in Sentry.

This change wraps the version-hash computation and translates those
pickle failures into a `click.ClickException` that names the most
common cause and points the user at the `version=` escape hatch. The
new ClickException short-circuits the Sentry filter added in #1039 so
we stop logging user-side closure mistakes as SDK crashes.

## Closes

- [FLYTE-SDK-21](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/FLYTE-SDK-21) --
`PicklingError: Cannot pickle files that map to tty objects` from
`cloudpickle._file_reduce`

`fixes https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk/issues/FLYTE-SDK-21`

## Test plan

- [x] New unit test in `tests/flyte/test_deploy.py` covers the
unpicklable-envs path.
- [x] `make fmt` clean.

examples: queue resource cap example (#1556)

Adds `examples/queues/resource_cap.py`, covering a queue's
`max_resources` cap the way the other examples here cover the integer
limits.

`main` submits six 200Mi actions to a queue capped at 600Mi: three run
at a time, in two waves. `too_big` submits one 200Mi action to a queue
capped at 64Mi, which cannot fit even an idle queue, so it is failed as
UNSCHEDULABLE before dispatch rather than held for room that can never
appear.

The docstring carries the expected timing for each half, the commands to
watch it from the scheduler while it runs, and how to create the two

fix(auth): honour slow_down and survive non-JSON errors in device flow polling (#1587)

## Summary

The device authorization grant's poll loop had three defects against
[RFC 8628](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628), none of them
covered by a test — `_token_client.py` and the device authenticator had
no test coverage at all.

Found while implementing the browser half of this same flow in the Union
login UI, and confirmed by running the existing code against a mock
transport rather than by reading it.

### 1. `slow_down` never widened the polling interval

`get_token` collapsed `slow_down` and `authorization_pending` into the
same `AuthenticationPending`, so `poll_token_endpoint` could not tell
them apart and slept the same fixed interval forever. Measured against
the previous code:

```
gaps between polls: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
expected per 3.5:   [1, 6, 11]
```

RFC 8628 §3.5 says the client **MUST** increase the interval by 5
seconds on each `slow_down` and keep using the increased value. As
written, a server asking the client to back off was ignored — which is
the one thing `slow_down` exists to prevent.

A new `AuthenticationSlowDown` carries the distinction. It subclasses
`AuthenticationPending` so existing callers (e.g. the refresh-token
fallback in `DeviceCodeAuthenticator`) are unaffected — which is also
why its `except` clause must come first, or the broader clause swallows
it.

### 2. A non-JSON error body killed the whole login

`response.json()` was called unguarded on the failure path. A gateway
answering with an HTML 502 — realistic during a poll that can run for
ten minutes — raised `JSONDecodeError`, which escaped
`poll_token_endpoint`'s handler and aborted a sign-in that should simply
have retried.

### 3. `interval` was treated as required

`from_json_response` did `j["interval"]` and raised `KeyError` when
absent. RFC 8628 §3.2 says `interval` is OPTIONAL and clients **MUST**
default to 5.

### Also included

- `access_denied` and `expired_token` now say what happened instead of
dumping `Status Code (400) received from IDP: {...}`. These are the two
outcomes a user actually causes, so they were the worst ones to leave
opaque.
- The loop measures elapsed time against the wall clock instead of
counting ticks. Previously `tick = tick + interval` ignored the time
spent in each request, so the loop ran past the device code's
`expires_in` and terminated via the server's `expired_token` rather than
its own timeout.
- `verification_uri_complete` is preferred over hand-appending
`?user_code=`, which produced a second `?` whenever `verification_uri`
already carried a query string. Servers return this field precisely so
clients don't build the URL themselves.

## Test plan

New file `tests/flyte/auth/test_device_flow_polling.py` — 9 tests, using
`httpx.MockTransport` so no network is involved.

**Seven of the nine fail against the previous implementation**, which is
the check that they are regression tests rather than restatements of
current behaviour:

```
FAILED test_interval_is_optional_and_defaults_to_five
FAILED test_verification_uri_complete_is_captured
FAILED test_slow_down_widens_the_interval
FAILED test_non_json_error_body_does_not_kill_the_poll
FAILED test_access_denied_reports_the_denial
FAILED test_expired_token_reports_the_expiry
FAILED test_polling_stops_once_the_code_expires
7 failed, 2 passed
```

All 9 pass on this branch. `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are
clean.

Two of these assertions were deliberately tightened: matching just
`denied`/`expired` passed against the old code too, because the raw
status dump happened to contain the error code. They now match the
explanation, so a regression to the dump fails them.

## Not addressed here

`get_token` and `poll_token_endpoint` accept `http_proxy_url` and
`verify` and never use them — the `http_session` already carries both
from `get_async_session`. Harmless dead parameters, but misleading; left
alone to keep this change to the polling defects.
