Bind artifact inputs to their stored literal instead of round-tripping

Addresses wild-endeavor's review of the artifact input path.

The Artifacts service already stamps `Literal.artifact_id` on the value it
stores -- verified against canary, where a fetched artifact's literal has
fields ['scalar', 'hash', 'artifact_id']. So the old path was doing needless
work and getting provenance from the wrong place: materialize the stored
literal to python, re-serialize it back to a literal, then re-apply an
artifact_id the original literal already carried.

Now a `flyte.remote.Artifact` argument binds its stored literal directly.
Provenance on the run's inputs is the service's assertion rather than one the
submitting process re-stamps -- worth noting for the signing question raised
on the thread: nothing verifies an artifact_id today, so client-side stamping
meant any submitter could assert arbitrary lineage. This removes the SDK as a
forgery point but does not make the claim verifiable downstream.

The type check is what the round-trip previously provided implicitly. An
artifact carries its LiteralType in spec.type, so we compare it against the
declared input type and fail at submit time instead of inside the task. Exact
proto equality is too strict (artifacts are usually published without a blob
format), so an unset format is a wildcard while blob dimensionality is strict
-- that is all that separates File (`blob {}`) from Dir (`blob {
dimensionality: MULTIPART }`).

Artifacts nested in a dict/dataclass/model now raise a readable error. They
previously reached the type engine and died with `Expected value of type
<class 'str'> but got 'Artifact(pb2=artifact_id {...`, quoting the whole
protobuf and never mentioning artifacts.

_unwrap_artifacts / _unwrap_artifact_value stay: the local/hybrid path runs
the task in-process and genuinely needs python values.

Also from the same review:
- convert.py: trim the nesting comment; the rationale belongs in (and is now
  fully stated by) raise_if_nested_wrapper's docstring.
- trigger_serde.py: the artifact-trigger comment said "no kickoff context key"
  without naming KICKOFF_TIME_INPUT_ARG_CONTEXT_KEY or saying why a schedule
  needs one and an artifact trigger does not.
- _string_literals.py: drop quotes on a common_pb2 annotation; the module

feat(plugins): bool and Literal battery fields, with the cut written down

Adds the Pydantic AI field shapes -- a plain value in the field, calibration out
of band -- alongside the answer types, for filling a model you already have.
`bool` asks what a Noul asks; `Literal["a", "b"]` asks a Choice over those
options and returns the option itself.

Two rules keep it from being a footgun.

A plain field is a question only when the field *says* it is. `Choice`, `Score`
and `Noul` are questions by their type alone, but `flag: bool = False` is
bookkeeping far more often than a question, so a `bool` or `Literal` needs a
`question` in its metadata before it is asked. Without this rule the bool field
in the pydantic example would have started being asked.

A `bool` must say where it cuts its 0..1 answer, per field
(`metadata={"threshold": 0.8}`) or per call (`ask(..., threshold=0.5)`). There is
no implicit default: something has to turn a calibrated number into two states,
and that belongs in the caller's code, which is the same reason `Noul` has no
`__bool__`. Requiring it also makes a misspelled key loud instead of silently
meaning 0.5, and it is checked before the request, so a battery missing one fails
without spending a call. A threshold passed when no field needs cutting is an
error too.

Nothing is lost from the call, only from the model: `CallInfo` gains `values`
(the float behind a bool, a Score's unrounded position) and `confidence` (for
pick-one and rubric questions) -- this plugin's answer to `provider_details`.
Both are `dict[str, float]`, so a task can still return a `CallInfo`.

Add `flyte deploy hello-world-task` and `flyte deploy hello-world-app`

Running a first workflow was the first half; deploying one is the second. Both
new commands need no files of the user's own, the same way `flyte run
hello-world` does.

`hello-world-task` deploys the environment behind that run command -- the same
example, so what the user just ran locally is what lands on the cluster -- and
then says how to run it: `flyte run deployed-task hello_world.main`.

`hello-world-app` is a minimal FastAPI service. `/` serves an index.html landing
page pointing at `/docs`, where the toy endpoints (`/hello`, `/line/{x}`,
`/mean`, `/health`) can be tried in the browser. index.html is not a Python
module, so the bundler only ships it because the env names it in `include` --
which doubles as the example of how to ship a static asset with an app.

The example carrier is now a small `Example` dataclass rather than a set of
module-level functions, since there are two of them and one has a non-Python
file alongside. Each gets its own scratch directory: the code bundle is rooted
there, so anything sharing the directory would be packaged along with it.

A deploy has no local mode, so unlike a run it cannot fall back to one when no
endpoint is configured -- it fails with the command that fixes it instead of a
connection error from deep in the client. `--dry-run` is exempt.

The doc walker's TaskFiles special case now covers EnvFiles too, so both new
commands appear in the CLI docs alongside `flyte run hello-world`.

fix(storage): auto-size multipart parts so large uploads don't exceed the 10k-part limit (#1175)

## Problem

A user uploading a large `.fastq.gz` to GCS (Flyte v2) hit:

```
InvalidArgument: Part number, 10002, must be between 1 and 10000
```

**Root cause — not a GCS or obstore bug.** `flyte.storage.put()`
delegated to fsspec → obstore-fsspec `_put_file`, which calls
`store.put_async(...)` **without a `chunk_size`**, leaving it pinned to
obstore's **5 MiB** default. GCS and S3 both **hard-cap multipart
uploads at 10,000 parts**, so 5 MiB × 10,000 = a silent **~48.8 GiB (~52
GB) upload ceiling**. Any file above that fails at `partNumber=10001+`.
(The reported "30 GB" file is larger than estimated — part 10002 ≈ a ~52
GB object at 5 MiB parts.)

The upload path exposed **no** way to raise the part size (downloads
already have `FLYTE_IO_CHUNK_SIZE` / `MAX_CONCURRENCY` via
`ObstoreParallelReader`; uploads had nothing).

## Fix

Auto-scale the multipart part size from the file size so the part count
always stays under the limit — **fully automatic, no user-facing knob**:

- `_compute_upload_chunk_size(size)` → `max(5 MiB, ceil(size / 9000))`.
- `_put_obstore_bypass()` calls `obstore.put_async` directly with the
computed `chunk_size` (streams from a `pathlib.Path`, no full read into
memory); handles single files and recursive directory uploads.
- `put()` routes obstore-protocol uploads (`s3`/`gs`/`abfs`/`abfss`)
through the bypass, guarded identically to the existing download bypass;
everything else falls back to fsspec unchanged.

Mirrors the existing download-side `_get_obstore_bypass` /
`ObstoreParallelReader` pattern.

## Behavior / perf

- Files ≤ ~45 GiB: identical 5 MiB parts → **no change**.
- Files > ~45 GiB: larger parts → **fewer** PUTs (these used to fail
outright). A 1 TB file uses ~117 MiB parts and succeeds.
- Only added work per file is one `os.path.getsize` stat — negligible
next to the upload.
- Recursive directory uploads keep the same concurrency (`BATCH_SIZE`)
and per-file path as before.

## Verification

- Confirmed the recursive bypass produces an **identical destination key
layout** to fsspec's `_put` (contents directly under the prefix, no
basename nesting) for both the async obstore backend and
`LocalFileSystem` — so `DataFrame`/`Dir` round-trips are unaffected.
- New unit tests: chunk-size math (small → 5 MiB floor; 60 GiB → parts <
10,000), put routing through the bypass with auto-sized `chunk_size`,
and recursive multi-file layout.
- `tests/internal/storage/` — **58 passed** (1 deselected = the
LocalStack `@pytest.mark.sandbox` test, needs a running cluster). Lint +
format clean.

fix: don't report a 405 from a non-Connect endpoint as an SDK crash (FLYTE-SDK-81) (#1525)

## Problem

[FLYTE-SDK-81](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7707816886/) — 4 events,
all from one host in a ~17 minute window on 2026-09-02, release 2.6.10:

```
RuntimeSystemError: Upload failed for /var/folders/.../fastc34306b3….tar.gz
  (org='flyte', project='flytesnacks', domain='development'): Method Not Allowed
  └── ConnectError: Method Not Allowed
```

The endpoint answered a Connect RPC with **HTTP 405**. connectrpc maps
only a handful of statuses (401/403/404/429/502/503/504) onto Connect
codes; everything else falls through to
`ConnectWireError.from_http_status`, which yields `Code.UNKNOWN` with
the bare stdlib reason phrase as the whole message — the same shape
`_is_non_connect_endpoint_response` already recognises for the 2xx
class.

The event pins the raise to `_protocol_connect.py:246`, the branch below
`if response_content_type == CONNECT_UNARY_CONTENT_TYPE_JSON: return` —
so the 405 response was not even in Connect's own JSON error format.

## Why a 405 is unambiguously not an SDK bug

**Every Connect RPC the SDK issues is a POST.** connectrpc's
`execute_unary` sends GET only when the caller opts in with
`use_get=True`; `execute_client_stream` / `execute_server_stream` /
`execute_bidi_stream` hardcode `http_method="POST"`. There is no
`use_get` anywhere in this repo.

A Connect handler always accepts POST on its own procedure path. So a
405 cannot be the backend rejecting *our* choice of method — it proves
the POST was answered by something that routes no Connect procedures at
all: a proxy, an ingress, a static-file host, a load balancer default
backend, or simply a misconfigured endpoint. That is endpoint
configuration the SDK cannot recover from, exactly like the 2xx case
(FLYTE-SDK-77/78) and the `text/*` case (FLYTE-SDK-7A/6P).

Because the whole filter rests on that premise,
`test_sdk_never_sends_a_connect_get` pins it: it walks the AST of every
module under `src/flyte/` and fails if any call site ever passes
`use_get`. If that changes, a 405 could become a legitimate backend
rejection and this filter would start hiding a real bug — the test says
so in its docstring.

## Fix

Add the 405 phrase to `_is_non_connect_endpoint_response`, beside the
existing 2xx and `text/*` discriminators.

**Deliberately only 405.** I ran the discriminator across the whole
unresolved corpus (75 non-Go issues) before writing it. Four issues
carry the bare-HTTP-phrase shape:

| Issue | Events | Status | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| FLYTE-SDK-81 | 4 | 405 Method Not Allowed | filtered by this PR |
| FLYTE-SDK-7C | 2 | 400 Bad Request | **untouched** — a 400 could be a
genuinely malformed request from us |
| FLYTE-SDK-64 | 276 | 500 Internal Server Error | **untouched** — real
backend signal |
| FLYTE-SDK-6S | 1 | 500 Internal Server Error | **untouched** |

Filtering the status *class* rather than the individual status would
have silenced FLYTE-SDK-64, the largest genuine backend signal in the
project. 405 is the only status in the corpus that is provably a routing
answer.

## Tests

5 new tests in `tests/flyte/test_sentry.py`, using the existing
`_wire_error_for_status` helper so they exercise the real
`ConnectWireError.from_http_status` path rather than a hand-built error:

- a bare 405 is not reported
- the real FLYTE-SDK-81 shape — the 405 as the `__cause__` of a
`RuntimeSystemError: Upload failed for …` — is not reported
- 400 / 406 / 409 / 410 / 500 / 501 all still report (parametrized;
covers 7C and 64)
- a `Method Not Allowed` carrying `details` still reports, since a real
Connect JSON error body always yields details and `from_http_status`
never does
- the `use_get` AST guard described above

The two behavioural tests were verified failing on clean `main` with the
exact production signature (`Expected 'init' to not have been called.
Called 1 times.`); the three guards pass on both sides by design. Full
file: 79 passed. `ruff format` / `ruff check` / `mypy` / `ty` /
`check-docstrings` all clean.

fix: filter InitializationError from Sentry (#1056)

## Summary
- `InitializationError` is what the SDK raises when the user runs a CLI
command (or calls `flyte.deploy` / `flyte.upload_file` / etc.) without
having first called `flyte.init()` or `flyte.init_from_config()`. The
exception's message is a clear, actionable instruction to the user — not
a crash report worth paging on.
- Sentry has collected several of these reports already (see linked
issues below). Add `InitializationError` to the existing user-error
filter in `flyte._sentry` alongside `DeploymentError` and
`ImageBuildError`.

## Sentry issues
Fixes [FLYTE-SDK-7](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7476258800/)
(InitializationError on `flyte deploy`)
Fixes [FLYTE-SDK-8](https://unionai.sentry.io/issues/7476262632/)
(InitializationError during `upload_file`)

fix(github): review fixes for dedupe, default branch, and rate limits

- dedupe_key now folds in the comment/review id. Keyed on the issue number
  alone, every comment on an issue after the first looked like a redelivery
  of the first and never launched a run.
- create_branch(from_ref="HEAD") resolves the repo's actual default_branch
  instead of assuming "main", which 404s on master/develop repos.
- create_or_update_file reads the existing blob SHA from the target branch;
  without ref= GitHub answers from the default branch and the SHA is wrong.
- request() now retries rate limits (429, and 403 with Retry-After or an
  exhausted quota), clamped so it never sleeps out a long reset window.
- Webhook signatures compare as bytes: a non-ASCII signature header made
  compare_digest raise TypeError, turning a 401 into a 500.
- The dashboard's recent-events table read the 25 oldest events, not the
  newest, so it froze after 25 events; allowlist values are now escaped.
- list_repository_files drops a ref query param the trees API ignores.
- repos allowlist docstring now states that unattributable events are
  skipped too.

docs: convert Sphinx roles in docstrings to Markdown code spans

flyte-sdk builds no Sphinx docs -- there is no conf.py, no docs/ tree, and no
sphinx dependency anywhere in the repo. The cross-reference roles in our
docstrings are a convention carried over from flytekit v1, and nothing renders
them: they appear verbatim as :class:`Name` in help(), in IDE tooltips, and on
the docs site, where 337 of them across 51 files reach the rendered pages.

Converts all 438 to Markdown code spans. The `~` prefix is dropped rather than
resolved to the last component, because the docs site's autolinker keys on
fully-qualified names for the SDK linkmap -- `flyte.report.Timeline` becomes a
link where a bare `Timeline` would not -- and the full path is unambiguous in
help() output. An explicit RST title (`Title <target>`) keeps its title.

Docstrings only; no code changed. `make fmt` is a no-op on the result and
`ruff check` passes.

feat(logging): stamp run/action context via LogRecordFactory (#1038)

## Summary

Replaces the per-logger `logging.Filter` approach for context stamping
with a global `LogRecordFactory`. The factory runs on every `LogRecord`
regardless of which logger created it, so any user-defined logger
automatically picks up `run_name`, `action_name`, and
`is_flyte_internal` attributes — no per-handler filter wiring required.

This also fixes a latent bug in main: the old `ContextFilter` and
`FlyteInternalFilter` mutated `record.msg` in place, so a record passing
through multiple handlers could get its `[run][action]` and `[flyte]`
prefixes prepended multiple times. Stamping attributes on the record
(and rendering them at format time) sidesteps that entirely.

## What changed

- **LogRecordFactory** (`src/flyte/_logging.py`) — stamps the active
flyte action context on every record, lazily importing `flyte._context`
to avoid import-time cycles.
- **`ContextFormatter`** replaces `ContextFilter` +
`FlyteInternalFilter`. The `[flyte]` internal-prefix marker is now a
formatter flag (`internal_prefix=True`), so the same record can be
formatted by multiple handlers without prefixes compounding.
- **`ContextFormatter(inner=...)`** — optional kwarg to delegate base
formatting to an existing `logging.Formatter`. Used to wrap pre-existing
root-handler formatters without losing their layout.
- **`initialize_logger(reset_root_logger=False)`** now wraps each
existing root-handler formatter with `ContextFormatter(inner=existing)`,
preserving main's "third-party log lines through root get
`[run][action]`" behavior. Idempotent on repeated init calls. Same
temporal limitation as main: handlers added after `flyte.init()` won't
be wrapped, but the factory still stamps the attrs so callers can format
them themselves.
- **`get_rich_handler(internal_prefix=True)`** — opt-out parameter; the
user-logger call site passes `False` so user-emitted lines don't carry
the `[flyte]` marker even under rich logging.

## Behavior parity vs main

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `[run][action]` on flyte/flyte.user logs | ✅ | ✅ |
| `[run][action]` on third-party logs through root (when handler exists
at init) | ✅ (via filter) | ✅ (via formatter wrap) |
| `[run][action]` on third-party logs through root (handler added after
init) | ❌ | ❌ — but attrs still on record |
| `[flyte]` marker on flyte internal logs | ✅ | ✅ |
| Compounding prefixes when record passes through multiple handlers | ❌
(latent bug) | ✅ fixed |
| `record.run_name` / `action_name` available everywhere | partial | ✅
universal (factory) |

## Why this matters for users

`flyte.logger` and any child of `flyte.user` continue to work as before.
New: anyone using a stdlib logger (`logging.getLogger("myapp")`) outside
the flyte namespace also gets `run_name` / `action_name` /
`is_flyte_internal` stamped on every record by the factory — they just
need a formatter that references them (e.g.
`"[%(run_name)s][%(action_name)s] %(message)s"`).

## Example

`examples/basics/reuse_concurrent_logging.py` exercises three logger
configs with a reusable container running concurrent tasks, so log
output from multiple actions interleaves on a single stderr — each line
correctly prefixed by its own `[run][action]`:

1. `flyte.logger` — canonical user-facing logger.
2. `logging.getLogger("flyte.user.myapp")` — child of `flyte.user`,
inherits the formatter via propagation.
3. `logging.getLogger("myapp")` — fully independent logger with its own
handler that references the factory-stamped attrs in its format string.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/user_api/test_logging.py
tests/flyte/test_logging.py` passes (23 tests)
- [x] `test_user_logger_no_flyte_prefix` updated to check the formatter
flag instead of the removed `FlyteInternalFilter`
- [x] `test_user_logger_no_flyte_prefix_after_rich_init` — regression
test for rich-handler internal prefix bleeding into user logger
- [x] `test_initialize_logger_wraps_existing_root_handlers` — covers
wrap path + idempotency on repeated init
- [ ] Manual: run `examples/basics/reuse_concurrent_logging.py` against
a cluster and confirm all three worker variants emit
`[run][action]`-prefixed log lines on the shared reused container

fix(io): skip the copy in File.download() when the file is already local (#1674)

## Problem

`File.download()` and `File.download_sync()` always copy a file that is
already on the local filesystem (for example one on a mounted volume).
With no `local_path` they generate a temporary path and copy the file
there. The async path does this with `await dst.write(await
src.read())`, so the whole file is read into memory and large files can
OOM the task.

`Dir.download()` already returns `self.path` in this situation; `File`
never got the same short-circuit.

## Change

When the file is local and `local_path` is `None` or points at the file
itself, return `self.path` without copying. This applies to both
`download()` and `download_sync()`.

Passing `local_path` equal to the file's own path previously truncated
the file in the async path (the destination was opened for writing
before the source was read) and raised `SameFileError` in the sync path;
both now return the path.

## Behaviour change to be aware of

Callers that call `download()` with no argument on a local file now get
the original path back, not a private temporary copy. Code that modifies
or deletes the "downloaded" file will now touch the source. This matches
`Dir.download()`.

## Not in this PR

Copying a local file to an explicit, different `local_path` is
unchanged, so the async path still reads the whole file into memory in
that case.

## Testing

- New tests cover the no-copy path (async and sync, with no target and
with the same path) and confirm an explicit different target still
copies.
- `tests/flyte/io_types`: 53 passed locally. The 12 tests that need the
S3 sandbox on `localhost:4566` could not run on my machine.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass on the touched files.

make the Agent callback event stream multi-agent compatible (#1288)

This pull request introduces robust tracking and attribution of agent
events to individual agent runs, especially in concurrent and nested
(sub-agent) scenarios. The changes ensure that each event is stamped
with the correct `agent` and `run_id`, so consumers (such as the UI) can
reliably distinguish between events from different runs or agents. The
UI now ignores progress events from sub-agents to prevent them from
interfering with the main agent's display, while still allowing
custom/unstamped events to pass through. Comprehensive tests are added
to verify these behaviors.

**Agent run identity and event attribution:**
- Added a `_RunIdentity` dataclass and a context variable `_current_run`
to track the current agent and run ID for each event, ensuring that
concurrent and nested agent runs do not conflate their events. The
`_run_loop` method sets and resets this context for each run, and
`_emit` automatically stamps `agent` and `run_id` onto every
`AgentEvent`. (`src/flyte/ai/agents/agent.py`)
- Updated the `AgentEvent` class to include `agent` and `run_id` fields,
and documented that these are now stamped automatically.
(`src/flyte/ai/agents/agent.py`)

**UI and event filtering:**
- Modified the chat UI event handler so that only events from the
top-level (first) run are processed; events from sub-agents (with a
different `run_id`) are dropped to prevent them from interfering with
the UI state, while unstamped events still pass through.
(`src/flyte/ai/chat/app.py`)

**Testing:**
- Added tests to verify that all events are correctly stamped with the
agent name and run ID, that sub-agent events are attributed to their own
runs without interfering with the outer agent, and that the run identity
context is properly restored after sub-agent execution.
(`tests/flyte/ai/agents/test_agent.py`)
- Added a test to ensure that the chat stream drops sub-agent progress
events (with a different `run_id`) but allows unstamped events, and that
sub-agent events do not clobber the UI attempt counter or phase.
(`tests/flyte/ai/chat/test_app.py`)

feat(extras): receive SaaS webhooks, at flyte.extras.webhooks

Product-agnostic machinery for turning an inbound webhook into a Flyte run, so
each flyteplugins-<product> package only has to say how to verify and parse its
own deliveries.

- WebhookAppEnvironment: one app serving a setup dashboard and a verified
  receiver at /webhook/{provider}, for whichever providers it is handed.
- WebhookEvent: the normalized event every provider parses into. Its dedupe key
  folds in the product's own timestamp, so a later change to one resource gets
  its own key rather than collapsing onto the first.
- idempotent_run: launch once per event key. Identity lives on a run *label*,
  never a name -- names race against concurrent launches and cap how many runs
  one key can ever have.
- Provider plus the verification primitives, written once because they are the
  part that is easy to get subtly wrong. constant_time_equals compares bytes:
  hmac.compare_digest raises TypeError on non-ASCII str operands, and these
  headers come off the wire, so a crafted one would turn a clean 401 into a 500.
- testing.assert_provider_conforms: the conformance check every product plugin
  runs, which replays a real sample delivery through verify and parse rather
  than trusting them to agree with each other.

No new dependencies. pydantic is already a runtime dependency; fastapi stays
behind the same lazy import flyte.app.extras._fastapi uses, so importing this
package never requires it -- only building the app does. Product plugins
declare their own [app] extra.

Tested against a stub provider, so the SDK depends on no product package.
examples/apps/webhook_custom_provider.py is a complete provider you can run
with no account at all.

fix(storage): don't clobber the global fsspec registry on import

Importing `flyte` (v2) inside a process that also runs flytekit (v1) broke
all of flytekit's object-store I/O: `flyte.storage._storage` unconditionally
ran `obstore.fsspec.register(["s3", "gs", "abfs", "abfss"], ...)` at import
time, replacing s3fs/gcsfs/adlfs in the global fsspec registry. flytekit then
called `fsspec.filesystem("s3", cache_regions=True, ...)` and obstore rejected
the s3fs-only kwargs ("Configuration key: 'cache_regions' is not valid for
store 'S3'"), failing every output upload and masking the real task error.

Two-part fix:

1. flyte's own I/O is now registry-independent: for obstore-supported
   protocols, `get_underlying_filesystem` instantiates a flyte-owned
   per-protocol subclass of `obstore.fsspec.FsspecStore` directly (mirroring
   what `obstore.fsspec.register` builds, including instance caching via
   fsspec's `_Cached` metaclass) instead of resolving through the registry.

2. Global registration is now non-destructive gap-filling: obstore is only
   registered for a protocol when nothing else is registered and no other
   implementation (e.g. s3fs) is importable, so pure-v2 images keep working
   `s3://` paths for pandas/pyarrow while hybrid v1/v2 processes keep
   flytekit's filesystems intact regardless of import order.

Parallelize the downstream consumer scan -- it was fully sequential

Profiled against the live playground cluster: a depth=1 request for an
artifact with the consolidated dashboard's watched_tasks/watched_apps
(10 tasks, 4 apps) took 4.68s wall clock across 34 RPCs averaging ~50-70ms
each -- but _consumer_runs_of_artifact and _consumer_apps_of_artifact awaited
every watched task, and every unmatched run within each task, one at a time
in a plain for loop. None of that work depends on any other task's or run's
result, so it's pure unclaimed concurrency: sum-of-latencies instead of
max-of-latencies.

Restructured both to fan out with asyncio.gather (bounded by a
_SCAN_CONCURRENCY semaphore so a dashboard watching many tasks doesn't fire
an unbounded RPC burst at once). Same RPC count, same result, run concurrently
instead of one after another.

Re-profiled after the change: same artifact, same 34 RPCs, 1.61s wall clock
(down from 4.68s). Verified the existing lineage smoke test (upstream/
downstream shape, depth truncation flags) still passes unchanged, and
redeployed to the live dashboard app, which reached ACTIVE.

rs_controller: publish flyte_core to crates.io (#1408)

## Why are the changes needed?

The Rust SDK at
[flyteorg/flyte-sdk-rs](https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte-sdk-rs)
depends on this crate by git rev, and crates.io refuses to publish a
crate whose dependencies are not on the registry:

```
all dependencies must have a version requirement specified when publishing.
dependency `flyte_core` does not specify a version
```

So the `flyte` crate cannot be released at all until `flyte_core` is.
This unblocks that.

## What changes were proposed in this pull request?

**`rs_controller/Cargo.toml`**
- Adds `description` and `license`. Both are hard crates.io requirements
— publishing fails outright without them. The repo `LICENSE` is
Apache-2.0 but sits outside the crate directory and would not be
packaged, so this uses the SPDX `license` key rather than
`license-file`.
- Adds `repository`, `readme`, `keywords`, `categories`.
- Adds `exclude`, so the published tarball carries only the Rust crate.
Without it, `uv.lock` (81 KB), the wheel-builder `Makefile` and
`Dockerfile.maturinx`, and three hand-run Python test scripts all ship
to crates.io. **This affects the published tarball only** — maturin
still reads `pyproject.toml` from the working tree, so wheel builds are
unchanged.

**`.github/workflows/publish-rust-crate.yml`** (new) — publishes on
`rs-v*` tags.

Deliberately separate from `publish.yml`: that workflow releases the
Python packages on `v*` tags and derives the version from the Python
release train. Folding the crate in would force `flyte_core`'s version
to track `flyte`'s, and publish a crate on every SDK release whether or
not the Rust code changed. Here the crate version stays in `Cargo.toml`
and is *checked against* the tag rather than rewritten from it.

It follows the conventions already in this repo: the `pull_request`
trigger runs everything except the upload (the same dual-trigger idiom
`publish.yml` uses to validate itself), work is delegated to `make -C
rs_controller` targets like the existing `rs-fmt` / `rs-lint` jobs, and
caching is keyed on `hashFiles('rs_controller/Cargo.lock')`. The upload
step warns and skips while `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN` is unset, mirroring
the `notify-docs` job — so merging this cannot break a release.

**`rs_controller/README.md`** (new) — required by the `readme` key, and
documents two things that will otherwise surprise consumers: the package
is `flyte_core` but the library is `flyte_controller_base`, and default
features embed a Python interpreter.

## What this PR deliberately does *not* do

Feature defaults are untouched. `default = ["pyo3/auto-initialize"]` is
what flyte-sdk-rs wants today, so changing it now would only churn.

A pure-Rust core split out from the pyo3 bindings was considered and
deferred: it is not achievable while `flyteidl2` depends on pyo3
unconditionally and annotates ~790 generated types with `#[pyclass]`.
Making that optional upstream, then splitting this crate, is a future
breaking release. The README records the constraint so the next person
does not re-derive it.

Note for downstream: `rs_controller` pins `flyteidl2 = "=2.0.40"` while
flyte-sdk-rs currently pins `=2.0.37`. Two `=` requirements cannot
unify, so flyte-sdk-rs moves to `=2.0.40` in the PR that consumes this
crate. Nothing changes in this repo.

## How was this patch tested?

- `cargo publish --dry-run` on a clean tree — **succeeds** (this is the
command that fails on `main` today).
- `cargo package --list` — confirms the tarball contains only Rust
sources, `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `build.rs`, `rustfmt.toml`, and
`README.md`; no `pyproject.toml`, `Makefile`, `uv.lock`, or `.py` files.
- `make -C rs_controller lint` — clean, unchanged.
- Both new Makefile targets run as the workflow invokes them.
- The tag-vs-manifest check was exercised directly: accepts `rs-v0.1.0`,
rejects `rs-v9.9.9`.

The `pull_request` trigger means this PR's own CI run exercises the
workflow end to end, minus the upload.

fix: validate a Trigger's automation and the fields of Cron/FixedRate

`Cron` and `FixedRate` are the only two dataclasses in `_trigger.py` with no
`__post_init__` at all -- their siblings `OnArtifact` and `Trigger` both raise
clean field-named `ValueError`s -- so every field on them reached protobuf
unchecked, and `Trigger.automation` was never type-checked either.

Three failure modes, all reproduced:

* Silent. `to_task_trigger` dispatches on `automation` with `is None` /
  `isinstance(..., OnArtifact)` and treats everything else as a schedule,
  handing it to `_to_schedule`, whose `if Cron / elif FixedRate` chain has no
  `else` and so returns `None`. `Trigger(name="nightly", automation="0 0 * * *")`
  -- the cron string where a `Cron` belongs -- serializes to a TYPE_SCHEDULE
  spec with the schedule field unset, deploys without a word, and never fires.
* Anonymous crash. `Cron(5)` dies as `TypeError: bad argument type for built-in
  operation`, `FixedRate("60")` as `TypeError: 'str' object cannot be
  interpreted as an integer`, and `FixedRate(60, start_time="2026-01-01")` as
  `AttributeError: ... 'str' object has no attribute 'utctimetuple'` -- all from
  inside protobuf, naming neither the field that was wrong nor the trigger.
* Silently wrong value. `timezone` is a `Literal` nothing enforces at runtime
  and it is interpolated into `CRON_TZ={timezone} {expression}`, so a typo like
  "US/Pacifc" corrupts the expression it prefixes. `Cron("")` and `FixedRate(0)`
  likewise serialize cleanly into a schedule the backend can never fire.

`__post_init__` on `Cron` and `FixedRate` now checks the fields, `Trigger`
rejects an automation that is not one of the three automation types, and
`_to_schedule`'s fall-through raises instead of returning `None` from a
`-> Schedule` function.

fix(cli): detect plugin-provided groups that have no callback

get_plugin_info returned early when cmd.callback was None, so a click.Group
that only dispatches to subcommands was reported as core no matter which
package defined it. The module path — the thing that actually decides — was
never consulted.

Three consequences in the generated CLI reference, all from that one branch:
the plugin marker is dropped, the "provided by <plugin>" note is dropped, and
because the variant filter keys off the same flag, the command is emitted into
the OSS Flyte variant. A reader of the open-source docs gets a full section,
examples and options for a command that needs a plugin installed.

flyte fork hit this. flyteplugins-union registers it as

    fork = ForkFiles(name="fork", ...)

a Group subclass instantiated directly, so it carries no callback. flyte debug
from the same package is unaffected only because it is written as a decorated
function. The two differ in construction style alone, which is not a fact about
provenance.

Now: prefer the callback's module, fall back to type(cmd).__module__. For a
plugin-supplied group that is the plugin's own module, which the existing
checks already classify correctly. An un-subclassed click.Group() resolves to
click's own module, which says nothing about provenance either, so that is
guarded and stays core — without the guard it reports a plugin named
"click.core".

Tests cover the regression, the decorated-plugin control that must not break,
core commands, a core Group subclass, the bare click.Group case, and None.
Verified adversarially: test_plugin_group_without_callback_is_detected fails
without this change. Full tests/cli suite passes (390).

Scope note: the fix is verified against a faithful reproduction of how
flyteplugins-union constructs the group, not against the shipped 0.8.0 wheel —
the local resolver's exclude-newer cutoff predates that release.

fix(remote): use OS DNS resolver in pyqwest transport

pyqwest defaults to use_system_dns=False, which routes all RPCs through
the bundled trust-dns resolver. trust-dns happily returns AAAA records
even on hosts with no usable IPv6 default route (e.g. tethered mobile
hotspots that advertise IPv6 via RA but don't actually route it). The
result is every RPC hangs and eventually fails with:

    client error (Connect): dns error: proto error: io error:
    No route to host (os error 65)

curl works on the same network because it uses getaddrinfo, which
honors AI_ADDRCONFIG and suppresses AAAA records when there's no v6
default route.

Setting use_system_dns=True on the HTTPTransport routes lookups through
getaddrinfo, matching curl's behavior and eliminating the spurious
EHOSTUNREACH failures on flaky/tethered networks.

Install code-server extensions in one invocation to avoid EEXIST race (#1417)

## What

Fixes a flaky debug-mode startup failure where `code-server
--install-extension` dies with:

```
EEXIST: file already exists, rename '.../.<uuid>' -> '.../ms-python.vscode-python-envs-1.36.0-universal'
```

aborting the vscode debug server before it comes up.

## Why

`download_vscode()` installed each downloaded extension in a
**concurrent** `code-server --install-extension` process via
`asyncio.gather`. Both `ms-python.python` and `ms-python.debugpy` depend
on `ms-python.vscode-python-envs`, so each process independently
downloads and extracts that dependency into the shared extensions
directory; whichever process loses the rename of its temp dir onto the
dependency's final directory exits non-zero, and `execute_command`
raises, killing debug-mode startup.

## How

Extension **downloads** stay parallel. The **install** step now goes
through a new `install_extensions()` helper that passes every vsix to a
single invocation (`code-server --install-extension a.vsix
--install-extension b.vsix`), so one process handles dependency
extraction exactly once.

## Testing

New tests assert all extensions are installed via one `execute_command`
call and that an empty extension list makes no invocation. Full
`test_debug.py` + `test_ssh_debug.py` suites pass (46 tests); ruff
clean.

feat: export Documentation from flyte (#1574)

## What

Exports `Documentation` from `flyte` and adds it to `__all__`.

`@env.task(docs=...)` (`TaskEnvironment.task`) and `TaskTemplate.docs`
are typed `Optional[Documentation]`, but the class lives in the private
module `flyte._doc` and has never been exported. Users can only reach it
with `from flyte._doc import Documentation`, which goes against
CONTRIBUTING's rule that users should never need to import an underscore
module. The Union docs had written `from flyte import Documentation`,
which fails with `ImportError` on 2.7.2.

## Changes

- `src/flyte/__init__.py`: `from ._doc import Documentation`, and
`"Documentation"` in `__all__`, in the existing order.
- `tests/flyte/test_doc.py`: the export is the same class as
`flyte._doc.Documentation` and is listed in `__all__`. Also tests
`extract_docstring`.

## Checks

- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` on the changed files: pass.
- `pytest tests/flyte/test_doc.py`: 2 passed.
- `make check-import-profile` fails, **but it fails identically on
unmodified `main` (1e949304)**: the only difference is `flyte._observe`,
so the recorded baseline in `import_profiles/` looks stale. This change
adds no module to the import set, because `flyte._doc` is already
imported through `flyte._task`. I haven't regenerated the baseline here,
since that's unrelated to this PR.

## Worth knowing: `docs` does not reach the deployed description

While checking this, I found that `docs=` has no effect on the
description a deployed task shows in the UI:

- `_deploy._get_documentation_entity` builds the `DocumentationEntity`
from `task_template.interface.docstring` only.
- The one place that reads `task.docs` is the CLI: `cli/_run.py:604`
uses it as the `flyte run ... --help` text.

Reproduced on flyte 2.7.2:

| Task | `_get_documentation_entity(task).short_description` |
|---|---|
| docstring only | the docstring |
| `docs=Documentation("Explicit…")` + docstring | the docstring (`docs`
ignored) |
| `docs=Documentation("Explicit…")`, no docstring | `''` |

The parameter's own docstring ("The documentation for the task, if not
provided the function docstring will be used") implies `docs` should
take precedence. If that's the intent, `_get_documentation_entity` could
prefer `task_template.docs.description` when it's set. I've left
behaviour unchanged here, so this PR stays a pure export. Happy to
follow up if you want it wired through.

fix(map): abort in-flight child tasks on failure, early exit, and cancellation (#1672)

## Problem

A user reported a run that stayed active for 11 days after `flyte.map`
child tasks failed (it had to be aborted manually), and child workers
staying active after the caller was cancelled.

A child action is only aborted server-side when its cancelled coroutine
gets to run `cancel_action` in the controller's `CancelledError`
handler, so cleanup has to cancel **and await** in-flight tasks. That
wasn't happening in several places:

1. `MapAsyncIterator.aclose()` was a no-op for the default
`concurrency=0` path, and on failure the remaining tasks were
`.cancel()`ed but never awaited.
2. `_map` never closed its iterator on failure, early exit, or
cancellation.
3. `map.aio()` drives `_map` on syncify's background loop. Cancelling or
breaking out of the consumer only cancelled the pending `__anext__`; the
inner generator was never closed.

## Changes

- `src/flyte/_map.py`
- `aclose()` handles both paths; `_cancel_unbounded()` cancels and
awaits pending tasks (also used on the `return_exceptions=False` failure
path).
  - `_map` wraps iteration in `try/finally: await iter.aclose()`.
- `map.aio()`, sync `flyte.map()`, and `collect()` close their inner
iterators in a `finally`.
- `src/flyte/syncify/_api.py`
- `iterate_in_loop` / `iterate_in_loop_sync` close the underlying async
generator on the background loop when the consumer stops (early exit,
error, or cancellation). If the consumer was cancelled, cleanup waits
for the in-flight `__anext__` to unwind first (`aclose()` raises while
the generator is running), and is shielded so a second cancel can't
interrupt it.
- ⚠️ This applies to every syncified async generator, not just `map` —
worth a careful look.

## Testing

- New `tests/user_api/test_map_cancellation.py` (10 tests): failure,
early exit, and caller cancellation, through `MapAsyncIterator`,
`_map.aio`, the public `map.aio()`, and sync `flyte.map()`, at
concurrency 0 and 3. 9/10 fail on `main`.
- `tests/user_api`, map, and syncify tests: 878 passed.
- Full unit suite (`-k "not integration and not sandbox"`): 6020 passed,
14 failed — 10 also fail on `main` locally (roundtrip, code_bundle,
keyring, serve); the other 4 pass in isolation on this branch and only
fail in the full parallel run.

fix: clamp Backoff.compute_delay to the cap instead of overflowing

`Backoff` requires a `cap` whenever `factor > 1.0`, explicitly "to prevent
unbounded growth". `compute_delay` then evaluated `base * factor**n` before
comparing against that cap, so the growth still happened and overflowed the
timedelta range: `Backoff(base=10s, factor=2.0, cap=5m).compute_delay(43)`
raised OverflowError rather than returning 5m.

This is reachable from a normal task. `RetryStrategy(count=100)` is supported,
and the local controller calls `compute_delay(attempt_num - 1)` on each
attempt, so a long-retry task with exponential backoff died on attempt 44 with
a timedelta arithmetic error raised from inside the failure-handling path --
losing the remaining attempts and pointing nowhere near the retry policy.

Catch the overflow and return the cap. `__post_init__` guarantees a cap
whenever `factor > 1.0`, and `factor == 1.0` cannot overflow, so a cap is
always available at that point; the documented `min(base * factor**n, cap)`
now holds for every n.

Send a Content-Type when uploading a local File

An upload that sends no Content-Type is stored as binary/octet-stream, so a
browser opening a presigned URL for it downloads the file instead of rendering
it. File.from_local / from_local_sync's lazy uploader never sent one.

This is also what kept artifact cards from rendering. Uploads are keyed by
content md5 + filename, so publishing one html file as both the artifact value
and its card writes the *same* object twice:

  PUT .../paper.html   Content-Type: text/html   <- card, correct
  PUT .../paper.html   (none)                    <- value, overwrites it

The card upload set the type correctly and the untyped value upload clobbered
it a moment later. Observed on canary, where the card uri and the artifact's
blob uri are the same key.

Content type is guessed from the file name. None when the extension is unknown,
or when it implies an encoding (report.html.gz) -- the guessed type there
describes the decoded bytes and would mis-serve the compressed object.

Dir uploads (remote.upload_dir) still send no Content-Type; left alone for now.

fix: don't crash-report a proxy answering a Connect RPC (FLYTE-SDK-77)

`flyte run` and `flyte deploy` from a Windows host failed with
`RuntimeSystemError: Upload failed for C:\...` whose cause was a bare
`ConnectError: No Content`, out of both CreateUploadLocation and
SelectCluster.

A Connect endpoint answers a unary POST with 200 and a Connect body, or
with an error status and a Connect JSON body. HTTP 204 is neither: the
request never reached a Connect handler, and something in the path — a
proxy, VPN appliance, captive portal, TLS interceptor or misrouted
ingress — absorbed it and answered on the backend's behalf. That is
endpoint/network configuration, not a Python-SDK logic bug, so it
shouldn't be reported as an SDK crash. This is the same rationale
already applied to UNIMPLEMENTED (a raw HTTP 404 from the ingress).

connectrpc only maps a few HTTP statuses onto Connect codes; everything
else falls through to `ConnectWireError.from_http_status`, which yields
Code.UNKNOWN, no details, and the stdlib reason phrase as the entire
message — the numeric status is dropped, so the phrase is the only way
back to the status class.

The filter is deliberately restricted to the 2xx-not-200 class. HTTP 500
produces an identically shaped error ("Internal Server Error", UNKNOWN,
no details) but means something genuinely broke and is real signal worth
keeping — FLYTE-SDK-64/6S/43 are exactly that shape and stay reported,
as does a backend that collapses an inner code into UNKNOWN with a
verbose message (FLYTE-SDK-67/4T). Two of the new tests are regression
guards pinning that behaviour.

fix: don't report click.Abort/ClickException to Sentry (#1039)

## Summary
- `click.Abort`, `click.exceptions.Exit`, and `click.ClickException` are
raised on purpose to display user-facing messages (Ctrl+C, declined
prompts, missing dependencies, etc.). They are not crashes and shouldn't
generate Sentry issues.

`capture_exception` so they short-circuit before any Sentry init/flush.

Release notes

Sourced from rustls-webpki's releases.

0.103.13

  • Fix reachable panic in parsing a CRL. This was reported to us as GHSA-82j2-j2ch-gfr8. Users who don't use CRLs are not affected.
  • For name constraints on URI names, we incorrectly processed excluded subtrees in a way which inverted the desired meaning. See rustls/webpki#471. This was a case missing in the fix for https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5.

What's Changed

  • Actually fail closed for URI matching against excluded subtrees by @​djc in rustls/webpki#473
  • Prepare 0.103.13 by @​ctz in rustls/webpki#474

Full Changelog: https://github.com/rustls/webpki/compare/v/0.103.12...v/0.103.13

0.103.12

This release fixes two bugs in name constraint enforcement:

  • GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5: name constraints for URI names were ignored and therefore accepted. URI name constraints are now rejected unconditionally. Note this library does not provide an API for asserting URI names, and URI name constraints are otherwise not implemented.
  • GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh: permitted subtree name constraints for DNS names were accepted for certificates asserting a wildcard name. This was incorrect because, given a name constraint of accept.example.com, *.example.com could feasibly allow a name of reject.example.com which is outside the constraint. This is very similar to CVE-2025-61727.

Since name constraints are restrictions on otherwise properly-issued certificates, these bugs are reachable only after signature verification and require misissuance to exploit.

What's Changed

  • Prepare 0.103.12 by @​djc in rustls/webpki#470

Full Changelog: https://github.com/rustls/webpki/compare/v/0.103.11...v/0.103.12

0.103.11

In response to #464, we've slightly relaxed requirements for anchor_from_trust_cert() to ignore unknown extensions even if they're marked as critical. This only affects parsing a TrustAnchor from DER, for which most extensions are ignored anyway.

What's Changed

  • Backport parsing trust anchors with unknown critical extensions to 0.103 by @​djc in rustls/webpki#466

0.103.10

Correct selection of candidate CRLs by Distribution Point and Issuing Distribution Point. If a certificate had more than one distributionPoint, then only the first distributionPoint would be considered against each CRL's IssuingDistributionPoint distributionPoint, and then the certificate's subsequent distributionPoints would be ignored.

The impact was that correctly provided CRLs would not be consulted to check revocation. With UnknownStatusPolicy::Deny (the default) this would lead to incorrect but safe Error::UnknownRevocationStatus. With UnknownStatusPolicy::Allow this would lead to inappropriate acceptance of revoked certificates.

This vulnerability is thought to be of limited impact. This is because both the certificate and CRL are signed -- an attacker would need to compromise a trusted issuing authority to trigger this bug. An attacker with such capabilities could likely bypass revocation checking through other more impactful means (such as publishing a valid, empty CRL.)

More likely, this bug would be latent in normal use, and an attacker could leverage faulty revocation checking to continue using a revoked credential.

This vulnerability is identified by GHSA-pwjx-qhcg-rvj4. Thank you to @​1seal for the report.

What's Changed

  • Freshen up rel-0.103 by @​ctz in rustls/webpki#455
  • Prepare 0.103.10 by @​ctz in rustls/webpki#458

fix(apple-silicon): review fixes for the bridge, client, CLI and serialization

Bridge and host processes
- Track the pods holding each workload (X-Flyte-Apple-Silicon-Instance): replicas of an app revision share its host
  process, which is torn down when the last pod lets go (DELETE or a lapsed lease); a second pod can't take over a
  task's run (409).
- A host process that fails to launch is marked start_failed instead of hanging in "preparing".
- Kill the whole process group, also after the leader exits; parallel shutdown under stop_bridge's deadline.
- A new run truncates its log before exec returns; reads end on a line boundary.
- Validate exec specs and bodies (types, NUL bytes, python version, size cap); 409 for daemon routes on host
  workloads; a catch-all 500 instead of dropped connections; proxy inflight on the right record, finite timeout.
- Injective, traversal-safe work-dir and log names. Owner-only log files.
- Drop only Kubernetes-injected service variables (not the user's DB_PORT), CUDA/NVIDIA vars, and container-only
  paths; forward pip index options from the image.
- The app's declared port is used on the host when free, so apps that bind it directly work.

Client
- Final log drains read to the end; partial lines are carried; one lock for the drain.
- Named errors for host-side failures (OOM, torn down, lost) and for an unreachable bridge after the lease period;
  signal exits map to 128+N. A rejected token is APPLE_SILICON_NOT_AVAILABLE (recreate the devbox).
- Bind the app port synchronously; half-close correctly.
- The container-mode opt-out also applies at run time.

CLI and host
- stop_bridge only signals a process proven to be the bridge (healthz pid or command line), and tolerates
  PermissionError; stale pid files are only removed.
- The secret is written atomically; an empty or short secret is replaced and never accepted.
- --apple-silicon requires uv (mlx-lm is only for container mode); --gpu can't be combined with it; a failed start
  stops the bridge it started; resume checks the devbox's baked secret still matches.
- flyte get devbox escapes workload text and tolerates odd payloads; it no longer creates state. A bridge from an
  older flyte is restarted.

Serialization and API
- Requirements files: continuation lines, -r includes, index options, flyte filtered by name; uv/poetry project and
  PEP 723 script dependencies; a warning for what can't carry over.
- RemoteTask.override keeps (or drops) the Apple Silicon settings instead of silently losing them.
- FastAPI and webhook apps listen on get_port().
- Error codes are namespaced (APPLE_SILICON_*), with a new AppleSiliconHostExecFailedError; deterministic setup
  errors are non-recoverable.
- Device("AppleSilicon") requires the APPLE_SILICON class; prefetch no longer offers AppleSilicon.

fix: accept dry_run in flyte.deploy, deprecate dryrun (#1573)

## Summary

`flyte.deploy` is the only public API that spells the dry-run flag
`dryrun`. Everything else uses `dry_run`:

| Call | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `flyte.deploy(...)` | `dryrun` | `dry_run` (`dryrun` deprecated) |
| `flyte.with_runcontext(...)` | `dry_run` | unchanged |
| `flyte.with_servecontext(...)` | `dry_run` | unchanged |
| `flyte.build(...)` | `dry_run` | unchanged |
| `flyte deploy` CLI | `--dry-run` / `--dryrun` | unchanged |

On 2.7.2, `flyte.deploy(env, dry_run=True)` raises `TypeError: deploy()
got an unexpected keyword argument 'dry_run'`. The user docs have
already tripped over this.

## Changes

- `flyte.deploy` now takes `dry_run: bool = False`.
- `dryrun` is still accepted as a deprecated keyword. It emits a
`FutureWarning` and maps onto `dry_run`. If both are passed, either one
being `True` requests a dry run, so disagreement errs toward not
deploying.
- The `flyte deploy` CLI now calls `flyte.deploy(dry_run=...)`, so it no
longer triggers the warning.
- Internal helpers (`apply`, `_deploy_task`, `DeploymentContext`, code
bundling) keep their `dryrun` names. Only the public signature changes.

### Why `FutureWarning` and not `DeprecationWarning`

`@syncify` runs the coroutine body on a background-loop thread, so the
warning can't be attributed to the caller's module. Under Python's
default filters, a `DeprecationWarning` raised there is silently
dropped. A plain-script check confirmed this: the `DeprecationWarning`
probe printed nothing, and the `FutureWarning` was shown.

## Tests

- New tests in `tests/flyte/test_deploy.py` check that `dry_run` is
forwarded to `apply` with no warning, that `dryrun` still works and
warns, and how the two combine when both are passed.
- `uv run pytest tests/flyte/test_deploy.py tests/cli`: all pass (35 and
462).
- `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy`, `ty check` and `make
check-docstrings` are clean on the changed files.

feat(logging): stamp run/action context via LogRecordFactory

Switch from logging.Filter-based context stamping to a global
LogRecordFactory. The factory runs on every LogRecord regardless
of which logger created it, so any user-defined logger
(`logging.getLogger("myapp")`, child of `flyte.user`, or a fully
independent stdlib logger) automatically picks up `run_name`,
`action_name`, and `is_flyte_internal` attributes — no per-handler
filter wiring required.

Adds `register_log_context(name, var)` / `unregister_log_context`
so users can stamp their own contextvars onto every record. The
JSONFormatter emits them as top-level fields; console formatters
can reference them via `%(name)s`.

The `[flyte]` internal-prefix marker is now a ContextFormatter
flag instead of a filter, so the same record can be formatted by
multiple handlers without compounding prefixes.

- `examples/basics/reuse_concurrent_logging.py`: demonstrates four
  logger configs (flyte.logger, flyte.user.* child, independent
  stdlib logger, register_log_context contextvar) under reusable
  containers with concurrent tasks.
- `tests/user_api/test_logging.py`: updated detection to look for
  the formatter flag instead of the removed FlyteInternalFilter.

Wrap File.read() in bytes() before decoding in the pipeline example

`evaluate` called `.decode()` straight on the result of `fh.read()`, which
fails against object storage:

    AttributeError: 'builtins.Bytes' object has no attribute 'decode'

The reader returns a Rust-backed `Bytes` that supports the buffer protocol
but has no `decode`. `bytes(await fh.read()).decode("utf-8")` is the idiom
in `File.open`'s own docstring and works for both backends.

Worth knowing: a local raw-data path returns real Python `bytes`, so the
broken form passes locally and only fails once the raw-data path is remote.
Verified both ways against GCS -- the unwrapped form reproduces the error,
the wrapped one returns the value.

Add support for .flyteignore file

This change adds support for a custom .flyteignore file that works alongside .gitignore to exclude files from Flyte code bundles. The GitIgnore class now explicitly reads patterns from both .gitignore and .flyteignore files.

Key changes:
- Modified GitIgnore to use --exclude-from flags for both .gitignore and .flyteignore
- Removed reliance on --exclude-standard flag for more explicit control
- Added file existence checks to handle missing ignore files gracefully
- Added comprehensive unit tests for the new functionality

Classify Azure 403 AuthorizationFailure uploads as a user error

refusing this client is deployment configuration, not an SDK fault. Raise
RuntimeUserError("UploadForbidden") with actionable advice instead of the
generic RuntimeSystemError("UploadFailed"), which Sentry reports.

Add 'flyte delete local-cache' command to clear local image cache

Adds a CLI command that clears the locally cached image lookups stored in
the SQLite cache at ~/.flyte/local-cache. This is useful when stale image

fix: serialize optional None task defaults (#1332)

## What/Why

Task parameters annotated as optional with a `None` default are
currently omitted from uploaded `default_inputs`. After registration,
remote clients consequently treat those parameters as required even
though their Python signatures allow omission.

This conflicts with the documented task contract: [parameters with
Python defaults can be omitted and their defaults are part of the task
input
schema](https://www.union.ai/docs/v2/flyte/user-guide/task-configuration/additional-task-settings/),
and [an `Optional[...]` input or any input with a default is not
required](https://www.union.ai/docs/v2/flyte/user-guide/task-deployment/run-command-options/).
During deployment, Flyte [analyzes and serializes task parameter
metadata into a
`TaskTemplate`](https://www.union.ai/docs/v2/flyte/user-guide/task-deployment/how-task-deployment-works/),
so the `None` default must survive this conversion.

<details>
<summary>Minimal reproducer</summary>

Run from the Flyte SDK repository root. On `main`, this raises the same
error observed when launching the RasterFlow integration workflow:
`ValueError: Missing required inputs: intermediate_storage_uri,
storage_uri`. It completes successfully on this branch.

```shell
uvx --from uv==0.9.21 uv run python - <<"PY"
import asyncio

from flyte._internal.runtime.convert import (
    convert_from_native_to_inputs,
    convert_upload_default_inputs,
)
from flyte._internal.runtime.types_serde import transform_native_to_typed_interface
from flyte.models import NativeInterface
from flyte.types import guess_interface


def task(
    intermediate_storage_uri: str | None = None,
    storage_uri: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    pass


async def main() -> None:
    local_interface = NativeInterface.from_callable(task)
    uploaded_defaults = await convert_upload_default_inputs(local_interface)
    remote_interface = guess_interface(
        transform_native_to_typed_interface(local_interface),
        uploaded_defaults,
    )
    await convert_from_native_to_inputs(remote_interface)


asyncio.run(main())
PY
```

</details>

## How

Serialize every declared default except `inspect.Parameter.empty`.
Extend the existing default-input conversion test to verify that an
optional `None` default is uploaded as the union `NONE` literal.

fix(crewai): keep native tool calling working with durable=True (#1430)

CrewAI's default executor does native tool calling: a tool-calling model
turn returns raw OpenAI-SDK tool-call objects, and the executor only
routes the turn as tool calls while the list elements still carry a
.function attribute. durable_step round-trips every turn result through
dumps/loads even on the recording pass, and the crewai serializer
coerced non-string results to JSON with default=str - so the tool-call
objects came back as plain strings, fell through the router, and were
returned as the final answer after one turn. durable=True (the default)
silently disabled tool calling on crewai 1.15.2, sync and async alike.

Tool-call lists now serialize under their own tagged record (dict form
via model_dump) and rebuild as real
ChatCompletionMessageFunctionToolCall objects on load, falling back to
the dict shape the router equally accepts, so recording and replay are
both indistinguishable from a live turn. Also resolve an awaitable tool
result in _dispatch: outside a task context task.aio forwards to the raw
function, handing an async tool's coroutine back unawaited, which
surfaced as a coroutine repr in the agent's tool output.

Verified with a sync/async x durable on/off matrix against a local fake
OpenAI-compatible server (tool executes, two model turns, correct final
answer in all four cells) plus round-trip unit tests; 30 tests pass
including the adapter conformance check.

fix: make module-level syncify wrappers cloudpickleable

`_SyncWrapper` transitively references a `_BackgroundLoop` whose asyncio
loop owns a `ThreadPoolExecutor` backed by a `_queue.SimpleQueue`.
When cloudpickle serializes a user function that captures a module-level
syncify-wrapped helper (notably `flyte._trace._fetch_action_outputs`),
the default reducer walks into the loop's state and dies with:
`TypeError: cannot pickle '_queue.SimpleQueue' object`.

Add a `__reduce__` that pickles a `_SyncWrapper` by reference (module +
qualname) whenever the wrapper is importable at its original module
path. The consumer just re-imports it on load, which is the only sane
contract anyway — the bg loop in the producer is meaningless in the
consumer process.

Falls back to the default reducer for unnamed (closure-local) wrappers
so behavior is unchanged outside the regression.

Signed-off-by: Kevin Su <pingsutw@apache.org>

Let a script task declare File and Dir outputs

A `slurm_script` task was terminal: it reported phase, exit code and logs,
so nothing downstream could consume its results. Not a policy choice -- the
interface was empty because an arbitrary sbatch script has no way to write
`outputs.pb` in Flyte's literal format, which is what the entrypoint does for
a native task.

Declared outputs close that without asking the script to know anything about
Flyte:

    SlurmScriptTask(..., outputs={"model": File, "shards": Dir})

The plugin exports a destination URI per output as `FLYTE_OUTPUT_<NAME>`,
under the same output prefix `outputs.pb` would use, alongside the
`FLYTE_INPUT_*` variables it already exports. The script writes there with
whatever tooling the site has -- `aws s3 cp`, `gcloud storage cp`, rclone --
and the connector records each destination as the declared File or Dir once
the job succeeds, through `Resource.outputs`. The bytes never pass through
the connector: the job already holds credentials to read its inputs, so a
large checkpoint goes straight to object storage rather than through a
connector pod.

Two constraints, both deliberate. Only `File` and `Dir` may be declared,
because a scalar would have to be parsed out of stdout and that is silently
wrong for any script that logs. And a declared output the script never wrote
fails the task even on exit 0, since the alternative is handing a downstream
task a URI to nothing, which surfaces much later as an unexplained read
error; that costs one existence check per output, once, on the poll that
finds the job finished.

Native tasks are untouched -- no destinations, no existence checks, and
`Resource.outputs` stays None, because their entrypoint writes its own.

feat(plugins): bool and Literal battery fields for typesafe-ai (#1612)

Follow-up to #1609. Adds the Pydantic AI field shapes — a plain value in
the field, calibration out of band — alongside the answer types, so you
can fill a model you already have from one Jev call.

| field type | asks | comes back as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bool` | a Noul | `True`/`False`, cut at a threshold **you** declare |
| `Literal["a", "b"]` | a Choice over those options | the option itself
|

## Two rules keep this from being a footgun

**A plain field is a question only when the field says it is.**
`Choice`, `Score` and `Noul` are questions by their type alone. A `bool`
or `Literal` needs a `question` in its metadata before it is asked,
because `flag: bool = False` is bookkeeping far more often than a
question. This rule is not hypothetical: without it, the `conflicted:
bool = False` field in the pydantic example from #1609 would have
started being asked.

**A `bool` must say where it cuts.** Something has to turn a calibrated
0..1 answer into two states, and that decision belongs in the caller's
code — the same reason `Noul` has no `__bool__`. So there is no implicit
default:

```python
hostile: bool = field(metadata={"question": "Hostile?", "threshold": 0.8})   # per field
facets = await ask(Facets, state, threshold=0.5)                             # or per call
```

Neither, and it raises — *before* the request, so a battery missing a
threshold fails without spending a call. Requiring it also makes a
misspelled key loud: a key that is not spelled `threshold` leaves the
field with no cut at all, so it fails rather than quietly meaning 0.5. A
threshold passed when nothing needs cutting is an error too.

## Nothing is lost from the call, only from the model

`CallInfo` gains two maps — this plugin's answer to `provider_details`:

```python
facets, info = await ask_with_info(Facets, state, threshold=0.5)

facets.hostile              # False   -- your model, plain bool
info.values["hostile"]      # 0.62    -- the float it was cut from
info.confidence["tier"]     # 0.77    -- for Literal fields
```

Both are `dict[str, float]`, so a task can still return a `CallInfo` —
there is a test pinning that round-trip.

## Testing

- 47 plugin tests, 9 new: compilation of both shorthands, per-field vs
per-call thresholds, the no-threshold and nothing-to-cut errors,
out-of-range rejection, non-string literals coming back as themselves
(`Literal[1, 2, 4]` → `int`), literal criteria and unknown-option
rejection, the bookkeeping-field rule on both dataclasses and models,
and the `CallInfo` round-trip
- One test asserts no request is spent when a threshold is missing
- `make fmt`, `make mypy` (902 files), `make ty`, `check-docstrings`,
`codespell` clean
- `examples/pydantic_battery.py` extended with a thresholded `bool` and
a `Literal`, and run end to end: `route=review intent=refund (p=1.00)
severity=BLOCKING@2.6 refund_requested=0.99 conflicted=False
asks_for_human=False channel=email`

fix(orchestrator): catchable condition errors and typed waits in the prelude

From review of unionai/sandbox-leaseworker#41.

- The sandbox has no exception classes of its own, so `flyte.errors` inside
  an orchestrator is a stand-in: ConditionTimedoutError is TimeoutError, and
  ConditionFailedError and ActionAbortedError are RuntimeError. A condition's
  wait() re-raises a timeout from the worker as TimeoutError, so `except
  flyte.errors.ConditionTimedoutError` catches only timeouts. `flyte.errors`,
  and those classes imported by name, are bound to the stand-ins.
- wait() passes the condition's name and data type with its handle, so the
  worker returns the value as the condition's type.
- new_condition checks prompt_type and timeout as flyte.new_condition does,
  raising ValueError.
- Run locally, a condition that times out, fails or is aborted is raised in
  the source as the worker raises it (RaiseInSandbox in the bridge), so the
  same handler catches it.

feat(task): raise SyncTaskCallInAsyncContextError on blocking sync-task call from an async task

A sync-style invocation (`child(...)`) inside an `async def` task blocks the
event loop driving the task body via `concurrent.futures.Future.result(None)`.
That loop also services `controller.watch_for_errors`, so if the controller /
informer dies (e.g. the actions service is down long enough to exhaust watch
retries) the process can never observe the failure: the error is never
uploaded and the pod hangs forever with the MainThread parked in
`fut.result()`.

Fail fast instead: `AsyncFunctionTaskTemplate.execute()` records the loop
driving the task body in a ContextVar, and `TaskTemplate.__call__` raises
`SyncTaskCallInAsyncContextError` — pointing at `await child.aio(...)` — when
the blocking call is made on that same loop.

The guard is loop-identity based, so the long-supported patterns keep working:
- sync parent -> sync child (body runs on the dedicated asyncify helper loop)
- calls from user threads / `asyncio.to_thread` (no running loop)
- sandbox orchestrators (Monty bridge already dispatches task refs via `.aio`)

Tests and examples that relied on the blocking pattern are migrated to `.aio`.

fix: honor batch_size on obstore uploads and make multipart part size / concurrency configurable (#1681)

##  Motivation

When many tasks upload with Dir.from_local() at the same time, S3 can
throttle them with 503 SlowDown. Users had no way to reduce the request
rate: part size (5 MiB) and per-file part concurrency (12) were
hardcoded,
  and the obstore upload path silently dropped batch_size.

 ## Summary

- storage.put() now passes batch_size to _put_obstore_bypass, which uses
it to limit parallel file uploads instead of the module-level
BATCH_SIZE. This makes Dir.from_local(batch_size=...) work on S3, GCS
and Azure.
The argument had been ignored since the obstore upload path was added.
  - New env vars:
- FLYTE_IO_UPLOAD_CHUNK_SIZE (bytes) sets the minimum part size. Values
below S3's 5 MiB minimum are raised to 5 MiB with a warning.
Auto-scaling for the 10,000-part limit still applies above it.
- FLYTE_IO_UPLOAD_MAX_CONCURRENCY sets parts in flight per file
(minimum 1).
- put_stream (used by hashed File.from_local) uses the configured part
size when it is larger than the 10 MiB writer buffer, even without a
size_hint.
- Defaults are unchanged (5 MiB, 12, batch 32). With no env vars set,
behaviour is identical.

  ## Test Plan

  - Unit tests in tests/internal/storage/test_storage.py:
    - peak files in flight equals batch_size (1 and 3)
    - the configured part size and concurrency reach put_async
    - env parsing: unset, empty, valid, and below-minimum values
    - put_stream uses the configured part size without a size hint
- Remote check on a staging cluster against real S3. One task uploads a
200 MiB file plus 8 × 6 MiB files with Dir.from_local. It reads back the
big file's ETag part count and records peak concurrent file uploads.

| | Part size | Parts (ETag -N) | Peak files in flight (batch_size=2) |

|-------------------------------|-----------|-----------------|-------------------------------------|
| 2.11.2 with env vars set | 5 MiB | 40 | 9 |
| This branch with env vars set | 64 MiB | 4 | 2 |
| This branch, defaults | 5 MiB | 40 | 9 (batch_size=32) |

  - To reproduce:
a. Set FLYTE_IO_UPLOAD_CHUNK_SIZE=67108864 and
FLYTE_IO_UPLOAD_MAX_CONCURRENCY=4 on a task environment.
b. Upload a directory containing a file larger than 64 MiB with
Dir.from_local(..., batch_size=2).
c. Check that the uploaded object's ETag ends in -ceil(size / 64 MiB).

fix(examples): inherit the plugin default images in the vLLM/SGLang apps

Every one of these examples hand-rolled an image that was a near-copy of the
plugin's default, and each copy had drifted: vllm 0.11.0 / 0.19.0 / 0.20.0 and
sglang 0.5.7, all below the versions the plugins now require, so the shims'
version check would have rejected them at startup. The copies also carried
flashinfer jit-cache layers from cu128/cu129 indexes, which cannot match engines
that pin CUDA 13 wheels.

Rather than re-pin nine copies, the examples now build on DEFAULT_VLLM_IMAGE /
DEFAULT_SGLANG_IMAGE, so the engine version, its matching flashinfer build and the
CUDA toolkit are maintained in exactly one place:

- vllm_app, vllm_app_sharded, vllm_app_artifact, sglang_app, sglang_app_sharded,
  sglang_app_artifact: use the default image as-is.
- vllm_app_triattention: `.clone(name=...)` + git + the TriAttention package.
- vllm_gpt_oss_claude: `.clone(name=...)` to keep its own build cache.
- nemotron_omni_voice: `.clone(name=...)` + librosa/soundfile. Its VLLM_VERSION
  constant is gone -- the default image is already well past the >= 0.20 floor the
  Omni checkpoint needs. README note updated to match.

The `transformers==4.57.6` pins are dropped: vLLM 0.26.0 requires
transformers>=5.5.3, so the old pin cannot be satisfied at all. Note that
vllm_app_artifact's pin carried a comment about newer transformers breaking the
fserve tokenizer path -- worth re-checking on a real deploy, but the pin was not
compatible with any vLLM new enough for the plugin.

feat: triggers without automation + flyte.run(trigger) to fire on demand (#1535)

Triggers no longer require an automation. A trigger without one is a
named launch configuration (inputs, env vars, queue, notifications) that
only fires on demand. `flyte.run(trigger, ...)` fires any deployed
trigger from Python, as the trigger, so the run carries its registered
config and is recorded as trigger-fired.

```python
import flyte
import flyte.notify
import flyte.remote
from flyte.models import ActionPhase

env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(name="reports")

# No automation: nothing schedules this, it is fired on demand.
full_report = flyte.Trigger(
    name="full-report",
    inputs={"region": "all", "days": 30},
    env_vars={"REPORT_VERBOSE": "1"},
    notifications=flyte.notify.Email(on_phase=ActionPhase.SUCCEEDED, recipients=("me@example.com",)),
)

@env.task(triggers=(full_report,))
async def report(region: str = "all", days: int = 7) -> str:
    return f"report for {region!r} over {days} day(s)"

# Fire it programmatically, with the trigger's inputs / env vars / notifications.
trigger = flyte.remote.Trigger.get(name="full-report", task_name=report.name)
run = flyte.run(trigger)            # region="all", days=30
run = flyte.run(trigger, days=3)    # override one input, keep the rest
```

Also: `flyte create trigger` no longer requires `--schedule`. Examples
in `examples/triggers/manual.py` and
`examples/triggers/programmatic.py`.

Jan/add dbt plugin (#1558) ## Summary Adds a new `flyteplugins-dbt` package for running dbt CLI invocations as Flyte v2 tasks. `DbtTask` maps one `dbtRunner.invoke(...)` call to one Flyte task. Project-level dbt configuration is set when the task is defined, while invocation-level CLI options are task inputs so the same task can be reused with different dbt commands, selections, targets, and extra arguments. ## What changed - Added the `plugins/dbt` package with `flyteplugins.dbt`. - Added `DbtTask`, which executes dbt through `dbt.cli.main.dbtRunner`. - Added typed direct and async invocation signatures for IDE help: - `dbt_task(command=...)` - `await dbt_task.aio(command=...)` - Added `DbtNodeResult`, a small serializable summary of dbt node results. - Added remote task reconstruction support through `DbtTaskResolver`. - Registered `DbtTask` with `TaskEnvironment` and inherited environment settings. - Added dbt project configuration on the task: - `project_dir` - `profiles_dir` - `profile` - `target_path` - Added invocation inputs for dbt command execution: - `command` - `select` - `exclude` - `target` - `extra_args` - Added support for multi-token dbt commands: - `command="docs generate"` - `command=["source", "freshness"]` - Added validation to keep plugin-managed flags out of `extra_args`. - Moved `project_dir` validation to invocation time so image-only project paths can be declared locally. - Added handled dbt failure support through `DbtInvocationError`, including capped failed-node details. - Added dbt node result reports. Reports are written before dbt failures are raised, so failed dbt runs can still show succeeded and failed node results. - Added support for user-provided dbt event callbacks, including import-path serialization for remote execution. - Fixed callback serialization for `__main__` script callbacks and dotted qualnames such as static methods. - Skipped non-node dbt results, such as `dbt ls` string output, while preserving dbt's normal printed output in logs. - Explicitly rejected caching for `DbtTask` until a dbt project-aware cache policy is added. - Added a dbt plugin example under `examples/plugins/dbt` using the jaffle shop project. - Added unit tests covering task interface, typed invocation signatures, environment registration, resolver behavior, callback serialization, dbt result summarization, report rendering, failure handling, unsupported cache behavior, and custom callbacks. ## Usage ```python dbt_build = DbtTask( name="dbt-build", task_environment=env, project_dir="jaffle_shop", profiles_dir="dbt-profiles", profile="jaffle_shop", report=True, ) @env.task async def main() -> list[DbtNodeResult]: return await dbt_build.aio(command="build", select=["customers"]) ``` For parallel execution from an async task: ```python @env.task async def main(): result0, result1 = await asyncio.gather( dbt_build.aio(command="debug"), dbt_build.aio(command="build", select=["customers"]), ) return result0, result1 ``` Multi-token dbt commands are supported: ```python await dbt_build.aio(command="docs generate") await dbt_build.aio(command=["source", "freshness"]) ``` Per-call Flyte task overrides compose with dbt invocation inputs: ```python @env.task async def main(): result0, result1 = await asyncio.gather( dbt_debug.override(short_name="dbt-version").aio(command="--version"), dbt_debug.aio(command="--help"), ) result2 = await dbt_run_test.override(short_name="dbt-run").aio(command="run") result3 = await dbt_run_test.override(short_name="dbt-test").aio(command="test") return result0, result1, result2, result3 ``` ## Reports When `report=True`, the task writes a `dbt` report tab with node names, resource types, statuses, failures, execution times, and messages. The report is emitted before handled dbt failures raise `DbtInvocationError`. ## Notes The plugin depends on `dbt-core`. Users still need to install the dbt adapter required by their project, such as `dbt-duckdb`, `dbt-bigquery`, or `dbt-snowflake`, in their task image. For remote execution, custom callbacks must be importable functions. The task accepts either callable functions or import-path strings. Caching is intentionally unsupported for now. `DbtTask(..., cache="auto")` raises a clear error until the plugin has a dbt project-aware cache policy. ## Testing ```text cd plugins/dbt uv run python -m pytest tests ``` ```text 33 passed ``` ```text ruff check plugins/dbt examples/plugins/dbt/dbt_build_example.py All checks passed ``` **Reports showing node status** --------- Signed-off-by: fiedlerNr9 Signed-off-by: Jason Parraga Signed-off-by: Haytham Abuelfutuh Signed-off-by: Michael Hotan Signed-off-by: Sergey Vilgelm Signed-off-by: Haytham Abuelfutuh Signed-off-by: Daksha1611 Signed-off-by: Daksha1611 <113719658+Daksha1611@users.noreply.github.com> Signed-off-by: Samhita Alla Signed-off-by: Peeter Piegaze <1153481+ppiegaze@users.noreply.github.com> Signed-off-by: Niels Bantilan Signed-off-by: M.
